Wanderland will reel you in with a good first impression; beautiful music, artwork, and a gameplay filled with coins and stars flying all over the screen. There are lots of quests and HOG elements, but there will come a point where you'll get slapped by a heavily inflated paywall influenced by slow Energy Timers you'd find on Facebook / mobile games. Artogon has tried to develop a storyline for the game, but the text is so badly written (incl. grammar and spelling), it simply becomes a nuisance.
To rub salt in the wound, the game is also a buggy mess.
You'll be lucky to actually be able to select the intended object.
There's not much you can do in this game without paying with real money.

STAY AWAY!
It starts out with promise for a HOG (which I tend to avoid)  but this one is so inviting with bright colors, nice music, cool locations, detailed artwork,  coins and stars flying into your inventory,  levels rising, glittery stuff we all like….. ?
But then. couldn’t go any further.. Need to build a bridge, need rubies to buy nails and boards.. So like everyone  (maybe) i clicked Buy Rubies for $75.00 there is a higher priced option too..
And it takes you to steam to literally BUY them! WTH?
NO THANKS! I assumed it meant buy them with all those apparently worthless coins I  earned IN the game.
Any idea Dev’s how many games we can get here for a 100 bucks?
It actually makes me MAD that this game is allowed!

I can't recommend Wanderland, although it's a decent game.
The game starts with a good first impression. Nice music, graphics and gameplay. You get lots of quests and hidden object scenes, but like in any of the so-called free to play games, you move over to free to pay very soon.
I don't mind those free to pay games, the developer needs to earn money, too. But this game is too much. The ingame prices are way to high, you can pay 100 € and use the rubys you get for it in a few minutes. And it's not like you are able to complete the game after that purchase. You have to buy more and more. I would never pay so much money for a single game. There are really good games from famous developers for about 50 or 60 €, and I can play these games for 40-60 hours.
So stay away from it, until you are really rich, or play just for fun and don't mind hitting a pay wall.

Through an old computer you have access to videoclips of a woman talking to the police about her missing husband. The videos were taped in 1994, and they were digitised, transcribed and made searchable so that it would be easy to find specific parts of the interviews that could be relevant in court. However, the footage of the detective’s questions have been lost so there are only about 270 short clips of the woman’s responses. The clips are not accessible in a straightforward manner, but they are at least searchable so you can type in a keyword to get the clips where that keyword is mentioned. Sadly, only the first five hits for each keyword can be retrieved. From this you will try to figure out what actually happened in June 1994.
From this description it is clear that Her Story is an unusual game. There is no other gameplay involved than typing keywords and watching videoclips, but it really works! It is not a straightforward story that is coming through the grainy taped videos, and I really wanted to know more about what happened. After finishing the game in a satisfactoily manner (actually watching all clips) I realised that I had spent more than four hours watching 90 minutes of photage of one woman responding to questions while enjoying it. This could only be possible through the excellent acting, and it may be the first time I think of excellent acting in a computer game. Well done Sam Barlow (creator) and Viva Seifert (the woman).
There an important flaw in the game idea of Her Story: it is certainly possible for a player to use certain keywords by chance and immediately receive crucial information about the case. Luckily for me, I seem to be very much into the other direction with watching almost all clips before getting a reasonable idea about the events. There is thus no guarantee that the order in which a player may see the clips makes sense from a narrative point of view. In addition there is absolutely no replayability value in a game of this type, but I think my experience from playing the game was so good that these flaws do not matter for me. I had four great hours!

Played for an hour then I clicked "Clear Session Data" to try and clear my session videos.
Clear Session Data clears all your progress.
10/10 would throw away an hour of searching for keywords again.

I happened to glance at the new releases on the Steam store page today (as I usually do) and was estactic to see ZE2 finally released! I couldn't have bought it any faster! I was feverishly clicking as fast as I could almost dropping my mouse in the process.
I highly recommend ZE2 for all arcade or twin stick shooter fans. It was one of my favortie indie games from the 360 and it continues to be one of my favorite twin stick shooters. As the self proclaimed "twin stick shooter king", this is saying something.
ZE2 includes tons of characters and hats to unlock using points obtained from beating waves of enemies. Characters have different stats and starting weapons and hats add bonuses. ZE2 also has different maps to play on and unique enemies. A shop at the end of each wave provides a chance to buy weapons, ammo, or upgrades to current weapons. With online MP and an endless mode, I see replayability being pretty high.
ZE2 brings back good memories from my 360 days. Can't go wrong with this gem, especially for the price!

One of the more satisfying zombie shooters there is. Just the way you massacre hordes of zombies, taking of chunks out of them and their swarm - MMMmmmm.
This game isn't just some cheap zombie shooter that you'll play for 10 minutes and get bored of or not understand; the developers have actually put time and effort into making the system user-friendly and simple enough for new players yet haven't dumbed it down enough to remove the depth and variety of weapons and characters.
Also, if you're worried that this game is a bad or lazy port from the Xbox, it isn't. I can sort of see why it took quite a while to port it from the 360 as they have made the game PC-friendly. In fact, if you didn't know it originally came from the 360, you probably wouldn't spot it; it has been implemented onto the PC platform very smoothly (V-Sync is toggleable, THANK GOD, and resolutions don't seem to be a problem which is good for someone with odd resolutions, e.g 1360 x 768 for me).
Basically, if you want a fun game to play with friends, offline or online, then this is a great choice. Enough depth to make it interesting but not too many features to be overwhelmed and confused as to to be able to play the game to it's full potential.

Started to play this game without too much expectations when the game was free for a day, since it has only a limited number of maps. I certainly didn't expect that this game would be fun even after 1k or even 2k hours. Admittedly this game has lots of flaws, but in part that's what makes it such a great game. The random elements in the game, spawns, enemy pathing and to a lesser extend the objectives, make the game unpredictable and failure is always around the corner. Unlike some Co-op PvE games out there, you actually have to play tactical and watch your HP (using "shoot and cover") to complete the heists on the higher difficulties (and for beginners even on the lower ones). Failing to do so will get you punished (although you can get away with it to some extend when playing with a VERY good team) and in all likeliness gets your character killed.
Besides the satisfaction of beating the game on the highest difficulties with a good team, you can basically make it as hard on yourself as you want. If the default difficulties aren't enough, install DAHM/DorHUD and play on an even higher difficulty with even more spawns (and yes, this makes a huge difference). Seeing all those helmets flying is a reason to keep playing the game and there's always room for improvement: more kills per minute, better accuracy, fewer downs, faster completion of the heist or just competing to be the best in the stats at the end of the heist when playing with other players, which can make for incredibly fun games ;).
The only downsides of this game is the crappy bots (although this can be seen as a factor that makes the game harder) and the fact that there are quite a few cheaters. As a programmer and creator of (an attempt of) an anticheat module (+more), DAHM/DorHUD, it's actually part of the challenge to find ways to beat the cheaters or at least expose them.
In fact, I didn't only have fun playing the game but also improving it. It's one of those things that are not for one or a small number of "uses" and I can get to enjoy the changes every time I play it. Of course there are also a number of downsides to this, but it feels good to help improve a game that I enjoy playing.
Since this is a review, maybe I should mention that it's worth even its full price. On sale it's only €2.48 (€3.47 with the soundtrack DLC that gives you an extra set of masks and some awesome music). It's roughly the price of one glass of beer, but you can play this game for a lot longer than you can enjoy that beer. You can even play this game after having drunk lots of beers (or vodka, if you prefer that).

Since the game was 40 cents at the time that I bought it (and I really just bought this to activate my account again so I can use the community store) I really didn't have hope for it to be the best, I went into this knowing I'm getting what I paid for.
Only took about 5 hours to beat the game, granted I took lots of breaks not because of difficulty but because of how headache inducing the sound effects were for me. In the small bits of story you get at the beginning and end of the game theres just bits of english that does not make sense, as well as gramatical errors. I'm still not really sure what the story was outside of "some guy is a bad guy". Ontop of that the controls are a bit wonky. There were times where I could not even move backwards, the key to walk back just would not register, even after restarting the client, so I would have to kill myself to get the game to work again. There was a time where I DID kill myself to fix the issue and the bonfire + enemies just disappeared, forcing me to restart the client afterall. Sometimes the client would close itself out of nowhere.
Boss fights were pretty one dimensional, in that a lot of the time in order to kill the boss you could resort to the simple strategy of just jumping back and forth around the boss, whittling down its health until it's dead.
On the subject of bosses, the art styles for each boss was so different from the game it felt like some of them were just ripped from RPG maker. I met one instance with a boss where they just simply glitched and did not move at all. Overall it was an interesting concept and you could tell where its inspiration came from, the pixel art for the stage itself, outside of enemies was fantastic but the game was definitely a miss for me. I really did not get any sense of achievement for beating this game.  Too many bugs and just too simple. If you're someone who collects games for easy achievements then this is probably for you.

Hey everyone, it's been a while. Tonight's game is Dark Throne, which looked great from the screenshots. I'm slowly starting to learn that visuals aren't everything but they're *usually* a good indicator. Maybe I've just been unlucky of late.
Anyways, on to this game. I was all set for a great 2D Dark Souls experience but straight away something seemed a little off.. the way the character moved and the UI leaves something to be desired too.
The enemies (who look like The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Of Bolton from Game of Thrones!) bizarrely bounce of your shield. The amount of endurance (green bar) you lose for each hit they do is basically nothing as you'll recover it all back before they even attack again.
The game is blatantly meant to be Dark Souls right, so why change the controls? I mean I can understand a little adjustment from 3D to 2D but why is right trigger block?! Why does the B button bring up the help menu instead of rolling? Why isn't there a roll button? Why can't you attack mid-air?
All of the animations are hilariously fast, yet the game play isn't so I'm pretty sure it's not because my computer's running the game mega-quick. Also why does my character, who is a knight in heavy armour, FLOAT when he jumps?!
The graphics are nice. and it's very cheap. The controls are alittle awkward (controller) but you get use to them. as far as i have played it seemed ok for the price.

Sometimes a game doesn't need a deep, complex, and intresting story. Sometimes a game doesn't need crisp, smooth, and polished combat. No sometimes a game needs to give you choice and my friends Blood Money does just that. Hitman: Blood Money puts you back in the well polished shoes of Agent 47 and tasks you to perform several hits and other assorted mission (That still involve killing people) of course once you are dropped into a mission a thought may cross your mind, "What am I supposed to do?" And that is the beauty of it. Players may approach there objective in any way they see fit, for example you could go Rambo on your targets, using a number of disguises to stalk your prey, or stealthly set up sinister traps ranging from poisoning food in some missions to swapping a prop gun at an opera for a real one. Hitman is a must play for those who call themselves stealth game fans or for anyone wanting a new fresh experince.

This game is more or less a bit of ARPG + LoZ, but more of a time-waster game than something with much depth.
You walk up to enemies and mash your attack skill, sometimes try to block or avoid damage, pick up loot that is better than your current stuff.  There are no abilities and the attack variety is purely in what weapon you use.  Find some caves with purchasable loot, stat upgrades, or hints towards your next goal.  Beat a set of dungeons and fight a final boss.  Dungeons are just small loops, switch 'puzzles' (more just like door triggers really) and enemies.
I've played about 1.5hrs and beat three dungeons, but the game has LoZ1-forest style mazes and an NPC who tells me the solution to a maze must have generated wrong because the solution doesn't work.  It seems there is a patch planned for an overworld map (which doesn't currently exist so prepare to get lost), so maybe some new content to improve the play experience is planned.  I don't really have too much motivation to play more because the gameplay just isn't that deep and I prefer multiplayer games for timewasting as the experience is at least more dynamic.  Nothing really wrong with the game, I just don't recommend the game because there are probably better games for you to spend your time on.

First off, this is an optimized version of a 1997 PC game that was an updated and ported version of the Super Nintendo original.
Welcome to the Starfleet Academy. You are a student captain attending classes in hopes of graduating and commanding your own starship. At the beginning of the game, you are given a crew that you have to manage while still accomplishing your missions. Each individual is in charge of a system and their view of you will determine their performance while on the ship.

The game is broken up into two sections the simulator missions and the academy where you interact with teachers and students. The academy is a bunch of videos with dialog choices. The simulator is where you will spend 90% of the game. For certain missions, you get to choose which ship you captain. This will determine the difficulty of that mission.
If you have never played a simulator game, the controls will be overly complicated. There are a lot of things you have control over which requires plenty of buttons. This is one of the many great features about this game. You control navigation, engineering, scans, combat, etc. Say you are in a fight and your shields are being depleted. You can switch to the engineering and increase power to shields by diverting other systems power. The game makes great use of the many features you see in the show and movies.

Since this is an academy, the missions are not all combat and depending on how you deal with some of the scenarios, the outcomes will be different.
The voice acting is quite cheesy for today’s standards. Back then they were a little over the top. Other than that, the sounds for the starships and combat are decent. You can tell that they did not try to update the sounds from the original game. The background music is not intrusive and goes well with the game environment.
Graphics…. Well, like I said, this is an optimized version of a 1997 game. The cut-scenes have been optimized for our larger displays but not updated to look any better (trust me, I am playing this on a 4k 55” TV). The 3D models are quite basic and are not very detailed.

With all that said, once you get used to the controls and are in the missions, you will easily overlook the outdated graphics and be concentrating on finishing of those cloaked Klingons that ambushed you while investigating that colony.
The game has its faults, but they are mostly due to how old the game is. Other than that, this is definitely a great game for any Star Trek fan who wants to feel what it is like to captain a starship. Just wish they also ported the expansion disk " Chekov's Lost Missions" to complete the experiance.
Also: if you kept a copy of your old game saves, they work perfectly in this version. You can load them up and visit your favorite missions or continue where you left off.

Pre-emtive TL;DR:
I love this game and I want more people to play it!  Buy it now, while it's on sale!
Long version:
Okay.  The game has its problems.  There are some match making and balance issues, but they're working on those.  And it doesn't seem to get along with AMD very well.  But I'm hoping to see a fix for that soon, and in the meantime, it's very managable.
But the only real problem this game has is that Overwatch came out so soon after it.  And they're being compared, which isn't fair.  Overwatch is a fast paced shooter, for people who like quick matches and lots of reflex gaming.  Battleborn, meanwhile, is A MOBA!  It just happens to be in first person.  But it. Is. A.  Moba.  It's a different animal than Overwatch.
And I, for one, like this game better.  I like being able to take some time and think through what I need to do, without having to worry about getting one-shot-killed the second I step out of spawn.  I like the leveling system.  I like the cartoonish art style.  I like the silly characters.  And I really enjoy the merger of moba & fps.
It may not be your cup of tea, but it won't hurt to give it a try.
Just.  For the love of God.  If you do?  Remember it's a moba.  The objective isn't glory kills.

The very definition of "short but sweet". This game is a mix of Metroidvania-style progression, beat 'em up combat (with a pretty deep combo system), and some pretty challenging puzzle-platforming.
As far as Metroidvania games go, this has to be one of my favourites; the pacing is excellent, combat is very fun, and the platforming is challenging without becoming excessively frustrating. Also, the game has a unique and striking art style, some great humor, and plenty of in-jokes and references to other games.
The game only took me around 5 hours to complete (without finding all the secrets), but I loved every minute. Highly recommended.

A rather simple Ghost 'n Goblins and Castlevania inspired plattformer that, for the most part, is a bare boned attempt at playing in the same category as those master pieces. Controls are awkard, animations are a tad lackluster and enemy variety leaves a thing or two to be desired. It adds some RPG flavor with three stats that you can upgrade; Damage, Vitality and Energy (stamina). While not being a Souls-, or Salt & Sanctuary-game by any stretch of the imagination, it's clear where the inspirations came from.
First off, the controls are clunky as you move with WAD (not S, that is used for showing your stats) and swing your active item with the cursor keys. Up arrow blocks, while the others perform various strikes. The game focuses much of its time on platforming, and most jumps require the use of "sprint jump". Now, the character doesn't run any faster when you hold "Shift", but your stamina meter will deplete. It's very strange to see that when you thought you'd be sprinting, your character instead moves at regular speed, while the stamina bars drains. Speaking of; as with all of these games you deplete stamina with your every action, but it does seem to refill rather quickly. Perhaps this is possible to upgrade, but the help screen do not show me where I can do so, even when the stats screen says I have points to spare.
Right, enough about awkward character movement and dodgy help screens, let's talk a bit about the enemies. For the introductory part they seem none aware of you unless you're on the same platform or level as them. However, they will move closer to the edge of the platform they're on, making it harder to get over to and kill them without taking damage. Thankfully there are spells, protection and fire, which allows for you to either take them down from a distance or protect yourself from all damage for a little while. However, these come in form of one-time use scrolls and you cannot stack up more than 3 of each. Fireball might sound useful, but when you require all of them to take out a lowly goblin from a far, it outlives its usefulness. Protection spell is better, but is usually just a short "let me move to that enemy without getting killed in the process" type of usage, meaning you rely on it more to get to the next plattform, than getting by in skillful 1-on-1 combat. You can upgrade your character, but this relies on rescuing Roger first, an NPC locked up in a cage.
On the audible side, the music in particular, seems to have been collected from a range of free music sources, including every Youtubers favorite composer, Kevin MacLeod. While the soundtrack for the most part is passable featuring your standard piano and baroccé ensembles, some are completely out of place. For instance, the song that plays in Kerbal Space Program when entering the upper atmosphere has for some reason found its way into Dark Throne (
) , which does not fit at all.
Sound effects are simple, yet serviceable, but leaves some things to be desired. Ambient effects would've added a ton of atmosphere to the game, and variation in enemy grunts is almost needed if you don't want to grow tired of fighting the same enemies over and over again.
I do hope the developer at least updates with controller support, as this game needs it - *badly*. Using Q and E to move your active selected item at the bottom is extremely tedious in the heat of battle and using the "Right arrow" to actually use the item is just downright confusing. Why can't you just map these to spesific buttons, since there are only a limited amount of items available anyway? Oh, and you can't rebind controls either, even when forced to use the keyboard. Also, if you like tons of typos in a game, you'll be well served here. Expect to see thing like "Demage" and "Come into a bonfire" (the what now?).  It's one of those. So far I've also had the game crash a couple of times, mostly after a death when it tries to save.
(Side note: Since this is a Java game, you won't find the game by its name in the task manager overview. You'll have to look for and kill a "Java (32bit) Platform task" in your task manager, usually the one eating ~600MB of your memory.)
After seeing this initial launch version and its hiccups, I'd recommend waiting a while to see if it gets some much needed patches even if the game is dirt cheap. If you want medieval platform goodness, I'd much more look into Maldita Castilla" or "Salt & Sanctuary" if 2D Dark Souls sounds interesting.

One of the very best games of the past generation. Hitman: Blood Money again has you perform several assassinations as the 'bald killer clone' Agent 47. You are dropped in about a dozen large maps, and have to figure out how to accomplish a set of tasks, which of course always include assassinations, as silently as possible. As a result, the game is essentially a puzzle game, and a very good one at that. No level has just one solution for attaining the optimal 'silent assassin' rating, which makes replaying levels worthwhile, as should be obvious from my time spent on the game.
Perhaps one of the game's strongest qualities is the variety in level themes, it takes you to snowy mountain villas, quiet suburbs, underground nightclubs, redneck weddings and many other locales. All this is scored by one of the generation's finest soundtracks by composer Jesper Kyd.
Blood Money is significantly more refined than its predecessors, which while good, are a bit too rough around the edges for the average gamer. This is also essentially Hitman's last hurrah. While Hitman: Absolution is not an irredeemably terrible game, it does move away from what is the core of the franchise. Where in Blood Money, the focus is clearly on planning and figuring out the solution, Absolution switches it more towards execution. I think the appeal of the two games as a result is rather different, this aside from several design issues Absolution has with one of its core mechanics.

I would consider this to be the best Star Wars game on Steam (if not, just in general). The main story and immersive side missions provide hours and hours of gameplay and getting to decide which side of the Force you wish to be alligned with makes for some interesting and entertaining gameplay.
With this being an older game, there are some bugs - some bigger than others. On my old laptop, I had a somewhat of a game-breaking glitch where the graphics would go beserk and glitch out all the time, but I have come to realize that this is somewhat of a rare glitch and I have only seen it happen on Windows 7 (so you Windows 7 users beware)...
The combat system in this game is liked by some and disliked by others - either you like it or do not like it. The combat system is not like that of the Jedi Knight series - the ever so popular hack-and-slash type...with this game being an RPG, the combat system is that of a click and lock-on based system where you choose your attack and your character performs it on their own. I for one am not the most fond of this combat system, but it in no way ruined the game for me in any way - that's how good this game is.
Having the ability to pick the gender of your character is a very interesting one, as it makes for some good alternate storylines
.
The game's world design is magnificent for its time and modern day mods that allow for quality and graphical improvements are useful as well.
The game's music is absolutely wonderful. It can go from being dramatic/cinematic to calm and relaxing which helps make the game as immersive as it is.
All in all, this game is truly worth the buy, especially for it's current price of $9.99. It is undoubtedly one of the best games I have ever played and I would reccommend it to any Star Wars fan, RPG fan, or just any casual gamer - it fits the bill for any player.

The name of the game and nostalgic but vague memories of the 1985 SSI version gave me high hopes.
Even if it didn’t measure up to my rose-coloured memories, I also harboured optimistic thoughts that it might play a little like a simplified version Victoria 2 in board game form.
What I actually got was a game more similar to a mobile port of RISK.
I realise that a few of the negative reviews have compared this game to RISK which is only partially accurate as there are some tactical considerations for terrain types and fortifications as well as about double the number of territories.  But in the end if you have ever played RISK with players whose only strategy is to make a giant hoard and bust loose every few turns then you know how this game plays.
There is really only 1 type* of combat unit (Infantry) and every battle more or less becomes entirely dependent on who has the larger stack, (with only a small consideration for forts and terrain). *(Yes there are ships but they are really only used as transports for your 1 type of land unit; and this is made tactically dull as any coastal province connects to any other coastal province in only 1 turn.)  So perhaps slightly more depth than RISK but certainly less than another board game classic like Axis & Allies.
The premise of managing an economy is also enacted too thinly as there are far too few things to spend your money on; infantry, ships, forts, or spies – that’s it. The card collecting strategy in RISK has as much or more depth.  Could we not have cavalry, artillery, fort upgrades, both transports and fighting ships, factory placements, research upgrades perhaps leading to aircraft?
Based on the current price of the game $7.99 USD / $10.99 Cdn compared to the play / replay value I cannot recommend this game.
Fun: 4/10
Tactical Depth: 2/10
Historical Value: 2/10
Playability (does it run): 8/10
Replay value: 2/10
Overall: 3/10

Colonial conquest is simplicity incarnate.  There is no depth to the game, there is no content, there is no strategy. Purchase your armies, and walk all over the world, gobbling up one territory after another until you achieve the preset number of victory points.  At this point the game ends - no cut scene, no message, nothing.  It just ends.
Colonial conquest fails as a strategy game. One game I played, the AI did absolutely nothing.
Colonial conquest fails to have any replay value. How many times can you create a mega stack of soldiers and walk over the world before you get bored?
Colonial conquest fails to be engaging in any way.   In less than 3.4 hours of game play, I experienced everything it has to offer.

I haven't play this game for quite a while, not because it's boring, but because of how badly optimized this game for AMD cards. Whenever I'm in a match, the FPS will drop insanely from stable 60 to something like 20-40. I get motion sickness easily, so this is a very big problem for me, and probably to lots of people out there. Maybe the problem is fixed, but I don't plan on returning to this game ever again.
Other than the poor performance issue, another major problem with this game is the community is pretty much nonexistent. I'm speaking from SEA server so I have no idea about the other regions, but from what I've read, it's more or less the same thing. There's one time I queued up with my friend, we waited for almost one hour straight, and not a single match was ready. I'm aware that you can switch region to queue up at other place instead, but then the latency wouldn't be optimum for me anymore. And for the record, I did try to queue up in other region, and it's taking a very long time too. For a multiplayer game to take so long to get into the actual game, I just don't see how I can be convinced to stay.
Although I'm very unsatisfied with this game, this game did provide me some entertainment. But it went completely downhill when the community dies off, so there's no reason for me to stay, or anyone new to hop in. Even with the 50% discount from Summer Sales, I just can't recommend this game to anyone. So if any of you out there planning to buy this game, especially if you are from SEA, take my advice, stay away from it and get Overwatch instead. I know both of them are two different type of games, but at least Overwatch can provide you entertainment moer than what Battleborn can offer. If you really feel like to try out this "Matchmaking Simulator", be my guest. But don't say I didn't warn you.
Tl;dr : Buy Overwatch instead.

The games title would give you the impression that this is a game that focus on Snipping but sadly it does not and has various bugs even after all this time. The story is forgetable and not all that interesting as it focuses on a hit gone wrong and the aftermath of trying to re-aquire and eliminate said target.
In terms of gameplay for the most part you'll be using a sniper rifle and sneaking through areas while quietly killing foes on your way to your next objective. However at the same time there are missions that take you out of this and place you in a Call of Duty style shooting gallery type of missions where you assault through areas where the foes almost know exactly where you are and for the most part your teamates are all but useless.
Now lets talk about the games many short commings and problems as they are here in bulk at times. For starters there's the games opening cinamatic and main menu picture. Both are upsidedown and can be diorenting at times. The game is also hard even on normal difficulty which can lead to some frustrating moments. The collision detection is flawed as sometimes you'll clip into opjects or pass through bits of them. Zooming in and out quickly with the sniper rifles can result in you sometimes seeing something off like a sort of clipping/temporary effect that can be off putting at times. Your AI teamates during the assault missions can feel like total useless teamates. If you plan on using a controller with this game which is does support nativly through the game itself you'll run into problems with the shooting portion. As sometimes you'll press your trigger and all of a sudden you'll get a quick double shot style action regardless of which gun you are using. This can be very annoying at times for obvious reasons all of which should be pretty clear if you've played other shooters or stealth games.
Be aware of the games many issiues and be prepared for some frustrating bits should you choose to get it if not then move along to something else.

I had the privilege to be part of the original beta testing group and entered into the game with the mindset of NOT to spend any money on it (after all I was doing them a service by testing it). The following review is based on my experience and strategy...
First of all, let me ask you, have you ever had a 'needy friend' in real life? What eventually happened? Did you ever tire of them continually selfishly wanting? Did they ever stop wanting? The more and more money you spent on them, did they ever become satisfied? Less demanding? Over the years you spent heaps of money on them, have you really got anything to show for all that money spent? No? Likewise if you think the more money you spend on this game the less demanding it is going to be ... boy are you in for a shocker. If you think that spending money in this game is going to give you some type of 'ownership' ... you really need to read the SMALL print.
Before we go on, let’s unmask the people behind this project, it comes from a small Russian company known as Artogon. They don't actually have a website at the moment, but you can find one of the head honcho's here
. This game 'Wanderland' has already existed for quite some time and just recently been ported to Steam. It is a casual HOS game, like so many of their other games which they often market to BIG FISH who in turn presents them with an award (that's like my mother telling you how wonderful I am. Do you think there maybe bias there?).
Predominantly this is an effective cash cow, because the game will constantly troll a player with a low chance rate with regards to a barrage of constant rare items, while at the same time exposing a player to constant limited sale offers flashing on the right hand side user interface. It's these two elements placed together which spell out 'MONEY' for both developer and publisher. Is it effective? Hell yeah. I was personally surprised at how many beta testers couldn't resist forking out real money, even before the game was even released. Basically it's some rich guy saying 'Here Sheepy' and the consumer hands over there credit card details and shouts 'BAAAAA!'
What do I mean by low percentage rate chance? Well one rare item you will constantly need in game is a mirror curse.  These are obtainable through the 'Hunters Hut' Hos. I played that scene 1200 times before it decided to give me one. Sure you can obtain by other means such as someone can gift it to you, you can get them rarely in treasure chests and sometimes rarely by defeating a goblin, but it does go to show what I mean by low chance. There are literally many items like this that have a low chance rating which constantly trolls you to grind away needlessly at HOS.
So a gamer really needs to ask themselves a couple of questions before they start this game.
1. Do I want to expose myself to this constant trolling need of items and sly effective marketing techniques?
2. Do I have the time to grind away hours upon hours at the same HOS thousands of time?
3. Do I have the money to spend if I become addicted to it?
4. Do I have the patience necessary to enjoy the game if I do not have the money to spend on it?
Now let’s do a complete flip in mind set. There are many gamers that DO have the money and are willing to spend it on a game they DO enjoy. For such ones this is an easy game to fall in love with and become addicted to. The games story revolves around various folk tales and children’s stories we all grew up with, from the world popular Snow White to less known characters from Russia. Most will just be delighted unlocking a new HOS or being rewarded with a 'Solution' which they must match up the discovered puzzle pieces with. This will often unlock a small animation and the artistry is often something that captures the imagination. The sound on the other hand I always found to be lacklustre in various places. For instance an exploding portal which you think would explode into existence doesn't even make a noise and a castle which quakes into two was accompanied by a tiny rumble which a hungry belly would probably drown out. I guess Artogon may have sacked their sound department recently?
Anyway if you enjoy HOS, and you've got money to lavishly spend then this is definitely a game for you. Alternatively you could always come over to my place and I will hide various items in my garden and you could give me money and I could hide them again. Just saying...
How about if you don't have money can you still enjoy it? Yes! If you enjoy the challenge. Personally, I did not spend any money on this at all and levelled up just as quickly as those that did. Here is how the game works.
* Save coins and rubies predominantly for your Golden Image and Wishing Well. Golden image gives you more and more coins as you level up every 10 minutes. Wishing well gives you more energy every 30 minutes as you level it up. To upgrade golden image will cost rubies. To upgrade wishing well will cost coins. Save them both as they can be difficult to come by since hos reward you barely with coins.
*Jumping in and out of portals will trigger new quests. Completing quests is where you will make your money.
* Utilise the community hub and add as friends as you can. You will be given two slots where you can put your item wish list in. This advertises to gamers what you’re in need of. It serves the interest of gamers to give you these items if they have spare as many quests involving treasure chests require to give things to friends. The other two slots in your wish list require rubies to unlock and are completely unnecessary. As soon as you have been gifted an item you can simply resubmit your wants again.
* In the early stages of the game are hidden wanderland tiles hidden inside the portals. Take time farming these tiles as they seem to be endless in the first three portals then become rather scarce later. These you use to unlock a pairs game where the last tiles you pair together is what you will be rewarded with. So take note what you really need and match that tile pair last.
* Archivist allows you to unlock a bronze, silver or gold treasure chest. Concentrate on the bronze ones only. The problem with the silver and gold is that the costs in obtaining them are quite extravagant and if you don't meet all the requirements by the time allotted then you have spent all those items in vain.
* Around level 16 you will be allowed to enter into tournaments with 3 varying objectives. While the gold, silver, and bronze chests look appealing, the cost of items you spend in obtaining them is insane if you actually sat down and looked at it on paper. Therefore the chests you obtain simply for entering into the tournament are actually the smarter way to go.
* Around level 22 you unlock a caravan which rewards you with two random items every 15 hrs. You need to click on it for it to renew.
* Very early you get to send a ship away packed or unpacked. If you don’t have the items the ship wants then send it away unpacked. When it comes back it will want something different. If you let it naturally come back it will want the same thing. Watch what the ship rewards you with. Only send it packed when it has a reward you WANT!
* Cursing the board is one of the biggest aggravating trolling mechanisms of the game as the curse is random in what it actually curses and since mirror curse it hard to come by, you don't want it going to waste. There is a way to force the game to curse the HOS you want. Lay your board with cheaper curses and free the one that you want the mirror curse on.
* My biggest tip, early in the game a sale where everything is for one gem in shop. Buy all potions and chests and activators with the rubies the game gives you. It will cost you no money and you will make all those rubies back quickly.
Hope this helps you decide if this is a 'needy friend' you want to stick around with...

Less of a video game and more than a run of the mill choose-your-own-adventure type of game,
is a delightful experience which goes to show that neither graphics, neither pre-order bonuses will make a game good. It is as bare bones as it gets, plain old text but the storytelling, the characters, the atmospheric immersion of reading and the fact that your choices matter (up to a certain point) will make up for a surpisingly dark yet at times funny story which unravels as you click on the choices appearing of the screen. I can honestly say that I've spent significantly more time trying to decide for an otherwise simple choice in this game than any of AAA games of a similiar fashion.
I have to admit that the entire premise of the game is reminiscent of the 1999 cult classic movie
, in addition from getting vibes from the now defunct MMO
and the same time feel like this could actually be a lost
episode. There's a near perfect mixture of seriousness, humour and meta humour, dark and mysterious twists and reveals, romance, resource management, entertainment, social issues, you name it. It is up to you to choose your own path and explore this fascinating world the author has created.

Help is supposed to be a horror title, though there is very little "horror" going on within this game. You're in an abandoned research bunker, in search of your missing daughter, and through a series of puzzles you're tasked to find out what has happened to her. The puzzles within Help are made up of three attributes; key finding, number solutions, and lever conundrums. All the while, you must keep your flashlight from dying by finding batteries.
It's your typical indie Unity Personal Edition "horror" game, by every sense of the phrase. However, Help is shrouded in overly cryptic puzzles, and it doesn't help that the few notes that you find scattered about are written in broken/poorly translated English. Nearly everyone who has attempted to reach the end of this game have been met with an abundance of frustration early on, and most do not make it past the first "level". There's zero guidance when it comes to any of the puzzles, and to make matters worse the items that you can interact with and pick up aren't highlighted or indicated in any manner.
The batteries for the flashlight drain far too quickly, and even if you obtain a surplus of them you will find that they disappear from your 'inventory' once you reach the next area of the game. You will discover keys, but you will get no leads on which door that they work for; this forces you to revisit every locked door in the area to figure it out. There's no soundtrack, and the only ambiance are some random whooshing noises and the occasional water drip. There are a couple of enemies that will chase you if they spot you, but their AI is so terrible they're really no threat at all; if you do happen to die to one, you'll find that the continue menu isn't even translated into English.
Overall, Help is just a terrible experience, and one that you cannot even call horror. It's an utter waste of time and money, and quite possibly the worst indie "horror" Unity Personal Edition game that I've ever had the misfortune of playing; trust me when I say that I've played a lot of them. Although the game runs at 60 FPS, it acts like it's only running at about half that, and the movement/camera is wonky at best. There were even some assets that I ended up walking through, and one of the enemies saw me through one of the lockers that you can 'hide' in. When you figure out what you're doing, the title only takes about 20 minutes to complete, but you could spend hours just figuring out the convoluted puzzles, all for an ending that's not even worth it. Ultimately, Help is a game to avoid, even if it's on sale.

The painfully uninspired art design, the unintuitive controls, and just the ridiculousness of the gameplay itself, made this game just a dreadful experience.
Art Direction:
It took hardly a second to see where this game was (and I say this with reluctance) artistically inspired, that being from The Legend of Zelda. When I say that bit Dungeon II is graphically inspired by The Legend of Zelda, I mean it is practically plagiarized. The first dungeon I entered was essentially just a recolour of the classic Zelda dungeons, right down to the chest sprite. Granted the layout was (kind of) different, it was as if the developer just took rooms from A Link to the Past, recoloured them, and slapped them all together with random-number-generation (which they did).
If a game is inspired by another, fine, that's great, but making it feel boring and done-before by outright copying a design makes it dull to play. A large portion of adventure games is finding something new and interesting that you wouldn't have expected, so when the first thing you see looks like a poorly copied version of something from over a decade ago, you start the game feeling like you won't find anything unique or interesting.
Furthermore, the enemies I encountered in my very, very short time playing, seemed lazy and tossed together. One minute there was jumpy, four-legged, insectoid monsters, next there were ghostly fireball-lobbing monsters, and then there was just a big snake. It didn't shoot lasers from its eyes, it didn't split into smaller snakes, it was just a big snake.
Now, when I think of a jumpy, four-legged insectoid creature, I think of the Tektite from the Legend of Zelda, which bit Dungeon II features a carbon copy of as a painfully common enemy. Continuing this trend, when I think of ghostly fireball-lobbing monsters, I think of the Poes from the Legend of Zelda. And when I think of big snakes, I think of, wait for it, snakes. One of the most common creatures to be featured as a starting enemy in RPGS. Oh, and, it was a mini-boss, did I mention that? I'm sure if I could stand to play this game longer I'd find plentiful amounts of ripped-off creatures from random games, but I couldn't stand the game long enough to look. I forgot to mention, the main character is an uninspired piece of crap. He or She or It or whatever doesn't have a name, doesn't have a face, or clothes, or any features what-so-ever, you're just some blue thing with two blank eyes. Making a character androgynous is one thing, but for it to be even vaguely relatable and entertaining, it should at least look semi-human. A big part of why people enjoy games is getting to put themselves into the game world as the main character, so they can experience and enjoy the adventure, I don't know about most people, but I don't feel that relatable to a blue-wisp-thing that doesn't have a name or personality of any sort.
Controls:
I personally believe that one of the most important things, in regards to anything electronic, is having an intuitive control-scheme. If you have a basic idea of how a video game works, nine times out of ten you can figure out the buttons pretty quickly without looking at controls.
Having played many games on many platforms from many genres, I cannot, for the life of me, think of a game that had Left-Mouse, A, and Spacebar, bound to the same control. if this was an interact control, maybe, just maybe, this could be a viable option. LMB/A/Spacebar was Attack, Block, Interact, and some sort of spin-attack/parry button all at once.
I'd like to digress for a moment to point out that the game is marked as having "Full Controller Support," now I didn't actually try the controller, but having seen that the only controls are directions to move, and LMB/A/Spacebar to attack/block/parry/interact, makes me question it using even four buttons of any controller. If this was twenty-or-so years in the past, maybe having so many options for one button could be understandable, but being sold on computers, wherein I can assume most have more than five buttons, it is just stupid.
So having thought that maybe I just didn't understand the controls, I figured I'd pause the game and look for a controls section so I could maybe rebind something to something else, hoping it might improve the gaming experience. Pressing Esc takes you to the controls and nothing else. I then thought that maybe if I just pressed buttons I'd find a proper pause menu with maybe some sound options or something. Something, I don't know what it was, took me back to the main menu when I pressed it, and pressing Enter when not properly in the main menu switches the game from Fullscreen to Windowed. On the topic of being either fullscreen or windowed, there is no form of resolution options as far as I could tell, so if you're rocking a made-up resolution like I currently am, tough nuts, you play it in windowed or you don't play it at all.
Another important aspect of controls is feeling as if you are in control, that's why they're called controls. It takes only moments to notice that at even a slight price of a direction sends you sliding removes any finesse from the movement, and if you hold down the direction you'll just start running at an out-of-hand speed before you know what's happened. This made walking into single-tile-wide doorways just a little bit too finicky to pass, seeing as every dungeon revolves around single-tile-wide doorways. This also caused a constant problem in the overworld where a monster dropped loot and I'd accidentally run off-screen trying to see what it was, causing it to just disappear. Would it have been so difficult to rebind a full-speed dash to double-tapping a direction, as many countless games from the past have done before? No, it really wouldn't have been. I'd like to add at this time that to attack in bit Dungeon II, you have to walk into an enemy if you're using keyboard, while when using mouse control you have to click on them, thie one random offset from the rest of the controls makes any movement feel sloppy and weird, and I often killed creatures upon entering a room without even noticing. What's the point of throwing monsters at your face every time you enter a room, if you can dispatch half of them by holding down one direction? as far as I could tell no monster had any sort of dodge or blocking happing, so if I walked into them, they took damage, and I didn't.
Gameplay:
No for real though, to anyone who has played the original Zelda or a Link to the Past, just imagine you played that, but at double-speed and being tactical in comabt didn't matter. I didn't have to dodge lasers or enemy attacks or even hit a weak-point, if I walked into an enemy, more than half the time they died before they even attacked me. One thing that the Zelda franchise did to prevent you feeling overpowered against everything around you, was waited until certain points in time to give you new tools. In a Link to the Past, when you enter the Dark world, everything hurts, always. Until you get that tunic upgrade and then bam! Everything is your ***** because it does half as much damage and you got used to avoiding their hits anyways. in bit Dungeon II, all loot was random, totally and utterly random, at the very start you're given the choice of an Axe, a Dagger, a Stick, and Shield, mind you it doesn't tell you the stats on any of them until you've picked the first one up, or at least it didn't for me. Being a fan of avoiding hits and dishing out lots, I picked an axe/dagger combo with the plan of just evading enemy attacks. Good thing I didn't need to though, because everything died too quickly for me to even notice. If I can start a game with weapons strong enough to turn any enemy to ash, and only get better gear from there on, it's not much of a game is it, it's just you walking into things until you get too bored.
I could go on forever but I'm already out of space, so in summary, this game sucks, don't buy

This game is too simple for my taste, but if you like simple games this might be a game for you.
You only get 2 units types: Land and Sea
Land units can only move to adjacent land area or board a sea units for a ratio of 1 to 1 to move to any coastal area.
You can only produce units in you zone with factories and it's not possible to build of capture more factories. If you lose all you factories you cannot produce any more units.
You receive a set amount of pounds per provinces to spend once a year and you can only spend you money on that turn. There's 4 turns per year, one for each seasons. You do not need to maintain you army so it's possible to build up an insane amount of troop which some time you need. With your money you can train troops, build forts and do 2 kind of 'political' actions.
To goal of the game is to get a set amount of victory points by capturing zones. Each zones is worth a random number of VP and revenu.
I've seen a couple of weird thing, like small neutral provinces with more troop then any super power. Panama had over 30k troops. If you own most of the map (90%+) you can build about 2k troops per year (unless you are Russia which build troops for half the prince of the other nations). So controling the world it would take you about 15 years to just match the force of a minor neutral nation and that would not even be enought to scratch their defence. That pretty much was a buzz kill for me.
You can also kill one by one the troop in neutral countries as a political action for the price of training 2.5 troops (5 for Russia) which make this action mostly useless. You can also give them money so they can buy troops to make it harder for other nations or you could buy the troop for you to conquer more land and get more money for more troop... so yet an other pointless action.
An other point is there is no real political mechanic in the game everyone is at war and that is it.
On a final note the AI is just horrible, play on hard if you want at least a tiny challenge.

Essencialy, the playes chooses one from out of six colonial powers and basically keeps piling up troops and navy to protect its territory and invade the other. The minors powers are just up there for the grab, and the AI is simply incomprehensible in its strategy even in the most advanced levels. Think of Risk without any specil objectives other than amass the most territories. Strategy fans will be certainly frustrated because the game is simply lacking content, whereas people looking for more casual strategy game, with an easy to grasp learning curve will find out that Colonial Conquest is simply unfulfilling.

While Colonial Conquest feels well put together, it plays more as a board-game rather than as a true video game. Which isn't a bad thing, if you were expecting a board game, but is something of a disappointment for a computer game. I would recommend the game if more effort were put into marking it more as a board game and rather than as a true video game.

Seeing the negative reviews for this game have given me a sour taste in my mouth so i plan to add my opinion in here. When it comes to gameplay and character complexity this game has it spades. When it comes to unlocking all the characters, every hero is perfectly obtainable with challenges, the two hardest ones being Deande and Ghalt. Then you have everyone's story to unlock which really gives a lot of depth to the characters. The Campaign is rather fun, as every playthrough the voice overs are a little different each time and add the Borderlands humor I've come to expect. Campaign is best for getting gear packs and leveling the character levels, while PVP is best for gaining commander levels. So going through some of the negative reviews are mainly about matchmaking, and the recent decision to add Platinum. a premium currency for getting new skins and taunts. I won't lie im kinda in the same mindset of "why does a full price game have any sort of premium currency?" to me this would be easily remedied by making them attainable with difficult challenges, so one could say they didn't pay for them. Then how Alani, without a key gained by getting the deluxe addition, is unlocked with around 45,000 IGC. I also won't lie thats a hilarious amount of credits. uh...easy way to solve that. put earning her by commander level or by a difficult challenge like the rest of the characters. Also there's many a complaint about how the average PVP match can go. Yes you will get pub teams vs. organized and higher level groups. welcome to PVP that will always happen. the problem is because theyre higher level people will automatically assume theyre going to lose...and with that mindset you will. If you dont like that you tend to lose playing with pubs...do what i did and get a crew of people to play with and just watch how much more fun it gets. Communication is such a big deal. One bud set up a Discord server for us and that boosted our ability even more. So really just get some friends. And remember...even if you're socially awkward...you're amongst the socially awkward. Play in groups!  There are certain characters that are much easier to use than others. the main one that comes to mind is Rath (who's actually voiced by Vegeta's voice actor), a melee character with plenty of player crowd control skills with very deadly skills. The game literally does describe him as easy first off...and I'm sure that Gearbox is thinking what to do with him, as Two others, Alani who was considered to be OP, and Galilea, who was hilariously OP for a very long time, have all been hit with the balance hammer! A lot of issues have been dealt with by the devs, and im sure with the heat they're getting with the skins...they'll take another look at it also. As the issue for playerbase...i think BB is hurting on that because the newbies theyre getting from the -50% sales are getting creamed by the more dedicated players who are still playing. but really after you gain every character and get the masteries for your favorite characters...there isn't a whole lot more to do right now. I'd say they could introduce a more serious PVP bracket...where you get increased credits and such for participating...and maybe at the end of a tourney people get that Platinum currency...you'd give something for more seasoned players to do, and would leave the newbs to fight each other. Anyway....i love gearbox but they are in new territory in a heavily pvp oriented game but ill stick by em. Don't look at the lower active players as a reason to never buy the game...we're all just waiting for more content

There are probably going to be plenty of people drawing parallels between this series and the HeroRise series, so I'm going to go ahead and jump on the bandwagon and give you my take on it.  Since this is just the first installment, I'm only going to compare it to HR: Prodigy.
So to start off, you'll be happy to know that this is not a complete rehash of HR: P.  CCH is its own thing entirely, and while there are similarities (
) I feel like those are general tropes that superhero stories have been using a lot recently.
As a whole I think HR: P has a better all-around story.  TbF is spending a more of its time getting you ready for the sequels and I feel like there was less resolved at the end than in HR: P.  If you only wanted to play one game and have no intention of playing the whole series, HR is probably the better choice.  TbF also had a LOT of characters, which made it harder to get to know them all.  You'll have to do several playthroughs if you want to understand all of them, whereas HR kept it more condensed which allowed more development for the characters it had.
That being said, I did thoroughly enjoy this game.  While it did feel crowded at times, I do still think that all the characters were developed well and had there own unique personalities.  The environment really did feel like a college, which helped CCH differentiate itself from other Choice of Games hero stories.  The plot was engaging, the mystery was fun, and it did a great job at getting me excited for the next installment.
So while I do prefer HR: P, I feel like CCH: TbF has done a fantastic job at making its own thing, and I can't wait for Eric Moser to publish the next several chapters.
Plus it was a thousand times better than HeroProject: Redemption Season.  So there's that.

This game is fun... until you hit the pay wall.
You need energy to play this game, in increasing amounts as you progress. At first, there's a fountain that keeps you going, handing out energy every half hour. It's a limited resource though, unless you fuel it with increasing amounts of gold it runs dry. There's also a golden idol that can be harvested for gold every ten minutes. It's also a limited resource, unless you fuel it with increasing amounts of rubies it also runs dry. Gold and rubies can be bought for cash, if you are a pretty active player $10 will keep you going for a day at first. The overall cost also keeps increasing, every time you fuel your fountain and golden idol you will have to spend more the next time.
There's also F2P, 1 energy every 90 seconds, which gets you one scene access every hour or two. Later on, you need to harvest a scene several dozen times to get the increasing amount of access keys required to play restricted scenes once.

I really wanted to love this game. I really did. But after just a short time, I knew that I never would.
The game is beautiful , with very nice graphics. The HOS scenes aren't terribly difficult, or terribly easy.  But...
Repetitive. After a little while, the scenes are all too much the same. You quickly figure out where the object placement spots are. So you can just click randomly and repeatedly on those spots and hit every item, fairly quickly. No penalties for random clicking either, so if you have a Macro on your mouse, just sit and randomly slide your cursor over the screen, while the mouse clicks away. So you can find everything while you watch pron on the TV in the room, or whatever. Does that sound like a good thing? Perhaps for some it would be. For me it created boredom and apathy. Yes, apathy.
Energy bar. So you run out of energy very quickly. The "Magic Fountain" that is supposed to reward you with more energy refills very slowly. 30 minutes to get another 35 energy. Which you will use in 2 or 3 HOS's. You use so much energy for each HOS, that you can only do 2-4 of them as you level up, tring to get quest items. Which drop somewhat randomy.
The Quests feel like they are out of order, the game telling you to do things that you won't be able to do for several more HOS scene levels or character levels. Not only do you level up your character, but you must level up each scene rating or diffculty, and many object you need for early quests will not drop for another 1-3 scene levels. So your Quest list grows, and piles up.
Microtransactions. Yes, the game wants your IRL money. And lots of it. And it does not give you much in return for a pile of your IRL money. The amounts of virtual currency you can buy, at ridiculously high proces, will be eaten up quickly by the in game currency cost for anything you need or want. It just feels like a very greedy cash grab. The in game virtual  currency flows very slowly, and the flow gets slower the further you progress. Basically funneling you into their pay-to-play microtranaction system.
Friends. Yes, the game is Singleplayer. But to complete some of the quest objectives, you MUST gift or recieve gifts from in game friends. And although the Steam forums does have at least one thread for sharing in game player ID's to add frends fior this purpose, you will end up adding a bunch of random people, who will be asking you for items, and may never return the favor.
Minigames. They exist, but they are really pointless IMHO. Find items through quests to socket into spaces. Puzzles (jigsaw type) are small and terribly easy. I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews - Game 24
bit Dungeon II
Playing bit Dungeon II makes me curious how the developers went about making this game.  It's like they knew they wanted to make a Zelda game, but couldn't figure out a story so they just penciled in a beginning sentence or two figuring they could come back later and add some more, but then never did.
The game starts out with you seeing I guess it's supposed to be the ghost of your girlfriend or something.  You click on her and she says  "Take my soul to my grave, and bring me back".  That beginning sentence is the only bit of story I got.  The rest of my time I spent running into a room and killing things, and then moving into another room and killing some more things.
I mentioned Zelda because the game definitely evokes the original Legend Of Zelda.  It has an overland area that is essentially broken up into a series of screens.  Most screens will have enemies you need to kill and then there will be an exit in one or more directions.  Some screens will have a door or opening that you can go through.
Some doors lead to rooms where you will get a random powerup, and others lead to dungeons.  The dungeons reminded me a lot of the original Zelda dungeons as well.  One drawback though is the complete lack of a map.  But the game will give you a sense of where you've been.  In dungeons for instance, rooms where you've already slaughtered the creatures within will still have the corpses lying about, giving you a visual cue.  As you clear rooms you'll acquire keys which unlock other rooms, until eventually you get to a boss of the dungeon.
The combat is pretty much just a bunch of frentic button mashing.  There isn't really any strategy to it.  As you kill creatures you will get experience and level up.  But there isn't really anything to leveling up; the game just picks a couple of stats to increase.
Enemies drop loot which you can pick up and upgrade what you have.  At first I was meticulously comparing each weapon drop to what I have, but then once I got a bow I quit caring because the game may as well have given me a machine gun.  The moment I picked up a bow I turned into Legolas, and the world was my swiss cheese.
The retro art style definitely looks like something you would have played on your Super Nintendo.  Same goes for the retro music, but it did get rather repetitive after awhile.
One other note, although the game supports keyboard and mouse, you will really want to use a controller.
I can't help but feel like the developers got bored of working on this game and went on to something new.  It's like they created the bones of the game around a combat system and some basic random map generation, and decided that was good enough.  I don't want to call the game unfinished, because it is perfectly playable, and there is fun to be had.  What the game does it does well, but once you get past those basics, the game just feels lacking in depth.
If you are desperate for a new roguelike game, or really want to scratch that nostalgic Zelda itch, then you'll enjoy this game.  But there are much better roguelike games that I'd recommend before this one.
It's Dark souls meets Link to the past. It's really really awesome, but not very long.

Bitdungeon 2 is a hard game to review pretty much because the combat sucks.  Like everyone is saying, you walk into the opponent to auto attack and you can do more damage by pressing RMB or A on the controller.  You basically just spam it until your stamina is depleted.  Killing bosses consists of literally standing in place and doing this over and over with very little moving out of the way of projectiles.
A few things I found annoying:
-When you enter a new room in a dungeon, you are facing the door and not the room, leaving you open to attack.
-The same button is used for pretty much everything on the controller.  A blocks, uses a special attack, and basic attack and picks up items.  So, many times you will be spamming attack and accidentally pick up a new item and equip it when you didn't know what it was.
There is a map that was added and for good reason.  BD2 desperately needs this as running around after you've cleared a few dungeons gets tedious.  You are supposed to beat all the dungeons on two lives.  So it's sort of a rogue-lite if anything.  The developer pretty much took inspiration from Dark Souls as when you die, you have one chance to retrieve your soul. If you die again, game officially over and you lose all the levels and gear you've accumulated.
The major draw for me initially was the way the gear looks even in pixelated form.  You can actually make your pixel avatar look pretty badass.  Things like capes will show up on your toon after you equip them.  Epic weapons look pretty unique too.  You will pretty much always want to equip 2 handers as they do the most damage.  1 handed epic weapons usually only drop after killing a boss, but they're supposed to be random so that may've just been my terrible luck.
For a 5 dollar game...BD2 is worth it.  It's a good lunch break game to just whip out if you're at home and play for 20 minutes.  Other than that, it get's extremely boring as most playthroughs look the exact same.  The dev claims each one is procedurally generated.  I suppose this is true. But the level design is so uninspired that each corridor on each playthrough appears the same to me.

You get an access to the old police computer, where are videos from interviews with... her. Yes, her, I mean that awesome actress you can see all over the screenshots. I think this is the first time I've been playing an FMV game but I've been enjoying it a lot. Game itself doesn't offer any typical challenge, it's up to you in what order you'll see the interview videos and when you'll decide that you know enough - but those who would be interested in complete story, will spend more time for sure, I'd say about 4 hours (and I'm not counting the time discussing speculations about details of the story on forum afterwards).

Seeing the negative reviews for this game have given me a sour taste in my mouth so i plan to add my opinion in here. When it comes to gameplay and character complexity this game has it spades. When it comes to unlocking all the characters, every hero is perfectly obtainable with challenges, the two hardest ones being Deande and Ghalt. Then you have everyone's story to unlock which really gives a lot of depth to the characters. The Campaign is rather fun, as every playthrough the voice overs are a little different each time and add the Borderlands humor I've come to expect. Campaign is best for getting gear packs and leveling the character levels, while PVP is best for gaining commander levels. So going through some of the negative reviews are mainly about matchmaking, and the recent decision to add Platinum. a premium currency for getting new skins and taunts. I won't lie im kinda in the same mindset of "why does a full price game have any sort of premium currency?" to me this would be easily remedied by making them attainable with difficult challenges, so one could say they didn't pay for them. Then how Alani, without a key gained by getting the deluxe addition, is unlocked with around 45,000 IGC. I also won't lie thats a hilarious amount of credits. uh...easy way to solve that. put earning her by commander level or by a difficult challenge like the rest of the characters. Also there's many a complaint about how the average PVP match can go. Yes you will get pub teams vs. organized and higher level groups. welcome to PVP that will always happen. the problem is because theyre higher level people will automatically assume theyre going to lose...and with that mindset you will. If you dont like that you tend to lose playing with pubs...do what i did and get a crew of people to play with and just watch how much more fun it gets. Communication is such a big deal. One bud set up a Discord server for us and that boosted our ability even more. So really just get some friends. And remember...even if you're socially awkward...you're amongst the socially awkward. Play in groups!  There are certain characters that are much easier to use than others. the main one that comes to mind is Rath (who's actually voiced by Vegeta's voice actor), a melee character with plenty of player crowd control skills with very deadly skills. The game literally does describe him as easy first off...and I'm sure that Gearbox is thinking what to do with him, as Two others, Alani who was considered to be OP, and Galilea, who was hilariously OP for a very long time, have all been hit with the balance hammer! A lot of issues have been dealt with by the devs, and im sure with the heat they're getting with the skins...they'll take another look at it also. As the issue for playerbase...i think BB is hurting on that because the newbies theyre getting from the -50% sales are getting creamed by the more dedicated players who are still playing. but really after you gain every character and get the masteries for your favorite characters...there isn't a whole lot more to do right now. I'd say they could introduce a more serious PVP bracket...where you get increased credits and such for participating...and maybe at the end of a tourney people get that Platinum currency...you'd give something for more seasoned players to do, and would leave the newbs to fight each other. Anyway....i love gearbox but they are in new territory in a heavily pvp oriented game but ill stick by em. Don't look at the lower active players as a reason to never buy the game...we're all just waiting for more content

I think Battleborn is fundamnetally misunderstood by a lot of people who expected it to be a lot more like Overwatch, and the timing of the game's release didn't help. Both are hero shooters, but otherwise, Overwatch is TF2 + Hero Shooter and Battleborn is MOBA-light + hero shooter. The differences make the games play very differently.
That doesn't mean Battleborn doesn't suffer from a lack of polish. The game feels, even with its delays, like a lot of important elements were underaddressed and underdeveloped: matchmaking, balance, interface, etc. Still, at its core, Battleborn is fun to play, has interesting heroes, is funny and well-written for the most part, and enjoyable. Sadly, the competition with Overwatch has led to a collapse of its population really quickly. The players who remain are mostly good, though, and the community is less toxic than many. I have hopes that the game will endure because of its specific qualities, especially in terms of the type of humor in Gearbox did in Borderlands. If you dug the jokes there, you'll dig them here too.

I 100% recommend this game for Spellforce fans. The nostalgia will be satisfied.
For non-Spellforce fans, I recommend it only if you're curious and are okay with a few hours of simple role-playing (the first hours in the game) that will grow more and more as you go and end with a blast.
Spellforce 2 is a blend of RPG and RTS. The old game played for over 50 hours, this one plays for 15-20 depending on your pace. You start with a level 1 Shaikan character and you get to choose, along the way, how you wanna build it as it levels up. The old Combat/Magic skill trees make a comeback and a new Shaikan tree appears. You also start with a Shaikan companion so that means you can choose how to build her as well.
As I mentioned before, the game focuses on the RPG aspect at the beginning. It starts slow, since you have little skills and basic af leather armor, but you also level up quickly. After a few hours you'll be level 10 already, which means you get to have a few of the cool spells, and start facing tougher challenges. Those hours might be a slight let-down for few but the rest of the game more than compensates for them. The game focuses more on the RTS aspect in the second half. It is not easy, but it is great.
The story is connected to Spellforce 2. It's a follow up. Several of the old game's characters make an appearance (one even joins your party for a while like Nightsong did) and the feats you performed in the original game are mentioned (which is great for nostalgic fans like me).
Two new factions are included in Faith in Destiny (for a total of 5-6) and I felt satisfied with them. But the best addition to this game when compared to Shadow Wars was the item sets (besides the autosave function). If you complete the sets you get added bonuses (some of them boring ones like +100 health, other ones fun like 25% heal when killing). There are lots of sets for every character class.
This game might be a little rough around the edges in a couple of aspects but it is still a good one.
If you really buy this game, just two tiny advices: first, don't make your first companion an archer; you get one later in the game. Nothing wrong with having two archers, since you can specialize them later, but I think you'd like to have a wider pool of magic spells in your party. And second, I've added a couple of guides related to loot and weapons that might help you out.
In the end, I wanna thank the devs for this satisfactory experience as an old Spellforce fan.
