Long time fan of the You Dont Know Jack series, so I was interested in the Jackboxes as soon as I saw them.  Ive played dozens of games from each Jackbox, and while I fully recommend the first two at the low price point, I think this one, while great,  isn't worth it until its discounted.
FYI: I have 50+ hours played, not the 1.4 it shows here...I play on a laptop connected to TV doesnt show i guess.
The Good:
- Custom Games - You can make your own questions... so if you are like me and starting to get repeat questions, you can make your own!
- Quiplash 2 - Quiplash XL was always a party favorite with guests in the previous jackbox, and this one doesnt disappoint!
- Trivia Murder Party - A new entry in the series, and its great!  Took a couple games to really understand the mechanics, but our group had a blast with it... some really great and exciting close games the way they end.
- Guesspionage - Another new entry... Simple and fun game with lot of surprises and its more challenging than it seems.
The Bad:
- No Fibbage - would have liked to see a new Fibbage in, this was a standout game
- Tee K.O. - Mediocre at best... the concept is ok, where you come up with funny slogans and draw T-Shirts, but half the stuff you draw and come up with doesnt get used in the game.  Also, the mechanics and scoring dont make sense... instead of a tournament style matchups, its just 2 random shirts, one gets voted off, and a new "challenger" shirt gets thrown in.  points for longest streak, and winner... problem is if your shirt comes out last, your max streak can only be 1, and if your shirt is first, highly unlikely everyone will keep voting for it to win, so it didnt make much sense.  we played a few games and moved on, wont bother unless it gets revamped in the future.
The Ugly
- No You Dont Know Jack??  Why a YDKJ episide wasnt included in a Jackbox, WTH?
- Fakin It - wow, what a mess.  Pass on this turd, we tried it a few times, and our group mutually agreed it was definitely the loser of the bunch.
Fortunately with 5 games included, its still worth getting even with one or two average or crap games, cause three are super fun with unlimited potential with the new ability to make up custom questions... well worth the price of a 12 pack of beer for the hours of entertainment value, so I still very much recommend.

Rogue Harvest is an Indie game with lots of potential. Don't let the graphics mislead you, actual game mechanics provide a depth to the game that is not immediately apparent.
In terms of genre, RH is an hybrid of sorts (featuring elements of survival, RPG, and rogue-like sandbox elements). It features crafting + building on an randomly-generated open world, where you must explore and strive to stay alive. The story starts out vague, and must be uncovered as you progress. In order to survive for longer periods of time, you'll need to learn from each failed attempt... improve bit by bit, even on aspects that in other games you take for granted (note to self: beware open flames near flammable stuff).
And so began my first playthroughs of the game. I had fun, and as usual took a few notes regarding gameplay elements and bugs I had found, heading over to the game's forum to provide some feedback. Genetix, the game developer, promptly responded, showing not only that he cared about the people that play his game but also about their actual experience of it. Each item was addressed, with suggestions being discussed and bugs noted (some were already being addressed).
So, not only is the game promising, it is also quite refreshing to see developers take the time to interact positively with fans in order to improve the game. The feeling that feedback has impact on how the game will evolve makes gamers more invested in its future.
Will be playing again, and look forward to future updates.

Let me start by pointing out that "Telltale Texas Hold'em" is an old game. It's outdated. So when you feel it, the graphics and the interface will probably bother you.  However that being said, even though its an old game, when you play it, you feel like you are actually sitting in a poker table, playing in a real tournament. The in-talk between the characters makes it really immersive. Characters are not so bad either, especially the character Boris Krinkle even inspired the character Leonard Steakcharmer from the Sam & Max series.
Other than that the AI is sometimes predictable, but it doesn't affect the game too much. You have the consider that this was the first poker game that Telltale games did, before the "Poker Night at the Inventory" games, they've built up so much more since then.
One problem that this game suffers is that the game has no replayability value, when you win your first tournament, you're done. No need to play another time, maybe except to hear the dialogues between the characters. It's not like the other poker games from Telltale, where you can get exclusive collectible items such as new decks, new tables, ot just new items from the characters in the game.
Normally if this was a brand new game or a recent game, i wouldn't recommend it, but considering its price being so low and its the first poker game from Telltale, i would say you can give it try, if the game is on a discount and/or if you want to the see the earlier version (kinda) of the "Poker Night at the Inventory". I have played this game on the PC for about 5 hours now, and I really want to like this game. I like Rogue style games and was addicted to Wizardry in the day. It is a compelling premise to combine these worlds.
Likes: I like th character development, and the ability to spec out your characters with different gear and classes. I do not even mind that you have to "eat" lower level characters to level up your more powerful ones. The use of animated miniatures is pretty cool as well.
Dislikes: I am always WJ currency poor in the game, and the ability to unluck the most powerful characters is highly dependent upon the WJ currency. It feels like they ported the game from an in-game purchase model where the intentional shortage is intended to motivate players to purchase more currency with real money, except there are no in-game purchases anymore (which I love) and they did not change the trickle with which you make more WJ.
The game is buggy as hell. Somewhat randomly certain characters when you Fortify them (level them up) or change their class get stuck on the animation screeen in which the game either gives you no way off the screen or the botton you are intended to push does nothing. I have had to CTRL-ALT-DEL many, many times to get out of the screeen and thus, had to restart the game each time. Interestingly, the game itself is apparently still running fine, you just cannot get out of that screen.
Finally, I do not like that the backrow characters seemingly do nothing unless you specifically get one of them to use a particular ability (like case a spell or shoot a bow). They do not seem to involve themselves in any obvious way in the head-to-head encoutners. The front rowers all swing, do apparent damage and take damage, the backrowers do nothing even when you have ranged or far-reaching weapons equiped. Additionally, you cannot intentionally target particular characters in the opponent party, particularly the characters int he backrow. Thus, you regularly clean out the front row, only to have their backrow get an automatic attack on you every time. Why can't my archers or mages attack their backrow characters while my fighters attack their front?
Thus, as much as like the compelling idea, the execution of the game seems like they missed some really obvious features that would seem to be obvious in a party-based game of this nature. Perhaps with a patch they can fix these things, but at the moment the game quickly becomes so frustrating it makes me want to stop even though it is a game I would easily play a lot with these minor fixes.

I bought this game because of the recommendation from one of my friends.

It was a good choice. I was pretty impressed by the way author implemented this investigation gameplay. Maybe it is not a new mechanic but I never encountered such games before.
In this game you will be behind some desk with a computer and you will be watching the records with interrogation of a woman. Unfortunately for you the records get mixed and there is no way to watch them in the correct order by default. Your only tool is the search string which will allow you to type words and look for the records with these words. So, every time you will learn something new from a record it will help you to move further in your investigation and to find more information.
The story is interesting, the gameplay is exciting and I wasn’t able to close the game until I found the answer.

I only got around to playing HER STORY at the end of 2015, after all the year-end hype had declared it to be among the best of the year. I figured I'd play it someday, maybe. But then a friend suggested we play it together and I'm so glad he did, because it's terrific. It's not that I object to FMV as a format, but I had my doubts that the storytelling or the acting would live up to its by-then stellar reputation. Nope! HER STORY is as great as everyone says it is.
I don't know how many people were offscreen, if any, but Viva Seifert is alone on camera and gives one hell of a performance. And by the end, or the beginning, or the middle (depending on where you stop digging) HER STORY is fascinating, more so than any run-of-the-mill crime story on television. Laid out in order, it wouldn't be as interesting: it is the mechanics of searching and analyzing that makes HER STORY so compelling. I hope we get more games like this.
Super addictive and fun.

Let me preface by saying I love most Choice of Games (and Hosted Games, its oftentimes less clever but sometimes still funny younger brother.)  This story appears to be published under Hosted Games, where you can submit your story to Choice of Games, and they can publish it if they think it's good enough (Stories published under Choice of Games are commissioned by professional writers.) Hosted Games can be good. Zombie Exodus is excellent, go try it. But I recognise that these authors are not professional, so I can forgive lesser quality for more creativity.
This story, however, is a disappointment on both fronts. There's no other way to put it: the writing is terrible. You can on ly play 3 cliched archetypes. I can't even immerse myself into the archetypes because the dialogue is awkward. I want to choose a dialogue option that fits my character but the lines are so bad I cannot imagine anyone saying them. The story introduces a whole bunch of characters without much characterisation at once. There are some scenes that might be considered technically good, like the early terrorism scene and the park capture-the-flag scene, but they're not worth it.
The writer should not be charging money for this fanfiction-quality of writing, let alone charging more per-installment (this is only the first installment!) than the all-around excellent Zombie Exodus. Choice of Games shouldn't let this quality be published under their name. I bought this game without demo-ing the game because I trusted the company to do quality assurance, because they made great games like Choice of Robots, Choice of Romance, and Heroes Rise. I'm just... seriously disappointed.
P.S. If you want a better superhero/villain game, try Heroes Rise or Diabolical. If you want powers in a school setting try Psy High. They are much, much better.

Original Review:
This game is one of my favourite genres.  Rogue-like Dungeon Crawler with random item spawns and random generated monsters with bosses. However, does it live up to my favourite Genre and do it justice? No. Let me elaborate.
Firstly the game has major flaws and it seems like the developers have left the game for dead (It has a 10 page Bug Thread and 90% of the bugs haven't been fixed). But without further ado, here is why I think you shouldn't buy this game.
Pros:
♦ Random Generated Monsters and Items
♦ Level up system that works
♦ Awesome system to tell where you have already explored (Say you've been in a room and killed everything and come back to that room, smaller enemies will appear to symbolize you've been there already, which is awesome)
♦ Unique controls that just work (You can use mouse entirely or keyboard entirely or both which is great choice. I didn't try controller, so not sure how this works).
♦ Achievements are easy (You can get almost all just by finishing the game)
♦ Awesome Graphics and Sounds
♦ Gameplay was fun for one playthrough
Cons:
♦ Devs seem to have abandoned the game
♦ No Storyline (There is a weak one, but there is no explanation as to why you are doing what you're doing)
♦ Achievement "Fiends, Wolves, Rats" which is unlocked by killing a unit is broken (Has been broken since launch resulting in you being unable to get 100% of achievements, which sucks.)
♦ All Achievements don't show up as locked on "Personal Achievements" page
♦ No way to remap Controls (Controls are awesome as mentioned but some people may like the option)
♦ No quit on main menu
♦ No way to tell how the game saves (It seems to just save upon going back to main menu, which is okay but would be better to let us know that's what happens)
♦ Version Number inconsistently says 1.96 in "Update/News" but in-game it says 1.95 (This is terrible as it doesn't tell us whether or not the 1.96 update is actually released)
♦ Opting into Beta doesn't do anything (Why have a Beta option but not make it change or add anything to the game?)
♦ No map/way of knowing when you've completed a biome (The map isn't really needed but it would be helpful to know when you've fully explored somewhere and or completed all dungeons and killed all bosses in that biome... but instead you're just walking around aimlessly not knowing)
♦ No way to tell if a Biome or Dungeon is recommended for a certain Character Level (This is lame as it doesn't set any order for you to complete biomes/dungeons and you have to figure it out yourself)
♦ Items seem based on luck and not on difficulty from what you've killed or from Character Level (All enemies even bosses seem to drop the same sort of items and level items no matter if you kill the first enemy you see to a boss, they'll roughly be the same which sucks as you'd think the harder the enemy the better the drop but that's not the case. Also I was level 35 and getting level 8-12 items dropping... go figure)
♦ Enemies don't seem harder per play through (I finished the game once and there seemed no difference in difficulty)
♦ Short (Took me 3hours to finish the game...)
♦ Very Repetitive (They try and make you play the game over once you beat it and the number of playthroughs gets added to highscores etc... but each playthrough is identicle and doesn't seem to scale in difficulty based on playthrough or character level which sucks and makes anymore than one playthrough extremely boring and repetitive. Also there is nothing unique per playthrough except the enemies are spawned randomly again, however the bosses are the same which makes it even more repetitive and boring)
♦ No Cards (Why? There is potential for cards but they are not included.. it would add to the game imo).
♦ Only way to see Stats is via a Fire (This is lame as you have to find a fire to view them and there is Stat Booster caves around and you can't check your stats before choosing which to boost which is annoying to say the least)
♦ Biome Path Puzzles are too easy (You are supposed to talk to someone to get the directions to take to beat the path, however you can easily do it by entering the path which isn't blocked by a rock or icicle etc depending on the biome which ruins the puzzle challenge)
Overall, if you like rogue-like games then this will definitely give you one playthrough averaging roughly 3hours. However, the game is very repetitive, has no storyline, you can't get 100% of achievements, the version number is wrong and the Devs have seemingly abandoned it... therefore, I'd recommend you boycott this game as there are many many more rogue-like games that are still being updated, are not repetitive and actually allow you to 100% them.

I bought this game because it was on sale and I thought it looked good. I was wrong.
Don't get me wrong, it isn't all bad. The basic ideas are fine, the dungeon designs are nice and the one life system is "interesting". I say "interesting" because if you die twice you lose everything, but don't necessarily have to start over completely.  You probably will though, because in this game your gear is the only thing pulling your through each dungeon. Losing your gear in this game is like having your stats reset in any other game. Continuing is pointless because you're not going to get far.
Now for the bad parts. Firstly, saying the controls in this game are simplistic is like saying Michael Bay enjoys explosions. You move with WASD and attack/pick up items/whatever with space or the mouse. Some of you might have already figured out the problem. Having every action linked to the same key makes this game a cluster♥♥♥♥ from hell. If you happen to be on an item while trying to attack, you'll go into an infinite loop of picking up the item, dropping your equipment, picking up your equipment, dropping the item and picking up the item again. When it happens in a dungeon it pretty much guarantees you're going to die. Killed by bad controls and a crappy pair of +3 Dodge boots.
That's another problem. The majority of the items you get in this game are junk. Sure, when you're starting out a crappy pair of boots is better than nothing, but unlike other games those crappy boots never stop appearing. It literally gets to the point where you'll use the same equipment through the entire game because the game won't give you anything better (or anything else.) There's no progression and almost no diversity. And to remind you, ITEMS ARE LIKE STATS IN THIS GAME. Sure, sometimes you get lucky and get a "good" item, but even then there's almost no diversity. The last time I played I got the same "epic" helmet (stats and all) five times in a row in five different locations.
Here's another problem: combat. Combat in this game is basically a drunken, anemic slap-fight against a boxer. The feel of your character's attacks ranges from hard and deadly to limp and sloppy. Some enemies will go down in one hit with the right weapon (reference the above paragraph), but others will literally brush your attacks off like you're nothing to them. It's ridiculously unsatisfying. More so due to the fact that combat in this game boils down to button mashing. There's no strategy, no rhythm, just repeatedly mashing space until everything is dead or you go into an item pick up death loop.
So to sum up: the controls are atrocious, the combat is weak and the item distribution is a game killer. I can appreciate what this game was trying to do (make a Legend of Zelda style game with RPG and rogue-like elements), but the flaws killed any fun I would have had with it right away. Which, frankly, is sad because I could have had a lot of fun with it. The best part of this game, I suppose, is that I only spent around three dollars on it.

A  simple action RPG with rogue-like elements.
Plot:
The game has very little plot to speak of, or not so much that I've been able to discover. Your objective is to take the spirit of your loved one to her grave, and to do so you'll have to kill a bunch of bosses in their dungeons, reminiscent of Shadow of the Colossus in theme except there are also ordinary enemies and minibosses.
Game world:
The game is set on an unchanging overworld map with dungeons that randomly pick from a set of designs to give a feeling of variation, taking inspiration from Souls for the bonfires scattered around where you can regain health and check your stats. The random generation is therefore not very significant.
Gameplay:
The combat is rather simple but not mindless: your character auto attacks when it bumps into enemies, but at a mouse click, key press or button push depending on what you're playing with they can attack instantly at the cost of some stamina. Holding down this key allows you to block attacks also at the cost of stamina, and perform a charged attack with your weapons. There's not much challenge to fights as the enemies and bosses are rather easy to figure out, and your greatest danger is underleveling or lack of good equipment.
The permadeath mechanic takes inspiration from Souls: the soul you're transporting is your only extra life, and you drop it at the place of your death. If you cannot retrieve it, your next death is final and you must restart, keeping only the coins you collected which can be used to purchase items at shops you must find yourself.
Graphics:
The game has charming "retro" pixel sprites graphics which work pretty well. There's not much animation to the characters but not much is needed either.
Replayability:
There is NG+, and if you enjoy collecting rare equipment or trying out different weapons and builds there is some replayability in this for you. The game itself is short. By the time this review was written I had completed my first playthrough after somewhere around 5 restarts, mostly late in the game. The game itself would only take around an hour to complete.
Conclusion:
This is a nice enough timewaster on a mobile platform. Outside of a mobile however, it is far too simple and with little challenge or replayability unless you enjoy farming for items (Borderlands fans, this is for you.) It was clearly ported to PC (the port works fine) and while it is a fun little past time, it's up to you if this is worth having it on your PC. I personally recommend getting this for your phone instead.

AUDIENCE

OPTIMIZATION
If you're computer, for example, can't run minecraft at 25 fps on a crowded server, then don't expect beautiful shadows and seamless movement. You will have to turn off shadows, settings etc. just to reach 60 fps, even 40 fps for some people. I came into Knights of the Old Republic expecting very little. The combat at first seemed bland and the graphics unappealing (especially the player character). But as I got deeper and deeper into the web of dialogue choices and skilltrees I found a game that so surprised me with its beauty the character count would not allow me to express it all.
The story begins 4,000 years before the rise of the Galactic Empire seen in the Star Wars films. It is a bold choice; to depart from the stock characters and scenes is to lose much of the iconic universe already known. But BioWare proves incredibly successful at creating a world of its own within the universe, delivering a story and atmosphere that would not be possible otherwise. I will not attempt to summarize it here- it is best recieved in its pure form.
The game offers two main paths for the player: that of the light and dark side of the force. I myself chose to follow the light side, making decisions along the way that pushed me towards the light. I was never once truly tempted to choose the dark side, however, as the two paths become rather black-and-white, but that is the heritage of the Star Wars universe, and I could not imagine it anay other way.
As for the combat, it takes place in a pausable real-time action-based system. Different abilities are gained by progressing through the skill tree of each character, called "Feats". These feats can be either direct upgrades to stats or abilities. I don't think it is much of a spoiler to say that the character is eventually allowed to utilize the force in a way similar to this, through a different tree. These abilities range from freezing an opponent (the ability I used the most) to choking them to death Vader-style. Equipment can also be customized, giving armor, damage resistance to different types of attacks, or reinforcing stats. All of these are available for every character in the game.
Now to my favorite: the characters. I loved them. Every single one was beautifully crafted, and I couldn't help but care about all of them. The character is allowed different dialogue trees with every one, learning about them and their backstories. Unfortunately as party size is limited to three I was not able to spend time with each one as I would have liked, but I understand that the balance is needed. There is so much I want to say about every single one of them, but I want you to meet and fall in love with them by yourself.
There is tons to do in each planet you visit, and I know for a fact I did not complete everything. Some adventures I didn't even find. Swoop-racing, pazaak (blackjack) playing, duelling are some of the blander activities. Others are best left for you to discover.
I know that I'm biased as hell in favor of this game, but that's 'cause I absolutely love it. I would definitely recommend this game regardless of your prior experience with Star Wars, RPGs, or even videogames: at ten dollars, it delivers a game better than the sixty-dollar massive productions spewn out of most big publishers today. Get it.

A great looking indie title headed in the right direction and with potentially compelling storyline, but seems to lack innovation.  Rogue Harvest is the top-down equivilant of Minecraft and Stardew Valley.
The player must survive for as long as possible.  The player must gather resources during the day to craft items in order to keep themselves alive and protect themselves from monsters at night.
Monsters are much more powerful than those found in most survival games.  These monsters can break the walls of your home and storm the house, therefore overwhelming and killing the player.  The player's "energy" meter will keep track of the player's food intake.  The player can choose to consume anything from leaves and flowers to good rabbit meat.
The player's home is more or less the only safe haven during the night, and it is as terrifying as it is brutal.  The game is permadeath and the player must struggle to keep the monsters out of the house my strengthening his defences and crafting swords to survive the night.  Rogue Harvest has a harsh difficulty spike as the player's time will mostly be spent on fortifying their homes at night, rather than exploring the vast open world which it has to offer.
Once the player has either killed enough NPCs or gathered a sufficient amount of resources, the player will level up.  Enhancing maximum HP and energy.  The player also collects these "souls" from killed NPCs.  As of now, these souls serve no purpose, but I'd imagine the developers have something planned for them.  Personally, I see the game following the path of Dark Souls, with the player meeting other NPCs offering services in exchange for souls.
+Familiar gameplay mechanics
+A good challenge for the "hardcore survivalist"
+Teases a story with depth and enough potential
+Features a character level progression system
-Absurd difficulty spikes
-Monsters need balancing
-Lacking innovation
-No multiplayer
-No trading cards
-Janky controls
Rogue Harvest is a great early access indie title and from what I can tell, it is still making great progress.  The game can sometimes be far too difficult for its own good and seems to takes far too many key elements and mechanics from other popular survival and RPG genres without introducing enough of its own to compensate for it.  The controls are janky, with the player only being able to effectively control the character using the mouse.  Pressing two keys at the same time will keep the player going straight as opposed to causing the character to walk diagonally.
Rogue Harvest has yet to show what it truly has to offer, but the game is slightly above average in its current build. I recommend it as it's cheap and still holds a lot of potential down the road.

Anyways, onto the review. Rogue Harvest was developed and published by Genetix, and was released on November 5th 2015. It’s genres are Action, Adventure, Open World, Rogue-like, Procedural Generation, and RPG.
Rogue Harvest is an open-world rogue like exploration game and those types of games in my mind are absolutely amazing.
When I first played Rogue Harvest, the very first thoughts in my mind was Stardew Valley, Terraria, and Don't Starve. Personally, I have never played Stardew Valley, but if you compare Rogue Harvest to Stardew Valley, you can see some interesting similarities in the art style. In my experience, Rogue Harvest connects very well with Don't Starve. While I have not played Don't Starve, I have played Don't Starve together, which is the exact same thing as Don't Starve just multiplayer. The biggest differences between Don't Starve Together and Rogue Harvest are, well,
obviously the graphics,pixel art vs a hand drawn style, lack of content, and modding capability.
In Rogue Harvest, the worlds are massive and procedurally generated, and mixed with it's rogue-like element, every playthrough is different.
The controls for Rogue Harvest are for the most part very good. However, when you first start the game, the controls are very confusing, but once you have enough time playing it'll get better.
When you play Rogue Harvest, you must keep an eye on your health, energy, and surroundings. If you run out of energy, your character begins to starve to death. If you aren't paying attention to your surroundings, monsters have a tendency to sneak up on your and could easily end your playthrough.
Crafting in Rogue Harvest was very easy, and compared to some other games that include crafting, Rogue Harvest had a very straight forward crafting system.
The soundtrack for Rogue Harvest is very, well, interesting. The sound effects are a little bit annoying, but are bareable. The music is what I find so interesting about the game. For copyright purposes, I will not be playing the music in question, but it sounds a lot like creative commons orchestral music. However, I may be wrong, and the musician is just really talented.
The graphics in Rogue Harvest are very visually pleasing, and aren't hard on the eyes, however, the sprites are enlarged in a very awkward way, and it stands out.
The story for Rogue Harvest is a confusing one. Your character is nameless, and is in some sort of accident. You wake up in a hut with some tools and a little farm.
The developer is very active and updates the game almost every week.
The downsides to the game are the really short day and night cycles. The days are short, and don't give you much time to harvest and explore before nightfall. The night is short and isn't long enough to provide any real excitement. The story is very confusing and bland, like the story of The Forest watered down. Another change I'd make to the game, although not a downside, would be multiplayer implementation.
Rogue Harvest is an interesting top-down survival horror game. Your goal is to survive and build your home in order to prolong the life-span of your storyless character.

In Rogue Harvest you play the role of someone who has found themselves somewhere they don't know with no memory of who he is or how he got there. You must survive in this strange place long enough in the hopes that your memories or some answers will come back to you.
Once you start the game you'll find yourself in a small wooden house with only an axe, hammer and pickaxe. You'll also find a little produce growing near your house but other than that, it's just you and your tools. You have main stats that you'll need to monitor which are health and energy and without keeping these full you'll die very quickly. Energy depletes over the day and can be regained by eating raw or cooked food, and Life will drop as you're attacked and can be refilled by using medicinal herbs. Keep an eye on these because once you die it's game over and you'll have to restart entirely but since the maps are procedurally generated, each run will be a little different.
You'll soon find that the world you're in is not a peaceful one and you'll need to find some way to protect yourself against those you encounter. Your first priority will be finding yourself some resources and crafting the basics such as a crafting table, oven, bed and a sword (though, maybe not in this order). You can easily find trees for wood and large areas of stone for any ore and stone needs you might have along with many other useful items either growing in the wild or dropped from mobs but you'll need to be careful; there is no map in Rogue Harvest so you'll only have your footsteps (which are marked on the ground) to retrace. Once you have your basics you'll need to  craft yourself a weapon fairly quickly so you have a little defence and you'll also want to expand your shelter. The rest is up to you.
As you interact with the world during resource gathering and combat you'll find yourself slowly levelling up which increases your stats. You have four categories which can be increased and these are Life Points, Energy Points, Luck and Souls but you don't get to allocate your stat points yourself, they are automatically distributed across the board evenly with each level.
The developer is very active with new updates every few weeks or so and engages regularly with the community on the steam discussion boards. I had a small issue with achievements and within a day I had a friendly and very helpful reply which was a pleasant surprise. Even though the game has a clear direction the developer is open to ideas, tips and feeedback on one of the threads and once again the dev is active there and seems to take things on board.
But I do feel obligated to state there isn't masses and masses of content currently. Though you can craft and build things you are limited in those options. The resources don't go much further than wood, stone, ores, a few items animals and mobs can drop a few different types of vegetation. Since the game is in Early Access I am sure we'll see a little more content as development goes on though I don't know how long it plans to remain in development. I also believe the developer is adding a little more to the story (I got this from the Early Access information on the front page so I could be wrong).
I have a few issues I've encountered. The graphics are something awful if you play them on a large screen. Now this is just my opinion but reading the tutorial alone was an unpleasant experience and it didn't get much better from there. There are no options to change your resolution and I am unsure on if the developer plans to add this so you can either play in windowed for a slightly better experience or you'll have to suck it up. There are also issues with seeing items on the ground. The small pieces of stone that drop after breaking a large rock blend into the stone floor and combining that with your footsteps dotted everywhere become impossible to clearly see. My second issue is the movement because right now it's clunky and doesn't seem to actually do what I want it to half of the time which has caused me some unnecessary deaths. My guy will mine the wrong rocks, not attack in the correct direction sometimes and for some reason get caught in walls and drawn towards them whilst walking.

You have to keep an eye on your energy and life meters, energy depletes on its own, so you have to stuff yourself with food whenever you can, cause when it reaches zero, you starve to death. Life gets depleted when you get hit by an enemy, you can get some life back by eating herbs or keeping a high energy level.
The land is inhabitated by a lot of unfriendly and vicious creatures, like fire flowers (no, you can't collect them, it's not SMB), walking mushrooms, and bunnies. Even worse enemies spawn at night, scary skeletons, etcetera. Make sure to kill lots of them, you can loot many important items out of them.
You have three basic tools: Axe for chopping wood, Hammer for destroying walls, Pickaxe for almost everything else. You can also craft weapons, like a sword, boomerang or a bow. Make sure to craft one of them, a woodaxe is not a perfect weapon for killing enemies.
Building a sturdy shelter is your main defense against the creatures of the night. Make sure to add extra walls constantly: enemies can and will destroy them while trying to get to you.
While I like the 16bit-like style of the game, I can't stand how poorly enlarged the sprites and menus are. I keep touching my glasses to see if they are still on my nose, cause the graphics are so blurry. What I liked though, was that your character's footsteps and blood of fallen enemies don't disappear for a long while: you can use this to your advantage by following your footsteps back to your home, just make sure not to stray too far, there is no map and it sucks to get lost in the middle of night.
All sound effects are pretty normal, nothing to say about them. Music is meh, I muted it after 15 minutes because it was putting me to sleep. Some tracks vary in recording quality, especially the new game song sounds like something ported out of an early PS1 game.
Walking sideways sucks. I've died 3 times because of that. That's the biggest issue, the rest of the controls are alright. You have a menu where you can craft/equip items and also mute music/sfx. LMB performs action on item that you are currently holding, so using a carrot makes you eat it, using a sword makes you swing it.
An interesting game. What it lacks in sound and graphics, it makes up with its ominous atmosphere and open world. Game was putting me on edge constantly, because I could die at every given moment. Sudden flashbacks to a plane crash were unnerving me even more. Nights are REALLY dark and enemies can kill you in mere seconds. Medicine gives very little of your health back, and you have to constantly hunt for food. This game doesn't funk around.

Great heist game, that rewards careful playstyle.
There is plenty to love in the game; colourful graphics, excellent music, and heist missions in various locations and some alternative ways to complete each of them. Some gameplay mechanics such as hostage system are fresh and very intresting and rewarding to use. Each heist lasts from 5-15 minutes on initial playthrough, and you cannot save during the heists. It adds to the tension, and I personally wasnt annoyed by the lack of mid heist saving or didnt find retrying a failed heist a chore. Usually the hardest parts of the heists are in the beginning of them as well, so you really dont need to be afraid of losing 15 minutes of time with every attempt.
What is a shame though, that some minor errors plague the game, that make it frustrating for many I believe. What is even bigger shame is, that the developers could have fixed these issues very easily, if they just were willing to give up some of their ideas  (ie. just remove the friendly fire, since the AI is too stupid to make the mechanic work). The game also has a memory leak, and will crash after an hour or so of continuous play, so better quit and restart the game after each succeeded heist.
Nevertheless, the game is still a fun tactical action/puzzle game for the ones  who can handle some small but irritating bugs in it. If you are a patient player and just take your time, they wont stop you getting a good experience from the game.

This is not a game a lot of people will enjoy. It can probably be best described as an "interactive fragmented imaginary documentary film about a curious case that never got solved", where "interaction" comes almost only in how you sort out the fragments of the story together. It's a weird and interesting experience that feels a bit... lacking, but still satisfying.
There's always something curious about things in life like that - when it's hard to be very definite about what actually happened. When all explainations you hear sound valid, despite being conflicting. When the mystery just stays with you in a "what do YOU think happened" kind of way. And in that regard Her Story is very good. Sadly, a lot of explainations and "twists" (although most don't really aim to be twists in an accepted way) are very predictable, which does leave the entire expirience a teeny tiny bit disappointing. Not because of "I knew that" feeling, but because you just feel like that since you know how it goes already you'd just wish there was more to do.
But still, it's an interesting experience, the acting is good and shattered narrative makes the game feel very unique and interesting, even though you can easily cheat it and watch things chronologically. But I'd advise against doing that until you feel like you see the picture and want to find the filler bits.

The less you know about this the better - it's a unique (style, story, and interaction-wise), singular experience, as good as reading a great detective book. Because a certain "effect" made me uneasy, to be clear: it is NOT a horror game. (no shocker moments)
If you like story games, it's for you. Boom.

The amount of praise and number of awards Her Story received compelled me to give it a try, so I eagerly sat down to the game with a pen and pad of paper. Everyone I'd heard talk about it stressed the importance of keeping notes.
The game exists as a simulated Windows 3.1 desktop with various sound effects and image filters giving you that mid 1990s computer vibe. That part is done well. Actually, that part is the best part of Her Story.
The gameplay consists of watching a 90 minute interrogation video, split up into almost 300 individual clips that are each a few seconds long. You consume these videos randomly, as you enter a word into the search field and it returns up to five videos which contain that word in their transcript.
I'm okay with "experience" games. Or "Interactive fiction". However, Her Story is really pushing this concept, in that there is no interactivity to this fiction (you are choosing which clips to watch in what order, but you're not making any choices) and the "experience" is . . . well, that of watching a youtube video, basically. I like your Dear Esthers and your 9.03Ms and your Dinner Dates and your TRAUMAs and your Thirty Flights of Lovings, but . . . Her Story is *really* pushing it. Kind of like that kid in school who responds to the teacher's demand for a "two page essay" by writing his with a 24pt font.
Anyway, I watched the five default videos that were on the screen when I started the game. Two of the videos contained names in them. I did a search on one of those names. Then a search on the other. After watching fewer than fifteen videos (twelve, actually), I wrote down what I thought the story was about and the two possible conclusions I felt were likely to be reached. On a hunch that I was correct, I went to google and did a quick search to discover that my conclusions were what the rest of the internet had arrived at.
That's it. That's literally it.
There are no other elements to Her Story. You watch short clips of a 90 minute interrogation until you don't want to watch any more of them and then you turn the game off. I do get the impression that I was supposed to find the story more challenging, though, and that I was supposed to furiously keep track of notes and keywords as I unraveled the story for hours upon hours, but it was really so clear after about two minutes worth of footage that I felt it was a better investment of my time to check if I had reached the right conclusions or not before spending more time at it. And I had.
This game seems to have a specific thing it is trying to be and it is that very well. It isn't broken or anything. It just isn't something I can recommend. There's not much to it and (having later gone back and watched the entire boring 90 minutes of interrogation on youtube), the story itself is just pretty . . . well, unoriginal. And not compelling. If this is what the life of a police detective is like, I'd imagine there would be more suicides in the profession.
Also, there seems to be a lot of contention over which of the two possibilities is "true" and the developer has hinted that there is one ultimate truth - but he's never going to reveal it. Personally, I'd say the title of the game does it for him.
Ultimately, my task is to say whether I recommend this game or not. I'm supposed to review whether I liked it and would encourage anyone else to play it. I'm not supposed to review whether it is or isn't broken or whether it is or isn't what it sets out to be. Just whether I would go to a friend and say "man, you gotta play this game". And, to that end, I have to say that I would not. I would be open to something along these same lines and this same format, but with a more compelling story in the future, but . . . this specific attempt . . . just did not do it for me. The only thing this game *is* is a story and not one part of the story or the characters maintained even a glimmer of interest for me.
The only reason I could really recommend this game is because it is novel. It's unlike most other things, right now. That, alone, doesn't seem like an adequate reason for me tell someone they need to spend five or six bucks to watch a chopped-up video, though.

Wizrogue is exactly what the title says: Wizardry meets roguelike game. I was impressed how well this blend works. Gameplay is very solid and balanced, underlying mechanics of Wizardry is a good background for roguelike game. As the additional bonus, the game is kept in the convention of the tabletop game, with mini figures representing your party and cards representing spells. The graphics are really good, I think that if that game would be considered as a pure roguelike, I'd say it has the best graphics from all other installments so far. Music and sound effects are also very good.
There is only one aspect of the game which can be a bit irritating: the mobile game roots of the game somehow got through to the surface. There are revive options, paid elite members and other reminiscent of In-App-Purchases which shouldn't be in paid version. My guess is that if those elements were fully eradicated, even with the certain death of the characters, the game would only improve.

Preliminary thoughts:
Pros:
-It's a unique spin on Wizardry. I never would have thought anyone came up with the idea of splicing it with a roguelike, but here we are.
-The translation is very well done (at least so far). Games like this typically have lackluster translations, but I haven't seen any of that.
-The tutorial clearly explains the mechanics of the game and how they work so there's very little guesswork to be done.
Cons:
-It's hard to really call this a con for everyone, but this game is a port of a mobile game that's been (I hope!) stripped of its cash shop mechanics (though the things you would typically purchase in such a game are still there) and it shows. The interface is very much what you'd see in a mobile game, and this may understandably turn people away from it.
-Following the previous point, some people may not want to pay $12 for something they don't have to pay for on mobile. IMO, it's not a terrible asking price given that there doesn't appear to be any IAP.
In all, it's not a terrible game at all, but a rather niche one. I would personally recommend it to anyone who is both a fan of Wiz and a fan of roguelikes, but anyone else should do some research first and see what they're getting into before pulling the trigger.

When I first started, I really thought I bought a F2P mobile game. After reading the forums it seems like it was ported from a mobile version, but they replaced all the premium currency packs with ingame currency. It's good if you don't want Premium Content to ruin the game, but bad, since it means you have to grind for Premium Currency now. So far, I'm not sure what the grind will be like.
Another gripe I have with this is, rather then customizing the character you want. You now get random characters with random stats. So you basically have to keep rolling until you get the character you want. However you do have the option the change classes later, if you decide to increase its age. The combat is also simplified because it was previously a mobile, so it's mostly point and click, with an occasional skill or two thrown in. So to summarize.
Pros
--------------------
*The game is an interesting twist on rogue games with a hint of wizardry IP.
*No $99 premium currency packs, so no P2W mechanics.
*Overall worth it for the price, since I've thrown more money then this on mobile games.
*Great achievement system to keep you hooked.
Cons
--------------------
*Characters are randomly generated with preset class/stats. (However class can be changed)
*Combat is simplified, eventually makes the game seem monotonous.
*Difficulty is nowhere wizardry level to far, for previous wizardry players. Your first R unit you get after tutorial just steamrolls the first couple of dungeons.
I'll update more, as soon as I put more time into it. Overall it's still an entertaining game and does scratch a rogue/rpg itch.

I used to enjoy playing this game back when I was younger and I recently saw it on Steam and decided to play it again for old times sake. But sadly, there was a one slight problem with it. The game crashed whenever I clicked the play button. HOWEVER, THERE'S AN EASY WAY TO FIX THE CRASHING ISSUE!
1. Open C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\SteamApps\common\Diner Dash Hometown Hero\assets\downloads\_default\restaurants on your computer and you will see a bunch of folders that should be called "ballpark", "boardwalk", "disco", "museum" and "zoo".
2. Go into all of those folders one by one and click on the folder inside each of them called "comics" and delete all the .swf files inside the "comics" folder that say "intro" or "outro".
3. If you did everything right, the game should work fine now (but be warned, the cutscenes won't be there anymore). Enjoy!

I really wanted to like this one. I really did. But this story just isn't at the same level of quality as others that Choice Of Games has released. I understand that this is under the Hosted Games label, but it's not even close. I own almost all of the COG games on steam, and this is the only one that has regularly made my choices feel forced and meaningless. This is also the only story that has regularly failed to provide me with the choice that I thought was the correct decision for the situation.
Things you need to know:
- Part of a planned trilogy. Nowhere on the store page does it say this.
- Incomplete story (Not even the story arc in this chapter is fully resolved and nothing is really wrapped up. It just...)
- Inconsistent quality. (Some spelling and grammar mistakes. Most of the problems are strange writing problems like scenes that are out of order or contradict things stated in previous paragraphs in the same scene.)
- Several choices require knowledge from previous plays to make the "right" choice.
- Many choices have unclear consequences.

If you aren't familar wth Choice of Games, they make CYOA games. The mechanics are flashy, but they are perfectly functional so it comes down to the story.
This is one of the best stories I've seen come from CoG in a while. It's written well, it's engaging, and it doesn't talk down to you. I particularly appreciate that, while it is the first installment in a series, it tells one complete story and you don't feel cheated when it ends. The world they create is unique, but not up it's own♥♥♥♥♥with thick lore.
My only other criticisms are that the stat screen includes "Stat A is 4 *Stat A=Strength" instead of a simple "Strength=4." There's more than a few times where clicking a different choice doesn't even give you a cosmetic difference, which is disappointing.
Over all, I recommend it as a pretty good CYOA.

Battleborn is a MOBA style first-person shooter developed by Gearbox studios.  Personally, as someone who played over 300 hours of Awesomenauts and loved every second of it, I instantly fell in love with Battleborn, as it has all the depth of a MOBA, but is easy to approach due to it's control scheme.  Below I will sum up some pros and cons I have with the game at the time of writing this review:
PROS:
- Easy to approach
- Everything that effects gameplay is earnable in game.  The only things buyable with additional money is cosmetic items
- Character designs are diverse and interesting
- Classic Gearbox sense of humor.  If you've played Borderlands, then you know what to expect
- Plenty of mission/challenges to complete for every character, meaning there's plenty of reasons to keep playing
- PvE modes for those who don't care for PvP or just want variety
- Gearbox seems fully dedicated to supporting Battleborn
- A large selection of playable characters, (26 and counting) all unlockable via simply playing the game
CONS:
- Playerbase is sadly very small due to (in my opinion) the game being wrongly compared to Overwatch, and in general being out-marketed by Overwatch
- Due to the above, queue times can be fairly long, but Gearbox is actively working to counter this
- Since the game is first-person, it can get a little hectic, especially as melee characters in the middle of a fight, and it can be difficult to know exactly what is happening or what happend until things calm down
- There are microtransactions for purely cosmetic skins/taunts, but personally I feel this is wrong in what is a full release title with a season pass
Overall, I highly recommend Battleborn to anyone who enjoys a MOBA style experience, or even just an explosive, action packed game.  It has a colorful cast of characters, and is obvious that Gearbox is behind the game all the way (or at least until season pass content is released)  and hopefully it stays that way.  It really does sadden me that so few people currently play the game.

This game is pretty fantastic. It's got a few quirks here and there, but it's fun, the characters are fun to play, there's build flexibility through talents and items (perfect for the min-maxers out there!), and it's written so, SO well.
Since everyone's biggest questions will be about how Battleborn stacks up against Overwatch, here's a quick rundown:
* Battleborn will require more time investment per game, whether you're playing PvP or PvE. (I haven't played much PvP, but PvE is usually 30–60 minutes.)
* Battleborn has much greater depth in its story, gameplay, characters, and settings right now; I'm not sure how Overwatch's characters will be developed as their other media are released (comics, videos, etc.).
* Battleborn missions give me the sense that the game requires more skill than Overwatch—I haven't had to take a break from Battleborn because I was getting killed by too many lucky or inadvertent shots, unlike Overwatch.
* Performance-wise, Overwatch runs more smoothly than Battleborn. Video can get choppy in Battleborn, particularly in outdoor areas. Right now, this is the single biggest complaint I have about the game.
* Overwatch doesn't have much in the way of player collision, but Battleborn does. You can't shoot or run through teammates. (That's my other complaint.) It takes time to get used to that and gets frustrating sometimes.
Ultimately, the games fill two different niches for me. When I just want something to play for a few minutes, I'll go with Overwatch. There aren't any gear changes or additional talents to have to think about in order to make your character the best at what you're trying to do. You can just jump in and start playing. When I'm ready to roll my sleeves up, push the furniture back, and spend some serious quality time playing a game that requires me to make gear and talent choices that'll affect my ability to fulfill a role, when I want to sink my teeth into a game with substance, Battleborn's the one I play.
Lost interest very quickly. It's essentially a more complex, but less interesting MOBA inspired version of Overwatch. Don't waste your money, get OW instead.

The mostly bad I encountered during my gameplay:
- Intro is bugged, everything is mirrored and upside-down, game is fine though, except one bug during a cutscene.
- Good, not great, graphics for it's age. Plenty of foliage, feels like the jungle. Looks good overall.
- Rifle gunplay is abysmal. Sniper rifle is fine, pistols too.
- No compass in game, it seems, yet you get occasional intel with directions in it. It isn't crucial though.
- Enemies shoot and hit you through barriers, even though, they shouldn't have seen you.
- Geometry blocks shots sometimes when shooting clearly through big openings like windows, fences or foliage. I shot some enemies in some trees and couldn't hit them. Since it's a shooter, this is annoying.
- Even worse, geometry when moving is also shoddy. When crouching you constantly get stuck. Sometimes you float over the floor and sometimes you clip into rocks. It's overall bad.
- Sniper missions are ok, assault missions are awful due to the mentioned bad gunplay.
- Enemies are heavily scripted and spawn after triggers have been tripped. This makes it a bad sniper game, since you can't scout out areas and pick off enemies before going in. Very occasionally you get those satisfying long shot. Normally it is medium range combat though.
Update:
- It's getting worse in the next missions. I just finished a mission where you suddenly take phantom damage without any visible source. You have to run to a stationary MG, but you will take damage no matter what. It is so damaging that you will lose half your health. After that there is another section, but you also get shot at by enemies. Very hard to get to the end of that level.
- I also want to say that the game helps you with showing enemies on the map and letting them glow. On medium difficulty this is a strange decision and I'd rather play without it.
Update #2:
- I'm now 90% through the game and whoever said the game gets better at the end should go see a doctor. the only thing that changed are more failure conditions.
- The detection indicator is also often useless. If an enemy spots you it goes red.... and it stays red until you kill that enemy. even if you are miles away, the indicator stays red. And in this state it won't give you hints if others might see you.
Update #3:
- Penultimate mission features lots of awful rifle gunplay. It really sucks.
End of this mission is cheesy AF.
- And while you can swap weapons, the selection is very limited.
- I forgot to mention that your NPCs never hit anything. You have to do all the work. But only in this mission I saw about 3 enemies being shot from someone other than me.
- Looking back, enemy AI is also awful. You can shoot their buddies in plain sight and often they don't even get alerted. Only when stealth is demanded, do they seem to care a bit more.
Update #4:
- I hate the terrain by now. Constant blocking by rocks, then you have to jump on them and risk detection.
- Also, the devs should be punished to walk down their own stairs and ladders for a whole day. Half-Life 1 had better ladders.
- Little Extra missions are ok
- Challenge mission is ok too, but while the minimal HUD and absence of manual saves is nice, why on earth do they disable resuming on a checkpoint? Dumb decision on a mission that can take you almost an hour.
Verdict: Get for very cheap in a sale if you like some sniping and otherwise mediocre gunplay. But after playing through the game, even this recommendation is hart to defend.

This game is great! It deserves more support for what it is. Its fun, a $5, retro dungeon-crawler with simple, but addicting gameplay. I really like the design and sprites in this game and the loot system! (i love games with loot). And a lot can happen in this game in a short amount of time, after countless deaths and only 6 hours on record I've already made it to the final boss. This can be a cool thing and a bad thing, if they could make the game longer, that'd be great, but its still very enjoyable. The sprites in this game are creative, cool, and just well made. I love the different themes of each area and dungeon in this game, it gives it a variety. The progression system is pretty good, as you level up the enemies seem to level up with you, so your never too overpowered. The weapons and armor also do this, so you can switch out your old "nooby" stuff to combat the enemies growing more powerful. The loot system is fun, with different rarities and qualities of weapons and armor, sorted by color. Nothing's more satisfying than opening the purple chest at the end of a boss, or finding hidden green/orange/purple chest. It's fun and satisfying to earn acievements, most of them after a boss. Speaking of bosses, the bosses in this game are unique, and have nice sprites, but are... easy. one of the only flaws of this game. You spend awhile going through an entire dungeon to get a key to go to the boss, then all you really have to do is repeatedly hit spacebar, pretty much stunning it, then killing it. It's like this with them all, except for the final ones. If only the dev(s) could've done what they/he did with the final bosses with the normal ones. anyway, I'd give this game a 9/10, especially since its only $5 and has alot to offer for a $5 game. :D

bit.Dungeon II is a unique little rogue-lite that draws from several beloved classics in gaming. It has the loot system of Diablo, the structure of Legend of Zelda, and a campfire system reminiscent of everyone's favorite Masochism simulator. Cool little features include a bonus life which can be retrieved if you return to the spot where you died, and a freeform leveling system which allows you to tailor your playstyle to the weapons you like to use.
The game isn't perfect. The combat isn't deep enough where I feel like it's based on skill. This is a game where stats are king and I shied away from the potentially tankier builds because damage seemed to be the top priority. Combat with the Bow and Arrow feels clumsy as does projectile based magic. Melee combat is fine on the other hand, and I had the most fun playing wielding two daggers and backstabbing for tons of damage.
The art style isn't going to win any awards for originality. If you're the type who's fed up with pixel art this game isn't for you. I do enjoy the way the overworld and dungeons evoke the legend of zelda but through the lens of Diablo's tone.
There's really no storyline to the game and the objective isn't clearly laid out for you. It's easy enough to discover on your own but if you don't have the patience for a little bit of trial and error and flailing about in the dark it might be best to look up a guide before jumping into this one.
I give the game a 7.5/10
It's definitely fun and charming, but it's kept from being a true gem by repetitive melee and lackluster ranged combat.

What do you get if you take the level design of the orginal Legend of Zelda and add the fighting mechanics of Ys, the random drops of Diablo, and colorful 16-bit graphics? You get the rogue-lite bitDungeon II. TL:DR: Cheap but fun roguelike survival game, some way to go before it's finished, but well worth the price with the current content! 7.5/10
Rogue Harvest is a roguelike survival game, with permadeath and gameplay similar to that of hardcore Minecraft or Terraria. In Rogue Harvest you play as the survivor of a plane crash fighting to make sense of and survive in the hostile world in which he's found himself. The gameplay is fun and currently semi-deep, there's several tiers of content for each item (from 2-4 depending on the item) and you are free to create some awesome looking houses to defend yourself with.
Graphics: 8/10
The graphics for this game are beautiful, the enemies are varied and interesting to look at, and the buildings look cool when finished.
Audio: 7/10
The audio is nice at first, and matches the game world well, but feels repetitive and can get annoying after a while.
Gameplay: 7.5/10
The gameplay is fun and interesting, similar to most games of this genre. There could be more tiers of items, and hopefully more will be added throughout the early access process. I couldn't find much of the story during my playthroughs, but I don't last long and I think I accidentally skip a lot of the dialogue.
Overall: 7.5/10
The game is enjoyable and interesting, for the low price of $6 I can't see this ever being a bad purchase, there's plenty of content to ingest and the randomly generated worlds keep things interesting.

Her Story is a pretty interesting point and click mystery game where you have to try and work out what happened to a guy named Simon. You're not told anything. You're just presented with an old early 2000's computer, a bunch of archived footage from an interview with some lady and a couple of readme files. You have no idea what it's about, what the story is, who the woman is or anything. You're just thrown into the ocean without a life raft and have to work out how to survive.
At first, the game is intriguing. You click through videos of an interview with some lady as she talks about Simon and other various topics. You're trying to work out a mystery that you don't even know exists. But you keep clicking, listening to clips of the interview and trying to piece together in your mind what's happening. It's confusing but you keep going, because you're dying to understand what the hell is going on.
Yet at the same time this is where Her Story, in my opinion, fails.
You see, while it is genuinely interesting and engrossing, over time Her Story begins to become more and more convoluted as the pieces of the clues start to disappear. Although you'll work out what is going on fairly early into the game, the further you investigate, the less you understand. Clues become thinner, context begins to disappear and confusion takes over your mind completely, causing a feeling of frustration as you seemingly hit a brick wall.
The thing is however, and without giving away anything, you're not really supposed to know what's going on. It's almost like a cruel game played on you by the developer. If you ever wanted to know how detectives must often feel, it's probably something like this. At some point in the game you are promoted to end the story and let the credits roll, but this gives no closure to the game what so ever. The game just decides you've seen enough clips to piece together the story but to be honest, by this point I knew as little as I did when I first booted up the game. You do however unlock a code that allows you to search for random clips, in the hopes of finding one you haven't already seen. But
you never really get closure in Her Story, just a sense of utter confusion that eats away at you for hours on end.
By the time you finish the game completely you'll begin to wonder if you really do understand Her Story. But the truth is that her story is so open ended you'll never truly understand.
As long as you go into the game not expecting closure, you'll enjoy Her Story. But know what you're getting yourself into.

First and foremost you should know what to expect going into this game, it's far from a traditional idea of a game. Usually I'm not big on kinda artsy games like this one, but I think dismissing Her Story as another Gone Home isn't giving it enough credit. Its experimental kind of gameplay system is really interesting and I enjoyed toying with it, and I enjoyed the game's narrative a lot. It's definitely not gonna be everyone's cup of tea, and you might want to wait for a sale in that regard, but for what it's worth I thoroughly enjoyed the game.

Summary: There are better Telltale Poker games out there, not much point here.
-----
Writing a review after 9 minutes of play?  Well, that's about all it takes to form an opinion of this game.  It is what the name says, Texas Hold 'Em by Telltale.
This was Telltale's first game released, and it has a lot of rough edges.  I would say it doesn't look bad at all for a 12-year-old game.
Gameplay is the same as Poker Night at the Inventory, but with an older, clunkier interface, and less interesting characters.  One of them is literally named "Ted 'Theodore' Dudebro", whose jokes are more late 80's/early 90's than Mid 2000s.  It doesn't take long to notice that the AI is very predictable and weak.  Characters and competition are just not a strong point here.
The game lacks graphics settings (you can only choose to toggle Fullscreen/Windowed), but has something the Poker Night series should have had: an option to turn off the dialogue.  The less demanding graphics, ability to turn off speech, and miniscule size (the whole game is about 40 MB) make this a decent game for low-end systems, but there's nothing else here that isn't done better in the successors.

***Disclaimer: I am a bit critical in this early access review coming into this game as something of an expert on these types of games. This game is comparable to Don't Starve, Terraria, Wayward, Unreal World, Lantern Forge, TownCraft and Darkwood. My experience of it so far is that it falls behind nearly all these titles in various ways. I still however recommend it because despite all my nitpicking and comparisons, I did find playing the game enjoyable even at this incomplete stage. I also believe it's on the right track to offering a solid alternative to the above mentioned titles.***
If you enjoy playing rogue-like wilderness survival games and/or Terraria - then you will find Rogue Harvest is a worthy addition to this growing genre. Especially for it's low asking price. Plenty of content being added during this early access phase and a developer who takes user feedback seriously. Where it differs most from other games of this type is it's story-based elements. Like Terraria you can expect a lot of combat and rough nightly raids. The crafting system still seems a bit lacking compared to other games out there - but the game is not yet considered 1.0 and I have every reason to believe the developer has a lot planned before it's considered "final". And of course games of this type almost always undergo consistent updates even after that point. One really awesome thing, the game gets trippy as f**k if you eat a mushroom. You can watch me take a second look at this game here:

tl/dr: I believe the game has room to grow before it really stands as a competitor to other similar titles. However, despite that, I found the game to be quite enjoyable as well as difficult. Ultimately I believe it's worth it's asking price and recommend it for fans of this genre. And... mushrooms.

=What is it?=
Firstly, this is not a Wizardry game of old, or even similar to one of the new installments. This is a *mobage*, a Japanese-style mobile game that has been ported to Steam without the microtransaction nonsense. As long as you know what you should expect, you will enjoy yourself.
Wizrogue is in a subgenre of mobile games which I like to call a 'monster battler', a game that derives its mechanics from similar games like Puzzle and Dragons, DBZ Dokkan Battle, Summoner's War, or even Star Wars: Galaxy of Heroes. Note that this game *does* require an online connection to play at time of writing this review.
=How do I play?=
The way it works is thus: You're given a starter party of some low-ranking  (read: low max-level) heroes, you select a dungeon from a list, and you progress in rogue-lite fashion towards the exit, stabbing monsties and collecting treasure along the way. You will often find coffins which contain other heroes, or are rewarded on a per-dungeon basis with Adventurer Tickets which allow you to roll for new heroes. All heroes have a ranking associated with them, and naturally uncommon or rare have higher stats, higher max levels, and better beginning equipment than common ones.
Your characters will level up based on enemies defeated after completing dungeons, which consist of a randomization of 3-6 floors of half a dozen rooms per floor, maybe, which include treasure and traps and the like, and whose objective is usually either get to the bottom or kill the boss on the last floor. You'll notice that you'll accrue a small army, however, with a large batch of useless characters. These characters are 'fed' to other characters (through training) which will give them experience and help them level up faster.
The core gameplay is essentially similar to the Japanese console-style roguelikes like the Fushigi Dungeon series. You'll recognize many similar mechanics, like attacking mid-air in order to reveal a trap tile on the space in front of you, or zooming through hallways to get to the next room. There is one caveat: your party has a collective HW (Holy Water) guage which depletes with every action you take. Luckily, HW recovery items are plentiful, and while it does act as a time limit, it doesn't necessarily force you to find the exit before clearing a room of monsters or search the floor for treasure.
Despite this, the gameplay has a distinctive Wizardry flavor. The base classes and races are all there, the class change system is present, as is the trapped treasure chest mechanic and the massive amount of pain dished out by certain enemies. The first few dungeons will leave you wishing it was more difficult, but the challenge ramps up fairly quickly. You'll find yourself digging around in the town screen for quite a while in between dungeons training your team, reorganizing, and micro-managing equipment, trying to find the right balance.
=Should I bother?=
Depends. Do you want a wholly immersive, first-person RPG with obtuse puzzles and a high challenge factor where you custom-make a party of six? In this case, no. In contrast, do you want a somewhat casual social dungeon crawler that rewards you for coming back day by day with a distinct Wizardry vibe? Or maybe you just want a Puzzle & Dragons-like game without the freemium nonsense and a bit more depth to the gameplay? In these cases, yes.
Pros:
+Solid mechanics
+Fast-paced, turn-based gameplay remniscent (but not identical to) the old Wizardries
+Board game graphical style
+Fun, easy to pick up and put down for quick play sessions
+Sweet title theme music
Cons:
-Obvious mobile port
-Getting used to this alternative model of gameplay may cause old-school Wizardry fans discomfort
-No overarching plot to speak of (though one faintly exists)
I give it a hard Yes to recommend, but be sure you know what you're buying first!

Now on to #2 and this is a BIG one for me....
2. I have been a fan of Wizardry since the early days of home computing when I first laid eyes on "Wizardry I - Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord" on my uncle's Apple III computer. The graphics in all its magnificent monochrome (single color green for you younger gamers who may have never experienced monochrome green, amber, and sometimes even red, it depended on the actual monitor you had. Back then color monitors were very expensive.) Anyhow, I've played the original games many times over the last 30+ years and I was happy to see familiar names and spells in Wizrogue. Halito = Little Fire, Dios heals wounds. I remember these from way back when I first braved the realms of Wizardry and yet they are here in Wizrogue and have the same effects. Also, Gilgamesh's Tavern seems to still be around! I wonder if an older Gilgamesh still runs the establishment? ;)
In short there appears to be a lot of nostalgia from the original series, just how much I don't know yet, but just the idea of familiar spells, locales, and maybe even monsters have me anxious to get back to the game. Saying that... that is what I'm going to do. I will definitely update this review once I have a few hours under my belt. I hope the experience continues to be great.

Well written and is similar to a table top RPG. Really enjoyed it! But don't be fooled that just because its a text game doesn't mean it isn't fast paced and full of action. It's a real "page turner" and it can be hard to stop and take a break from it as you just NEED to know what happens next.
It's a well written story that immerses you in a world filled with characters that you can connect with. As it is a game written solely in text, it lets your imagination create the characters and in doing so you make it part of your own. You can make choices and choose your story and it's more than just playing a game and completing tasks etc. Like I said before, it's more like a table top RPG with only your imagination to visualize the world described in words. A great deal of skill is required to bring a world to life with graphics, but it is just as skillful to paint it in words while still leaving enough mystery for the reader to fill in the blanks with their own interpretation.

This game may not be for everyone as it makes you think out of the box, I understand that the box these days is "Here is a gun, go shoot things" but I'm talking about in adventure game terms.
Sure, there's quests to do which are pretty straight forward involving helping the homeless, pimp business and corrupt politicians. Your standard adventure game staples you might think. But you're some white dude with blonde hair who definitely has a disorder of some sort who can be talked into trying to disguise themselve as a Yakuza to aid the mafia.
If that paragraph didn't really make sense then the rest of the game will make less sense. If it did make sense to you then you're probably the protagonist of the game.
I may edit this after a few playthrough's, but somehow I think leaving this game in people's minds with a little morbid curiosity might fare better. If you've seen it and read about it and/or put it on your wishlist just do it. It's one of those games that you think you'll fire up for a few minutes to see what it's like, think "everything is fairly standard and boring, nothings really happening. That's the first bit over, what's the fuss? I'll play a bit more and... what? Wait! What? Seriously? Is this?... Yes it is happening" and will just continue on.
If you want an adventure game that really makes use of you interacting with it for Steam achievements then this is for you.
If you want an adventure game that makes you try to find inventive ways for you to be killed then this is for you.
If you want an adventure game that tries to make you find ways to steal babies and then eat them then this is definitely for you, and you should probably seek help.

This was my first Hitman game, and probably made the biggest impact on me. It's difficult, entertaining, immersive, and overall a lot of fun.
One of the best things about this game is the lack of handholding. You're given a simple, introductory course at the beginning of the game, and virtually everything else is up to you to figure out. I personally love this. It warrants multiple playthroughs to try and find something that can help you perform the hit, or perform it better.
Couple things to note: this game has not aged well at all. Predominantly this is due to the controls and slow crouchwalk speed they gave Agent 47. Thankfully both of these were improved with the games that came after this one. There are also a few issues with some of the levels: one level has guards that are horribly glitched, and in order to obtain the "Silent Assassin" rating (the best rating you can get), you have to do the exact opposite of what you would expect. Another level is nearly impossible to get Silent Assassin because the AI is prone to walking in front of cycling trucks. They are run over and their dead bodies are discovered and attributed to you automatically.
All that said, this game is a lot of fun. It's still the most memorable Hitman game for me, and I still think its worth wading through the outdated gameplay to sit through.
