PAYDAY The Heist is a 4-player co-op FPS game in which you and your friends heist your way to wealth and glory. with nine well designed heists(Two of them DLC) to keep you busy.
Somehow, it manages to be better than the sequel, Payday 2, with better and more balanced weaponry, better heists, better balanced hostiles and smooth, mostly intuitive controls. That said, it is not without flaws. The stealth system is not entirely as great as in Payday 2, but that's pretty much all I can think of at the moment.
The progression is decent, giving you new guns and abilities over time while giving you plenty of gametime to unlock it all. You can choose what general direction to unlock things in on leveling up, and things unlock at a steady pace that doesn't leave you grinding for levels just so you can play as you prefer. All in all, it's well made and works fine.
The gameplay itself is pretty good, with cover playing an important part and no enemy feeling unfair or like an unreasonable bulletsponge. It makes sure that almost every thing you're doing is of importance, with a good pace where sometimes it is tense and other times you can take a breather. It feels like you're always doing something, whether its rejoining your group, running from cover to cover, or taking out a few special units. Somehow the drill jams less than in Payday 2 as well.
Of course it's not all bad, the AI is just good enough to work, and the hordes of cops make you sometimes feel like you're playing L4D with cops instead of zombies, zombies with guns. There are surprisingly few negatives to Payday The Heist.
Overall, it's a bit old, but it's still great. I'd even say better than its sequel. And with regular sales it's easy to grab some friends and go heisting. If the regular price tag is not worth it to you, a sale will probably start soon.

Funny storyline, interesting setup. The gameplay is more of a puzzle/planning game with some very minor tactical elements. If you are looking for depth of action, look elsewhere.
The downsides are really all in the mechanics though, a lot of the games difficulty comes from unresponsive controls and the clunky interface that doesn't do what you want it to do "in the moment", leaving you frustrated when one of your goons runs off and trys to circle around the building when what you wanted him to run over and do was directly in front of him but some stray box told him to go the long way.
Also of interest is the metagame style used here where you evolve your crew and its tools between missions (or by going back and redoing missions to perfect them) which should in theory make every play through unique. Unfortunately there's not alot of depth to this either and the customization ends up coming down to generic thugs with random names and sometimes just redoing missions over again to get the money you need to finance a tool you need for the next mission.
There's a lot to like in this clever little strategy/puzzle game, but it's also pretty unpolished and it's not terribly long. Unfortunately it also started to glitch and hiccup. During the pause screen (which is like a bullet time where you set up a series of moves) the game would often hiccup (pause within a pause) and not actually accept your input commands. And since its not actually stopping the action you get to watch in slow motion as your goons don't obey your detailed commands. (And than trying to reclick on the person you need when there's 5 of them overlapping to redo a command sequence that was multistepped is an excercise in frustration)...
I wish I could write a glowing review for this game, the core elements are there it's just not quite perfected and it's probably never going to be.
In the end I would still recomend the game but only on two conditions:
1. you can tolerate some frustration in your puzzle interfaces
2. get it on sale, I don't regret spending $5 on it, but I'd be pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off if I'd spent $20
I'd kill for a less buggy version of the game or a "pause while planning" that isn't in glitchy slow motion, that would have been worth $20 instead of $5.
Anyway if you played cops & robbers as a kid and were always the robbers, you'll probably find something to like in this game if you pick it up on sale.

Ridiculously enjoying this game. Play 1-5 hours almost everyday with friends. Even about 97 hours into the game, I still feel like I have so many characters to try out and enjoy. Haven't maxed out a single Battleborn yet even!
Every gamer is different, and not ever game can be enjoyed by every gamer. (Sad I have to set that as a reminder, but there you go). You might like this game (or love it as much as I do!) if:
1) You are a fan of the humor from Borderlands 2 - I love the cheeky humor, the awful people with hidden hearts of gold, the complex robot and human relationships, the great voice acting, etc.
2) Enjoy engaging and different playstyles outside of the typical shooter - While this is all first person, a lot of the characters are melee based or highly movement based. Very few straight up shooter characters. This is a really fun aspect, and a lot of my favorite Battleborn are the melee characters.
3) Enjoy planning out party composition, communicating with your team, coming up with tactics - this is a highly tactical game. Your enjoyment will drop insanely if you expect to be able to rush in all Leroy Jenkins style. My friends and I like coming up with new team compositions and treat the PVE chapters like raids. Fun times!
4) Enjoy unlocking new characters, new lore, new recolors, new titles, etc - Rather than a permanent level up system, you instead unlock more content as you play. My favorite aspect is unlocking new lore for the characters. You get story bits, audio logs, etc. It's fun to discover the background stories for your fave Battleborn.
5) Enjoy experimentation - Not every Battleborn will work with every playstyle. Part of the fun is figuring it out, and then seeing how they play early game versus midgame, and discovering new playstyles you didn't know you'd like! (There's an in-match/in-chapter leveling system for each character, and you can make different choices each time. This encourages more experimentation and refining your playstyle)
A lot of my friends enjoy the PVP mode, but personally I like playing the PVE chapters over and over again. The typical problem in Borderlands 2 is that all this amazing dialogue and story was happening, but I was too busy shooting things to notice. Replaying the chapters means I get to enjoy the story more, and seeing how certain characters change the dialogue is also super fun.
TLDR; version:
- If you like to experiment and come up with tactics, this game is awesome.
- If you like weird BL2 humor, this game is awesome.
- If you like playing as a team focused on objective, this game is awesome.

Some people are inclined to say "Her Story isn't a game". Well, no. It is a game. And shut the ♥♥♥♥ up.
It is a game because the mechanics aren't what make it, the actual murder mystery is what makes it. Your goal is to unravel the mystery, or more likely, come up with a minimal half-baked theory that could be a solution as to what is going on. And that's the big part of Her Story - all those searches will paint a broad, weird picture of things I will not care to spoil for you. Let's just say that
The proto-vaporwave look of the game is important because the game needs to separate you from the things that are going on. The grainy Windows 95 ugliness and the warped VHS-to-digital transfers of video really aid in the immersion, putting you right there in the seat of that crime database, ready to do some super-sleuthing. Hell, even the search engine is archaic, because it won't give you more than five entries at a time. That's where you gotta put on your thinking cap and figure out how to narrow your search to get what you want. Or you could, like I did, type in random swear words and get an achievement for it.
I can't say anything reliably about the bigger topics that the game wants me to explore, but I liked how I simultaneously felt lost and yet still in some kind of control in the game. The game's narrative is very non-linear and is largely powered by whatever keywords you pick that sound interesting, and by either accident or design, you'll either come to how the murder was done, what the murder was about, who the interviewee (played by Viva Seifert) is, or even what happened in certain cases. You'll find out some things and other things will be completely in the dark. The thing is, the game still manages to lead you to where the necessary facts of the case are just through topics brought up in the discussions, and that's how I played - jumping from one topic to another depending on what was brought up. I don't understand it all (and if the discussion boards are anything to go by, there is no real solution), but I enjoyed getting lost.
So yeah, it's cheap and it's a mind-bending experience that threatens to change your look on the case at every turn. Fantastic stuff to play through!

Her Story is definitely something completely different. The gameplay involves you searching through fragmented video files, trying to understand a possible murder case. The visuals really give the feel of staring at an older monitor, for better and for worse. The best, and likely intended way to enjoy this game is to search through the files in the fragmented format. Once you begin to piece together an interesting story, the game kind of abruptly ends. There is no goal, you see. The entire purpose of this game is to deliver it's story in an interesting and different way. It's very much an experiment, and I feel it did well.
Ultimately, if it seems interesting to you, you'll probably enjoy it. If not, well, this game doesn't have much to offer other than the story.

Zack Zero is a game for an obvious young child target audience, although some of the content is questionable, the story is narrated and designed for children roughly under the age of 10.  The visuals are quite good and the characters designs as well are something out of a saturday morning cartoon. The game's platforming isn't bad with the multiple forms you can transform into offering a variety of ways to progress (some forced), and although easy, it keeps in mind its target audience. The combat is also easy, and can be summarized by pressing attack and letting the lock on do its work, it takes essentially no skill but does allow the game to be accessible again to the very young demographic. Dying also seems to be of minimal penalty, further lending to the genre, which is made to be accessible.  The drawbacks to this game are twofold, the first are that there are some technical issues and even I got frames per second drops occasionally without any apparent cause and the second is that if you are outside of this game's target demographic you likely will not enjoy the experience. That being said, if you are looking for a platformer for your child under 10, this game is a decent choice.

Jackbox continues their streak of pushing out some of the best party games in history, with the trifecta of Quiplash 2, Tee K.O., and Trivia Murder Party being the highlights of this pack. Guesspionage is alright but the actual outcomes seem to have been polled from a completely different pocket gathering of social outliers for almost every single question, and Fakin' It relies on both physical presence and the sort of on-the-spot improvisation that is probably not the forté of most of the Steam audience.
Quiplash 2, along with its new bag of prompts, adds the ability to make collections of your own which can be amazing but is otherwise basically the same, Last Lashes excepted. Trivia Murder Party is probably the most high-octane quiz game I've ever played, and genuinely starts pitting people against each other in surprising ways.
Good value, good pack, good online functionality with the right streaming services (hint: pretty much anything but twitch). Worth it.

The Jackbox Party Packs are quite possibly my favourite party games I have played so far. The games are incredibly easy to pick up and play for a wide variety of people. Not all of them are gamers, but everybody I've played these packs with so far including myself has really gotten a lot out of the games included in each pack. The Jackbox Party Pack 3 is no different.
The game is very fun, but reminds me more of the first pack where some of the games were far superior to the others. This meant you would only be playing around half of the pack, while the other games gathered dust. If you like the look of Trivia Murder House, Tee K.O and Quiplash 2 or want a very fun party game to play with a wide range of people, you should absolutely buy this pack. However I do not recommend buying it for only one of the games, especially if it is at full price or slightly discounted at the most. If you are new to the Jackbox Party Packs, I would also advise getting the second pack as it is still the best one so far in my opinion.
I decided to play this at a small party I hosted and it ended up becoming the main focus for the seven of us that were there. As this was the first time buying one of the packs at launch, I was a little nervous but it had turned out to be great! Trivia Murder Party in these first 4 and a half hours of playing the pack has ended up becoming the group's favourite game choice of all the packs to date, which is remarkable. It reminds me in some ways of You Don't Know Jack, except the sharp edges of that game have been ironed down incredibly hard to make this one as close as you can get to perfection.
Tee K.O is absolutely hilarious. It is a hybrid of Quiplash and Drawful where the captions and drawings created by the other users are given to other players and they create a t-shirt out of it. This has even spawned many inside jokes amongst the group. My only issue with this game is the rounds where you are drawing and writing captions feels a little slow and is not always fun to play through. However, the chaos of battling t-shirt designs more than makes up for it.
Quiplash 2 is just Quiplash, except it now has a lot more replayability due to being able to create custom episodes with user generated prompts. Jackbox have really gone all out on this sequel similar to how they have done with the standalone Drawful 2 by giving a lot more options compared to the first Quiplash. If you want to experiment with user-generated content, then by all means consider this game as a factor to your purchase. If you already own Quiplash as a standalone or from the second Jackbox Party Pack, then it may not be worth your time.
The best way I can describe Guesspionage and Fakin' It is that they are the equivalent to Word Spud and Lie Swatter from the very first pack. Guesspionage has an interesting idea and will generate a few chuckles, but there really isn't a lot to get out of the mode with me and friends wanting to play another one of the games after trying it once and finishing a game. Fakin' It sounds great on paper, but is a lot worse in practice. This was mostly due to confusion when me and friends tried it, as the player who was meant to be the Faker had no idea because there was no text given to him at any point in the round. It is also the only game where you can only play with six players maximum, so keep that in mind when playing with more than six players at a party (As I do not have much time spent on these two games, I may change this section of the review after playing with more people).
As this game is still fairly new, bugs are to be expected. I have encountered only a couple of these, but they were minor. An example of these graphical glitches would be the one such as below, however I expect they will be quickly fixed.
Any other issues I have with this game are very personal and only affect me as a person who has bought all three of the party packs and the standalone Drawful 2, so they are not worth bringing up.
Overall, I recommend this game if you have played the Jackbox Party Packs before but I would recommend playing one of the other ones before the third pack. My favourite one so far is still the second pack and I highly suggest playing it first as all of the games are enjoyable to play:
However this is up to you and if you like the look of Trivia Murder Party, Tee K.O and Quiplash 2, then this is a worthy investment. This game is best played with everybody in the same space playing the game. This is because in order to have other people see your screen while playing this game with your friends over the internet, you will need to use something such as a Steam broadcast which has a delay of 10-20 seconds. The game is also more fun when you are laughing in the same room together :3

First of all I'd like to say I like these sort of games, but I currently feel that buying this game was a mistake.
The controls are really weird - you just walk towards the enemies and the game swings your weapon for you, this makes the game feel really weird, especially at first. You get used to it fast, but I don't see why the dev decided this was better  than having a separate button for attack.
The second bad thing about this game is the deal breaker for me - sometimes (quite often) when you enter a room you instantly get hit by monsters, or a big monster might even block you from moving which means that you will 100% sure take damage and theres nothing you can do about it. And if you are not strong enough to kill the monster right away you might just die.
Also sometimes monsters dodge or ignore your damage so even if you're just meleeing easy monsters that you know you can one shot, you often end up missing the hit and taking some damage.
Sure the latter can be avoided by being extra careful against even the tiniest guys but in this game a new set of monsters are spawned everytime you enter a room - even if you had already cleared that room previously.
Apart from these things, it's a fun little game and the price is very affordable so definitely check back on it later, but I wouldn't recommend buying it as it is.
I'll give this game another shot later and hopefully I can recommend this game to others by then.

bit Dungeon II is a minimalistic roguelike that pays homage to games like The Legend of Zelda. Upon loading the game, you feel like you're in for a fun, difficult, nostalgia-inducing treat that will keep you hooked for hours. Sadly, this isn't necessarily the case. bit Dungeon II is fun for the first 15 to 20 minutes of playing, but it quickly wears thin of its flare. One button to attack, block, and perform special abilities while you explore dungeons that are vastly the same as the previous.
The description of bit Dungeon II mentions Dark Souls, a brutal third-person game where death is inevitable and unforgiving; I expected the same experience from bit Dungeon II. While you may have a similar experience while playing with sword and shield, you'll find that archers are ridiculously overpowered. It's too easy to just sit in a corner, where monsters won't even notice you, and then just spam arrows into their backs. When using a bow, even the bosses become a cakewalk. The only downside to using a bow is the boring downtime you have while waiting for your stamina to regenerate. Fully depleting your stamina for the first time while fighting a boss introduces an interesting element when you notice that your tiny dungeon crawler is moving at half speed. This is easily remedied by quickly shooting four arrows at your enemy and then moving to a safer position while your stamina regenerates. However, even when using a bow, you're prone to being swamped with monsters when entering a new map. More than half of the time you go to a new map, you're placed on top of enemies that can quickly rid you of all of your health if you don't act quickly.
After defeating a boss, you're taken back to a familiar overworld with the same, old faces ready to claw your guts out. Exploring in this game becomes a bit tedious. Many paths will lead to dead-ends, and there's no map or guidance of any sort to even point you in the direction of your next mildly-exciting dungeon. While exploring, dungeons, combat, and bosses may be lackluster and bland, you can always have a good time searching for more loot, which is randomly generated; as a wise man once said: it's like a box of chocolates; you never know what you're gonna get.
Overall, this game is bland and has very little excitement to offer. However, it is cheap, and if you love endless roguelikes with random loot, this one may be one to pick up at some point.

Hitman 2: Silent Assassin is a game developed by IO Interactive and published by Sqaure Enix and is the sequel to Hitman: Codename 47. As the enigmatic Hitman, you must use stealth and tactical problem solving to enter, execute and exit your assignment with minimum attention and maximum effectiveness
One of the finest stealth games of its generation, it puts you in the role of Agent 47, a shadowy assassin who is equally capable of slipping in and out of target locations un-noticed, the game provides a wealth of memorable situations you will talk about years down the road.
However, the game is not without its flaws. For a game nearly 10+ years old, gameplay mechanics can be somewhat clunky. Probably the biggest gripe however is the in-game saving option, which does not exist. If you are spotted in the middle of a mission or die, you will need to start the mission over. While not a big issue in the earlier missions, this can become extremely frustrating on the later missions where you need to navigate a huge mansion with tons of guards and one mis-step means you're killed and need to restart
However, Hitman 2: Silent Assassin is a brilliant stealth game for its generation and a welcoming sequel!

Remember that this game is still in Alpha...
First off, this game is not for the feint of heart or someone looking for the 'Easy Button' - you are going to die, you are going to work, and you're going to have to think.
Second...if you're a crafter then this game is definately for you.  Ever since Istaria (aka Horizons), whether it's building a house, making that fine sword or elegant Chest Plate to whipping up a delacacy, I've been and will always be a crafter.
There are a few minor issues, but all-in-all this is perhaps the most enjoyable alpha I've played - wouldn't be saying that if I didn't already have well over 100 hours in the game.  As long as the developers keep at it I can only see the game getting better and better...not to mention addictive like Civilizations.
You start out quite primitive picking up stones and pieces of wood to craft primative weapons and tools that allows to make a Dominium (claim some land).  Food is always on your mind and you'll have to tend to that as well while you fashion your land, create better tools, weapons, and armor.  You learn as well for during your travels you will come across 'Godsends' - small stashes of Knowledge Fragments.  These allow you to learn how to craft higher grade items - some need only a single fragment while others require 3, 5 or even 10 fragments.  Learn enough and you can use what you've learned on any server.
There is nothing more...fulfilling than watching your character grow, your knowledge increase and even more importanly watching your small piece of land develop into a massive holding complete with Castle.  Yes...you will eventually be able to build your own Castle.
This of course all takes time...and some will say it is grindy but in a lot of ways this game mimics real life - nothing comes easy or for free.  If oyu want it you have to work for it and that makes it something you can sit back and smile about once you have accomplished that next goal.
Pros: Crafting Galore - from tools, weapons, food, farming, and living structures everything is player made.  Large world which is supposed to grow as the population grows (supposedly this already happened once before I started playing) - an interesting concept indeed.
Cons: Balance - some notable gaps in skills, crafts and combat...especially noticeable againt creatures that fight back - even wily old fox will decimate you early on.  Also noted in some foods...where an easy food can't be accomplished without a high level structure which makes it useless and thus it has to be skipped in order to advance cooking skills.  A few memory leaks that requires relogging (I have noticed that fleeing crows seems to have the largest impact).  There is very little documention and if not for those who have been playing for a while (the community is very helpful, at least on the PvE server) a new player would be completely lost and overwhelmed not to mention easily frustrated.
I put up with a lot worse from games I spent 4-times as much on out of the box - so far I can say hands down this is the best money I've spent and would have paid two or three times more than what I did.

Disclaimer:  Steam does not have a neutral review rating.  Just recommended or not recommended.
I have completely rewritten the review so if some of the people in the comments section don't make sense this may be why.
Since I had a negative experience with the devs, I will leave the review as not recommended.  I will cover this below.
Wild Terra as it stands right now is an early access title.  It has been getting regular updates, usually small ones sprinkled with larger ones here and there.  The title has come a long way in the last 6 or so months before it hit Steam just in terms of character movement which has helped immensely.
I have only played on a PvE server so cannot vouch for the play on a PvP server.  The game is slow paced which I like.  I can sit back and relax while playing.  Game play consists of running around the map collecting resources for building up your dominion (what the game calls your base of operations).  Once you have your dominion built then you can work on expanding it and/or collecting resources to make into useful items needed for the extensive amount of recipes found in the game.
While wandering the map you can find godsends, which come in the for of decomposed adventurers or crashed wagons.  Inside the godsends you can find items as well as recipe fragments.  The recipes you cannot make from the beginning of the game can be found in these godsends.  Each recipe requires a certain amount of fragments to be found before you can create that item.  From what I can tell it can take from 1 to I believe 4 or 5 fragments to unlock specific recipes.  It seems that once you do unlock a recipe that some recipes have a gold recipe that can be unlocked.  The crafting is deep in the game.
The Map:  This is the biggest issue I have with the game.  Everything is player driven (which isn't a bad thing).  There are no NPC cities or towns.  Everything on the map is one flat surface with trees, water, wild life, and resource nodes.  There is absolutely nothing that stands out that you could reference as to where you are in the world.  Once you have a dominion, you get a marker on the edge of the screen that you can use to get back, but that's it.
Player base:  This is where the game shines for the most part.  Most people in the global chat are very helpful and willing to help people out with questions and issues they have.  Some people leave a chest or storage outside for others to come along and rummage through for anything they may need.  During the Christmas event (before the devs lowered the cost) the stockings were hard to make because they needed a loom which unlocks from recipe fragments (found in godsends) and most weren't able to  make them.  One good person on the server would make the items you needed if you brought them the resources.
The devs:  I was wrongly banned from the Steam forums and it took a week before they realized I was wrongly banned and unbanned me.  The devs seem to just willingly ban anyone from their forums that speak bad about the game or the cash shop or in my case ban the wrong guy.  Instead of making a sticky at the top of the forums that lists exactly what is in the cash shop and opening it to discussion.  I feel everyone that is on the fence about the game has a right to know as much information on the game before they make a purchase.  So that brings up the next part.....
Cash Shop:  Once in the game, you can bring up the cash shop.  Inside you will find titles you can bestow on your character along the lines of Duke and Knight and a handful of others.  If you want a mount, you can pick from horses, deer, wolves, and bears.  If you want to dip into their premium  offering you can get a bonus for your character for a period of time based on how much you wish to spend.  I tried to see what the time length was for this review but the cash shop wouldn't come up for me at time of writing this review.  The premium is described (I wrote this down earlier when I was replying to someone) as:  Doubles chances to get rare items, gathering, building, and crafting speed.  As a PvE player this doesn't bother me in the least.  I don't care what the other guy is getting or what he is doing.  In a PvP setting I can see this as being an issue as the other guy is now pulling out double resources on some of the harder to find resource nodes in the world.  If the rare drop is (no clue what the actual drop rate is) 10% then the premium player is getting 20%.
Due to how the premium is worded this is how I see it as working.  It could be double to getting rare items and an increase to gathering, building and crafting.  Even though an increase in rares can still be an advantage depending on the drop rate imposed in the game.
Is the game bad?  No and I feel I more than received my monies worth during my past and most likely future game play.  As an early access title the content is limited despite the large amount of items you can craft.  This is an issue that plagues many early access titles and is the bane of the whole ea system in general except for a few exclusions.
I do recommend Wild as the game itself, but you must realize what the game is and what it isn't.  It is not an action packed game full of dazzling sword play and fireballs whizzing inches from your face.  In fact there is no magic to speak of.
I do not recommend Wild Terra based on the actions of the developers.  They seem like they care about the game and are definitely actively working on it, but deleting posts in the Steam forums and banning is definitely not the way to go and sends off bad vibes to current customers and prospective customers.  They need to take the good with the bad, embrace it and use that feedback to allow the game to flourish.
Verdict: Neutral.  If what you have read appeals to you and you can get past the developers then you can find a nice little time sink here.  If you're like me and try to answer questions for other people in the forums and just be an all around nice guy, then beware that you should probably not talk about the cash shop in any form at least until the devs smarten up and just embrace the contents they provide in the shop and not try to hide them.

It is also worth noting that much of my opinion here is just that - purely subjective based on my own preferences. For example; while I do like Wild Terra's skill system (similar to the likes of UO, or simply, 'doing things makes you better at them') - I don't like how unlocks are (currently) managed.
You have to find (randomly?) placed 'Godsend' items on the ground, which come in the form of deceased hunters or wrecked carts which have random crafting recipe fragments in them. You cannot tell what recipe it is for beyond a broad category description until you've used it. Using it simply being putting it in your inventory - so if you're playing with friends, there is no way to specialise your crafting/construction efforts and you're hit with RNG at two levels (finding, then what you get). You cannot even give something of a broader category to your friend unless they've run out in the same direction as you, as picking it up automatically consumes the item.
Salem handled this through a research tree (and quite a detailed one at that!) - I'd dearly love to see Wild Terra adopt something similar.
In fact it is this element of knowledge progression which most kept me from enjoying WT as it currently stands.
WT has a lot of potential - have no doubt, and the oft repeated refrain of, 'If steam allowed neutral reviews I'd probably give this one' is true for the current state.
No - Salem had a cash shop which in many ways felt mandatory. (It wasn't - but progress was punishingly slow without.)
So far WT while yes,
, seems to allow for pretty good rate of progression without ever touching it.
The 'dominium' stones which mark your territory are craftable from objects in the world alone (at least the tiers I've seen so far) and don't require any bought currency for upkeep, which is a
plus in WT's favour.

I'm a longtime fan of the original, just like many of the people posting reviews here. While I admit this version of the game is a pale shadow of the original, but it still can be fun. You have to remember that back when the original first came out and I was playing it flash games were in the golden years. It was everything a game needed to be:
Eventually they did release a "premium" version of the game called "Goldium Edition" which at the time I didn't think added enough value to consider the purchase. (I think it was like $7 USD). You have to remember this was back in the pre Steam pre Smartphone age where most kids got "allowances."
Motherload did have a shelf life though, so despite how amazingly fun it was you could only play it through a couple times before it did get boring, despite how satisfying that BZZZT drilling sound was. It was one of those games you remembered and thought back on "Oh yeah that was a great game" and then went on with your day. Memorable but not so much that you went to go pick it up again you know what I mean?
To be honest I didn't even know this game existed until it showed up as a featured sale item. I did not purchase this game at full price and honestly I can't recommend anyone to do so. This version really only waters down the original and while the new powers are interesting the fact that the map is the same everytime means you will never be able to afford them. All the characters with unique abilities are also neat, but don't add enough to the game to make you want to try them all.
While I understand the want to add a "story" to the game I feel that Motherload really didn't need it. I think it stems more from the fact they couldn't leave the final boss as SATAN HIMSELF due to obvious reasons. Thus they had to find a "new" final boss and therefore had to create a story to explain it all. Personally I think THE LITERAL DEVIL hanging out on Mars and exploiting humans for profit was pretty amazing. But keep in mind the original was made before "PC culture" even existed so they could get away with that. Big Bird with a pirate hat does not cut it in my book.
Also on a side note: While I did enjoy the final boss fight I feel that it should have had a sequence at the core before the surface race began. You two duke it out and then have to escape the rising magma and the destruction of the planet is due to your climatic battle for the planet. The whole Death Star laser was just in bad taste I think.
Not worth it for full price.
Get it on sale and its a great purchase. Besides it comes with the Goldium Edition of the original so if you hate the new one you can live it up with the classic.

This game, ho boy.
I'll be upfront: I liked this game in beta, I liked this game on release, I have come to not like it recently. The community seemed to filter out all the good players and just left all the terrible, toxic people to spam their mics and chat with hateful comments while performing worse than those they chose to flame. I cannot get over how frustrating this game has become in the past few weeks; someone could easily write a thesis about Battleborn's rapid decline.
Community aside, the game feels okay. I use that word very deliberately: Battleborn controls just okay. The jumps feel floaty but don't ever seem to have the height to jump up anything; allied minions and players constantly get in the way of your shots, even if you position "better"; and support characters feel like they have either no impact on the game or way too much. As for the rest of the roles, DPS has its good picks and bad like any other game, with no one really outshining anyone else substantially; tanks feel the same way too.
The single player is by far the best reason to buy this game, which is sad because it's also the shortest thing about this game; it feels like they wanted to make a solely PvP game, then someone complained so they slapped together some quick and easy campaign just to shut them up. The gameplay throughout the campaign is pretty much the same as it would be if PvP but it's less hectic, and there aren't as many people concerned about their KDA, so very rarely do you get toxic players matched up with you.
If there was any way to restore the community to how it was back in beta/release, I would play this game non-stop, on the daily; all of my qualms with this game would still be there but it was tolerable when everyone was having fun and not concerned with being the most MLG ever.
This game will eventually make it's way from middling popularity to ghost town to shut down, and I can't say it doesn't deserve that fate.

I played the original bit Dungeon on my phone a year ago and was pretty excited to hear a sequal was in the works. bit Dungeon II is vastly superior to its predecesor. I will say it does have some faults though.
The general gameplay is a roguelike 2D zelda style. You don't have a story really but you have an overworld with dungeons spread throughout and a few very basic random events that can happen such as being attacked when healing at a fireplace. Enemies and bosses are mostly simple but some have special attacks that must be avoided and you'll randomly find dungeons where enemies are harder than you may expect.
Overall the gameplay is addicting and fun. Many of the items can have cool stats that allow you to do fun setups with your character. The thing the game truly suffers from is how simple the controls are. This is due to it being a game designed for phones. You can use your keyboard to play which is a simple WASD and spacebar setup however this can be annoying when your attack button is the same way you pick up gear. I have often dropped my items on accident. This is worse when you don't realize it and move off the screen and anything on the ground vanishes. These are things that can be fixed though and hopefully will be.
Another thing is imbalance. The bow is absurdly overly powered. If you don't want to make the game too easy I suggest avoiding it. If you want to get further into the game then pick one up. Using the spacebar you can spam the bow many times before running out of energy.
Anywho for the low price the game is very much worth getting, and I find it more enjoyable on the PC with the keyboard than on the phone with the touchscreen.

A game that is inspired by Diablo, Dark Souls, and Legend of Zelda sounds completely awesome. Which way would you take a game that is trying to mash together so many greats? What do you strip away? What can you enhance about the experience? Bit Dungeon II seems a bit of a strange amalgamation, including the button-mashing frenetic-ism of Diablo, overworld and dungeons with puzzles reminiscent of Zelda, and dropping your soul when you die… Leading to permadeath if you don’t find your way back to it. Some things seem to have hit home, while others leave me questioning. Without further adieu, lets look closer at Bit Dungeon II.
Firstly, I love the retro aesthetic and top-down view. The music is enjoyable, although seems to have a hard time looping since there is a rather long fade in/out for each song. The armor upgrades show on your character, which is always a positive thing when you’re grinding gear. There isn’t a massive selection of armor, but having every piece show on your character is a great feeling. Especially because when you first start you’re completely naked, with nothing but a ghost-wife. You will be given a staff, shield, and a few melee weapons to choose from. The weapon animations basically consist of the weapon flipping sideways for a couple frames, and could use a lot of work… Jabbing with spear, slashing with knife, etc., although I do appreciate any attempt at all. The magic animations are much better, but still not extremely flashy.
I enjoy the scope of a lot of things in the game, huge statues and bosses that make you feel like a boss yourself when you bring them to their knees. The puzzles in this game aren’t really difficult, but I feel like this is somewhat made up for with the frantic fighting. I would like to see things a bit more skill-based… Because while there are spells and skills to use, most challenges can simply be overcome with some mashing of the A button. The character feels pretty overpowered past level 10, which is fun at first… But walking into a room and dispatching every enemy in the same way (A,A,A,A) doesn’t really make for an epic adventure, no matter how much I love scraping stats.
I want to like this game… I really do. But LoZ, Diablo, and Dark Souls sets too big a precedent for this simple little button-masher to overcome. There are fantastic choices in the game, I love collecting gear to put on a fashion show, I love dropping my soul and getting smashed on the way back, and having to start all over. The bosses are good, the music is great, but the random generation of the overworld map with no actual readable map to lead the way makes me want to gouge my own eyes out. I also feel like more time should’ve been spent on the combat side of things, and the puzzle side of things. The combat will wreck you as a level 1 melee, but with a few levels and a few items you will absolutely fly through the game. And the puzzles, well… They’re just plain easy. Such high hopes for this game, and they all seem to have fallen a bit short. It’s got some nice ideas, quite a bit of fun to offer, and is quite probably worth the low asking price… Especially if you’re really into pressing A.

Final Score: 6/10 for aesthetic design and respawn mechanics. 8/10 with improved combat/puzzles.

I can assure you that the developers have worked hard on Bit Dungeon II, and it saddens me to say that half of that work was making the game worse.
I cannot recommend it at full price, you may want to take it at 50% off, which nets you a decent value for what it currently is.
I would like to state that I believe that the developers have handpicked the material shown on the store page to lead you into believing this is more than it is. This game is a one-button "ARPG" game - it is mechanically lacking in every way possible. Controls, movements, "skills" and enemies are perhaps less than one-dimensional. It is primarily a mobile game and for that platform it might actually be good and unique, it has not been greatly improved upon for its PC release.
The game:
Your objective is to kill the big baddy at the end of every dungeon/maze. The big baddies are slow giant sprites with absurdly large hitboxes that shoot projectiles when you get close and after a few seconds, sometimes. Each giant sprite has slightly different ways of shooting projectiles.
There are ranged monsters and melee monsters, that's pretty much the only relevant difference. The monsters have two types of AI: Shooty and Chasy. I'll let you figure out which enemy type uses which one. All regular enemies have the same attack patterns, the only noticeable changes are attack frequency and movement speed.
Now here's your journey - pick either a melee-type weapon or a ranged-type weapon. The subtypes make no difference other than attack frequency.
If you picked melee:
Walk next to monsters and wait for them to die - you attack automatically. If it's a stronger monster, hold the button to avoid damage. Your journey is now to poke enemies and quickly back off until your attack cools down - if its a ranged enemy, approach holding the button and then let it go.
If you picked ranged:
Hold the button and let go to kill enemies. Do not get close to enemies. Your journey is to shoot stuff from afar and hope that the game does not spawn two melee monsters with fast attack speed on top of you.
Your offhand item will either stun nearby enemies when you hold the button or do something that serves only as extra DPS. Choose it wisely, this makes a bigger difference than weapon subtypes.
Up to this point - it is a decent game and would actually be worth its full price. From this point onwards, "features" are actually making the game worse. This is mostly a bitter rant, you might wish to skip it if the previous statements do not turn you away from the title.
ARPG elements:
In total, there are about 12 different attributes; you will level up as you play. The game automatically picks the attributes for you based on your weapon so it doesn't make much of a difference... other than the fact that there are 4 different attributes that raise damage for the "different" weapon types. This makes it so trying other weapon types in the same playthrough offers a great way of experimenting slightly diverse ways of greatly reducing your damage output.
Most chests you open and all of the dropped loot is of a random type, with random attributes. As you might have guessed, this makes it so most of the weapon drops are completely worthless. There's also the fact that the weapons are pretty much the only piece of equipment that make a noticeable difference. Other than item type, there are no special effects or interactions. This means that the best you can get from your random drops is... linear stat progression... which is exactly what you usually get in games without randomized loot... without the need of having to get a random drop and hope for the right item.
"But if you had played the game you'd know that there are special eff-" No. You stop right there - because there aren't. There are additional attributes you might find less often - these raise your chance of triggering a certain "action". Those attributes are not unique and add an extra chance of either doing extra damage or not taking extra damage. At this point you might think I'm oversimplifying it - and I am. The fact that all of this happens by not pressing/pressing/holding a single button and every animation is bland makes it so everything feels pretty much the same.
The game has an elemental damage system. It works really well with how you cannot choose the equipment you're getting. Here's what it feels like from the player's perspective: you either do normal damage to everything, or normal damage to something, less damage to one thing and more damage to another. You do not get to choose which element you will get or use - you can only refuse the options that the game will pitifully spit in your face.
Rogue-lite-like elements, hooray:
Dungeon layouts change, but the only thing you will notice is that you are going in different directions. All the dungeons feel exactly the same, but in different colors. Room layouts are: kill monsters and the doors will open; press the buttons; find the key elsewhere and come back.
You start every "run" in one of the checkpoints next to a dungeon (the map itself is always the same)... so you guessed it - every area feels the same in regard to threat level. Threat level starts out at mild and drops as you level up.
Every screen gets randomized monster spawns - you can get anything from one useless blob to 5 of the only monster that poses any threat.
There's permadeath too! Hooray! Except this only makes it so you have to replay the same content every time you get the one mob who can actually deal damage to spawn on top of you. There is NOT enough difference in content to justify this. Playthroughs are too long and slow-paced for the additional content you might have missed.
There is a "permanent progression" system based on coins that you get by killing things. You can use those to buy underwhelming starting equipment. Oh, you can also buy random loot chests, you can choose between a chance at a random bad item for 5 minutes worth of coins or a 90% chance at a really strong item with the wrong attribute/type for your current playthrough for 50 minutes worth of coin farming.
"That clearly means that the best strategy is to start off opening one of those chests you dummy!" Certainly a great idea! Oh yeah, they're actually in very specific locations that require you to either get lucky and spawn at the correct place or walk for 15 minutes before actually starting each run.
You can also find special secret caves on some screens! Except that they show up on a random chance and actually disappear/reappear on screens you have already visited! And they always use the same visual cue! And they all have pretty much the same thing inside! Hooray.
I apologize if I was rude, I tend to be overly sarcastic, but it deeply saddens me to see promising devs throwing their time and hard work to produce something worst than they're capable of - just because.
The game seems to be doing well, take that opportunity to make even better games in the future, avoid tacking on "fashion" features, "cool" features. If you want to homage your favorite franchises - do it right. Study them. Find the elements that work together. Make them work together. Do not throw a pile of references and interactions on top of bare-bones mechanics without fleshing anything out.
This one is still rough.
Make the next one shine.

"Her Story" is interactive fiction told through well over 200 video clips searchable by keywords. The first keyword was "murder". Who... are you, the searcher? Why are you there? As you explore the archives of videos, and piece together the story, you will learn a lot about Hannah, her family, her husband, and perhaps, gain some insight about what made her do what she did... if you can figure out what did she do, that is...
The format is strange, and there's really no "obejctive" per se other than to unveal all videos and figure out the story, and people are still debating about the story today... What exactly does the story mean? Without any spoilers, let's just say, when you figure it out, you will be... surprised, shocked, dismayed... annoyed... whatever. But it did make you think, and that is what the best fiction do, right, make readers think?

If you're looking for a AAA storyline and impressive cinematic quality cut scenes, or even decent humor, forget about it.  However, as craptacular as the narration, which comes off more like story time in the kids section of the book store, it starts to fall in to that "so bad it's good" category.  The plot is flimsier than dollar store toiler paper, but that's what makes it funny.  It feels like it was written by a grade schooler, and the character designs reflect a lot of those same sensibilities.
The gameplay is your typical run and gun platformer ala Megaman X8/9.  I use that example specifically because the different powers enable you to reach certain areas, depending on what you're trying to achieve.
The models and environments are fairly well detailed, so I think I would've liked to have seen more in-engine cutscenes as opposed to the concept storyboards and  would've liked to have had a voice attached to the comm notifications.
All that said, I paid a buck for this and got a lot more than that in value.    Zack Zero shows a lot of promise, but go in it for the old school run and jump gamplay of the nintendo era, and try to not cringe too much at the storyline or the narrator's booming voice.
Other games like this would be Rochard and Shank.

the essence of zack zero is awkwardness. completely, though with degrees, frustratingly. I do believe the entire work is misguided. somehow, I still believe it is based on a love of videogames, but its process of modernization only offered oversights and misinterpreted tropes. to point it out basically, crocodile entertainment struggled with the basics of their game. controlling zack in the air is lacking entirely in finesse. either right or left moves zack very quick and much too far through the air. to complete most jumps, you’ll need to alternate between left and right so you can stay centered. usually this occurs in platformers that retain momentum, but zack zero has no aerial momentum to speak of. this careless implementation makes platforming more busy than it actually demands and kills its organics. the core problem demonstrates a lack of awareness that, at least, is consistently inhibited in other areas as well. however, the game is not without merit. its environment design exhibits a convincing technical competence and obvious visual excellency.
the pallette, visual direction, and quality of models are rather impressive. most especially the pallette, zack zero is uniquely bright and colorful. a bright, saturated, bordering cel-shaded platformer, it certainly wins out on first impression. any given scene in the game is delightful, at least especially, when not in motion. as for the execution of the 3D in general, a trine comparison is an exact science. a trine foil can carry too, both games have a talent in visual design to make you stand up and say “wow is this really indie?” (through irony; indies containing excellent 3D have been relatively commonplace, we still enjoy the disparaging perceptions). yet, still like trine, there isn’t much of a visionary execution. their gorgeous assets are liberally applied to reproduce a world of cliche. trine is, however, more comfortable with its setting, and achieves an otherworldly effect to a much fuller degree than zack zero. that saying, trine doesn’t even strive to make its world especially otherworldly, I would use the word fantastical, so the obvious fault of zack zero is demonstrated.
zack zero’s beginning sequence of levels does have an offworld impact. it’s not truly alien or anything like that, but a normalized sci-fi influence at least shines through. the planet seems to be an arid jungle, inwhich is the nonstandard appeal. altogether, it’s expressive and effective. to a general degree, anyway. never does this game go above and beyond. the after locations are metallic bases and underground caves nigh exclusively. they are visually disappointing, not only because the ideas are plain, but because crocodile entertainment could only bring plainness to their ideas. in their enemy design this remains a symbol. the enemy race is, well, a barney-like dinosaur and through the game you encounter a generous maximum of 4 barney variations. most every encounter is a mob of these same bipedal reptiles, with little visual and no mechanical variation. the resulting plainness in visual and scenario design is not surprising given the example set after the first level sequence.
to put it simply, this game is unable to cope with the platformer genre as it has stood since 1988. zack zero’s platforming is seemingly competent, at first, yet after the first 2 or 3 hours, the player has experienced the majority of what zack zero has to offer from its platforming, and is expected to play through variations of the same method. I can’t even say that every level contributes at least a few new ideas, there are levels in the mid and endgame that are plainly a wasteland of ideas. it was determined that the baseline of jumping on platforms, vertically and horizontally, would suffice for the majority of the game. it can be supposed that the weakness and tapered off nature of the game’s enemies contributes to the inability to differentiate. I cannot determine what is not there. crocodile entertainment banked on zack zero having an adventurous feel, with long levels coming in all kinds of shapes and sizes, topped off with zelda puzzling. the puzzling is nice and has far more thought put into it than the platforming, but it is not good enough to carry the deadweight of the game’s core. never, if maybe one time, are the player’s powers expected to use in tandem in the game’s puzzles. they’re more like glorified locked doors; the player finds then performs the told and unchanging solution, with the variable being only which power is the solution.
zack zero’s implementation of fighting combat is, as very well expected, ignorant of its placed genre, and as a result nothing other than offensive. there are two identical punches, a homing disk-something shot, and a myriad of elemental powers. zack zero’s model is unemotive and his bland animations could be called serviceable. the fire and ice powers have particles that go beyond and obscure their hitboxes, blind the player, and look particularly garish, most especially the terrible bloom-or-whatever happens when you do a fire explosion. earth attacks are relatively goofy but at least look and feel the best. enemies typically have more exciting fighting animation and presence than zack does. in between boss phases are combative cutscenes - these really show how dead and uncharismatic the protagonist is during combat. zack always has super armor, his attacks are all fast and strong, there is no clear reason to use some attacks over others, the depth of strategy is close range or long range. which of course means that long-range is the best option. that besides, earth attacks do overwhelmingly more damage than other attacks with little sacrifice, when it comes to melee. bosses go down comically fast with nicely timed ground slams.
enemies do no more than approach zack and swing, or approach until contact. minibosses have attack patterns even more lame than a super mario boss, that is, they have one extremely easy to dodge attack performed over and over again. it doesn’t need to be said, though I’ll say it: the combat and enemy design all suck. in a complete move of utter unaware travesty, combat happens more than not within encounters, where every bad enemy needs to be beaten in order to progress. combat and platforming is rarely integrated and it is with flying enemies if it ever is. bosses start out as more puffed out versions of minibosses, then become the best part of the game. zack zero’s boss fights are the only aware and modernized aspect of the title and I can’t help but feel they’re not studied, just coincidental. nevertheless, the patterns become inventive, though never chaotic or dense, which is good and bad. since the game checkpoints between phases, bosses never offer a working challenge, yet it doesn’t stop the fights from being enjoyable.
sometimes the game has walkable floor that looks like it’s in the background. it’s really impossible to differentiate those sections from actual background. sometimes background looks like walkable floor, but then you find out it was the background. checkpoints are very frequent, so while I couldn’t get mad, I still found these moments so incredibly stupid. there is a leveling system, with experience points gained through collectibles, that locks out abilities. the combat sucks, so again I couldn’t get mad. either upgraded abilities deal no extra damage, or enemies level up with you, who knows, but I seemed to do the same damage throughout the whole game. the story is embarrassingly, hilariously bad, and the game would have been better off without any attempt at writing. the soundtrack is largely unfitting and I rarely if ever get that feeling about accompanied music. it’s strange how catastrophically bad elements of zack zero are and how it isn’t really felt in the game. it’s pitiable, the feeling I can’t shake, that crocodile really did try their best.

I played this game as far as I could, until the crashes got to me and I figured - screw it.
There are plenty of positive reviews that state what is good, and for the most part, I can agree with them. However, the following are the reasons that, for me, made me give up on this.
Firstly - The crashes. It crashed a lot. coupled with the fact that the game only seems to autosave AFTER the current heist is complete, it left me having to redo heists again and again - not fun.
Secondly - The way the character's inventories are handled; Right clicking on a character will bring up a circular inventory which surrounds the character. Sadly, the way you tell characters to pick up items/use items is also right clicking. This means that it is virtually impossible to pick up an item that the character is standing over, because you just continue opening a characters inventory. Not a great problem, just very annoying when it happens for the 7th time in 10 minutes.
Thirdly - This game is NOT a 'plan a heist' game. There is no 'casing the joint', for example - Its a puzzle game. When you find a solution to a heist, that solution will always work. It'll work for me. For you. It'll work a year from now. There is no random elements apart from, perhaps, the public that wander into the stores now and then. Not that that is a bad thing - but i didn't want a puzzle game. I wanted something more.
Fourthly - The whole hold-up mechanic. Seriously, If i have 2 guys with shotguns pointing them at a security guard, I don't expect that guard to wait 45 seconds or so, then draw his baton and charge me. But that's what happens. People will not be held up indefinitely, but instead you have a short time to either shoot them or beat them into unconsciousness.
Now, im aware that I didn't play THAT far into the game. Perhaps there will be items to permenently placate people - ropes or handcuffs - but I didn't see anything like that.
Don't get me wrong - Its not a terrible game. Its just has several flaws.

Would I reccomend this to a friend? Nope. This game was removed from early acccess too soon. Review is for v1.2.2
Unstable.
Crashes too often (Seems to be a memory leak. Perfomance gets worse the longer you play), especialy on the later levels that take longer to complete. Can't complete my current mission (3rd to last) as the game will crash before the mission can be completed. By design, you can't save durring missions. I'm ok with the lack of saving, but having to rush to try and finish a level before the game will crash, is not ok.
Controls are bad.
Opening/closing doors are a large source of frustration. Game uses swinging doors with physics. To open a door to a room, you have to walk in to the door and then in to the room to open the door all the way. Until the door swings out of your face, you can't see anything past the door.
Closing a door when facing it is often a two step proccess. You click the door to close it, and it swings on to your goon. He then has to turn away and walk away from the door as it will push him in the back if he does't move quick enough or of another goon is too close and blocking his path. Once the goon has cleared the door jam, he can turn around to face the door to lock it. This process takes WAY TOO LONG to complete. Have fun doing this when you want to lock enemies in a room before they can rush the door, push it open and punch your goons silly.
Due to the bad controls, you are required to use two or more goons to do what should be simple tasks for a single goon. One to close/lock the door, second or third to hold a gun on the enemy to delay them breaking control. Sure you can knock everyone out and drop them in the room you plan to lock them in. You end up having to do that anyway, but it feels forced as the other method is so bad.
Pathing can be bad. Tell a goon to backup to move a small distance away from an enemy or anything actualy. Instead of turning and moving to that spot, they will try to move far away (often in to another room) and then loop back to the spot you told them to move to. It then turns in to move, cancel order, move again.
General bad stuff you can find in this game.
Hire goons based on their stats, yet once you hire them you can not see those stats again.
Goons can be killed by gunfire (including your own). OK that's fine. Goons can be killed by melee attacks. These are the same attacks that only temporarily knock out the enemies. Can't revive your goons durring missions, nor can you carry them back to the hideout to be revived. They can be killed from being punched with bare fists. Not OK.
Enemies can have melee weapons (baton) yet will not drop them when knocked out or killed.  Late game you find 1 brass kncukle. Whoopty-doo.
Achievement to hire enough goons to reach a team of 6. What's the point when you can only bring 4 on any mission. Outside of that achievement, there is zero reason to have more than 4 goons at a time.
Pro's.
Sound and Art are nice.
Edit: Went to double check the version of the game v1.2.1 or v1.2.2 and now it crashes on launch. Avoid this game.

Well this same is probably worth waiting for it to be on sale. As much as the first game "Art of Victory" was a complete failure, this game get a second chance and trying to redeem itself. So let's start with the good.
It was more fun to play this game than the first. The graphics and scenery are great. I had a Far Cry 3 feeling to it. It was interesting to play because you had an AI parter with you half the time, so it made for interesting moments. Most of the time you played as sniper, other times you were the tagger, and even forced to use a rifle as well. Which brings me to the bad stuff about this game.
So you are a sniper so stealth is a big part of this game, and you are also camflauged. So what is the problem then?
It's actually not so funny when you have a silenced sniper rifle, you shoot one enemy, and the rest of the enemies can, with pinpoint accuracy, shoot at you, even from a long distance. Though unlike the first game when you died almost instantly, you still lose health if you don't move. They somehow get alerted sometimes. AND then you will have an unsilenced sniper gun; you fire that and no one seems to be bothered by it. This is actually quite frustrating when there is one level you have to get through by stealth alone. You shoot one guy silenced, and everyone in the area is on alert. So if your foot is exposed, forget it, you are dead.
The next thing which I consider pretty bad are the weapons. Not the weapons themselves mind you. I can say it was interesting to play where distance and wind are a factor to how your bullet will travel. There is on easier levels, a red dot on your scope to help you.
You see. I am a Counter-Strike player and the only weapons that you use for zooming are scoped weapons. In this game, the cross hairs are so open that you are forced to use iron sights to shoot, and by doing so, you cannot see your target properly due to the visual of your gun being in the way. The takes out the presicion of aiming when you are trying to strafe and hell, even to try locking a position down.
I was enjoying this game, but because of the issues I see here, I found myself rushing to finish the game fast, just to get it over and done with. The maps are good and unique, which is why I continued to play the game to completion. I won't discredit that.
This game does have potential, but due to my observations on it, I am not even inclined to want to play multiplayer. Becasue I bought this in a bundle, I hope Sniper 2 proves to be much better than this game. We can only hope.
If you try to compare it to the Sniper Elite games, they are similar, but not the same kind of games. I would suggest watching YouTube videos for this game, just to you know what you are in for.

This is a game where you dig, find valuable minerals, and return to the surface to deposit said minerals and refuel. You spend your funds on upgrades that allow you to go deeper and deeper, receiving cryptic transmissions along the way - eventually reaching the center of Mars.
That might sound boring but this game does a pretty good job of keeping it fresh. Soon you will encounter rocks that block your way, find upgrades that reward you for picking up specific minerals in order, and lava that you can drill through at the cost of a good portion of your health. Soon, the game becomes a puzzle, trying to figure out the most efficient way to drill in order to reach the valuables.
If you want a basic idea of how this game works, look up Motherload. It's an old (free) browser game this one was based on.
This game's presentation is fantastic, featuring a powerful and atmospheric soundtrack by Eric Cheng and beautiful art by Scott Carmichael. Despite being a simple digging game there is crazy amounts of atmosphere.
The voice acting ranges from "good but weird" to "unintentionally hilarious". It can break immersion but usually it's not a problem.
Regular mode is fun for a while but it gets boring when there's no consequence of being stupid. Enter Hardcore mode. Hardcore mode is not for giggles with your buddies.
If you die, that character is dead forever. You'll need to start a new save to use that particular character.
If you run out of fuel, you die. Also, all players in the session share fuel so die, die, die, and die.
I love it.
It's pretty good. It's not absolutely captivating, but it's... reasonably compelling. You are an employee of Solarus corporation, mining into Mars. As you drill deeper and deeper you hear strange transmissions from the other miners and discover that something's gone wrong - and that's not Solarus talking to you.
It's a good game. It isn't fun in the same sense that some games are, but it's absolutely worth playing. Again, if you're on the fence, look up the original Motherload.

Is this a perfect game? no, it's an alpha. But I think a lot of the reason this game receives a bad rap is because of the initial impressions that some have given by clubbing new players. Sprinkle a little bit of addictive survival gameplay elements, add an improved Ultima Online look, finally throw in a load of people and what you have is Wild Terra Online!
Wild Terra Online
Journal – Entry #1
I awoke in a land not knowing where I was, what to do, or how I got there. Moments later only my name came back to me, a great Wild Terra Onlinesign. I did what anyone else would do and I started to explore my surroundings. I had nothing on me, nothing at all, not even clothes, except underwear. Greenery was everywhere lush pine trees were strewn about the land, lakes, and snow filled the landscape. It was a beautiful sight.
Survival mode kicked in. “Okay, most importantly I need food, and water”. I went to a tree and tried getting anything I could to make a weapon to hunt prey. Nope the branches were to strong and tree too sturdy. I would need to craft a tool to cut down branches from the trees. On my way to this tree I noticed piles of stones in random areas. “Okay” I thought, “I could use these to make a stone knife and then use the knife to cut down branches”. I was happily collecting rocks, I only needed about three or so, but I collected one hundred and thirty. Something so damn addictive about gathering these things, something that would extend to everything in my game session.

Wild Terra Online 2Time went by and finally I had enough rocks. I needed wooden scraps to make a knife. I explored more and right when I was about to give up, I found them. A knife was made and I quickly went from tree to tree. I cut down every branch I could so that my next tool. ‘the stone hatchet’ could be made. With the hatchet I could cut down trees for wood, and with wood I could make spears, with spears I could now hunt. Do you see the progression? It was pretty damn fun going through it, the carrot on the stick game play kept me wanting more.
I won’t lie, I died a few times, I mean a fox put me to sleep a few times. Thankfully the run back to your body isn’t too long and all of your equipment is still there. I was warned however, each time I left the peaceful area. I don’t know much about it but I believe if you leave it you’re fair game for anyone to kill, so tread carefully.
Overall I enjoyed my short session with Wild Terra Online, and I look forward to seeing what else it has to offer.

Needs ALOT of root level work before it really playable.

-- 90's Isometric Interface/machination
-- Solid crafting and base building system
-- Medieval and tribal aesthetic
-- Mounted combat
-- Sandbox roots
-- Sandbox roots. Good because there's enough 'free will' to explore most crafting/combat types with progression in each one, but there's not a lot of options available to you in terms of progressing or leveling up each skillset (except crafting), and you're forced to harvest from a node-like world (like The Forest or Subsistence) instead of being able to use absolutely everything on the map (like 7 days to die or Ark)
-- Combat is definitely lackluster. It doesn't entirely suck, but projectiles and melee leave a lot to be desired.
-- Recipes for crafting decent equipments and structures are gated and require a LOT of searching and grinding to find and unlock
-- Population scarcity.
-- Every screen looks identical to the one before it. The only variation comes when you get an identical screen with snow covering the same backdrop you just saw 20 seconds before. Environments need a huge upgrade/expansion.
-- Early hunting on anything other than a grouse or hare is frustratingly disparaging. A 120% quality bow still takes an average of 10 shots to down a deer, and more for a wolf or boar. Chasing animals gets to be a big ordeal that feels more cumbersome than rewarding.
-- A nearly non-existent soundscape. Most of the sounds are recycled and there's not much variation between things like landing a javelin throw or hitting a tree. There's hardly any ambiance as well-- half the time you'll probably find yourself seeing if you didn't accidentally mute your computer because there's just no sound coming from the game.
-- Everyone looks like identical twins. :-/
-- Hunger system needs a revamp. The requirements are a bit absurd and unless you've got a good system going, staying fed becomes your primary focus/activity more than expanding your base does.
I'd recommend this if you're a fan of isometric sandboxes lke Ultima Online. It feels almost like a successor at times (in the absolute most basic sense of the term), and I have a strong suspicion that this game will see a heavy improvement over the next year.

Again, as always, Jackbox has produced a great group of really fun games to play.  Some of them are especially great
Trivia Murder Party is great fun and tense as well-it really makes you double guess your own actions and your friends actions.
Quiplash 2 is just as great as the original, probably better in fact. You can write your own prompts and the game is just improved in every way I can think of.
Tee K.O. is an interesting concept of a game, where you design a few t-shirts and then come up with a few random titles-someone else will pair the two and then it will be voted on and the person who paired them will win, not the person who designed it, which we found odd but interesting. This doesn't make the game any less fun though, it is a great game
Fakin' It is also a good game-however, you need to be able to see each other perfectly. Considering we were playing over Skype and therefore I could only see one person at a time because I was sharing my screen, this made the game a bit more difficult and so we agreed to say what we would do. It is an interesting game though, where there a different rounds that you can pick-for example, you will have to write something, hold up a certain number of fingers or point at someone. Everyone gets given the same prompt to do something, apart from the faker who either gets given a roughly similar prompt (for example in the writing round, one prompt was "the last book you read" whereas the fakers was "your favourite childhood book") or no prompt at all and they just have to try a persuade people that they are not the faker. However I am not entirely certain how the points system works.
Another good point is that once you have finished the game and select to play again with the same players, it will remember and you will not have to sit through the introduction again-in fact, in the Trivia Murder Party this is incoperated into the game and if you lost in the previous game-and thus "died"-it will add "Jr" to the end of your name.
As well as this when you log onto the Jackbox.tv website and join a game, the format of the webpage will change dependent on what game you are playing, which is a nice feature.
You also have the ability to look at the answers at the end of the game via the webpage. In Tee K.O. It even gives you the option of buying the T-Shirts that everyone so lovingly designed.
All in all, another great Jackbox Party Pack that is super fun to play with friends, with new more experimental games that are just great fun to play with your friends.

This is one of the greatest games ever made.  As Star Wars games go, it is virtually unparalleled.
HOWEVER...
The game is riddled with bugs, and is largely unplayable.  Here are the problems I face when attempting to play the game;
-The game doesn't launch, but Steam and my computer recognize the game as running.  When I try to end the process, it doesn't respond, and Steam can't close until the game is closed.
-If I can get the game to launch, the game crashes as soon as I set up my character.
-If, on the rare occasion I can actually play the game, various issues and intermittent crashing occur.
I'm sure there are some complicated ways in which I can solve these problems, but I'm not interested in spending hours trying to fix the game, and I imagine that the average consumer on Steam isn't either.  In its current state, I can't possibly recommend this game.  And frankly, I'm disgusted with the people who can't run the game but are so nostalgic about KOTOR that they give it a positive review anyway.  If you can't run the game, DON'T RECOMMEND IT!  Until someone patches KOTOR just like they did with KOTOR II, this game will remain a pleasant memory, and nothing more.

No, it's not the next Borderlands. The game is a first-person shooter MOBA that has hints of the team behind Borderlands in the artwork and humour. It has a few short "stories" that are completed by cooperative play and three different types of competitive play: a capture the flag; destroy opposing sentries; and escort minions. It's the first MOBA I've enjoyed since Team Fortress 2 and I'm still enjoying it after about 40 hours. But, it's going to die. While not the same game as Overwatch, it directly competes with it for players. You see this in the lengthy time it takes to match up teams and the woefully unbalanced teams that go head-to-head.
Game mechanics are good, the complexity of the characters vary tremendously so there is much to learn and ample opportunity to grow. I just don't see many people sticking around for the long haul and without a player-base the game will be harder and harder to actually play. So, while I reccomend the game (and enjoy it), buyers should be aware that it has a potentially short play life.
