Word of warning to anyone looking to buy this game: it is an FMV game, which means you watch videos and solve a puzzle on your own. Some people have said that this is not really a game, but more of an interactive story. I'm inclined somewhat to agree. There is an end goal, but there is no possible way to fail or really muck up. I suppose you could stop trying, which could be considered a failure. In essence, you're a person on a police database searching through some 90s videos of a woman discussing a murder (I doubt that's a spoiler). You have to figure out whether or not she did it based on her responses. As you listen to her talk, you can get new ideas for terms to plug into the database. So, it goes along like that and eventually you solve the mystery or give up.
This experience is incredibly short, but I liked it a lot. I've played a lot of Herinteractive's Nancy Drew PC games and was majorly into Myst, so I'm kind of used to puzzling things out. Not that there was much to puzzle out here, of course. You're just searching things. Anyone who has done any sort of degree knows how to utilize Boolean search techniques to gather results.
There is nothing innovative here and Her Story isn't really a game, but... well... it is an enjoyable experience and the price is fair. I found the actress good, particularly given the role she had to play. I enjoyed following her story (hyuck) and I think you will too.

It is pretty entertaining and will keep you questioning for awhile. But it is short and spare one achievement it is pretty easy to finish all there is in the game. The actress does a really good job and it does make you debate which of two things are real. The way they have you discover the story is unique (or if there is a game with similar style I haven't played it at least). Downside is though, if you're not careful it is easy to run out of options on where to go and at times it feels like you've seen the same video. And of course the short amount of play time. My time is with me getting lost and rewatching videos to figure out a new path.
Verdict: Buy on sale. No offense meant to the people who made it, but I feel like the $4. something price I paid was a fair price.

I got this game gifted to me by a friend of the developer, and was pleasantly surprised with the quality of the seemingly-simple gameplay.
If you like rogue-likes, minimal mechanics, dying a lot, and straight-up fast-paced violence, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are good - the detail in the character sprites and background are decent. The music and sounds are an appropriate fit for the retro theme. Whenever you pick up new equipment, it will show on your character, which is something I always appreciate. The feedback on how much damage you are doing and taking is quick and not intrusive. You can bring up your stats on the left side of the screen at any time.
The controls are very simple to pick up, and the learning curve is moderate to challenging depending on your experience with rogue-likes. There is no tutorial - you are immediately thrown into the game, but you can press ESC and read the instructions. Something very important to realize (it took me too many playthroughs to realize this, making the game unnecessarily more difficult, heh): if you interact with the campfire in front of you, it will heal you to max health.
YOU DO NOT start off the game at full health. I kept dying because I thought half the HP gauge was what you were supposed to have. Also, interact with the ghost in the beginning of your run for an extra life. I believe there is a higher chance of finding a +1up to life if you go back to the area wherever you died.
The gameplay is nice and charming, I personally prefer to play with a controller, but the keyboard works just as well. You can just move your character up to enemies to auto-attack, however, you can hold the attack button down to block and charge your special ability (dependent on your weapon equipped). Enemies respawn whenever you enter a new area, however, once you clear an area a few times, significantly weaker enemies will respawn instead. There are at least 4 different biomes (map areas), and each contains a campfire/shop, and a dungeon. You will start your runs in a random campfire/shop area, and you can walk to each biome. There are also structures in each biome that offer permanent bonuses to your stats, however, you may only select one attribute to boost.
Dungeons are the meat of the game - each has a very, very challenging boss at the end. You can leave without killing the boss, and this is strongly advisable because the global enemies will boost in difficulty whenever you defeat a boss. Grinding is fairly quick in this game, and you should invest in doing this before tackling a boss.
Random drops are frequent, ranging in item type (armor, weapon, rune) and quality. Staves offer you ranged attacks, however, I have not picked up any other projectile-based weapons (like bow&arrows, crossbows), so I do not know if this is included in your potential armory.
The game auto-saves your progress if you quit the game, however, only one slot is allowed.
Overall, a very fun, fast-paced game. Definitely give it a try if you are into the rogue-like genre.
Recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

is pretty terrible.  I spent my entire playtime grumbling about its bad physics, confusing graphics, and groan inducing story.  And yet, for some reason, I would still say that I enjoyed it overall.
You play as a superhero who can switch between four elemental forms, each with special powers for both fighting and moving around.  Jump on platforms, fend off bad guys, maybe collect gems and treasures if you feel like it.  Fairly standard platformer.  The game is generous with checkpoints, so if you mess up it's no big deal.  Perhaps the casual nature is what kept me going.  When badness creates difficulty, progress ceases and I quickly stop caring.  This game may have been lackluster, but at least I was moving through it at a decent rate.
The use of the 2.5-D perspective is one of
weakest points.  The camera often zooms and rotates as you move through the level, which can be disorienting.  It's also sometimes ambiguous what you can and can't stand on.  The physics are also pretty bad.  Jumping feels subtly awkward.  I can't really explain it, it just feels somehow off.  Then there's this glitch where you clip through a wall or floor.  If it's the floor you just die and go back to the last checkpoint, but if it's a wall you may get stuck and have to go back the the main menu, which is annoying.  In all cases it happened when I was touching stacks of crates, so I guess destroy those from a distance.
The art style seems to draw inspiration from Man of Action and Filmation fantasy.  Cutscenes were fairly entertaining.  The story is an F-5 cliche storm in which you rescue your girlfriend from an evil overlord.  It has the good sense not to take itself seriously, but I don't think a silly tone excuses lazy writing.  Good mechanics could more than compensate for it, but this game has no such luck.
One thing I'll say in the game's favor is that it has a handful of actual boss fights.  Not just recycled minibosses (though it has those too), I mean unique enemies with lots of health and attack patterns and weak points and the like.  That seems to be missing from a lot of modern games, so it's nice to see it happen here.
As I said, I enjoyed
despite its problems, and to an extent because of them.  If you like casual platformers, have a soft spot for cheesy adventure cartoons, and can get it cheap/bundled, this game may prove... acceptable.

In a nutshell: if you like the game's visuals and platformers as genre, buy it.  (If you can get it from bundle or on sale, it's actually a great deal.)
Little longer: Zack Zero is a classic platformer: linear levels with secrets, enemies to defeat, and coins - in this case green disks? to collect. There is a little tweak: Zack has his human + 3 elemental-imbued form, each with different abilities (faster, can surf in air, slow but great defense) besides 2 activable abilities. In combat each of them can be useful, but managing over the map and storyline or reaching certain spots (and secrets) you need to use specific abilities.  These features are good additions to the gameplay, but nothing broundbreaking or really new here.
The game is quite family friendly: there is absolutely no blood or gore in the game - robot enemies explode, others just "shatter". You can watch it in the game's trailer. It's like a saturday morning's superhero cartoon.
Positives and negatives
+ Nice graphics with beautiful elemental power effects
+ Enjoyable gameplay: platforming not too hard (experienced players will find it rather easy), and there are lots of checkpoints (not indicated ingame)
+ Cool-looking cartoon animation to the storytelling between levels
+ Easy achievements: can be done in 1 walkthough, or artifact collecting by "select level" option.
- Bugs (RARELY) : Not as bug-ridden as older reviews claim, but there are some clipping issues with animation. In my 26 hours of gameplay ( ~ 1.5 walkthrough) I found one platform I kept falling through when tried to jump from, and one wall I stuck in it. Second can be considered as game-breaking, had to exit to main menu then continue from prev checkpoint. Lost ~ 5 minutes of game, nothing serious.
-You start with your suit at level 20, then it gets downgraded to level 1. You see each abilities with power levels decrease, losing powers. Yet during the game your suit levels up, but you can't check/there is no indicators, for when will you get  for example the stone spikes power.
- And sadly a real pain: at certain points denied backtracing. Platforms cease to exist backwards, you fall somewhere and can't climb back, things like this. But there is a "select level" option at main menu, so you shouldn't be troubled if you're going for maximising points or collecting artifacts.
- I don't remember which one, but one boss fight was just plain terrible: the camera focus is glitched or something, I had to fight while being outside of the screen. As there is 3 or 4 checkpoints even in bossfights, it's not that hard, just a really awkward situation.

Think Don't Starve with a blend of Haven and Hearth and you will have a feel for this inde sandbox.  Once you have decided on PVE lands with pvp zones or the full-blown open world pvp, you are dropped into your choice with nothing but a deep desire to gather and explore.  Animals are plentious but not all friendly.  Fashioning primitive tools allows you to  hunt rabbits, birds and small game while locating a suitable place to claim for your own.  A primitive house and a bed of branches lead up to further construction and production while watching over your claim from poachers who would take what they can reach.  The grind is not too grindy and the pace is relaxing.  Skills are gained by using them and death is very certain if you get too close to the dangerous bears, boars, wolves and other obvious predators.  But there are some much appreciated helps in the game.  Rather than a map, a floating icon always points in the direction of your home and/or your body as the case may be.  Building walls can protect your claim from poachers and give you room to set up production properly.  The game is in early access but already there is a wealth of things to do.  The crafting is of the typical gather this to make that, and there is lots to do.  It is very solo-friendly, at least in the PVE lands.  The most frustrating part of my first 15 hours was failing so frequently when my skills in a particular thing indicated low percentages of success - but it was expected and makes crafting a rewarding passtime.  There is a wiki but it is deficient of content.  Global chat seems to be the best way to get information on the many crafting stations already in the game.  This game has much potential and is already a fullfilling experience.  If you like sandbox crafting coupled with a survival experience, you will feel at home in Wild Terra.  Get it.

Star wars: Knights of the Old Republic is a truly amazing and inspiring game. for fans of the rpg genre it is a ride you won't soon forget which tells the tale of the light and dark sides of the force in constant flux and the backstory of Raven; a character who became famous and a fan favourite of many. Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, or KOTOR, is by far one of the best games I have ever played. It has recieved over 40 Game of the Year awards, and it is what I believe to be one of the all time great RPGs.
You start off by waking in a starship, the Endar Spire, under attack by the Sith Fleet that have bombarded the Republic. You will make your way to an escape, whilst fighting through Sith soldiers that have boarded the vessel, meeting two characters on the way, one of which is the war hero, Carth Onasi. You and Carth flee the ship and crash land on a nearby Planet, the urban world of Taris, where you will start your search for Bastila, a legendary Jedi without who the Republic would be all but finished.
After you find Bastila, you and many other characters you meet on your way, travel to Dantooine once discovering a cunning plan to escape the Sith quarantine on the planet, due to the help of Canderous Ordo, an ex-mandalorian (Mandalore in KOTOR 2), in the nick of time as the Sith armada begin bombing the planet once they learn of Bastila's whereabouts on the surface.
Once you reach Dantooine, the main plot is revealed and you set off travelling from system to sytem on your quest, which will lead up to an epic finale.
The amount of detail is astonishing for a game that came out in 2003, and you will find no better storyline or characters anywhere else in the Star Wars Universe, and in my opinion, in any other RPG. The graphics are not amazing, but I believe that they are appealing and the game is extremely atmospheric, partially due to the great ambient music.
The story is essentially linear, however you get to choose the path you take, what ending you will have, and your actions have influences on other characters and NPCs, which can often be very rewarding and satisfying.
Few small glitches and bugs, and it has turned-based combat, which may not appeal to some, but offers a more strategical outlook on combat. Also, this game is relatively dialog-heavy, however it is extremely interactive, with little in the way of characters droning on and on.
It is likely to take around 28 hours to complete the game first time, even for more experienced players due to the main story and sidequests.
Pros:
-Amazing Story
-Interesting Characters
-Feel like you are in control, e.g. character influence, path choice
-Strong atmosphere
-Plenty of playtime
-Great replayability
Cons:
-Handful of annoying (but minor) bugs
-Aged graphics
-10/10 - Would get arrested on Manaan again
Overall, the best £7.99 I have spent (I would have payed easily £60 for this, now I know what it is like). The screenshots really don't do it justice, and if you like excellent stories and/or Star Wars, play it.

Battleborn is a good game released at a bad time. It released at a time with a fluid of first person MOBA's came out the biggest Overwatch. The week of Battleborn's launch was the week of Overwatch's Beta which had over 9,7 million users playing. The internet was already raving about Overwatch due to Blizzards marketing even before the beta, after the beta forums and blogs were just completely overwatch. Pushing Battleborn under the rug, the only people really fallowing it devotedly was fans of other of the makers games such as borderlands. But lets focus on the game itself now...
Battleborn fallowed in the same footsteps as borderlands with its cartoony art style (which I like very much) over the top action and sense of humor. The characters were over-all delightful but lack any real depth to them. You don't really build any type of feeling or relationship with them, so there's no connection. As such you never fully feel immersed in the world, which is a real downer. They focus heavy on the multiplayer aspect of the game which frankly I found to be the least fun part of it. They only have a few levels with 3 or so modes, switch characters is the only way to make it feel fresh but even that gets old after awhile. The real fun of Battleborn was in its co-op story mode which unfortunately is also lacking. There are only about 7 missions (although I'm sure more will come via DLC but lets focus on the main game itself) and you'll find yourself protecting and guarding things very often. The best parts are in between those areas, and the boss fights. They also have different difficulties to keep things fresh, and the reply value is high. Trying different team set ups, and making your way through missions together you grow a bond between players much more than you get with online mode where 1 out of 3 teams you join will just try to get kills and ignore the goal. Its due to the co-op story mode that I recommend this game, its charming, silly and has a very uqinge story to it, the only down side is the lack of a story mode when this was the best part of the game.
Pros:
• Co-op Story Mode
• Fun and entertaining Characters
• High Reply Value
• Good for both the Causal gamer and more hardcore one
• One of the best Intros/ending cut-scenes seen in a game
• Lots of dialogue, it even changes sometimes when replying a level or playing as a different character keeping things fresh
• Interesting Level Up system, really makes you able to custom a character to your play style
• Lots of Loot to go through
• Lots of achievements to get for each character
• Unlockables
Cons
• Lacking in Story Mode length
• Lacking in Multiplayer options
• Lacking in depth/background story/character development for its "Battleborns"
• Even once you do everything your felt wanting and not in a good way
In short:
Its a good game. Its not great, it wont blow you away but its solid and plays good,and fun. Its worth getting but I'd wait into the price drops or it goes on sale.

This is an interesting diversion of a game.
You are presented with an interface that resembles a custom corporate PC OS, complete with added screen glare (which can be turned off!) and a variety of desktop icons.  You're given only the most limited instructions, and then sent off on a sort of treasure hunt where you unlock fragments of a story via associative reasoning, deduction and straightforward hunches.
The story as revealed is an interesting one, although maybe a little less enigmatic than it thinks it is, but the true triumph of this game is in the atmosphere it conjures - at times I really did feel I was in the basement of some local authority archive, late at night and alone, trying desperately to find out what had happened to the protaganist and why.
The keyword guessing mechanic is also pretty addictive, and I ended up with a whole scribble of notes which is pretty rare for me as I'm generally good at retaining info from games, but felt like I needed to keep reminding myself of the things I knew (or thought I knew! There's a couple of curveballs along the way,..)
I definitely recommend this game if you're a fan of slower paced experiences and interested in playing detective in a novel and interesting way.  Total game time for me was about 8 hours, but that was to max out everything.  You could easily reach the end game in half that time.

Kaiju Panic by Mechabit is one of those games that mix tower defense with action/strategy, and it does it fairly well. Yet I had troubles liking it fully. Why? Well, Kaiju Panic is a kind of fun, kind of boring type of game. I know, I just confused you, didn’t I? That’s okay, that’s how I felt about it at first too.
The story follows the aftermath of an asteroid crash. Within this asteroid were these little monsters called Kaiju, which are apparently coming to destroy us. Your job is to mine the asteroids for resources while avoiding the Kaiju and also gathering survivors to bring them to safe places. The places are only as safe as you make them, though, and this is where the tower defense kicks in: you will have to build towers to defend it (and the people you just saved) from all those monsters coming to get you.
Simple enough, right? Of course, as you go through you get to improve buildings, research, gain perks, etc. Some survivors won’t want to go with you until you complete a requirement (ie. Find their dog first), which gets a bit annoying.
I rather enjoyed the visual aspect of the game, even if it has a bit of a ‘mobile’ feel to it. The cutesy cartoony graphics are lovely if you’re into that type of art style, the variety of Kaiju is enough to keep you entertained, and the colorful atmosphere will make you forget you’re essentially in one of those aftermath games.
The maps are interesting, though nothing out of this world. After a while they all more or less start to look alike.
That said, the controls were a bit confusing at first, but once you get used to them, they’re only moderately annoying. You use a combination of mouse and keyboard, where the space bar pops up the build menu and the mouse is mostly used to look around and select buildings.
The music is annoying as hell, but the sound effects were decent for the type of game - pretty much what you’d expect from a mobile-looking game.
My biggest pet peeve with the game is that while it’s really entertaining to play when you just start, after a while it just gets repetitive and boring. And I did enjoy the first few levels of the game - but as I progressed, turret placing became a bit of trial-and-error as you have no clue until you’ve played it where monsters will be coming from, and with an already repetitive style of gameplay, having to re-do entire levels can get really frustrating.
Mechabit has recently added a co-op option, which I haven’t had the chance of trying, but I think would really add some to the entertaining factor if you’re not playing it on your own.
Would I recommend it? Eh, I give it a very hesitant yes, particularly if you’re into tower defense, but I would certainly not pay full price for it. Better wait for a sale or a bundle.

Super Motherload is a game about mining.
The essential mechanics of the game should be familiar to anyone who’s played a mining game before: collect ore, sell for cash, use cash to upgrade miner. Collect even more ore… rinse and repeat.
Usually this process is addictive enough to compel your average gamer to play until the miner is maxed out, but Super Motherload dresses this in slick 2D graphics, 80s Communist era charm and an intriguing story which develops via a series of increasingly ominous transmissions from the bowels of Mars. While the focus remains on mining, the story and the quests that it brings does add a welcome alternative motivator and rewards you at the end with what I consider to be one of the more interesting and bizarre encounters of recent gaming memory.
Unless you’re playing in Hard-core (which is ridiculously stressful and difficult), for the most part the game is rather forgiving: death is mere short delay on your quest to wealth. The exception for me was the final checkpoint which I found too far from the finale to be any fun – instead ending up with a little too much ‘grinding’ (pun intended!) for my taste. Hard-core gamers may disagree.
The co-operative multi-player allows for up to four players. You and up to three friends can either pool your resources and strategies to help each other out... or bicker and race each other to the Motherload. This turns a good game into a great one, so if you’re buying a copy make sure you get copies for your friends too.
Overall, Super Motherload is a great way to ‘sink’ a few hours and have legal fun with your friends for a few £s. What’s not to like?

9.9999999/10: A faithful re-creation of the original flash game I killed hours and hours on in the library in elementary school, Super Motherload was one of my best purchases... on sale. Keep that in mind for this review.
No, I don't think it was worth $15. I bought it when it was about $3.99, and I still feel like that was cheating the developers, but I wouldn't have paid $15 for this.
I noticed a lot of people were not happy with this game, and for some reasons, I can see why: the minimap is really tiny, especially when playing on a big screen. Sometimes blocks just float a little strangely, don't break in the right way. The controls sometimes get a little soggy feeling on the keyboard (so it's worth shelling out for a controller!), which can lead to some enraging drops, and upgrades process doesn't really keep you updated on what you've actually bought, and what that does. Some of the explosives challenges are annoying, and can lead to some aggravating situations (That one unobtainium up on the top edge! Damn it!)
But. For a game that brings back my memories of the original Motherload (which is included in buying this, by the way!), I couldn't think of anything better. A beautiful world, spectacular design, a great update to the filling/selling/upgrading process (just... driving over the buildings? Holy cow!), the checkpoints and bases system, the smelting/combining system, which totally revitalised my joy of mining... the list goes on. The music is amazing, though I wish I could have had that original jam updated... could have listened to that on repeat for days! The replay value is... okay. For some, getting to the end is all they wanted. For
, the replay value was through the roof: I could drag a few friends over, throw the game up on the TV, and have a hysterical time. I could put it on my laptop and kill some time mining instead of writing press releases. I could put it on my screen in my room, and play it before going to bed. I enjoy mining way too much. I have issues.
So it's a good purchase. Play it with your friends. Play it by yourself. Go mining.

This is a game that had enormous potential from the getgo. It uses the Five Nights at Freddy's model of horror...however it makes the deathly mistake of doing things that made FNAF 2 a chore to play. One of the great things that made FNAF 1 such a joy to play was its ultra creepy visuals, its innovative haunted house feel, and the jumpscares. OMG The jumpscares. This title does one better. It lets you roam around...which is something we've always wanted to do at Freddy's. (and were sort of able to do in a map on Garry's mod). And from the start of tattletail you are immensely creeped out.
You play an 8 year old child 5 days before christmas who gets out of bed and wanders about the dark house wanting to open his Christmas presents early. We ALL did that and it was an awesome premise. However the premise goes astray and actually starts to tick you off more than bring joy and actual fright. Your present is a talking toy called Tattletail, which is a parody of the 80s (scary) Furby toy that talked. Also TEddy Ruxpin. This name is immensely clever seeing as how the thing that constantly gets you killed is this toy that JUST WON'T SHUT UP! I guess that's the reason. That's the premise. You carry around this toy...and this is where the choices of gameplay borrowed from FNAF2 cause the game to take a wrong turn. In that game you constantly had to wind a musicbox to avoid getting killed by a jester doll...and this caused you to not be able to enjoy doing ANYTHING else (like enjoy the visuals or actually enjoy getting creeped out by the sound and visuals and tension that was there in FNAF 1.) Nope. You had to do what felt like work. Wind the box all game. In this game you have to do three things. None of which make any difference. You have to feed it, brush it and charge it. If you let any of them go too long without doing them, tattletail whines until you do. And this voice is of the fingernails on a chalkboard variety. It never shuts up. And even after you do these things, it whines about other things. It keeps talking. In the early levels you really aren't in any danger at all making you wonder why you have to be so quiet all the time. It never really explains why. Then suddenly you are afraid of another toy called Mama which it doesn't really accurately explain but rather you are instruced via an abstract little scene. Then it becomes like FNAF. Now strangely enough while I found the distant pinpoint eyes great I wasn't as scared by them like say when I saw them in the recent IT. Probably because they were used so much it ceased becoming a fear thing and was more just part of gameplay. And the jumpscare itself (which happens a LOT) never ever shocked me out of my seat like Freddy, Bonnie, and Foxy did. I don't know why. Maybe the music. Maybe the animation wasn't really spooky enough but more satire and funny looking? Perhaps if the shocks were scarier I would not have minded some of the plotholes. Like if this thing is getting me killed, then why don't I put it down. Why don't I call for help? Oh yes that reminds me that there is a door to your mother's room that you can pound on til your fingers bleed and nothing will happen. This smacks of comedy sure. This also smacks of a developer trolling us. No help will come. Where are the parents. We find evidence (I think ) that you are being raised by a single mother. Well the fact that an option says "Knock on Mom's door". But then the logic breaks down night after night, day after day. And is this toy really bullying you? There's fear in that. In fact I was scared from the beginning of this game when I was walking around in a dark house alone and once the furby I mean tattletail carrying started I wanted to shoot myself. Really the fear left because of gameplay and annoyance at that voice. Perhaps a different actor would have made that part more palatable. There is also an extension called Kaleidoscope which continues the story in quite a neat science fictiony way. More logical in its logic than the previous bits. I wanted to get through this game. I wanted better. I wanted more. Everything in my head about this game was scarier than the things that actually happened. And I was stuck doing night four for what seemed an eternity, constantly failing because of something out of my control. I think there's the rub. The game at least is cheapish and when on sale I'd suggest playing it. But there will be fingernails...on a blackboard. And the voiceacting in the expansion gets so much worse. And there's something else audibly irritating to add to all the Tattletailing. Whenever you are making noise, it puts a megaphone icon in the corner of your screen and beeps in a high-pitched, dog-summoning tone until you stop. Does this increase tension? Yes. Does this increase the irritation? Yes. It really feels like the game is nagging you to death.

I love Dateline and Murder Mystery books------This was like a glorious interactive version of that genre.  There are still unanswered questions and 2 very strong theories from folks who have completed the game (seriously thesis paper length theories from fans).  The actress is AMAZING.  Her Story is better than most of the movies I've seen in the last few years.  It gave me chills at one point.  I waited till this game was on sale for half price and it was delicious.

The gist:
"Her Story" is an experimental game in which you explore a murder case from 20 years before. The game gives you a database of 270 short video clips that show the victim's wife during several interviews at the police station. Gameplay consists solely of entering search terms into that database, and watching the clips that the search resulted in, which will give you ideas for further search terms. There is no (obvious) way to see the clips in chronological order, and you only see the wife's replies to the detective's questions. You never see or hear the detective. Your task is to understand what happened those 20 years ago, and why.
I found the story well-designed and interesting to explore - it provides a good amount of detail, you learn a bit about other characters and their backgrounds, and there are several revelations that kept me engaged and gave me a sense of progression. The non-linear presentation enhances the mystery (by never giving you complete information) and fosters immersion (by letting you feel like a detective exploring a set of data). The non-linearity also makes it possible to discover some very revealing bits early on, but the story is complex enough to not give all of its secrets away easily.
The acting of Viva Seifert is spot-on. This is not immediately obvious because her role doesn't give her many opportunities to show off - most of the time, she is supposed to play a realistic British middle-aged woman in a rather formal situation. But after closing the game, I realized that I had just watched the same single person talking monologues for 90+ minutes, without me ever getting tired of it, and without her ever giving me the impression that the scene was rehearsed. That's pretty impressive.
The game is quite short. All the clips combined amount to 95 minutes of footage, and you probably only need to watch one third of that to get the gist of the story. My own rather thorough playthrough took 2 hours, and then I spent two more for finding all the clips and getting one rather obscure achievement. It seems possible to "finish" the game in 45 minutes while understanding most (but not all) of the story. The game has no replay value, actually it defies the concept of replayability entirely. You cannot 'restart' a game that consists solely of collecting static information and piecing it together in your mind, though you can of course go back and look for more info, as long as you haven't seen all the clips already.
The game is heralded as being very innovative, probably more so than it actually deserves. "Dear Esther" experimented with non-linear storytelling 3 years earlier (though "Her Story" does it much better). "Tesla Effect" proved one year earlier that FMV has a place in modern gaming, and had much higher production values for its clips. "Cloud Chamber" already used FMV in an "explorable database" setting that was, due to the integration of social gameplay, considerably more innovative than its plain implementation in "Her Story". The main achievement of "Her Story", I think, is to condense the benefits of FMV into a minimalistic setting that allows for shooting 95 minutes of footage, and telling an intricate story, while still keeping the production cost low. Another potential achievement is that the game might be very appealing to people who aren't gamers already, but enjoy watching detective stories; it seems suitable for introducing TV watchers to the gaming hobby by adding a bit of interactivity to an experience they are already familiar with. The game does not require any gamer skills, they only need to observe, listen, and enter terms in a search box.
"Her Story" has gathered considerable praise in the media, and consequentially some customer backlash. It's the usual controversy around an experimental game that gets hyped up to a mainstream audience, which may have different expectations about games. On metacritic, the game currently has a critics' score of 85, and a user score of less than 60, and the Steam forums sport several of the usual "this isn't even a game" complaint threads. I think that this particular complaint is silly - it reminds me of old people trying to tell me 30 years ago that Rock music wasn't music just because it didn't have the instruments or melodies they liked. But I can understand why "Her Story" may disappoint players who focus their gaming on action, overt puzzles, or traditional means of interactivity. If your enjoyment of a game depends on the presence of these things, then I don't recommend "Her Story" to you. However, if you appreciate a well-crafted narrative and good acting, and enjoy unraveling a "detective story"-type mystery by observing clues, then the game is definitely worth a try. In that case, give it a shot, it's not expensive (even less so when discounted). :)

Reviewing this one is a tough call. There are so many things wrong here that a non-recommendation looks obvious - however, it manages to be fun at times despite all the flaws.
The best part is the actual sniping - the game seems to simulate it quite well, and when the level design doesn't get in the way (it often does), then the game is quite enjoyable. It has flaws, but it's still fine.
On the "however" list are, however:
- The aforementioned level design. Rails all the way, and narrow ones, even. Situations are heavily scripted, and the environment is often anti-stealth, with no other options than being discovered.
- Enemies dumb as hell. To compensate, they have eagle sight and pinpoint accuracy. They see your muzzle flash if you shoot their friend from 200 metres while they show their backs. Or, they don't realize their friend is actually dead and keep talking to him. Flip the coin.
- For some reason, the game has standard FPS sections, which are purely horrible. No more words wasted here.
- Unrealistic situations. Example: your friends keep screaming for sniper support when they are hardly outnumbered and have safe cover. All they'd have to do is sit on their bums for 30 seconds while I take out all the attackers, who are not that keen on a suicide rush in any case. But they don't, and you can fail missions that way.
And then again, on the upside - it still has quicksave.
So how can I recommend it? Be aware of its flaws and buy it at heavy discount. After all, you can always refund it.

Wow, only 8 hours in-game and I'm already thinking this is a solid 9/10 as far as sandboxes go. There's a lot of things I absolutely love about this game, such as:
The fact you can see Team Members/Your Home via arrows on your screen (Loved this in Don't Starve Together)
They make it easy for you to craft your respawn point and it's not one use (step up from Ark)
Also love the way the land claiming system works and how you can upgrade the amount of protected space you have
Can't get enough of the fact that you can travel between PVE/PVP/Faction Zones at will (Loved this part about Albion Online to an extent) Really makes you feel like you've got the best of all worlds, if you want to live on the wild side and live/fight in the PVP zones you can, or if you want to play it safe and stick to the safe zones you could still travel to the PVP zones whenever you wanted.
And they balanced it a bit by making it so if you built something outside of your domain (your dominium) it would start to decay and eventually be destroyed. Causing you to be very careful about what you place and how you place it.
Not to mention it's really not grindy at all, I've only been at it for 8 hours and have already got a shelter, anvil, stone oven, workbench, multiple storage containers, dry tanning rack, all incased in a box of wooden fences followed by another layer of wooden fences stretching all the way around my upgraded dominium. (Hated the grind of Life is Feudal because it felt like you couldn't do it all yourself but here they totally change that.)
Only thing that I could say really about having a gripe with the game is the hunger system. The hunger goes down extremely fast so be prepared for that if you're looking to get into the game. Look into crafting a bow as soon as you can and start leveling your archery to make sure you can start racking up the raw meat. That's the only thing that makes it a 9/10 instead of a 10/10 for me. Other than that it's a really really REALLY good sandbox.
I've got to say without a doubt it's one of the best sandboxes I've played to date, and for the price of 13.49 (regular price 14.99) it's practically a steal for avid sandbox lovers. This one is definitely worth a try and I have to recommend to all who are wondering about it. With our without friends!

The Masterplan is an entertaining game and concept, however the -constant- crashes at this early access stage ruins the fun, and I find it difficult to complete heists at times.

The learning curve is stiff, and the controls are a little odd at first, but the game's not too punishing that it's a hassle. Once you figure out what you're supposed to be doing, this is one of the best heist games ever made, if not the best. The threat of violence always trumps violence, and stealth is to be preferred, if not always feasible. You control the crowds as well as you can, and if things go♥♥♥♥♥♥up, it turns into a smash-and-grab, trying to get out before the cops arrive and you end up in a firefight, which will at best be expensive (you're responsible for paying for "cleanup") and at worst devastating, with a party member dying. It's like a very slow-paced, straighter, prettier Hotline Miami, if Hotline Miami was about working your way from knocking over convenience stores to robbing Fort Knox. I haven't heard a ton of buzz about this, but it's been occupying my attention for short bursts for the past few weeks.

After the flawed but interesting Codename 47, Hitman 2 is a step in the right direction. Everything here, from the stealth to the score by Jesper Kyd, is improved tenfold over the first game. But this is from 2002, and although it runs on a modern low-end computer damn well (although a few tweaks are needed to raise the resolution), it's a game limited by its engine. Silent Assassin wants to be two things at once - a stealth puzzle game, where the most direct solution is rarely the best, and an action game where the aforementioned action is detrimental to the player.
It succeeds... mostly. In Silent Assassin, 47 returns from a short hiatus to rescue a kidnapped priest he worked for. This quest takes him from Sicily to Japan, Thailand to Russia. It's visually decent although marred by simplistic models and animations that, while impressive in 2002, look odd in 2016. Anyone looking for a challenge should invest in Silent Assassin; the perfect hit takes patience and the will to experiment with approaches. If you found Blood Money or Contracts too hard, Silent Assassin is not your friend. Certain levels are downright tedious to sit through as a result of one  mistake, and each misstep is punished accordingly. Though almost unrecognisable to the later games (containing no accident kills or elaborate assassination methods), Silent Assassin is worth your time - if you've got the patience for it.

The GAMEPLAY also has some much needed improvements: the controls are a lot more "mainstream", I had a hard time to find a suitable configuration to play Codename 47. Just like any other respecful Hitman game, you have tons of creative options to take out your targets. Poison, silenced weapons, sniper rifles, malee, the iconic fibre wire... Hell, you can even get some anesthetic and go for a non-lethal approach towards the guards (it is HARD AS ♥♥♥♥ tho).
This time a loud and dumb approach can be an actual option, as I said there's tons of weapons to choose from, it's all up to you.
The graphics...well of course they don't hold up, but the maps really give you a sense of scale. They're REALLY HUGE.
THE SOUNDTRACK! OH MY GOD THE SOUNDTRACK! The music in this game is GLORIUS, and they know it, they shove it in your face as soon as you start the game up. There are soooo many epic tracks. It is SURELY ONE OF THE BEST IN GAMING HISTORY.
Of course it has some minor issues, for example, it felt short, at least for me. I finished it in a little more than 10 hours, and I scored professional in almost every missions, even silent assassin in a few of them, which should take longer.

But overall, this game is really solid. It's worth it just for the soundtrack. I'm listening at it while i'm writing this review and oh man... THE chills...

Got this game during the weekly sale for $0.99 USD, and it is definitely worth paying and playing if you enjoy action platformers.
If you like platformers, chaining different combos for that wonderful score multiplier, and large areas to explore, then you will really like this game.
The aesthetics are very good with lots of detail in the environment. The music is nice and is appropriate for the action and atmosphere.
The controls are not overly complicated, however, chaining different combos can be fairly challenging. The learning curve is moderate, again with most of the difficulty due to the combos (if you care about increasing your multiplier to maximize your score). I strongly suggest using a control instead of the keyboard. You do not use the mouse when you play this game (even in the menu screen).
I think the game may not be fully optimized for Windows 8.1, as I cannot seem to be able to change the resolution to anything besides the default (1280x760 i believe). If I change it to anything else, the game appears to zoom into the top left, so it seriously obscures your field of vision (impractical to play this way). I do not believe there is a resolution fix at the moment.
The game starts off with a helpful tutorial that lets you most of the available skills - its similar to the original Assassin's Creed where your character is maxed out, then you start the real game debuffed back to level 1. You even get to see the stats screen that strips away all of your skills and levels.
You have 4 different suits: regular, fire, ice, and earth. You can switch to any at will, but the elemental ones drain energy - and you will automatically switch back to regular Zack once you deplete your bar (it refills fairly quickly). Each suit has different abilities and uses. For example, the fire suit can shoot fireballs (surprise!), glide in the air, and also moves the fastest. The ice suit can slow down time (extremely useful for navigating through numerous environmental hazards) and use ice attacks, freezing enemies. The earth suit cannot jump, however, it is essential for breaking through destructible obstacles and getting to secret areas.
During combat, if you switch suits and vary your attacks, you will boost your multiplier (resulting in boosts to your score). This can be tricky to master in the beginning, especially if you are not using a controller as the keys bindings are very close to each other. The game progresses in difficulty at a reasonable pace. The first few boss fights were pretty easy to defeat.
As you pick up the collectibles, you will gain experience for levelling up. I am pretty sure leveling up is automatic, as I have not been able to select which skills to invest in (mind you, I did not get very far into the game at the time of this review). There are secret areas with collectible trinkets for the achievement hunters. The stages are pretty big, allowing you a lot of space to explore.
Overall, I think any platformer junkie should give this a try, especially if you love chaining your combos and watching that multiplier go up. There is a scrolling bar that provides feedback on your score's global ranking, as well as its comparison against any of your friends who may have the game.
Recommend.

So, this game looks super cute and fluffy, you're a little general leading your little Duplo citizens in fending off cuddly alien monsters.  The theme pays homage to Japanese monster films of Godzilla fame (there's even a Chibizilla end-stage boss), whilst the gameplay is an innovative take on the tower defence genre by mashing it up with some RTS action.
Be warned though, If you let the cutesy character design and bright lollypop colours lull you into a false sense of security, then you're going to get your cream buns handed to you on a plate.
Whilst its family friendly graphics may make it look like something that's aimed at children or at the "casual" market, it's most certainly geared towards people who have cut their gaming teeth on various tower defence games.  After two cursory simple levels to get you accustomed to the controls, it throws you in at the deep end once the kaiju appear. It's a little like paddling about in the shallows one minute and then finding yourself in dangerous Kaiju-infested waters the next.  I was definitely caught off-guard when I expected the entirety of stage 1 to be a breeze, instead, I found myself barely passing level 1.2 by the skin of my teeth!  (WTF? Level 1.2? I guess it turns out that I'm crappy at tower defence games after all?)
That's a pretty steep difficulty curve, I can only presume that they've decided it to ratchet it up right from the beginning as a way to offset that cutesy image.  It ensures that your first impression is that at its core, this is a serious game, it just happens to be wrapped in a sweet candy shell.  Ultimately, I'm glad that it does so, often times, I feel that the hand-holding portion of some games last a little too long, and if you're familiar with a genre this can make for a boring experience.
My playing style generally means I keep replaying levels I've already completed (I like seeing a neat row of gold before moving on to the next level rather than blasting straight through the game) so I found upgrading my weapons and stuff relatively simple.  As such, it didn't feel like a particularly grind-y game to me, i.e. I didn't have to repeatedly replay levels that I'd already gone gold on just to get the research points.
The first playthrough of any level can be a little bewildering so some players may become frustrated when they find it super difficult, but I relished the real challenge of developing the best strategy to approach each level.
There is a unique scenario for each level, so you never feel like you're playing a "filler" level which keeps things interesting, and keeps the urgency and "panic" cranked up to 11.  (Did I mention how cute your little minions look when they panic and run around after they've been hit?  Annoying mid-game, but they do look ever so sweet.)
The music is ok, I guess it's kind of generic sci-fi game music, each continent had its own theme, but I could barely tell the difference, to be honest.
It's moderately paced, with a driving rhythm such that even when you're in the quiet lull at the beginning of each level, there's a sense of urgency.  Whilst repetitive, it's saving grace is the fact that it's not obnoxious and annoying.
I'm an avid point'n'click adventure game fan, so I love a good story.  But let's be honest, these kinds of games are all about the action and the story such as it is only exists to provide a scenario with thematic level/character design and a bit of glue to tie everything together.  In this instance it's: Monsters Attack!! Save the earth!  Kill them, kill them with fire!
I guess I should reserve judgement on the story, though as I'm not even halfway through the game yet.  There could be a massive twist awaiting me for all I know.
The story is told, quite charmingly, with comic strip panels and a little bit of instructional dialogue.  Kaiju Panic keeps things light with splashes of humour and pop culture references which make for a fun game with quite a few genuine laugh out loud moments.
So, ultimately, would I recommend it?  It depends... are you a fan tower defence games?  Are you calm and collected with a steely determination in the face of adversity?  In which case, yes, the game is a fun and refreshing take on the genre, and if you're a bit of a completionist, then there's many many hours of gameplay that you'll be able to squeeze out of it.
+ Looks cute, easy on the eyes
+ Fun, refreshing take on a tired genre
+ Richly designed levels and monsters
- Music may not be annoying, but unfortunately it's kind of unmemorable
- Difficulty curve is possibly a little too steep at the outset

tl;dr: The game feels unfinished, unpolished and offers only very mediocre hack & slash gameplay. Also, it's not even close to being a rogue-like as one of its user-defined tags suggests.
Dungeon graphics resemble Zelda (A Link to the Past) graphics. The 5th (last) screenshot on the store page points this out, and it touches the border from homage to blatant plagiarism.
If you can get over all the flaws mentioned before, you get a game that primarily focuses on equipment grind. You find items with different stat bonuses to finetune your character, and you gain stats each level based on the kind of attacks you used. The monsters level along with you, but do this in a rather strange fashion. Monsters I could one-shot when I first met them suddenly took a lot more hits after I finished a dungeon. The loot is random and there is no inventory to save your items. You carry only what you have equiped and leave the rest behind. You also don't have any consumables.
If you are attracted by the "rogue-like" tag, then I must disappoint you. The game has no procedural level generation (at least, the areas look so much alike it's hard to say. Starting a new game drops you at a different area, though, but on my third game I got the feeling this is the only random part of the level generation), no turn-based gameplay, and there is no tile-based movement/graphics. This game offers perma-death, but gives you extra-live(s), and it has randomized loot. Perhaps this is what the definition of rogue-like has boiled down to.

I Like this game, most levels take multiple play throughs to get 3/3 objectives (Stars, in most other games), and although I can understand grinding may make it easier I have not had to do any grinding for upgrades yet (2 of 6 worlds complete). The biggest advantage in the second play through is knowing the enemy types and directions, as there are four tower types in this game and each is very effective at countering certain types of enemies. Using the right tower types in the right zones is key to winning, unlocking all of the upgrades is not required.
The actual gameplay is a lot like revenge of the titans, where you have harvestors and turrets and have to defend with the limited resources that your harvestors provide, except you actually have to collect said resources and build the towers within your characters range. You are also encouraged to be close to the enemies to pickup science upgrade points for your permanent upgrades to towers / character. I find that this keeps me busy for every map on the first play through and only on repeat playthroughs (If I missed objectives) do I find myself with enough time to wait for the waves to spawn.
The game provides a fun amount of challenge and gives you the tools to overcome it.

While at its' heart Kaiju Panic is a tower defense game, the game actually does some new things that distinguishes itself from other tower defense games.
To gather resources Kaiju Panic borrows from the RTS genre where you need to build extractors that gather resources from deposits on the map. In each level you can also rescue civilians which you can use to man your turrets (increasing their power) or use them to build towers faster or repair damaged towers. The tower defense mechanics in the game are also pretty good. These two mechanics make Kaiju Panic stand out among a lot of the other tower defenses out there.
When talking about Kaiju Panic you need to bring up the art style which is fantastic. The graphics are cutesy but are really well done.
The art style hides the fact that Kaiju Panic is not an easy tower defense. I would say that it is a medium to hard tower defense. The game requires a lot of trial and error and at times you might have to grind to get enough research points to purchase new upgrades.
While Kaiju Panic might not be for everyone, I liked it. I thought it was a good tower defense. If you don't like tower defenses I don't think it will change your mind. Due to the price of $20 I can't really recommend it to people who only casually enjoy tower defenses. I would recommend that these people wait for a sale on the game. If you really like the theme and tower defenses though I think you will like Kaiju Defense.

Note: I received a free review copy of the game.

FULL DISCLOSURE: I was given a press copy of this game prior to release. It is your right to disregard my opinion based on this fact, but I assure you that this has never affected, and WILL never affect, the way in which I construct this or any other review I write.
If you’d prefer a video version of this review have a look here:
Kaiju Panic, a new Tower Defence kind-of-action hybrid developed by Mechabit Limted. This is their first game on Steam, they’ve released a couple of smaller games and one or two VR games but for all intents and purposes I consider this their first major release.
As I said, it’s a tower defence game, but it has some atypical elements to it. I called it kind-of-action, but that’s not even really accurate. You basically play this game from a perspective that you’d imagine wouldn’t really mesh with the genre. Though I have to say it’s been done before by Orcs Must Die, and Orcs Must Die manages to achieve this gameplay from an even stranger perspective. Though, Kaiju Panic certainly has it’s unique elements and we’ll get into that in a sec.
Presentation
The game looks good. The art style certainly stands out and it was, as it usually is, the reason I requested a review copy of this game in the first place. Presentation is massively important and I feel, while it doesn’t blow me away, it certainly does the job. It’s bright, colourful, and varied between the different locations in the game. The character design I found to be pretty cute, and I while I liked the enemy design, aside from a few exceptions, the enemies were relatively generic looking. The boss-type enemies were definitely the highlight we’re talking design. They looked pretty sweet.
Mechanics
The game is standard in a few ways as you’d expect; you have a base that you need to protect from enemies that will, usually, make a beeline to the base. I say usually because about half-way through the game the enemy AI is upgraded, and they begin calculating the best places to focus their efforts which is pretty cool. I love it when games find a way to up the difficulty without turning all of the enemies into damage sponges. Really refreshing. There’s also a ton of variety, aside from the upgraded AI there’s also the lab that you can use to purchase new technology with research points -- though that’s pretty standard. You have three different types of weapons -- Cannon, Laser and Acid; they all serve different purposes, and you’ll find yourself using them all, which is nice to see. There’s also a bunch of unique mechanics; the currency you use to build weapons are these crystals. So, at the beginning of every level you must construct mining devices, and I found myself gathering people to help me while the crystal was being mined. Getting people to help you is probably the coolest mechanic of the game, where you can order civilians to man certain weapons and each civilian has their own strengths that can help add to your turrets. It’s got a really deep strategy to it and, as a tip for you if you choose to play this game, MAN THE TURRETS. I spend the first couple hours or so losing to the 5th level because I underestimated the importance of placing civilians on turrets.
Story
Story’s ok. Serves it’s purpose. Like the presentation, it’s good, but nothing to write home about. It’s there to give context to the gameplay, and that is totally fine. I don’t want to undervalue the importance of context in games, because games without any context feel slightly soulless. They feel like a tech-demo rather than a full game, and this game certainly feels like a full game. I guess what I’m saying is: it’s good the story is there, but no one is going to playing this game FOR the story. It’s super simple, like Mario saving Peach.

Verdict
Now, Kaiju Panic is $20. That seems like a lot, but hear me out. The game is long. There’s a lot of content here. Now, I’ll fully admit that I haven’t finished the entire game, but it took me around 6 hours to reach the third area, and there are six areas. Generally the levels in the third area were longer than in the second area, and the second longer than the first. I could easily see, on the high-end, this being a 15 hour game, and on the low end being a 10 hour game. That’s also backed up by the fact that new elements were being introduced in the third area, and there were tons of different weapons that I hadn’t bought yet in the lab; so the content is relatively high quality. So, is it worth $20? I’m gonna say yes if you’re going to play a lot of this game. One of the reasons I couldn’t finish it before release - and by the way I like it so I will finish it - is because I couldn’t play it in long stretches. In my opinion this game is best experiences over a long period of time where you keep coming back for more.

In 1998, when I was eight, my mum took me and my younger brother's furbies, and strategically placed them around her apartment. Mechanical, fuzzy sentries. She had grown tired of he and I sneaking around once the lights were out. Gobbling candy and leftovers and stealthily playing on our Playstation.
Somehow, when we rose that night, thinking our mum was asleep, the two of us failed to notice the animatronic creatures were missing from our room. We carefully padded through the apartment, giggling like goblins. Only for us to scream at the top of our lungs when a furby lit up on the hall table, and proclaimed its love for us.
Our mum, needless to say, was not pleased.
Tattletail lets me relive that PTSD-inducing night of childhood terror. Thank the Gaming Gods it exists. It's nigh therapeutic! (And pretty funny too)

I was given a furby as a child and kept it on a shelf in my room. I didn't play with it often and every once in a while it would wake up in the night and yell in that gravely, low-battery skewed voice "feed me please." I hated that thing but childhood guilt wouldn't allow me to throw it out or give it to Goodwill.
This game reminded me of how much I hated that thing, so I think this is a good game because it cements that hatred even further so I don't feel stupid for still holding onto said childish grudge that I didn't even know I still had.

I really expected to lke this game more than I do. The premise is very clever, and the visuals are well-done for a Unity budget title, but the gameplay feels very much like a more free-roam take on Five Nights at Freddy's, which I just don't find particularly interesting or scary. The core gameplay revolves around getting out of bed, finding Tattletail, doing whatever activities the game's objective prompts tell you to do, all while keeping your flashlight charged (which drops way too fast) and keeping Tattletail charged, fed, and groomed (those meters also drop way too fast). If you fail to do so, Tattletail will start making all kinds of noise, and the Tattletail Mama will find you and kill you (with a jump-scare right out of FNAF).
Bottom line, if you're the sort who thinks Five Nights at Freddy's is a neat horror series, and you want to try something new, you'll probably really dig Tattletail. But if you're like me and find managing meters to avoid canned jump-scares a poor excuse for horror, I'd recommend you stay away from this one.

Often called a MOBA-Shooter, Battleborn is (at least in my opinion) quite far away from that. Its a team-based Shooter which takes some elements to MOBAs.
It has distinct hero classes, at release 25 which will get expanded to 30. The heroes are highly specialized, everyone serves its specific purpose, but are not very flexible. If you want to play solo, that could make things tricky as not every hero is supposed to do that and can fail, depending on the mission. During a mission or match, every hero can level up 10 times, with each level a new, passive bonus from two (or sometimes three if you have them unlocked) can be chosen. Each hero as a number of skills which are available from the start except for the ultimate ability, which are often very strong and are onlucked upon reaching level 5. In each mach, three pieces of gear can be take with which provide more passive bonuses, but can also have negative sides. Gear can be aquiered by playing the coop missions or by buying lootboxes with ingame currency, which is awarded after completing a game. In general the game is heavy on the unlocks, only five characters are available from the start, they all have additional choices for their passives to be unlocked as well as cosmetic stuff.
If you expected and epic campaign with a long playtime, then you've come to the wrong place.
It consits of eight missions (and a prologue), which can all be done in around 30mins. They are pretty linear and only offer a handfull of different objectives: get to a certain point, defend it from waves of enemies or escort a sentinel (spider-like robot) to a specified location. The environments offer a good variety and the levels are in general well done. The story does not use its potential, the story and setting are interesting, but only very little is done with it, as it is simply to short for that. It also tries to emulate the Borderlands humor, but tries to hard and instead goes for lots of swears (which are all censored).
Its not that the story mode seems like a complete afterthought, but it does not live up to its potential.
The competitive multiplayer has three modes: Caputre, which is your basic domination mode: three points, stay near them to capture them and earn points, first to 1000 points wins. Nothing bad, but also nothing too exiting. In Incursion the goal is to destroy the two enemy sentries while defending your own. This mode has the most in common with a MOBA, but still plays quite different. You can hire mercenaries and giant minions in addtion to the ones that automatically spawn in waves and walk towards the enemy sentry. My personal favorite is Meltdown, where you must escort minions to a grinder to sacrifice them to earn points, the goal is 500 and bigger minions bring more points, reaching the halfway point will move the grinders to a new, a lot harder to reach location. I like this mode since it does not focus so much on taking out enemy heroes, I've played quite a few games where the enemy team got a lot of kills but still lost horribly. Controlling the minions is key.
If your looking for a coop-successor for Borderlands, Battleborn is not your game, as its focus lies with the competitive modes. Those are very well done and complex, mastering a character and mode can take quite some time. There is a coop campaign, but its no match for any Borderlands game and serves better as place to play around with different characters and gear before going into the competitive modes.

I want to write a personally honest review, so here we go. My experience with Battleborn has been pretty great so far. It's not a perfect game, but it brings things that interest me into a FPS arena, delivering some pretty fun gameplay in the process.
For the positives, my favorite thing has got to be the characters. There is just a lot of variety. Each character has their own gameplay nuances and their personality quirks are really entertaining. My second favorite thing is the MOBA style gameplay. I tried a few MOBAs before, enough to get the gist of the core mechanics, but at the time I wasn't really interested in the point-click aspect of it. Battleborn really solves that problem for me, combining FPS skill/style with MOBA-like strategy/goals. Ganking, feeding, harassing, wandering, ... fun stuff. I thought I wouldn't do so great, but at it's core it's a shooter. I did fine.
For the negatives, there's a fair number of starting maps, but they're divided amongst the game modes. For a few modes, there's a clear preferred map. It would be nice to get more maps. I haven't experienced as much MM problems as others have, but I would like better lobbying. Sometimes you meet-up with people that are fun to play with and just want more of a good thing. I think they patched in something along those lines, but in general I prefer having a list of my favorite servers with their various server configs/mods and usual suspects (e.g. valve style).
All-in-all I recommend this game. I'm 130+ hours in and it's been a blast, but I still need to try out all the characters. (I stuck to a few that I liked, but recently I've been forcing myself to try new heroes and .. now I have new favorites.) At this point, I just want more loot, more maps, more characters, more gankings, MOAR! (Seriously though, it's a fun game. Check it out if you can.)
(I checked the box that I received this product for free, because I did. I also bought a console copy, though.)
Seriously, don't buy until matchmaking is fixed.  You will spend hours of your life looking at a waiting screen... If that is your thing, then this game is for you.

The best word to sum up SteamWorld Dig is "transparent".
The game loop consists entirely of going into the mine, collecting ore, going back up, selling it, buying +1 to your pick, and repeating. It is an extremely mindless and unchallenging way to spend 3 hours. It's not fun or interesting at any point.
I get it. All games require some sort of loop to keep you playing it and keeping the feel consistent. But SteamWorld is, as I said, completely transparent. Nothing exciting or shocking happens, there are no interesting puzzles to solve, challenging monsters to battle, or interesting characters to talk to. There's nowhere to explore, and nowhere to go but deeper into the mine, where the gems are a new color and the numbers are bigger.
If, like me, you play this game to the end, you will hate it and yourself all the way through for being so obviously manipulated into dull, glassy-eyed complacency by a skinner box's "reward" of a bigger number next to your mining pick. Do yourself a favor and don't buy it - and if you have bought it, just say no. Life's too short for this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

For those that don't know, or are interested in buying;
.. with polished gameplay with many awesome features and unique and appealing graphics. There is a lot to this game and I'm going to try and cover most of it.
When I first bought this game, I was dissapointed. The first mission is quite confusing to someone who has never seen gameplay or a video of how it's done and the game's version of a 'tutorial' is confusing and quite unhelpful. This, being a con. However because of easy controls and UI you will figure it out within a minute or so. After you complete missions you go back to your hideout, which, is mostly pointless other than for you to mail order yourself weapons and accessories, or to hire another goon (Hitman/robber/whatever you want to call it). The more goons the better. Once onto levels with security you will want to hire another goon and make sure two of your three goons have guns. It takes two guns pointed at guard(s) to make their resistance level stay at 0 (Full circle), while your third goon beats them up. The gameplay is quite fluid and there is no pause button, but there is slow motion which is essentially the same thing except that the game is still moving. (reaaaaally slowww)
Due to the top down, slow paced aspect the game can probably run on any PC or laptop. The graphics aren't really changeable (Not like you would want/need to). And the game rarely crashes and doesn't ever crash on startup (for me, and I haven't seen any crash on startup reports on the forums). The developers and moderators on the forums, to those interested in the community, are very very nice. They seem to be open to critisism and are nice to the players and those asking questions on the forums. They reply to nearly every post, crash log, bug report, suggestion, etc etc.
Lets talk about how the game does in its genres.
. Very strategical, will have you dieing/running to your car from cops/shooting cops, picking places to hold people up, hide bodies, etc. Needs some working on the paths your goons follow but that is it.
. Not in 5 as bad but 5 as in it depends how you play. If you are the other 50% you will refrain from any 'action' and only hold people up and knock them out. If you are the other 50% you will be seeing lots of action, like shooting at cops, security, civilians, running to your car before the police show up, etc. So it heavily depends on how you choose to play.
. Most people are probably suprised when I classified this as a Puzzle game, however, most players would agree. It's not really a puzzle game, it just has puzzle aspects of it. The whole mission is essentially a puzzle that you have to figure out how to get through a room and get the pieces inside of it using means of holding people up, telling hostages what to do, hiding bodies, locking doors and lots more. Since the game only has puzzle aspects, and isn't a puzzle game. So if you aren't into puzzle games, but this title has caught your eye, keep looking. If you are looking for puzzle games, this isn't one.
Now, to other qualities of the game..
. It has its own unique, and good looking style of graphics. Whereas, if you are looking for an HD clean realistic looking graphics, you won't find it here.
. The game has bugs/glitches but they are few and far between. Most that get reported get patched that same day/week.
. Challenging as hell, exciting, keeps you on the edge of your chair hoping you don't slip up and ruin your heist.

Slowly belly-crawling through the underbrush, I scan the distance for signs of enemy troops. I come to a sudden stop; inexplicably, an invisible wall blocks my forward progress. I crawl to the edge of the brush, frantically run across an exposed trail, and into the foliage to the left of the path, figuring that a different route might be in order, but I'm stymied again as I find myself stuck on a rock that raises only six inches off the ground. Finally, I find a way past these obstacles in the brush and silently arrive at my GPS designated destination marker, but my objective won't clear. I give up. Defeated, I walk back up the hill, walk down the path, which triggers a voiceover, which enables the GPS marker, which spawns enemies on the path ahead of me that kill me.

Hitman 2: Silent Assassin
A classic entry in the Hitman series which sparked many sequels, Hitman 2 is a solid, fun stealth title.
+ There are many different ways you can approach missions - poisoning the food or water of your target without being detected, choking them with fiber wire, using silenced guns or just running in rambo and ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥up. Maybe you want to cause a power outage by turning a generator off, then slitting their throat in the dark. Fancy placing a bomb on a target's helicopter and watching it expode? It's all possible. The ability to choose how you will carry out your hit is pretty cool.
+ Lots of unique disguises to use, which vary according to mission. From the typical bodyguard attire to dressing as a doctor to infilitrate hospital surgery rooms, or as a pizza delivery boy - you'll have many options to pursue when trying to reach your target.
+ Huge array of weapons to select prior to each assassination. You do need to collect these guns throughout the game's levels to have access to them however. You've got submachineguns, M60s, assault rifles, crossbows, desert eagles, revolvers, silenced pistols, multiple shotguns...numerous sniper rifles - tonnes.
+ I loved the variety of missions available. You'll travel to Russia for assassinations then to Germany, Japan, Singapore and India. Each segment contributes to the overall story of Hitman 2, which I thought was pretty clever (no spoilers on that).
+ Awesome music throughout the game. Really helps you feel like an assassin and a badass one at that. Truly top notch.
- Graphics haven't aged well, but the game is old so no surprise there. Not a real problem but it should be noted regardless.
- Clipping issues (at least with the steam version). Check my screenshots for examples. Enemies walking through trucks seemed to be the major one.
- One of the biggest problems with Hitman 2 is the lack of information you're given on how the game works - how enemies interact with your decisions. If I dress up as a bodyguard, will civilians be suspicious of my outfit? Or will it just be other guards? If I dress as a doctor, will guards see through it easily or will civilians? No one tells you how the suspicion metre in Hitman 2 actually operates. Sometimes it seems to do whatever it wants.
For instance, in one hit I placed a smoke bomb in a laundry chute to activate the fire alarms and then sneaked into the firefighter quarters, taking a uniform. I walked out and towards the metal detectors - then a civilian INSTANTLY recognises me (without the suspicion bar even rising) and alerts the guards. Why? I still can't figure out how this happened. Same deal with one assassination I had in a hospital. Dressed as a doctor, I shot a guard dead with a silenced pistol and concealed his body. But the nurse somehow alerts the guards, even though there's a ♥♥♥♥ing BLACKOUT because I cut power to the generator. Certain parts of the game don't add up logically.
- Difficulty is outrageous on anything over normal. Enemies see through disguises straight away, leaving you no choice but to mass murder your way to the target. Pretty poor design really, making the whole point of the game (silence and stealth) impossible rather than a challenge.
Overall Score: 8/10

At the beginning I have to deny some informations pointed in negative reviews.
- Button delay - I had no problems like this one. Controling character was intuitive and easy.
- Graphics issues - I've played Zack for over 10 hours and I never had any problems with visual side of game.
- Game crash a lot - Never happened to me... not even once.
- Bugs - During gameplay I saw only one type of bugs - in-game enemies.
I do not know why so many people have problems with this game, but maybe you should learn how to properly configure your Windows and gamepads before you blame developers for all the evils of this world?
This is not a hardcore platformer. Even Steam achievements are enough easy to make 100% and get another "perfect game". It's a platformer, where you can experiment while searching for hidden objects. Even if you fail, game saves your progress every time you do a few steps, so it's not a problem to do searches like "I don't think there's a precipice, but let's check that place just in case...".
Puzzles are not very challenging and even a child should be able to resolve all of them very quickly.
As everyone can see on screenshots game is maintained in cartoon style, which is very similar to Pixar movies. In my personal opinion it's a good option for 2,5D productions like Zack. Animations are fine and cutscenes are quite interesting.
In-game music stimulates the atmosphere appropriate places, but is definitely not memorable. I forgot it already, and just 2 days have passed since I've finished this game.
Story is trivial, but be serious... do you seriously expect every game to be Sherlock-Holmes-Story-Telling-Level?
In Zack Zero storyline fits gameplay and game concept. I think it's more than enough.
I can truly recommend this game to young players and for everyone who like platformers, but not hardore ones where you can easily break your gamepad.
