tl;dr: Its like Borderlands 2, Serious Sam, and Helldivers all had a glorious baby together.
Do you love the chaos and waves of enemies from Serious Sam? Did you enjoy taking over worlds for the sake of freedom (and sometimes saving lives and other nonsense) like in Helldivers? Did you spend so many hours in Borderlands 2 that you don't know how you didn't wither away into a husk wrapped around your computer? Good. Then you'll probably love this game.
I loved all of those games listed above, but I was jaded after the experience in Borderlands: TPS. I was reluctant to get this game, so I spent too much time looking at videos and reviews rather than trying the game out. Obviously, I heard everyone elses opinions and didn't really experience it myself. I finally bought it and I realize now I should have done it much earlier. I don't really care about the fight that is going on between this game and its competetor. I wanted a game that when my friends weren't around, I could play single player, and especially a single player that didn't feel like an extended tutorial for the online portion of the game. I have spent so much time in just the single player option I keep logging in and thinking "I should probably play more online..." but then I click on the storyline once again.
The difference of playstyles that each character brings to the table is pretty fantastic. Sure you don't get the millions of guns that you did in any of the Borderlands, but you do get different gear and loadouts that you can set up that you can pop on to whatever character you want. There is lore and achievements for each character and more skins and taunts to unlock while you do that.
Overall this game as worked its way into the many different tastes of video games that I enjoy. When I just want to chill out and kill stuff, I have single player. When my friends log on and want to co-op, I can do that. When we all want to team up and challenge people online, we have that too. And with the achievements and lore unlocks, it gives me a reason to really want to play every character to their fullest.
Overall, I liked this game and I'm still having fun with it. I felt like it was getting pretty bad reviews so I thought I should give it my thumbs up to try to get more people to play it. I really don't regret it at all, and this game will sit in some of my permanently installed games (honestly, it may even take BL2's spot).

I have to say this game is not palatable to everyone, but still it is a fruit of painstaking work. It's not something you would usually expect when you buy a game today. The essence of this game is experience. Here is my humble advice on how to enjoy this game:

2) Focus on the feeling and emotions, not on rationality and the completion of the game.
3) Be careful. There are many elaborately designed details. How much you can acquire from this game largely depends on how many details you find.

Her Story shows that games can serve to make a linear story unravel in a way that a movie or book either couldn't achieve, or would have a lot of trouble pulling off. The player interacts with the game by typing in keywords in interviews with a woman, and as you reveal more clips, more things will be mentioned to be looked into. I never found myself without a new term leading to a revelation, and despite the low interactivity, the experience made me feel more like a detective than anything else I've ever played.
While it doesn't necessarily take advantage of all the interactivity games provide (really it's just a chopped-up set of clips from some longer videos), it's still a damn good experience that wouldn't be nearly as good without the "unraveling" quality the keyword-searching provides.

--Counter argument to those who chose not to reccomend the game--
Quite a few reviews are disatisfied due to the fact the story has a linear plot. Guess what, that's what every good story has. It's interactive, not infinite. You get to propel a character that you *influence* through a predetermined set of events. You don't *decide* the outcomes, you *choose* the outcomes. It's *choose* your own adventure not *decide* your own adventure. It's not *your* character, it's a character that you can *influence* not *create*.

I keep going back to this game from time to time. As I change as a person, my choices change, and so does the story.
As you can see, I've played this game for quite a few hours. I really enjoyed the story, and I found it highly immersive.
I could, for the most part, act in such a way as I would have wanted to if I was in such a position myself.
When facing ethical dilemmas, as the altruist that I want to be, I usually did what I thought was right. Sometimes that led to events that I hated, but that is the way the world works.
The main complaints I've seen in regards to this game, are from people whom possibly are choosing very different paths from the ones I have chosen. If you're the kind of person that loves to play the bad guy, maybe the game would unfold so dramatically differently that it simply would be a bad story. I don't know, I like being the good guy.
Still, the choices can be quite narrow, and generally depending on who and what you are as a person, it might be a good or a bad experience.
I don't know how many times I've played through this game, and does it really matter? Whether it be 5 times or 10, I know I loved it every single time.
You are the new CEO of MetaHuman Inc., and that's where the story starts, more or less. You guide the company in the direction you desire.
Do you focus on technological advancements, witchcraft, or both?
Do you try to outplay your competitors, or try to work together with them?
Throughout a year of making tough decisions, you might save humanity from a dystopian future, or be the one to reap the benefits of such a world.
Your choices matter. A small mistake can end with your romantic partner leaving you,
What drives you? Money? Power? A better future for humanity?

Super Motherload is a game about digging downward and hoarding materials.
Pros:
+Fun gameplay
+Couch co-op
+Great graphics
+Material rarity is well balanced
Cons:
-Repetitive music randomly triggers
-Some controls/mechanics unclear from the start
-Horrible bossfight
-If a player stops moving for longer than 5 seconds they disappear and have to rejoin.
-The bossfight is truly terrible
-One of the worst bossfights I've seen
Info:
This game supports local same-screen co-op, with controllers, which is great.
Explanation:
Really, the biggest issue with this game is the ending. If you don't want spoilers stop reading now.
For some reason, the developers decided to end a game with no enemies with a bossfight. Not only a bossfight, but a grueling minutes-long escape sequence during which you can easily die at any second. Quick reflexes aren't required for any part of this game until the bossfight. The bossfight is sudden, and not very well explained. You essentially have a choice of two bosses, who behave exatly the same. I played this game all the way through to the end with my girlfriend, but at the bossfight we had to quit after four or five attempts because it just wasn't getting anywhere. It's like we were playing a soccer tournament and then for the last match they decided we had to play tennis instead. Bad decision on the devs part.
Once you get to the bossfight you won't want to play anymore.
Other than that, it's really an enjoyable game. There are a few nits to pick here and there. The amount of idle time you're allowed in co-op before you get unspawned and have to rejoin isn't enough. The music seems to trigger at certain depths or something, but ends up starting at random since you're constantly changing depth. Your goal is pretty unclear when you start the game. But for the most part it's pretty enjoyable up until the very end, when it's discouragingly difficult and infuriating.

Super Motherload is very underwhelming.
First off; I really liked to original back in the day, and while this game has some advantages in that the visuals are much better than the original, it also does a lot of things worse. First of all the start of the game is rather overwhelming in that there's so many blocks at once, which of many can't be destroyed which is very annoying (in a larger extent than the original). Furthermore  the upgrade screen is a major downstep as you can't skip upgrades or see the numbers to an upgrade (I want to know how many litres different tanks hold, how fast different drill speeds are etc). There's also no way (at least I found none) to open your inventory to overlook what you're carrying and also to drop certain ores. You take much more damage from crashing in Super Motherload than in the original, and it really is annoying to have to micromanage every foot you travel, both going down AND up.
There are some quests and the first half of the game is decent gameplay this way, although the Quest-boxes being invulnerable initially (as in before you knew what they were) was yet another confusing element. As you approach the end game you come to the realization that there really aren't many high end resources available as you'd expect when you go really deep, and even to the end the world is dominated by mid-tier resources.
And then you decide to go all the way down there anyways despite being unable to farm enough to max out all your upgrades. You have no idea what the boss is going to do and perhaps die a few times (it will one-shot you in phase 2 as well). You respawn at the station, which means you're in for 5 minutes or so of really boring travel just to have another go at it.
In sumary, the game it really does feel underwhelming in terms of content, as the asking price is 14.99€. The quests were decent, but there's only three of them! The game should definitely be at least twice as long. There defeinitely could be much more imaginative upgrades available late game; being able to drill through different kinds of previously invulnerable materials for example. There should be more kinds of ores and generic (fuel, drill speed etc) upgrades available.
At least you don't have to deal with the earthquakes from the original in this one, but the original still reigns supreme by far in comparison because of the reasons above, and because it's free.

Keep in mind I didn't play very deep into this game; it didn't grab me at all, so maybe some of my critiques become invalid further into the game.
Motherload's main mechanic really isn't all that terribly interesting -  it's not *bad*, but it's not good enough to hold up the experience on its own. The original Motherload held it up with the character progression elements and the story, such as it was anyway. The need to upgrade your capsule kept you mining, and the curiousity as to just what the heck is going on keeps you interested.
Super Motherload doesn't have that. The character progression is there, but it doesn't feel as satisfying; it's too fast, too easy, and upgrading your engine or your drill no longer feels like an accomplishment, nor does it feel satisfying when you actually get the upgrades. In the original each and every upgrade made you feel like you were riding a substantially more powerful mining machine, digging twice as fast or staying under twice as long - but in Super Motherload I'm not sure what the effects of the upgrades even are!
I honestly think the UI streamlining detracted from the experience; in the original, going through the motions of refueling, repairing, restocking, and finally checking the upgrade vendor to see what you can afford made returning from the pit each time feel a little bit refreshing, a "yes! I made it!" experience and a breath before you go back to the main gameplay - which is, after all, literally nothing but grinding (well, drilling, but that's close enough). In Super Motherload you literally just swing past the dropoff, fuel, and repair vendors and then it's right back into the pit with you, feeling less like an accomplishment and a break from grinding and more like a pointless "do you wish to not lose the game" prompt that comes up every five minutes. The fact that the resource indicators are less obvious and harder to read, and there's no audiovisual cue that you're about to run out of fuel doesn't help either.
The story in the original definitely isn't going to win any Pulitzers, but it was simple, clear, and served its purpose. You're a miner on Mars. You dig for a bit, your boss occasionally congratulating you on your successes, and then you pick up a transmission from another miner just like yourself, except he's trapped deep underground, and there's something there with him... followed by your boss telling you that it was probably just a radio glitch. Things progress pretty predictably from there (did I mention your boss's name is "Natas"? Yeah...), but it's an interesting enough mystery to keep you engaged, and there's a clear situation (you're a miner on mars and your employer is Up To Something) and a clear goal (find out what he's Up To, or else you might well be next!).
Super Motherload may have that eventually, but not in the amount I played. Instead you first get a few minutes of a robot literally just text-dumping you the game's instructions (which can never be called up again, of course) and then as you dig you intercept a message from some underground base that their life support has been sabotaged, demanding your employer send help. Maybe I screwed up or something but there doesn't seem to be a way to get to them and help them - the message is literally pointless to you. And then you get a call from another base telling you "base xyz isn't a ___, it's a laboratory, they're experimenting on us!" "They" is presumably the company you work for but... so? The player character can't do anything about it, no-one's asking them to do anything, and there's really no mystery; the company is doing evil♥♥♥♥♥♥ okay, yeah, so what do I do? Apparently nothing. So the story is more annoying than compelling.
I wanted to like this game; had good memories of the original. But the new additions add nothing of value and ultimately, all the good parts are the ones copied over from the original Motherload, except oftentimes not even as good. Super Motherload has little to no redeeming value; go play the original, it's better and it's free, or indeed any of XGen's old Flash games.

Do not get me wrong; Pandemonium is a classic from the days of yore.

This game is a true nostalgia trip for those that played it in the 90s. Yes it is a port but this is the original port found in the 90s that has an emulator capable of running it on modern machines. As for the 'trouble' with key bindings, it's simply a change in the options menu. I'm no computer geek but if my idiocy can figure it out I'm sure other people can to and rebind their keys accordingly as SURPRISE! you can do that. The issues I had with sound were due to my actual sound being too loud, not the games. Easily sorted by alt tabbing out of the game and adjusting my volume that way along with the in game sound. I don't see people's problems with this game. Yes the response from the game can be lacking but quite frankly this isn't a modern game, this happens all the time with older games (and even some more modern ones from the 00s). It isn't perfect, it came from a time without HD graphics and modern controls and computing power. But if my computer can run this perfectly fine (considering it is a laptop and not a gaming one either) I'm sure that there may be the odd issue here and there for some as things go wrong, but there is no need to rage about how you haven't managed to figure things out and blame it on the game. As to the save mechanic... what save mechanic? Games from this era in time didn't really have saves so to speak. You would bust your guts beating the level to be rewarded with a level complete screen and a PASSWORD for the level so that you could go back to where you left off. It is not some modern game that lets you have 30 different saves because quite frankly it didn't need to at the time of creation, again showing it's age a little. Too many people appear to have come into this expecting the game to have suddenly been remastered.... when it is a release of the original port.... and not labelled as a REMASTER of all things. Again, people probably requested the game get revived and that is more than enough, as lets be honest Crystal Dynamics and Square Enix probably don't want to spend the time or resources on producing a complete remaster due to their busy schedule with other games that people want. Count your lucky stars that it actually got released rather than being locked in a vault and everyone having to break their disks in rage while trying to get the game working on modern machines.
All in all I would highly recommend this game to those who played either the PS1 version or PC version as it is a great nostalgia trip if you can manage not to rage quit because older game is showing it's age. Defintely worth it as I am a fan of the games, particularly this one in the series. And as to those who have so many problems, maybe being patient and asking for hep might be better than blaming everything on the game... like people do in call of duty... all the damn time

A good game that with a little more effort could have been a great game. I've currently played 15 out of 20 maps.
The good:
- Good game mechanics. Hold up hostages, disabling camera feeds, line of sight, fog of war.
- Nice graphics that combined with the music, suits the game very well.
- Nice map design that combined with the game mechanics offers different approaches to reach your goals.
- A lot of potential if the developers decides to improve the game or make a sequel.
The bad:
- The UI is lacking. Too easy to make mistakes
- The AI is lacking. The NPC are too naive
- The game is too easy.
The ugly:
- Others have experienced game crashes and I've sadly exprienced that a couple of times myself.
- Some NPC are too (and unrealistically) trigger happy. The police chief at the impound started shooting my goons that had stood idle beside the van during the whole mission. He never saw the one goon that had been active and who also was the guy that "unlocked" the chief (I hid behind the door when I unlocked the southern door). I just ran outside and started shooting like a maniac. So that was police brutality at it's worst.
As I said, this is a good game that could have been great. Even if the game mechanics is good, the game itself is just too easy. When you've gotten the basic and you have hired 1-2 more goons, found a guards uniform, you will, with a little patient, most likely run through most of the missions without much drama and no collateral damage. Basically, you send the guy in dress as a guard, and he will get you all the keys and cut of the camera feed without any problems. And then it is pretty much straight forward for the rest of your goons. You find yourself a room where you can lock off all exits (and make sure that it doesn't have a phone inside). And then you just "invite" one after another of the guards/civilians to that room.
Much of the problems is that the NPC, especially the guards, are too naive. Other problems is that the guards don't try to fix the missing camera feeds.
So what I would have liked to see regarding this is:
- Guards try to fix the camera feeds. And if they cannot fix it, they become a lot more alert.
- The guards communicate with each other for instance, via wire less (walkie talkie). So if the see something suspicious like a broken window, the call over other guards and they conduct a search. Also, they have com-checks now and again. So if you have lock guard A inside a room and guard B calls out for guard A and does not get an answerer, he will conduct a search.
- More random behavior from NPC. For instance a guard get bored standing/patrolling, so I go to chat with colleague or goes to the kitchen to make a snack or go out for a smoke.
- Different skill level on the guards. You can have one slacker who don't care if he saw something suspicious, others are extremely professional. And maybe having somebody that is completely paranoid.
- random behavior when you hold up an NPC. For instance that some NPC can panic and try to run off.
This is not part of the review, but more on how I would have liked to the game to be.
I would have liked to see a more complex campaign where the police will investigate your heist. Basically, your goons can leave evidence during a heist which may increase the chances for the police to find you. For instance if you get caught on the camera, if you don't get the tape containing that recording, the police will know how your goon look like. NPC can become witnesses if they see your face. You can leave fingerprints at crime scene. So to counter this, you can wear masks and gloves. But using this when you are only gathering intel, it will increase the rate of suspicion by the NCP's. Also, there should be a notoritey level, so the more aggressive you are, the more public wants your arrest, and hence, more resources will be put into trying to solve who is behind these heites.
Also it would have been fun if the game focused more on gathering intel before a heist. For instance you must have contacts to get the blueprint of buildings. Without these blueprint, the layout will be covered in the fog of war. Also you should be able to buy more intel, for instance how many guards there is at duty, how professional they and so on.
And of course, it would have been cool having some RPG elements on your crew, learning skill and so on.
And if all the above was include, it would the be put together with a sandbox career mode were you can include fan made maps to, and the "plot" is just to "earn" as much as you can until you either get caught or until you decide to retire. A little bit like Pirates. And this would also require a time-line where new technology becomes available both for you and the police (DNA for instance).
And if you get caught, it would have been cool with a some prison break maps so you can arrange an earlier release. And if you don't decide to escape, you also can continue your career after you've served your time, if your health allows it.
And what to do with the loot? Well, buy a lot of cool stuff, a mansion, a yacht and so on.
Multiplayer would also be pretty awesome.

First we have to stake the place out. There’s a guard at the entrance and another one is patrolling the interior. Security cameras are active. There are a few customers inside and they’re going to be a problem as well. We don’t want them calling the cops from the phone booth on the corner. We have to sneak inside, grab the key to the back room and knock out the guy watching the security monitors. Then we can get to the safe. We don’t want a bloodbath. However, if things go wrong, we’ll do whatever it takes in order to get out alive with the loot. Everyone know what to do? Alright, let’s do it.
As you might have surmised from the opening paragraph, The Masterplan is a real-time tactical heist game in which you plan and then carry out robberies all over town. You start small, with a kiosk and the local bar, but over time your ambitions will grow and you’ll get to rob a bank, break into a police station, take out a rival gang and finally take on Fort Knox for that massive payoff that’ll secure your retirement in the Caribbean. The Masterplan is a top-down 2D game set in the 1970’s. You start off with a single goon and a toy gun, but as soon as you get to your hideout, more options will appear. You will be able to hire up to six goons, but you can only take four on heists. As you hit more places, you’ll earn money which you can use to hire goons and buy weapons. You can also use the hideout to practice some mechanics such as locking a door, shooting and so on.
The first heists are rather simple, but very soon the game design starts to open up and manages to provide a nice amount of open-ended gameplay. You can choose to go stealthy and use non-lethal force. Most guards and civilians will surrender once you point a weapon in their direction which gives you the opportunity to knock them out and lock them in a room so you can carry on uninterrupted even after they come to. However, you can also choose to go in guns blazing and just kill everything in your path. Naturally, in most cases someone will survive and call the cops and you’ll have to kill them as well. What it comes down to is planning, but even that doesn’t guarantee success. In almost every scenario you will encounter an unexpected situation which will cause you to repeat the heist quite a few times.
Of course, if a heist goes wrong, you can just carry on and try to salvage the situation, but I found it better to just reset the level due to several things. First off, the interface and the controls are very unintuitive and unwieldy. Even though you have a slow down button, when things go hot, it simply becomes a massive drag even to pull off things such as aiming, turning around and closing doors. Basically, issuing any kind of orders in a pinch is far more convoluted and clunky than it should be. Coupled with the trial-and-error design, the game does get pretty frustrating at times, especially in the beginning while you’re still learning the ropes. Another reason why it’s better to reset is that the amount of money you get away with gets reduced if you kill anyone. The game explains it as the evidence cleaning fee. But here’s the thing. The only things you can spend money on are goons and weapons. So if you go the stealth route, you don’t really need the money. But if you go the violent route, you’ll get less money and you won’t be able to buy new goons, weapons or ammo. Clearly the stealth route is the way to go, but it also makes the money sort of worthless. However, pulling off a perfect heist is its own reward.
The Masterplan’s presentation is humble yet effective. Both the art style and the soundtrack faithfully recreate the feel and the atmosphere of classic heist movies and TV shows of the 70’s and 80’s. Unfortunately, the game suffers from some stability issues. I’ve experienced multiple crashes and considering there is no checkpoint system, the game crashing can induce some infuriating moments. One of the crashes I’ve experienced was during a particularly tough heist just as I was directing my goons back to the getaway van after successfully pulling off a perfect heist. Needless to say, I wasn’t happy. Also, the game starts to slow down considerably when played for longer periods of time. Quitting the game and starting it up again alleviates this issue, but obviously it shouldn’t be there in the first place. As of writing, the developer has already released three patches which removed the crashing issues. However, the slow down remains and the game froze on me a couple of times.
The Masterplan can be extremely frustrating at times due to its trial-and-error design, unintuitive interface, wonky controls and certain technical issues, but somehow it does manage to successfully portray the exhilaration of planning and carrying out heists. It does possess that inexplicable addictive element that makes you want to repeat that heist until you get it just right, no matter how much it drives you nuts. Definitely rough around the edges, but still recommended to anyone who finds the concept appealing.

The fountain (or whatever that blue aura is) in your starting area, for example, will replenish your health when you interact with it (so don't forget to do so before heading out).  All in all, not bad for five bucks...though it could stand to be improved upon in some areas.

This game is exactly what I was hoping it would be.
If you want to sample what is effectivly the same game in a different enviorment, go play the original bit Dungeon. It's a free flash game.  I bought this game the day it came out as I felt that this game would live up to my expectations, and it has.
The gameplay very clearly uses the same solid base as the original bit Dungeon, which was very solid. A lot of niche elements (such as the music fading out during combat in new areas) are still very present, and I would say that this sequel did not lose much of its original mechanics or quirks.
The primary type of controls you use to play the game is a loose combination of positioning your mouse to change the facing of your character, using WASD to move freely, and pressing/holding left click or spacebar to attack/block. This may sound incredibly simple, and it is, but the game does require you to think carefully and quickly to prevent a swift death. I almost feel like it was a bit lazy to have the game play nearly identically to the original, but I will say that the gameplay has yet to feel stale. The basic layout of the game is a semi-randomized overworld layout you run through to find the next dungeon. The game is less about exploration and more about dungeon clearing, which was the entierty of the original game.
As far as graphics  go, the game uses a fairly good quality and consistant pixelart style as many other games have chosen to do. I give this game special props for making all equiped weapons and armor fully visible on your character, which gives you a rolling appearance based on what gear you have. The music is generally the same as the orginial, and is fitting to the game itself very well. Rescaling the game in a window also works much better than I expected, and although there are basically zero video settings, I seriously doubt any modern computer would have trouble running the game.
The main problems I see with the game as of now is that there is no overworld or dungeon maps (which doesn't bother me at all), and the game actually feels a bit too easy sometimes. I expect some sort of 'hard' difficulty with higher scaling on enemies to be implemented at some point. Also, your offensive stats are autoleveled based on your equiped weapon, and although it really streamlines the game, I would rather be able to manually assign stats, so what I have in my hands at the time doesn't influence what my character would be better at using later.
Overall, the addition of more status procs, weapon types, new movement mechanics, redoing the magic bar, and better hybridization has made me happy with this game. bit Dungeon is one of my all time favorite flash games and I expect to burn a good amount of time on this game as well, if it has even close to the amount of replay value of the first game.
EDIT: Difficulty update fixed some problems with the game, the developer clearly cares about the status of the game. Buy this game.

At first when I tried this game it was on a whim.  I've always been a huge fan of the borderlands games since their inception and I stumbled across the open beta on logging into steam one day, saw the gearbox logo, and decided to give it a go.
What I saw, was astounding.  Smooth, genuinely fun gameplay, well written characters and story, it felt every bit like the borderlands games I've enjoyed.  I jumped into the pvp and before I knew it I'd met and joined up with others that enjoyed the game as I did and the hours just flew by, before I knew it the day was gone.  I picked up the game that day, and I've never looked back once.
People are probably going to compare it to Overwatch, and the simple fact is the only thing similar about them is they both were called 'Hero Shooters' and had a similar launch window, but the simple fact is they couldn't be more different.  In addition to the episode based story campaign, which is good on it's own, there are three modes of pvp.
Capture - Simple enough, one just has to focus on holding the three available control points in an effort to amass a team score of 1000 before the enemy does.  This mode is quicker than the others and focuses less on controlling minion waves and dealing with structures and more on player versus player combat.
Meltdown - A classic Moba style of match with two lanes, except rather than breaking down an enemy base, the goal is to destroy the enemy minions and to guide yours safely to the goal on the enemy's side of the map.  At 250 points, half way to the 500 point goal mark, the goal point closes and one farther back will open up, widening the feild a bit and increasing the distance you'll need to push to get your minions in.  This allows for some excellent counterplay and turn arounds in the latter half of the game.  Of course to reach these goals, one must often get past enemy structures.  Accellerators speed the team that owns them and slow the enemy team.  Turrets, much like towers in other mobas, attack enemies that get too close. Supply Bases restore the health of nearby friendly players at a modest rate, and all structures have three teirs, costing an increasing amount of crystals for each tier.  The structures can be destroyed by the opposing team, and give exp like enemy minions would, however they can also be rebuilt for a cost of shards, little of which can be found around the map and of course from the large shards which spawn by the bases of each team and the middle of the map, control of which is often disputed heavily by each team.  All in all this mode is the most true to the moba formula in my opinion and really stands out as one of the more distinct types of pvp I've played in any game.
Incursion - The goal here is to breach the enemy's fortifications and destroy the two heavily armed and sheilded sentries that guard the opposing base.  To aid in this, in addition to the standard minions, there are a variety of defensive and offensive structures to build, super minions to summon, and unique to this mode are the outcast thrall camps.  Outcast Thralls are like mini bosses which you can fight in three strategically placed control points on the map.  On defeating them, you can capture the point, which will summon that thrall to temporarily join your team and it will deal major damage to the enemy minions or sentry if left unchecked.  Of course, with these and particularly with the heavily sought dual thrall camp in the middle of the map, there is also the chance of ambush while attempting to take these points.  Unlike meltdown or other moba style games, this mode has only one lane, funneling the whole of the players into one area which can lead to some truly spectacular team battles.  All in all this mode is my personal favourite, and when you finally break through the enemy team and their defenses to claim victory it can be quite satisfying.
This game is really something worth looking at, and honestly it's a shame it wasn't advertised more, but the quality of the game speaks for itself.  Look it up, watch some gameplay, ask a friend to let you watch them play if they do, and I'm sure you won't regret it.  Also Toby ftw.

Her Story shows that games can serve to make a linear story unravel in a way that a movie or book either couldn't achieve, or would have a lot of trouble pulling off. The player interacts with the game by typing in keywords in interviews with a woman, and as you reveal more clips, more things will be mentioned to be looked into. I never found myself without a new term leading to a revelation, and despite the low interactivity, the experience made me feel more like a detective than anything else I've ever played.
While it doesn't necessarily take advantage of all the interactivity games provide (really it's just a chopped-up set of clips from some longer videos), it's still a damn good experience that wouldn't be nearly as good without the "unraveling" quality the keyword-searching provides.

In two hours, we uncovered 50% of the videos, learned the main story, but yeah, there are still some holes left to fill. We hardly saw any of Interview Six. And I keep saying "we" because I'd really recommend playing this in a small group. One person on the mouse, one on the keyboard, and a couple others taking notes with the suggestions and such.
Of course, you don't NEED to do any of that, but it makes the experience more fun. It'd be nice if there was a bit more of an "ending" to the game, or a clear "final" video. But maybe the fact that there isn't makes the experience more authentic. I dunno.
Good fun, and well, I'd even pay full for this if I had to buy it again.

This is my first review to a game guys and boy I'm I happy that Her Story is the one I start with:
It's a captivating journey putting you in the driving seat of a police detective and give the feeling that you are one at least regarding one aspect "searching through loads and loads of clips" for clues to connect the dots.
Sounds: And I wanted to start off with sounds because it truly left a mark on me, the in game sounds are solidly crafted giving you this retro feel that blends in in a wonderful manner with the overall theme of the game; nothing short of a full mark for me.
Gameplay: The gameplay is nothing but unique, I'm not even sure if you can actually call it a "Gameplay" all I know is I got addicted to it way too fast way too early in the game, I Basically was stuck in front of the screen and finished the game in what you can call one session, not a very long game but believe you'll feel satisfied when it's finished and it definitely is worth the money.
Visuals: The visuals are all that is needed for this type of game, solidly cementing the retro feel that gives this game its glam.
Acting: The model performance is quiet solid, not sure it's going to win her an Oscar but she is a delight, and I really hope to see her in future works, whether gaming related or in movies.
Story: The story unfolds in a wonderful "connect the dots" manner, I wish there was a method to re-watch the clips you already opened filtered with respect to in clip history which would give the chance to view the story in a more cohesive manner each once in a while, I can't say I understood a 100% what was going on in the game especially when you finish it, but I'm sure I there's tons of theories and lore out there that I can check to gain wider perspective, what I do know though is that even though it kind of left me hanging at the very end, it wasn't a fairly major  detail and perhaps other players got it and it's just me overlooking some details that will give me this lost insight.
Oh and, PLEASE DON'T GO LOOK FOR SPEED RUN CLUES AND OTHER THINGS THAT WILL SPOIL THE GAME FOR YOU AND MAKE YOU SAY IT'S A SH**Y GAME, the best way to play it, is to let the game unfold itself on its own.
Overall, could this game have been better? Yes. I believe there where places where you can add wonderful extra features to the game, and there are some missing opportunities that would've made this game put its mark in gaming history, nevertheless as I previously said this is one unique experience you don't want to miss, and for the price, it's well worth your money.

An enjoyable Hitman/Murder Simulator experience. While not as good as Blood Money, which I consider the height of the series, its still an enjoyable game. While lacking some mechanics, stream lining, and smoothing out of the later games and being much more simplistic it still offers a core gameplay that I really enjoy and is why people play hitman games. Everything thats here is what makes Hitman games Hitman games and this is what Blood Money, Contracts, and I beleive the new 2016 Hitman game all build on (♥♥♥♥ Absolution).
Unfortunately it can be fairly janky, it does not offer 1920x1080 as a display resolution though it did run fine on my Win7 64 Bit machine. The display resolution maybe fixable with mods but since the game ran fine I didn't bother. Occasionally NPCs will stand in the wrong place making it impossible to do something your supposed to and other stuff like NPCs animations not lining up and them doing weird funny stuff.  I did get a few crashes here and there especially when trying to alt tab, as was common with older games.  There is an inate jankyness to the AI and gameplay. Sneaking up behind someone is extremely difficult because you must be in "sneak" mode and AI really love to walk around. Sneak mode makes 47 move extremely slow so I did what I did when I was a kid and just ran up to people I wanted to strange while spamming the Fiber Wire, eventually you will fandangle yourself behind them and get the kill. Its easier just to use the 9mm silenced and just pop people unfortunately.
Its still a fairly good game and has some interesting and fun points in the story. The games best if you play by the rules and try to be as stealthy as possible but there are points where you just can't stealth through a level or an area and have to shoot.. atleast thats what I found in my experience.  There are times you get caught doing something from someone who could not have possibly seen or heard you unless a glitch happened but for the most part you learn to adapt and overcome and save alot. You only get a certain number of saves per level so you can't just turtle your way through though. You are really free to accomplish the objectives by any means necessary and with any combination of tools at your disposal. You can load in with an M60 and blast everyone in the map or load in with only a fibre wire and kill the target with a scalpel while hes on an operating table after you shut all the lights off. This game is one of the best games I've ever played.
The story, the gameplay, the soundtrack, the atmosphere and environment, is all executed extremely well.  For a 2002 game, it was ahead of its time.
The player gets to have control of a man who goes by the name "47."
He had worked as a hitman for quite some time after escaping an asylum in which he was born as an artificially made human clone, born and raised to be a killer for the wrong reasons.  He becomes accustomed to killing for the right reasons considering his targets wind up behind horrible people who do bad things.  However, his motivation seemed to be money and fulfilling his habit of professional stealth and murder.  But, he did eventually clear things up and manage to put an end to what was bad in the previous game.
At the start of the game, our once notorious protagonist is an ex-hitman seeking forgiveness working at a church somewhere in Sicily.  He befriends "Father Emilio Vittorio", who is eventually kidnapped.  The individuals who captured him leave a note demanding money from 47 in return for his priest friend.  47 is to then rejoin his employers at the "International Contract Agency (ICA)" and work with his handler Diana Burnwood.  Throughout the game, she gives the player a contract or hit to perform in exchange for the agency's attempts at finding Father Vittorio.  Within these levels, the player is to take control of 47 and take in really huge levels with plenty going on.  Not only is there a target (or targets) within the level, but there are probably guards, civilians, security cameras, et cetera.
After realizing all this, the player must painstakingly calculate how he or she is going to get the job done and escape with as much precision and stealth as possible.  It is allowed to go in guns-blazing, however it can be pretty darn difficult, and it's not necessarily the ideal way to play the game.  If one were to play the game like it's normally supposed to be played by the means of stealth, there are rewards.  Such rewards happen to be new weapons that could be used to improve stealth abilities, or non-stealth abilities.  Every once in a while, 47 will wind up back at that church so that he could wait on another job by his work computer, or take a good look at all the weapons the player has unlocked throughout the game so far within the garden shed.  It is also important to know that 47 can take disguises on individuals that he either kills or knocks out, which is a feature in every Hitman game that is always fantastic.  It allows access to parts of the level that would be restricted otherwise.  But, if you're up for a silent assassin suit only challenge, be my guest.
By no means do each level feel the same or repetitive, for 47's job requires him to work on a global scale.  The excellent level design also helps make each level feel like something new and difficult.  And by difficult, I mean really difficult.
Even though it is tough, there are many opportunities within each level for the player to improvise and figure out within every level, and it is well worth the time.  Such opportunities allow the player to pick and choose equipment before starting a level, as well as using things in the environment that can be found to assist in performing the hit.  That is awesome.
---
The game isn't without its faults, though.  One thing that bothers me particularly are the possibilities of getting compromised and realized by enemies even when in a disguise.  It happens by the most dumb means possible...
If you were to run within a disguise (which is something players do in almost every game, because why would you want to be really slow...) you could be shot at.  And so, to avoid suspicion, you *must* walk when close to other non-played characters that happen to be guards or wearing the same clothes as you.  If you're in your original suit, you can run all you want.  But otherwise, nope.  And it does makes sense to get suspicion for it, but it doesn't make sense to be immediately shot for it.
Thankfully, every other Hitman game does not have this problem, and the idea of there being suspicion is done a lot better.  But it is something to think about and prepare for before playing this game.  You could preform a glitch where you can quickly switch between running and walking and not get shot at for it, but it really looks stupid and it kills the illusion that the game is not just a game, but something seemingly realistic.  This poorly designed mechanic is really annoying.  But, if you have the patience, it can be overlooked and the game could still be a lot of fun.
There is a notorious bad level in this game known as "Hidden Valley."  In this level, there is no target.  Which could have been okay if it were still fun and managable.  But it's not.  There is one disguise option.  If you get it, it still doesn't stop the difficulty of getting through.  It's not the fun difficult you'll get at every other time in the game.  No.  It's the stupid difficulty that only exists due to bad mechanics.  Every time a guard gets you in their sights, they run to you to check your "ID" or whatever, even though your face is completely covered up in a mask and you look just like one of them.  But for some reason, even though they could have literally run up the anybody else who looks the same and check their ID, they check yours.  I recommend getting through this misery as much as possible before you die of pain from trying to get a perfect "Silent Assassin" rating from completing it.  Ironically, there is no assassination in this level, making the idea of getting the Silent Assassin rating seem pointless.  Just get through it, and never play it again, unless you really want to, for some reason.  You might unlock a weapon from doing it, but you could probably find it and exit the level with it instead.  This is the worst level in the entire Hitman franchise, in my personal opinion.  Get it done.  Then move on.
It is really, really, bad.
Another thing that rubs me the wrong way is the fact that you awkwardly have to load a level you last saved in, then exit it to get back to the menu, then be able to pick a level in order to play whatever level you want.  After you beat the game, it does save, so it's not that you would have to beat the last level over and over again, and that's great.  But still, this is something that is a little annoying.  Thankfully, Hitman 2: Silent Assassin, and the third game, Hitman: Contracts, are the only games in the franchise to do this.
--
The atmosphere and vibe from each level (except Hidden Valley) feel ecstatic.  Even though the graphics are dated, they're still nice to look at and are far from ugly.  Even if you don't have a super computer that allows amazing detailed graphics and insane frame rate, the game still looks cool in gameplay and in cutscenes.
The levels are also beautifully designed, making almost every level a joy to complete.
Not only did I feel like a professional assassin when I executed levels with intense precision and stealth, but I felt like one whenever the ICA moved me into these locations.  These locations range from being civil parties with wealthy scumbags to top secret locations where you need a disguise to not get shot on sight.  I always felt like I was on an important job, causing me to feel like a real professional.  If I wasn't a professional in the first place, I wouldn't be able to have the ICA send me on these jobs.  Trail and error is the key to success in becoming the professional this game will want you to be.  So have at it.
--
The soundtrack is some of the best I've heard in a video game, let alone a form of entertainment.  It was composed by Jesper Kyd, and it is perfect.
--
Overall, the game is really great.  The game offers a compelling story revolving around a character who manages to be a cold-blooded killer and a human being seeking justice.  Buy it.

- Sniper Ghost Warrior -
After having completed this game, I believe it deserves a review. So here it is:
Sniper Ghost Warrior is a Sniping FPS, made by City Interactive. You play as a small US Military unit, which consists of several members. The one you'll be playing in about 75% of the missions is Sergeant Tyler Wells, known as 'Razor Six Four.' He is the Sniper of his unit and in an unbelievable turn of events, you'll be doing most of the sniping in the game as this guy. The game has an interesting way of interpreting each squad member's role, as since you'll be doing most of the sniping as Sergeant Wells, you'll also get to play as the Spotter, O'Neil, in which you'll have to help out Wells in picking targets to snipe through your binoculars. You can also play as a couple members of a Ground Assault Team where most of the gunfighting is done, but I'll get to that in a minute.
I'd like to keep this review simple by first covering the game itself, then the different gameplay aspects you'll be diving into throughout the campaign.
First off, the game itself looks really pretty for a 2010 release. The foilage and jungles look lush and thick, and well rendered, and the buildings in the urban areas all look convincing and well modeled. The draw distance is very far (which I would expect from a game which focuses on shooting people at extreme range) and the lighting is impressive. On the other hand though, the character models look pretty bland and even look like plastic up-close. The enemies throughout the game literally have about four different models and the animation isn't great. Enemies won't do things such as take cover, instead preferring to stand in the open and shoot right at you, despite the range disadvantage, which leads me to another issue.
The AI are either omnipotent or brain-dead. Sometimes they will be doing the sniping with bursts from their rifles, killing you very quickly and being able to see you from a country mile away, or they'll look about in horror having seen their pal collapse from a .45ACP to the head, even though you'll be standing right behind them as they panic. They never do anything other than shoot or throw grenades at you, and on missions where detection = failure, some may raise the alarm as they die - despite having nobody nearby to see or hear them die. They'll gladly stand still as you shoot them up, trying to return fire.
One of the features of Sniper Ghost Warrior affect your ballistics, or in non-sniper jargon, how your rounds travel over a distance. You'll have to account for bullet drop and lead your targets, and ensure you keep your heartbeat at a low BPM to maintain optimal accuracy. You can use the Mil-Dots on your scope to ensure kills at longer ranges, or the chevrons on a PSO scope. The issue is however, most of the sniping isn't done at a long enough range to even need to adjust your shot. You'll be trying harder to stay undetected, and if you're like me, you'll be relying more on your sidearm to eliminate sentries and slip past. A feature which also bugged me was that on both the Easy and Medium difficulties, a little red circle will appear on your scope to tell you EXACTLY WHERE TO AIM, which pretty much renders most of what I've mentioned in this paragraph redundant. Having discovered that this circle is disabled in the Hardest difficulty, I immediately restarted and went for this option. Things were better then, and it was more enjoyable for sure, but with increasing the difficulty, another problem surfaced...
Remember when I said the AI were sometimes omnipotent and could spot you anywhere? On Hard, you'll be utter screwed if luck isn't on your side, as you'll literally be one-dinked from No Mans Land by a kiddie conscript in his early twenties if you don't see him first. It's pure Rocket-Tag gameplay, and whoever gets the first shot in usually wins the fight. This wouldn't be an issue if the game was completely stealth. You'll have scripted events where you'll have to retreat under fire, and if the game rolls a 'Screw You' on the dice of fate, you'll die instantly and will have to try again, regardless of what you do otherwise. I remember on the chapter 'Steal From Under Their Noses', where as soon as you grab the intel, you'll be compromised, and forced to swim to safety. Two guards will spawn behind you after you start swimming, which will nine times out of ten, kill you while you're defenceless. I had to repeat this part countless times, before I managed to escape. I had a similar issue later in the game when I was playing as the Spotter, and only had a MK.23 (A .45ACP Handgun) with abysmal range to defend myself. I had to sneak past a bridge, but the guards seen me nearly every time and I was shredded. I couldn't fight back as my MK.23 just couldn't hit them at the range I was at.
Now, referring back to the other characters, you'll be playing as the Ground Assault Team in some chapters. This is where the game often turns to mud. The gunplay is horrible and any weapon will have ridiculous recoil and shake more than a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dog. There is no stealth at all and you'll have to make do with only a few weapons to fight your way through. There are very few weapons in the game at all, with most of them being Sniper Rifles, naturally, so at these points you'll only have a few AR's and maybe a USAS-12 to hand to get by, all of which suck. You'll still have the never-missing AI blast you to bits though, and an occasional dose of 3 to 4 grenades being hurled at you at once. You play as these guys in more than one chapter too. The Spotter, O'Neil's missions are brief but rather lacklustre. Simply consisting of marking targets though a set of binoculars for the aforementioned Wells to snipe. (I suppose it's more realistic than the rest of the game). Chances are you'll be here for Wells' missions, which ARE the sniping aspect of the sniping game. Previous issues apply and you'll often be potshotting rookies from less than 100 metres away, nullifying the whole point of having a Sniper there in the first place. You'd be as well sending Solid Snake. You can pick up enemy weapons but they're as jerky and inaccurate as playing as the Ground Assault Team, once again ruining the purpose of being a Sniper to begin with.
The story is pretty generic, with the US finding another dictator that doesn't like them much, a la Castro, so they send your team in to liquidate them.
AND THE GAME ENDS RIGHT THERE. RIGHT AFTER YOU TAKE THE FINAL SHOT. What. The. Hell. (It literally fades to black, 'THE END' appears, credits roll.) Well wasn't all that build up for nothing or what?!
To put an end to this review, I'd have to say first that I got this game in a bundle. I may not have bought it otherwise but after having played it I would have to say that it isn't worth your time, unless you get it in a bundle yourself or get it very cheap. It wasn't a huge studio that made the game, fair enough, but I feel as though they make their own game pointless by giving you Assault Rifles at any time, and telling you where your bullet will land. It is, as I said, very pretty to look at, but not much to it. A 4-5 hour campaign at most and dead multiplayer. If sniping is your bag and you can't get enough of it, I recommend to get this and play it on the Hardest difficulty from the get-go. You'll still get absolutely mullered at the scripted events where stealth is not an option (more common they should be), but at least it'll provide a challenging experience. Aim high.

A SIMPLE REVIEW: Only buy this game if you can get it for less than $5. No more. Best aspects are sniping, sneaking, and planning your shots/kills. While the sniping and sneaking are a lot of fun, the more "action" like parts are NOT! I recommend this only if you can grab it in a cheap bundle (I paid, mathematically speaking, less than $1 for this game). If you want more details, continue below.
SNIPING/SNEAKING: A lot of fun, actually! Don't play this game on easy, just start it out on hard. You'll have a much more challenging and enjoyable experience. I had more than enough fun sneaking through the jungle and carefully picking my targets. Many enemies I had to leave behind in order to remain undetected. DO NOT PLAY THIS LIKE A RUN-AND-GUN! (as should be obvious) The mechanics of this game and your gear will not help you in the slightest and you will die easily. Which brings me, sadly, to the next part...
NON-SNIPING PARTS: Due to the poor mechanics of this game and the overall design, the hardest, most annoying, and least fun parts were the ones where you have to use an assault rifle in a 3-man team. Recoil is terrible, accuracy is non-existant, and everyone else can take you out since they are shooting from all directions. Simply AWFUL! No other words needed to articulate this problem. Oh yeah, and the AI is either incredibly clueless or has the perception of a hawk, depending on your current status or location in a given mission. (sometimes the game just "automatically" made me detected even though I was never spotted and never raised an alert).
I only recommend this game IF you buy it for less than $5. Otherwise, wait till the price drops. The sneaking and sniping through the jungle was a fun experience without a doubt and outweighs the terrible assault mechanics.

I've read all sort of bulls**t in the reviews about this game. This is NOT a PS1 port. It is the very same PC version of 1996, but with a 3DFX/Glide Wrapper to emulate the 3D cards of that time. I have the original version of this game in CD, and if you don't use a glide wrapper, you have to run in software mode, where you can't change the resolution, neither use filters like anti-aliasing. People with a little bit of effort, can find the game folder and change the graphics configs using the nglide_config app. Of course it will not change like water into wine. It is a 20-year-old game, one of the first 3D-accelerated games. Give a break.
So I recommend the game to the people who likes old games, because this IS an old game, with the limitations imposed by its age. The game runs fine in Windows 10 and with a Xbox 360 controller, you can set the resolution to Full HD (or even more), but, as I said, it's a 20-year-old game in Full HD, with pre-rendered backgrounds that doesn't change with the resolution and low-poly objects. You can see the result in my screenshot gallery. ;-)

Bit Dungeon is an endless roguelike with a light Diabloesque loothunt for the ultimate gear. The objective of the game is simple: beat each boss in every area's dungeon to unlock the portal to kill more demons and save your girl. I finished my first "playthrough" with a game controller in around 2 hours. When you beat the game, you get sent back to where you first started with all your progress intact and the difficulty increased. The entire map is always the same but the enemies that spawn change each time you enter a room. Once you memorize the entire map, you could probably do runs in under an hour or so. Truthfully, there isn't anything else to see once you've downed the last boss. It's not much of an ending either but it plays to tell how you start over. The game is absolutely designed to be played many times over to get the best loot while seeing how deep you can go.
The battle system comes from Zelda, where A is to slash or shoot your bow and holding it down either blocks or charges your weapon. Simply walking up to an enemy will make you attack. Take your pick: dagger, 1h sword, 1h spear, 1h hammer, 1h staff, 2h greatsword, 2h blade, 2h axe, bow, spellbook, or shield. You can dual wield any of the 1-hand weapons but my personal preference is my best 1-hander and a shield for stuns on demand. I tried bows but they consume too much stamina per attack while melee weapons can be spammed and kill a boss without having to rest.
Luckily, I found an amazing set of gear that just destroys everything.
As I mentioned, I play this game with a controller and this is the best method to play the game IMO. You can also use just the mouse or just the keyboard and WASD all the way or a combination of both.
There's some cheapness to the enemies that have fast multi-hit attacks because getting hit stuns you for a brief moment. (Edit: this issue has been patched as of 12/19/2014) It's best to attack and kill first before mobs have a chance at attacking you. The AI is slow to lock on and slow to attack so take advantage of that.
Those weapons come with random stats and that's where the Diablo inspiration shows. Each item can have up to a handful number of affixes with various effects like life steal, a death strike, phase (dodge an incoming attack and teleport away), berserk, and so on. I'm a big fan of crazy loot and the system satisfies for what you can do in this game. Quality of items I've found so far: white, blue, orange, purple, red, cyan, and green. There doesn't seem to be any set pieces. You'll often loot black stones along the way and you can use these to purchase equipment from merchants. Hidden rooms also often give good stuff stashed in a chest.
The developer mentions some love of Dark Souls and it shows. Resting at a campfire restores your health. Sometimes, upon waking, a powerful foe may appear and pronounce "I have found you..". A nice surprise and these fights are fun but you can easily escape to the next room and they'll despawn. It would have been great if they locked you in for a minute and drop loot too.
If you die, it's game over and you lose everything. There's only one save file so try your best to stay alive. Fortunately, black stones carry over across deaths. There is however a softcore touch to this in that if you have a blue heart (you start with it), you can respawn at the last campfire you used. And if you manage to get back to where you died, you can reclaim a blue heart.
There are some other negatives:
-There is no explanation of what all the stats and effects do. You can figure what the primary stats do but some of the effects aren't too obvious (i.e. I think of cleave as a wide arcing attack but it's merely a damage multiplier).
-black side borders with any aspect ratio over 4:3
-non-customizable controls (the developer may patch this)
-utterly short, moreso if you play till just the last boss (but remember, it's designed to be played continuously till you die)
8.5/10 from me. It has the makings of a great action adventure RPG with cool loot but ends up being repetitive and gets there quickly right after the "ending". However, the chase for epic loot is fun and the developer is actively improving the game so you can look forward to this game only getting better!

bit Dungeon II has a little bit of Zelda, rogue-likes, and Dark Souls in it.
The action is fast, spammy combat, with some unique controls. Walking into an enemy causes a slow attack. Tapping A controls both parrying and quick attacks, which draw from a voluminous pool of stamina. It's unclear why you would ever want to use slow attacks, since quick attacks cause dramatically more damage, and as a bonus you might accidentally parry enemy attacks in the process.
Enemies consist of melee enemies, some of which have tough shields, and ranged enemies. They almost universally have a single-frame windup, followed by a single-frame attack. You can see the inspiration from Dark Souls here, but it doesn't translate. Since the animation doesn't show attack progress, and since there is no cost to blocking as long as you want, there's little point in timing the enemy's attack. Plus, most enemies can be killed long before they actually manage to land a hit.
More generally, the game did not feel difficult enough. On my first play-though I became godlike far too quickly -- within about ten minutes. I felt like I was cutting a bloody swathe through enemies made of paper, which is very not-Dark Souls/Zelda/rogue-like-y. I killed several of the bosses before they were able to make a single attack. And while I died to some once before I learned their attack pattern, I never felt like I was in danger of losing my second life.
The lack of a map is also a problem with the maze-like quality of the overworld. Zelda 1 may not have had a map (I don't remember), but its overworld is more varied and easier to remember. At some point I lost track of what I needed to do next, and that's when I stopped playing. Not all things about the eight bit era are good things.
All in all, it was a nice attempt, but not a game that held my attention. I don't recommend it.

I don't usually take the time to write reviews, but I wanted to toss this game some praise. If you have a look at my collection, I am a huge fan of Rogue-likes, dungeon crawlers, Dark Souls, etc. While this game isn't perfect - it certainly shows an evolution from the dev's earlier work (the Kongregate bit Dungeon). Both games feature some flavor from the Souls series and Rogue-likes, and I think that if take these games and their complexity in sequence...we could be looking at a very fun formula for an indie dungeon crawler in the future.
What I like -
1. Combat: While combat is simplistic, I rather like the frantic pace.
2. It borrows well: Souls elements are here - you get a shot at recovering your heart (like your bloodstain in Souls games), and leaving it in a rather precarious place in a dungeon has the same vibe as in the souls games. Perhaps my favorite Souls feature is the way that there are even quality weapons (Dex+Strength scaling) and the fact that stat scaling is at all part of the game is super fun. My favorite game series by far, so any homage is welcome!
3. Loot and Gear: Loot variety is promising and will only improve over time assuming the game is supported. I found myself building a Dex character with Berserker and life steal, which was quite potent towards the end game.
4. Locales and Aesthetics: Areas are quite gorgeous and dungeons (while procedurally generated and featuring very little in the way of features like traps or special mechanics) at least have a common theme and unification of art style. I enjoyed enemies that took advantage of stealth and range, and found the game to be quite fun.
5. Replayability: Another Souls feature, the infinite playability of the game (i.e. when you beat it the game just keeps on going) seems interesting and I'd like to see this dev take that somewhere even cooler in a future game or modification to this one. It seems as though loot that drops at higher levels rolls affixes and then sets its stats according to item level, meaning there will always be upgrades to find (even if its just rehash of gear found at lower levels). There are enough inventory slots to make sure that finding perfect gear for each slot (i.e. affixes you like and stat distributions that are effective) will take quite some time.
What I don't like -
I think I tried to put my little quibbles in with all of my positive points, but overall I will say there just needs to be more. The developer is quite possibly on to something in terms of a style of play which is addictive, accessible, could have depth, and borrows from games people genuinely enjoy in dungeon crawling (Zelda/Souls series). A lot of fans of the Souls games are currently looking for anything at all to sate that urge until Bloodborne comes out in a few months, and since it is a PS4 exclusive this market (PC) is ripe for the taking.
Indie seems to be a viable option for exploitation of that gap in the market. All this to say MORE. Perhaps try to get some DLC features patched in or propose a game via Greenlight or Early Access when you're ready for a sequel?
Thanks for reading!

I don't know whether I approve of this game or not. So we're just gonna say no. But keep in mind I had a good amount of fun with this game for the roughly 2 hours I played.
First off, lemme get this out of the way, I can't get past the frozen maze. I dunno if my copy/version is just buggy or something, I'm going to uninstall and redownload and update this review. But, I follow the directions the dude in the cave tells me to exit the maze (ala, original Zelda), it won't let me progress. I simply keep repeating the maze never moving forward. I've restarted multiple times and there was no fix.
On the topic of replayability, once again I don't know if its an issue only effecting me, but the map just doesn't change at all. When I go into a rogue like game, I expect a big difference in the game on new playthroughs. I was expecting something closer to Binding of Isaac, but instead the only difference was (Possibly) slightly different dungeons, different item drops, etc etc. If you know where the caves are on the overworld, you're free to casually stroll and pick up all of your stat buffs before even walking into your first dungeon.
Not that you need to. Grab a bow or an axe, and you're going to rip right through the game like a hot knife through butter. I originally started off using a staff, and enjoyed the challenge of the game for a while... That is, until I walked into a dungeon room with very unfortunately placed enemies who immediately gangbanged me without a chance for me to fight. My next character had an axe, and every enemy died near instantly, including bosses. Just spam the quick attack and they get wrecked.
The enemies were incredibly similar in tactics. Waddle towards you, maybe shoot an arrow or magic attack. Charge them and they die, it doesn't make a difference. The bosses suffered the same fate. They looked different, but there were no differences in strategies for killing them.
The game was fun enough. But because I couldn't progress it's flaws became apparent super quick. It's not balanced, with some weapons providing an incredibly easy runs or a horribly unfair experience. It became stale quickly, wandering the exact same overworld moving down slow moving and easy enemies became boring fairly quickly.
Would I pay 5 dollars again? Nope. If it had multiplayer? Still probably no, which is a rare thing for me considering I absolutely LOVE co-op games. I'd rather spend a few extra bucks for increase replayability, such as Binding of Isaac.

Like all other Choice of Games games, this one gives you a non-linear story that will be shaped by your choices, for better or worse. This time out, you're thrust into the role of a CEO of a research company dabbling in making humans metahuman - sort of like superpower capitalism, except instead of being a superhero story, it is a cosmic horror story due to the price you have to pay for the research. Nice twist, that.
Unfortunately, like some Choice of Games games, unless you choose a polarized approach and stick to it 95%, you're not getting a decent ending. This makes your first playthrough, the blind one, essentially poking at the game to see what major milestone mistakes you can make, and then prepare for a 'proper' run to see a specific storyline formed by taking a coherent approach.
On the one side, it's a good thing, since this allows multiple reruns of the same game while seeing tons of new non-repeating content. On the other side, like in imperfect gamebooks, you can clearly see where the tracks cross, like "here's a dialogue option I would have picked if I picked THAT dialogue option two chapters ago... what I'm more interested in, is why there isn't a follow-up to the option I DID pick?".
The game suffers a bit from what I like to call the "Mass Effect Dialogue Issue": sometimes, the options you are offered aren't 100% related to what your player character ultimately ends up doing, although it has a lot less issues with it than, say, Hero Project. It's also highly unclear at times whether a decision result is calculated based on your stats or RNGed, a traditional issue of Choice of Games games that messed up my enjoyment of Mecha Ace greatly.
All in all, yes, it's a nice addition to the collection and a worthy recommendation to anyone, especially since the corporate backstabbing angle is weirdly complemented by the cosmic horror setting, but if you had doubts about these games before, this one will not change your opinion in the slightest.
Also, if you don't mind me saying this, the ending feels somewhat rushed and disjointed due to the need to tell three outcomes as a singular story, since way more focus is given to what your shareholders think of you rather than what state you leave the world in or what your decisions or indecisions did to the various characters. Yes, this will make the next runthrough as a heartless embezzler easier to do, but also sort of undermines any intent to play a person with a stern moral compass, I'm afraid.

Yes, this is definitely a game.
In Her Story, you begin by interacting with a database.
How you play is simple: watch the clips and try to piece together the information by spotting something interesting she says and search a new term to see if there's more related clips.
To me, this is very simple yet it really drew me in because the more I noted her attitude, her statements, and even her body language, I was intrigued with what really happened.  Who is this person she mentioned?  Does he mention him again in another clip?  Hey, this happened at a certain location, what else happened there?  And so on and so forth.
I've never played a detective game in which I actually had to take notes.  This had me taking notes by saving certain clips and jotting them down in the user tag box so I can tell not only what she's saying but piece together related video clips as well.
And then there's the story that the collection of testionies itself builds up to: Damn.  Talk about food for thought.  Believe me, this game WILL make you think.  Also, don't even get me started on the theories surrounding the story.

First off, this "game" is not a game. Just as there are popular story-based games that are just called "walking simulators," this one is simply just thinking and repeatedly typing phrases to watch something over and over.
Does that mean the game is necessarily bad? No. But it's not something amazing I would say that must be played. It is simply unique because I do not think I have seen something like it before, or at least not in the same style when it comes to FMV games from years ago.
There really is nothing to say in terms of general review material. I cannot say much on graphics, sound, or gameplay. The graphics are an old computer screen showing FMVs. The sound is generic computer noises and the woman talking. The gameplay is clicking videos and searching for them with words to solve a murder mystery.
I enjoyed it for what it was, simply because it is new (and simultaneously nostalgic). Some videos are interesting and even pretty creepy, while there are many very short videos that are filled with fluff. I just wish they hadn't separated videos so much like that. It wasn't really necessary to have THAT many videos when a lot do not have much useful information. I understand not all videos should give main story points, or else that is pointless. But having many videos with a single word was also pointless.
But really, the biggest flaw of this game is how easy it is to get a grasp on the story. Within just over 30 minutes, I already found some videos that basically gave me the general idea of what to expect to find in the rest of the story. And less than an hour or so after that, I had found all of the most important videos, really.
I wrote things down as I went along and by the end of the game I had utilized 130+ search terms or phrases to find 100% of the videos. But I had come up with some phrases that led to the most important videos within the first 25 phrases that I had come up with, and by the 40th phrase, I had found the one which signified the possible "endpoint" for the game. But instead, I purposefully didn't watch videos with terms that I thought were most important, because I thought it would end the game and destroy my progress.
I found out eventually that it didn't, so I ended the game, then just continued and found the rest of the videos because I was being a completionist, and not because I was that excited to look for more videos. In fact, the majority of the last videos I found (like the last 25-35% of the videos I found) were mostly boring and had no story to them.
In the end, I liked the game, but don't think it's a masterpiece by any means. So, if you aren't genuinely interested in the whole idea of trying to search for and watch videos in a disjointed manner to piece together an alright (but nothing too great) story, then do not bother. But if it intrigues you, give it a whirl.
