This game is truly addicting.
A game that is truly addicting is a rarity. Smotherload uses textbook skinner box incremental numbers to keep you playing, but it does it so well and so flawlessly that you barely notice. For once, making those numbers go up is truly fun. It's FUN.
Too bad it only has a lifespan of about 2 hours, and very little replay value.
Motherload is a pseudo-rogue-like game where you dig down down down and collect ores ores ores in a randomized crust of minerals on Mars. Sell the ores, upgrade your miner, mine more ores, sell more ores, upgrade more parts untill youre strong enough to dig to the core and uncover a conspiracy. It's great, incremental gameplay with a solid ending.
The game plays like butter, which is strange because there is not really any call for tight controls in this game (apart from the pitiful boss fight). The game is all about thinking laterally and not getting greedy. In the original motherload the entire point of the game was not to get greedy, because there is SO much ore to collect that it blinds you to your health and fuel reserves. So many gems and minerals... calling for you. You can spare the fuel to go get that last ruby right? No, wrong. Stop it.
The game expands it's lifespan via randomly generated puzzles that spawn under the surface, you have to think long and hard about how to get the valuable gems without blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up and causing them to be unattainable forever, it's rewarding gameplay and a good player can use them to help speed up the grind. Unfortunately the game hits a wall only 1 hour into gameplay. After the first hour of solid fun, the game turned into a long, wet fart as I grinded ores to upgrade my miner to get to the bottom, at which one of the stupidest boss fights was waiting for me.
If you played the original motherload you'll want to get this. There are no longer random deaths from gas pockets, running out of fuel doesnt make you explode anymore (seriously what was even with that?) and it's a lot harder to die. These changes go together to make a much better feeling game... it also kind of took away the challenge, somewhat. The game is not very hard. I'm glad the changes were made, but not enough was added to make the game's difficulty curve up.
At the end of the day though, I was enamored by this game, it's short and♥♥♥♥♥♥in spots, but the gameplay, the story and even the graphics are wonderful. If it were any longer it would be in danger of being far too grindy. I'm sure this game could have been far better, but as it stands, it is still a fantastic way to waste an afternoon.

Fantastic game. Typically, I find stories with this format rather unappealing due to the vast scope of the world and its unnatural setting combined with a familiar story (magic/Aliens - CEO of corporation). Which typically make getting immersed in the story difficult because you are given such a narrow view with which to see what’s going on around you and with so much is going on its easy to get confused or hung up on certain details.
However, that is not a problem with this game you very quickly learn its focus and what you are setting out to achieve which lets you focus on the intrigue of the main story and the satisfaction of seeing your metrics improve month on month make you feel like a real super powered CEO with plenty of scope to be the good guy philanthropist or the brutal cut throat businessman.
I love that fact that you get to play a little allocation of resources game month on month as a method of establishing focus and showing the player the consequences of their actions and I hope to see more of this kind of mechanic in future games.

Use keywords to search a police database for fragmented video clips related to a crime. Try and figure out what happened.
Simple concept, pure execution but over too quickly. I would love to see this idea developed further in a future game.

+ Interesting concept - who knew that searching for 200+ fragmented interview clips and trying to piece it all together could be so much fun? Having to scribble down notes on pen and paper was engaging.
+ Retro 90's atmosphere achieved with minimal graphics
+ Convincing acting by Viva Seifert, who single-handedly carries the game
+ Trying to find all of the video clips without cheating is genuinely challenging
+ Slightly ambiguous story open to interpretation (2 theories about Her Story have been analyzed in detail by players)
- Extremely short (2-3 hours unless you are trying to find 100% of the clips)
- A bit too easy to find key clips that reveal major details
- A few pointless, "filler" clips that consist of one word
- Not easily able to play discovered clips in chronological order. It would have been nice for the UI to handle this for you at the click of a button.

Hopefully, this might change with future editions of The Masterplan, but it would require some rethinking of the user-interface/controls-implementation on the developers' side.

* I've never written a review before, so bear this in mind.*
Battleborn, I was hesitant to purchase this; that I admit. Infact, I waited until it went on sale, even at that I was a little worried.
Well, my verdict? This is an absolute blast, I regret nothing! I wish I dove into it sooner.
You will LOVE this game, if:
1) You like the gameplay of Borderlands.
2) A MOBA fan.
3) Oh you like Smite? Well... Guess what?! This is less clunky feeling!
As for the nay sayers in previous comments.
This game isn't DEAD, sure it's not BOOMING. But, I've yet to play the same opponents twice.
I blame the negative reviews on perspective:
People are saying OverWatch is better. Y'know what? OverWatch is a strictly FPS shooter, their competition is of another breed. Meanwhile, Battleborn is an FPS MOBA. It's really not hard to get into at all. The playerbase isn't so toxic to hate on you during a match.

Their cries for OverPowered characters? Look how much time they've put in the game.
I find most of these critiques a joke. I dont only mean on Battleborn, but for the rest of Steam.
Sure, balancing isn't perfect♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's not nearly as awful as the woeful make it out to be.
Perhaps it wasn't their cup of tea? Maybe they had a rough day? Bugs are really not game-breaking.
Unbalanced matchmaking? That's also a joke. I don't know who thought it was funny, but it's not true. We were a groupd of lowbies (1-18) and we still rocked a game where their accounts were 70-100. It's means nothing. It's not a measure of "True Player Skill".
Perhaps they've got more account experience due to the previous "Double XP weekend" (Which I wasnt apart of, regretfully). You know what? That equates to nothing. It doesn't significantly or even marginally give you an advantage. Sure, they might have an extra "Helix" unlocked. Truly though, what you start with most of the time is better, it just serves to fit your character into a niche role.
You need to decide for yourself, and not be too relient on other individuals judging on what YOU may like.
Final Thoughts:
Give this game a chance. It's had low publicity, perhaps bad marketing. I truly think you'll enjoy yourself in their world of Battleborn.
-There's unlocks to the Helix System = Optimizing attributes to your character.
-There's enough characters in here to make your own, to suit your playstyle. Shooters, Casters, Melee, Skirmishers, Snipers.
-You've got frikken loot! You accumulate said loot, from the story, obtaining in-game currency to purchase packets, etc.
-It's 2K Games, If you've never experienced Borderlands, there isn't a moment I havent laughed. The characters feel emersive, yet hilarious enough to keep individuals entertained.
-The Campaign mode is really not as bad as what I was expecting, due to reviews. They're fun, and always with a chance at different narrative from played characters; Yours, or your allies.
If you're hesitant as I was; Don't be. This game is safe, and has an update every week about their roadmap, features and what-have-you.

I love this game so much. While there are things that make me grumble on occasion, they aren't things that happen often or can be patched out. So, here's the rundown.
Pros:
-Super fun PvE campaigns, with Advanced difficulties. They're also relatively forgiving if you want to try out a new character since most people on your team will know what they are doing.
-Every character feels uniquely different, and has a full fledged skill tree for every match to try new builds, unlockable skills, unlockable lore, and unlockable taunts, and not all of them are show in the command menu.
-Speaking of lore, all the characters are very well developed! Their lore will explain how they became such badasses and their trials before you met them like Rath, or reveal things like Oscar Mike's terrible fear of spiders.
-Very humorous, and all the
characters have dozens of different lines. Even the campaign dialogue will change depending on the characters present.
-Tons of replayability due to the unlocks.
-PvP is challenging but satisfying when you win.
-The soundtrack is pretty damn good.
-Fast paced crazy action, just like Borderlands.
Cons:
-Sometimes enemies will bug out and be stuck behind a wall, where you can't kill them. This can prevent progress, but can usually be solved by AOE abilites, waiting, or in the case of timed levels walking away.
-PvP is HARD when you first start. Expect to die a lot.
-Not everyone thinks to be mindful of their teammates and stick together, or they stand in front of you where you can't shoot around them. This game is very cooperative in every aspect but single player, so you can't leave your healers and snipers out in the open.
-Getting pushed into a wall by an Attikus and Kelvin then pummeled sucks, because you're literally stuck between a rock and a hard place.
-Melee tanks are a little squishy, so you have to be very mindful of staying in motion.
-Poor optimization. I run this on medium settings and still get  big FPS drops on certain levels, (*cough* I'm looking at you Saboteur...) whereas I can run MGSV on high and never get any drops except for maybe like 30 seconds rarely.
I'm hoping I wrote about an equal amount for both, as I can't really tell on my phone. But really, give this game a chance, even if you wait for a free weekend, a sale, or even have a friend that owns it share their steam library with you. Hitman 2 Silent Assassin is to my mind a true classic for me even though this game is now about 14 years old it is still an excellent game and a great source of entertainment. This game brings you into the world of Legendary Assassin Agent 47 who comes out of retirement and is plunged into the criminal underworld as the ulimate assassin all with you at the controls. The gameplay in this game is obviously quite dated by the standards of games today but in my opinion you should not let that deter you from buying or playing this game because the controls still feel great and are easy to learn and memorize.
This game possess great variety in the methods to which you conduct your assassination attempts throughout the various levels. The great thing about the Hitman series is that the game gives you alot of freedom in how your aproach it you are in no way stuck to a linear setup in the levels and as such this game grants you a great deal of replayability as you can choose to play the same missions many times but go about them in very different ways ranging from the coveted Silent Assassin rank or to other more brutal and straightfoward methods. In addition to this you can take lots of different routs and use different tools and scenario's to perform your hits.
With an exception level count of 20 missions which is the most in any Hitman game you will be playing this game for a considerable time even following a guide on how to go through this game still grants up to 15 hours play for just 1 playthrough but you could decide to take your time and study each map and try all the different methods which would great you up to 25 hours plus and that is just one playthrough you can do it a totally different way in another playtrhough.
Now this game is not perfect and there are a few negatives such as glitches that can imped you from getting the best rank in some levels but they dont always happen so they are not to bad and also the AI can be quite finicky and strange at times which can be frustrating but once you learn the pattens of this its really not a huge issue at all.
On another note i should bring up the outstanding soundtrack by composer Jesper Kyd who quite simply creates an amazing soundtrack for this game which so wonderfully helps to immerse you in this very fun game to my way of thinking soundtracks and game atmosphere are very important to a successful and enjoyable game experience and this game delivers that with flying colors. All in all i would highly recommend this game for those who are thinking about it its a true classic it may be old but it is excellent and still holds up well in todays gaming if you ask me you have to really think about what you are doing and there is alot of variety to keep it fresh i give it a solid 7.5/10

There's plenty I don't like about the game. But there's WAY more to love, it's simply a massive game.
Bad:
-Really lacking tutorials to a game that has so much mechanical and tactical depth.

Good:
-Incredible tactical depth; You can really implement forms of maneuver. Understanding ADRP/FM 3-90 will greatly improve player experience.

-Tactical versitility; I have over 1000 hours logged and I still find new tactics, or new combinations of forces to implement tactics, etc.
ALB fits it's niche very well, and unfortunately that means it's not for everyone. I really didn't enjoy Red Dragon, and am so dissapointed that it stole basically all the player base for ALB and killed the multiplayer. I think I've seen the end of an era.

Also, you can enter your own name to be referred to, and pick a gender INCLUDING options for "It's complicated but I guess I'll put ___" or "I won't answer this question". Nice touches.

Oh, and before I forget, the story is well written and memorable, with characters that I found interesting and believable in the world they're in. I caught myself sacrificing my own needs to protect them on occasion, and I was trying to be self-serving.

I was originally finding at least some fun in this game at the start, so my orinigal review, despite being more of a "meh" kind of situation, was going to be positive. That said, having finished the game in just over 4 hours and 30 minutes (Steam claims 6, but that's likely due to leaving the game running while doing other things away from my computer) and finding merit in the complaints of others, I think a negative mark would suffice.
The AI can genuinely range from dumber than a sack of hammers to eagle-eyed geniouses, and they are indeed somehow more accurate with hipfire than the player can be while looking down the scope/iron sights of their rifle. While I somewhat appreciated the change of pace from sneeki breeki sniping to run-and-gun action, I'm left scratching my head as to why the latter was even added in a game that, if you were to go by the title alone, would/should be about sniping and stealth. And on that note, the sniping isn't even satisfying! How do you mess that up?
I had hoped to go through the "Unfinished Business" storyline after completing this game, but now I'm not so sure it would be wise to do so, even with the supposed "revamped AI." All I can say is I'm glad I bought this on sale in a bundle, so now that I can honestly say I've played this, I can now move on to the (hopefully superior) sequel.

I have no idea whats going on in this game whatsoever.
The story is rather odd to be honest.
You're stuck somewhere in south America, trying to disrupt some general from doing some bad things. But before that you're rushed through a training mission that emphasizes how important stealth is in the game, then it immediately forgets all pretenses of stealth as it confusedly tries to rush you through an action campaign, which it feels like there was a rift going on here. Half the studio probably wanted to make the next Call of Duty game, and then the other half wanted to make something more like the Sniper Elite series.
So you run through an earlier part of the mission with your buddy who has a weird callsign that you'll forget three seconds after hearing it, then you go through some combat and he gets taken back for his six o clock dental appointment on a boat, which you're glad he's gone because he's a terrible teammate anyways. Then you're supposed to escape using stealth, meanwhile you can't actually be stealthy. Like one area of the map where you're supposed to get from one end of the village to the other while being super sneaky, you climb through the tall grass, taking everything super slow, waiting for enemies to move, learning their pathing, generally being super good with your tactics. And then out of nowhere, ♥♥♥♥boy davey decides to shoot you with his gun because he somehow saw this elite trained sniper in his native environment... Yeah, GG on that one.
But then because the game gets bored, they quickly drop you on an oil rig where you're supposed to be doing some fast paced actiony shooty shooty sections, all the while I'm sitting here thinking "I bought Sniper game, but right now I'm not even carrying a sniper rifle at all!" That section ends and then you get back to the mainland, 'whew, time to do more sniping!' but nah, one member of your squad (oh yeah, you pick up a few guys at one point and then they go break on tea time, really I don't know where they went, I just looked up at one moment and they left me) gets hit by a sniper bullet, and then you have to go through this terribly designed village in order to uh..... do a thing I guess? I have no idea what the main goal for this game is yet, and I feel/hope I'm most of the way through the game (Honestly I was just playing and sorta raged at a certain section of the game, I'll get to that later) But this village has very few paths, actually really just one path, there were only maybe multiple paths because I found a way to get around some invisible walls. And by this point the AI have somehow downloaded an aimbot.exe because they're outsniping the trained sniper. Also this particular section was frustrating because the amount of cover was minimal, the enemies were spread out far, (meaning that if you move your character half an inch to the side, like five of them now have an angle to shoot you from) and even with the lack of cover, there's no good way to work around it. A decent peeking system would have made this part much smoother without providing an unfair advantage to players. Not to mention moving around the tight corridors in the building nearby is nearly impossible when your character feels like a piece of clay with two wheels and a gun attached to him. After you've finished that area you go and try and kill some more guys that you quickly realize are nearly indistinguishable from the vegetation nearby (though somehow they instantly see you when you're climbing around in the brush, actively TRYING to be sneaky) and then for no reason whatsoever, the game teleports you to a lighthouse for you to shoot people from. (I should mention that I wanted to test out how amazingly easy it was for the AI to spot me, so I went prone at the top of this tower, just observing them, and then boom... one guy popped out of a truck and shot me just about immediately after his boots touched the ground....) At this point I don't know whether I'm playing as five different characters or not. Like how the hell did I randomly get to a lighthouse? I really thought I wasn't going to like Her Story but, as it turns out, I really, really did.
That doesn't mean it's perfect, however.
The decision to leave out the questions being asked to the character on the screen is problematic at times. I understand that lining facts (or lies) up and painting a bigger picture is made more challenging if the designer completely removes questions from the equasion, as it leaves facts lingering in the air which may stirr up interest or present an inevitable "A-Ha!" moment later on. The problem, however, is that without any form of context, a lot of facts will invariably be burried under dozens of other videos that the player will be watching consequently.
Unless the player is familiarized with the core concepts of the experience, it's likely that they won't keep a lot of important discoveries in mind from the first videos they watch. Again, while I understand that this was intended, it shatters conveyance and theming in a single blow. After all, the character who the player is technically playing as, knows exactly what they went to that computer to do. If the objective of the game was unrelated to the character's motivation, it wouldn't matter. However, it is. Because of this disconnect, the reveal may lack the emotional punch it requires to be as effective as it needs to be. As it stands, while it retains its value as a very good twist, it's more or less contingent on the player's emotional maturity, and I don't feel the subject matter really needs to be contingent on anything but itself in order to be effective.
Secondly, it's important to admit that the "custom keywords" section of every video is a glorified .txt document. The designer should have known that the player is likely to write comments on it for later reference so they should have made sure to cater to that notion by providing a slightly larger box to work with. This leads me to the back up storage section below, which can get pretty cluttered, since there's no function to remove videos from the back up line. This is made even more of a problem because of the absense of an easy way to visually confirm why each video that the player has stored for later, is important to the player (i.e. you have to click every video to see what keywords you've applied to them).
I understand that the game doesn't need to cater to the user's utmost convenience in this way but it's worth keeping in mind, I think.
All of that said, this was an experience and a half, I must say. I played Her Story with one of my best friends through a stream and it was incredibly fun to discover her titular story. The amount of narrative intrigue, mystery and depth that this experience manages to pack into such a relatively small timeframe is staggering.
This review was largely devoid of positive points up until this point but this is mostly because this is a very simple experience from a user standpoint. There isn't much I can positively comment on without giving too much away, so I'll simply commend Viva Seifert's performance. I was completely stunned by her performance and I truly hope to see her in more acting duties beyond her musical career. She presents a very clear theatre style performance which I, personally, welcome. I thought it would sound very excessive but it doesn't sound the least bit hammy or forced, unless that was absolutely intended.
Some say that Her Story doesn't need to be a game at all, but the fact is that it does. Without the ability to go back and forth between videos, putting the story together wouldn't have been possible. So, Her Story completely and undoubtfully deserves its place as a bonafide videogame.
I absolutely recommend Her Story. Couple of slight oversights do not sully an ultimately great experience that I'm not likely to forget any time soon.
A nice, relatively short (you can, and probably should, beat it in one sitting) experience that uses the medium exceptionally well.

I had the pleasure of playing The Masterplan back in October 2014, during its Early Access phase. When I played the game then, The Masterplan was essentially a single player version of Payday. You had a crew and committed several heists. Every part of the plan was left up to you, planning, execution, and escape. There are new features in the game, the ability to hire goons,  buy weapons, and equipment, Including a new items that lead to other heists or weapon orders.
As of June 2015, The Masterplan has left Early Access and the game is now complete. I am happy to say the game is fantastic and fun. Everything here still works rather well as it did in Early Access, combat, sneaking, and general law breaking. In case your not familiar with The Masterplan, you control a team of criminals from a top down view. The best example is something like Door Kickers or a more far more tactical Hotline Miami. If things get a little hectic you can use a slow-mo button to issue commands and order your goons to perform tasks ranging from, shooting, taking hostages, or safe cracking.
Now while I covered most of how I felt about the game in my
. I feel It's important to note how awesome the over all tone of the game is and how well it all works. While the graphics are simple they really do a good job of conveying the grit and crime of The Masterplan, almost in noir style. The music and sound effects are great and fit in perfectly as well.
For the purposes of this particular article, I wanted to cover the new things I enjoy and the things I wish worked a little differently. There is a story now intricately woven throughout the levels, little snippets of paper building the mystery of whats going on. There are cut scenes telling the tale of how your character broke bad during the Nixon administration. All of these add a little flavor and life to the game.
The hideout has seen a bit of updating as well. You now have the ability to hire goons and purchase weapons, as long as you have the right contact for the weapon. These can be acquired throughout the levels and add an extra objective aside from getting cash. This is all fine and works well but can lead the game to feel a bit grindey in the beginning as you have to repeat missions to earn enough cash. In later parts of the game this isn't a big deal. For the most part the hideout stayed the same, I would've liked to see a bit more added to it. Perhaps some sort of secret or way to expand upon it and make it the seat of your criminal empire. It just ends up being a stash place for your left over equipment/weapons and the place you go in between missions. Not a major complaint just my own personal wish.
There are several new missions and places to rob. Including new levels to finish out the story/campaign. All of these are crafted well and requires your keen focus as your order your team of goons. In general the gameplay felt smoother in controlling characters and maneuvering them, as opposed to the EA version of the game where it was a bit more difficult. Such things as being able to pass through your own men made things much easier. With that said there are still some things that are hard to control. Doors in particular are a nightmare and being such a vital element to the games strategy, I thought this would've been corrected a bit more.
Things such as goon skills and multiplayer have fallen to wayside or replaced with simpler mechanics. I feel that The Masterplan will benefit from simplifying and focusing on the single player experience. While goon skills would've been nice, that is something that perhaps can be added later. In the final version of the game the focus on singleplayer can be seen and the game is very enjoyable.
So if you haven't checked out The Masterplan yet and you're looking for a heist style game that is solely based off your skill. You definitely want to check out this title.

It's a cool concept, I like the idea, but there's a LOT more work to be done. Maybe 1 hour of gameplay currently with no replay value yet. But there's definitely potential here, particularly if it goes fully procedural.

As of Build 1:
The Masterplan is a heist sim with a 70s heist movies look and feel.
Take Monaco, mix in a bit of Hotline Miami, add your typical strategy game controls for all of the characters - and that's how the game feels in general.
It's definitely quite more puzzely and requires more planning than fast paced Monaco. And may be as well not so insanely tactical and quick as Hotline. But it has it's moments, plenty of blood if you are not careful, and tons of quick decisions to make.
Even with lacking features (no skills, no level editor, no gadgets, they are coming though), only 4 levels to play (last one is hell, wasn't able to beat it) - The Masterplan offers a pretty solid experience that will most likely only get better.
No serious bugs was noticed during ~2h playtime.

Fast colorful and kind of insane, this game feels fresh and interesting if a little bit short. The 6 degrees of freedom make it a very interesting experience. Being forced to play 12 levels I've already played to get to the final boss is kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and I would've liked if it were optional.
Also, beware that there's few if any instructions. There's no hand-holding and the game expects you to explore and learn things on your own. Don't be discouraged if at first you don't really know what's going on or where are your enemies or how do they move.
That said, the gameplay is strangely relaxing in some wierd way so I play it while listening to podcasts to wind down.

This game tells the tragic story of a crash test dummy sentenced to perpetual torment. Players lock the poor dummy in a vehicle and send him into extremely dangerous situations. Oftentimes the impacts destroy the dummy and his vehicle. But it doesn’t matter, for they always rebuild him, but only to break him again, and again, and again. There is no escape.
Turbo Dismount is a physics-based simulation game with the goal of inflicting maximum destruction upon the protagonist, Mr. Dismount. You are the antagonist, Mr. Dismount’s permanent nightmare. With a considerable catalogue of levels, vehicles, and customization options, Turbo Dismount offers players considerable choice in overseeing the catastrophic life of Mr. Dismount.
Perhaps the most impressive feat of them all, Turbo Dismount continues to receive updates – including new content – nearly four years after release. If you’re looking for a chaotic simulation game complete with mass destruction and slow-motion replays of huge crashes, Turbo Dismount is worth the purchase.

I bought this game when the price dropped to 3-4 dollars and for that low a price, I think it was a worthwhile buy, but let's be real ... at that low a price we can write this game off as a failure for the company that made it, and I largely think they have "social justice" to thank for that.
The overall gameplay from a coded standpoint is fairly enjoyable. The rts aspect of it is pretty basic in comparison to something more polished like Starcraft or a Total War game but it's nothing that couldn't have been touched up with future patches if the game hadn't bombed on release.
I love the magic and steampunk mixture they have for a gameworld setting, and the cartoonish cutscenes cgi animations are very well done. The game also tries to blend together a card game, a campaign style kingdom management system, and rts, and an RPG style story into one big epic package ... and on every front but the story it does at least a decent job.
The story though ... jeez. I honestly can't tell if it's actual gender studies graduates self failing, or trolls making fun of gender studies graduates via satire. The writing is so on the nose and lazy it's like they just cut and pasted segments of CNN into the elves and lizard people and Fox News into the dwarves and undead. The imps ... to their credit ... pretty much just wanna blow stuff up.
But yeah, listening to the political dialogue made my spine cringe out of my back. It was about as poorly done as Seige of Dragonspire with the transgendered shopkeeper lecturing your D&D adventuring party about how terrible they are for observing traditional gender roles ... ... because that's what you want in a video game ... a preachy moral busy body who doesn't even like games but feels the need to make everything about politics.
I think we all get enough of that from relatives at Thanksgiving Dinner thanks.
For 3-4 dollars ... I can suffer through the cringe worthy writing. But it's that cringy writing that specifically made me not buy the game when it was being sold at a price point the developers needed to sell it at to actually make a profit. Hopefully if enough of these "progressive" themed games bomb the developers will get the message that consumers don't want to be preached at when they're doing their hobby.

Feels a bit like four simple games stacked on top of each other to make one fairly complex game.
Each turn is made up of four stages. Take turns until you own every capitol city on the map.
Stage one is a political simulator.  Visit each room of your flying fortress, managing your tech trees, and speaking to your various generals and ambassadors while choosing which of their demands to appease.  This determines your modifiers in stage two.
Stage two is a turn based war boardgame.  Move your pieces around the map.  Buy more pieces.  Play modifier cards on territories.  At the end of this phase, a random number based battle happens in any territory with opposing units.
Stage three RTS mode.  Once per turn, you can play one of those contested territories as a real time strategy map, which potentially gives you much better odds of winning than letting the battle be decided by numbers and dice rolls.
Stage four, after a minute in RTS mode, you can enter the battle field as a flying dragon, which can dramatically change the pace of the battle, but also makes it much harder to micromanage your base and units.
Larian Studios had to figure out how to top playing as a dragon in Divinity II.  Their answer: strap a rocket to the dragon.
It was a good answer.

I really thought I wasn't going to like Her Story but, as it turns out, I really, really did.
That doesn't mean it's perfect, however.
The decision to leave out the questions being asked to the character on the screen is problematic at times. I understand that lining facts (or lies) up and painting a bigger picture is made more challenging if the designer completely removes questions from the equasion, as it leaves facts lingering in the air which may stirr up interest or present an inevitable "A-Ha!" moment later on. The problem, however, is that without any form of context, a lot of facts will invariably be burried under dozens of other videos that the player will be watching consequently.
Unless the player is familiarized with the core concepts of the experience, it's likely that they won't keep a lot of important discoveries in mind from the first videos they watch. Again, while I understand that this was intended, it shatters conveyance and theming in a single blow. After all, the character who the player is technically playing as, knows exactly what they went to that computer to do. If the objective of the game was unrelated to the character's motivation, it wouldn't matter. However, it is. Because of this disconnect, the reveal may lack the emotional punch it requires to be as effective as it needs to be. As it stands, while it retains its value as a very good twist, it's more or less contingent on the player's emotional maturity, and I don't feel the subject matter really needs to be contingent on anything but itself in order to be effective.
Secondly, it's important to admit that the "custom keywords" section of every video is a glorified .txt document. The designer should have known that the player is likely to write comments on it for later reference so they should have made sure to cater to that notion by providing a slightly larger box to work with. This leads me to the back up storage section below, which can get pretty cluttered, since there's no function to remove videos from the back up line. This is made even more of a problem because of the absense of an easy way to visually confirm why each video that the player has stored for later, is important to the player (i.e. you have to click every video to see what keywords you've applied to them).
I understand that the game doesn't need to cater to the user's utmost convenience in this way but it's worth keeping in mind, I think.
All of that said, this was an experience and a half, I must say. I played Her Story with one of my best friends through a stream and it was incredibly fun to discover her titular story. The amount of narrative intrigue, mystery and depth that this experience manages to pack into such a relatively small timeframe is staggering.
This review was largely devoid of positive points up until this point but this is mostly because this is a very simple experience from a user standpoint. There isn't much I can positively comment on without giving too much away, so I'll simply commend Viva Seifert's performance. I was completely stunned by her performance and I truly hope to see her in more acting duties beyond her musical career. She presents a very clear theatre style performance which I, personally, welcome. I thought it would sound very excessive but it doesn't sound the least bit hammy or forced, unless that was absolutely intended.
Some say that Her Story doesn't need to be a game at all, but the fact is that it does. Without the ability to go back and forth between videos, putting the story together wouldn't have been possible. So, Her Story completely and undoubtfully deserves its place as a bonafide videogame.
I absolutely recommend Her Story. Couple of slight oversights do not sully an ultimately great experience that I'm not likely to forget any time soon.
A nice, relatively short (you can, and probably should, beat it in one sitting) experience that uses the medium exceptionally well.

An easy title to review and can be summerised in one short paragraph: this is probably the finest FMV (full motion video) game ever released and a proud salute to a long lost genre that very was popular in the early-to-mid ninties. A series of grainy FMV clips have to be viewed in no certain order concerning of a pair of "twins" portrayed with aplomb by a stunning English Rose being invterviewed in a police station, it is of course up to you to find out who killed who and reach your own conclusion(s).
I have played this game on and off for quite while now and although I could complete it fairly quickly, instead I am just savouring every moment I sit down and be transported back to '94 and gaze longlingly at Sam Barlow's lead actress.
Her Story becomes an instant classic and should become your story when this modern classic finds a home on your hard drive.  It is a masterpiece of FMV and the story telling has been written by a genius.  RECOMMENDED 9.75/10

The Masterplan is a game where you pull of various heists as you see fit, the heists can range from small shops to jewelry stores and even to warehouses (No banks or such are currently in the game) there are as of now 4 heists to pull off and they are designed really well. You can pull of these heists in various ways such as walking in the front door and pulling your gun out and murder everyone inside, of course anyone who sees you doing this will imediately call the cops and you will have 30 seconds to get the hell out. Or you could walk inside, wait for the owner to go someone secluded, follow them, take them hostage and then get your friend to beat the hell out of them and then continue with only the customers to worry about. But of course some are much more difficult as guard will be involved.
-Gameplay-
You control various men (in the future you will be able to hire your own men and such but for now you are given 'goons' on different heists) using your mouse and you tell them what to do and they do it. If you pull out a gun and aim at someone then they will freeze meaning they won't move and now you can control them but if you lose LOS a meter that slowly drains will drain much faster and when it runs out they will make a run for it or if they have a weapon attack you. There are various keys that open different doors and security guards that will watch cameras for illegal activity.
-Conclusion-
This is a very well made game even for Early Access, I have high hopes for this game and definately reccommend picking it up now even though there are only 4 heists because they are highly replayable as you can approach in loads of ways and possibly improve on your last run. There are of course quite a few bugs and issues such as if the game lags it causes the characters to fly across the screen which is hilarious until it screwes you over, also something I 'hate' at the moment is if 'you' call the cops from a phone even if you haven't even entered the building yet when the cops turn up they will kill you on sight. I learned this because I wanted to see how they responded to calls incase it went south but the cops wanted to shoot first and ask questions later.
For now I give it an 8/10 for being fun, unique and amazing even if it is a tad buggy at times. Hopefully there will be some sort of MP as that would be incredible for this type of game.

The Masterplan is an action/strategy game focused on pulling off different heists and set in the 70s. If you enjoyed games like Payday 2 or Monaco you’ll most likely enjoy this one, too, even if they are entirely different games. Still, this game can easily hold its own and has more than enough content for an Early Access version.
The comparison to aforementioned games isn’t a completely honest comparison because Payday 2 is a first-person shooter focused on a whole lot of shooting (if things go wrong, that is) and Monaco is really more about stealth than tactics. But The Masterplan masterfully combines several of the elements used in these games: first of all, you view the action from a top-down perspective and there are several ways to finish a mission; guns blazing, with careful planning or - if things go wrong - a combination of both. You will also holdup civilians and cops among other things related to heists.
You can walk freely to wherever you want, as long as it’s not towards a place that raises suspicion. You’ll control several goons, which can be controlled individually or as a group. It’s usually a good idea to just walk around and see where everything is located before taking any action. Once you have an idea of what to do you can strategically place your goons and let them do what they’re supposed to do.
As an example you could have a goon set up near the entrance of the place that holds people who are entering or about to leave hostage, one that holds the store manager hostage (which you can then control to open things, for example) and another one could knock the store manager out once he’s done with that (or before that, and have a goon open the door him-/herself). There are many ways to complete the heist, and there are many ways a heist can go wrong. The store manager could call the cops, which will then arrive shortly after, making it nearly impossible to get out without killing anyone. Do something suspicious on camera and again, the police will be alerted. Or civilians could see an unconscious or dead body and, yup, could call the cops.
It’s a game that requires a good bit of strategy but thankfully the developers have implemented a feature to slow down time for people that usually don’t play strategy games or have a difficult time improvising when things go wrong. It’s a feature that doesn’t use a time mechanic so you could play the entire heist in slow motion if you wanted to. It makes the game very accessible to all sorts of players.
The maps aren’t that big to begin with and that’s actually something that I liked. It’s hard to manage your characters when they’re miles apart from each other. Some of the maps of the later heist missions are just big enough for them to become cluttered. But I think there will actually be bigger maps in the final version. I just hope they don’t become too big.
There’s also a hideout map where you can eventually hire new goons and do some other stuff, and this is also where the game tells you about the game’s mechanics, besides the tutorial level (which basically explains the controls).
This Early Access version has 5 different heists, ranging from very simple to pretty difficult. There are a few features missing right now, like goons having specific skills, a connecting story and, obviously, more heist locations. The developers states that there is about 1,5-2 hours of gameplay in this version and I agree. But you could add an hour or even a few hours more if you want to play things in a different way. So far, this version is already extremely polished and it runs great without any problems. I also didn’t encounter any bugs so far, but maybe I’m just lucky. Who knows ?
The graphics are 2D and shown from a top-down perspective. The characters lack a bit of personality because of this but the graphics are just beautiful in general. It has a nice 70s look mixed with what looks like some sort of comic book effect(s). It’s absolutely gorgeous to look at, and it’s all made with higher resolutions in mind.
The soundtrack consists of some smooth songs that have a jazzy feel that reminded me of old school heist movies. And that sounds exactly what they’re aiming for. So they did an excellent job there. Same goes for the sound effects which have an authentic feeling to them.
The Masterplan is on its way to become one of my favorite indie games. There’s still some work to be done, and I’m not talking about fixes here, but more about adding (final) content. This current version is already very stable and very playable and if you enjoy strategy games or heist games then this is a game you just must own. You can clearly see this game was made with passion and that’s absolutely something that should be rewarded. And the best way to do this is to just buy the game.

Quite possibly one of the most functional 3D shoot-em-ups I've ever seen. The player is given a great range of control of the ship, allowing you to zip around and take ridiculous paths through the environments, The music has a pretty good range between calm, atmospheric tracks when first entering a stage before combat starts, to ramping it up a few notches when blasting your way around.
The environments themselves are full of sharp geomoetric shapes, cubes, and abstract machinery that always finds a way to look interesting, not to mention be exciting and terrifying with its sheer size and emptiness. There are points where you will be warned that you're going out-of-bounds, but it's still neat to try and probe each stage to see just how far you can go. Not only are the stages nice to look at, but there are plenty of hidden objects, rooms, and items to find, though you're probably better off exploring before you start combat so you're not being swarmed by enemies.
There are a few problems, however, namely dealing with combat and general gameplay. Almost all of the enemies and their movement is based on tracking the player, so they will constantly rubber-band their way around the place based on what direction you're facing or in which direction you're actually moving, and while it can be predictable, some enemies take entirely too long to settle down so you can pick them off and get them out of the way, and some enemies have attacks that are nearly unavoidable because their tracking is just too spot-on.
Couple this with the fact that there are only two pick-ups in the entire game that enemies can drop, one being an advanced boost with a limited capacity, and the other being a single shield point, with the player's max being four units, the length of the stages and amount of enemies seems a little unfair.This can get really obnoxious because you'll be picking up tons of boost pick-ups that you don't need, meanwhile barely hanging on with only one hit-point left, only to eventually get knocked out by a stray bullet or asteroid and being set back a few checkpoints. The drop-rate for the shield unit is so low that it might as well not even exist as an item, because it's not really dependable at all.
Another problem is that while the environments are neat and there's plenty to see and do, you're gonna get sick of them after you realize that you need to go through each stage four times, one time for each of the four weapons you unlock. Not only does it get repetitive, but some of the weapons just aren't well-balanced for certain bosses and feel a little unpolished. With one boss and weapon combination in particular, the weapon deals so little damage over time that it's hard to determine where or what its weak-point is, whereas the first two bosses have more obvious weak-points that change color dependant on the weapon you're using.
With the different weapons to unlock and the extra items to collect throughout the game, it teases the player into thinking there will be more abilities to use, but SPOILER ALERT: there's only one unlockable ability, as well as five different weapons. Outside of that one ability, the rest of the items are just collectibles, and the ability you unlock is honestly more dangerous than helpful in a lot of cases, being a grappling hook that can bring you up to insane speeds and potentially kill you.
All in all, Kromaia is a pretty neat exploration of the concept of a fast-paced 3D shoot-em-up, with great presentation and fun gameplay.

This game was only average - 6/10 at best when it was released.  It hasn't aged well, and the things that were annoying about it 6 years ago are only magnified in this age.
While a million miles better than CI Games previous effort at the genre - the woeful Sniper Art of Victory - it still falls short of a pleasant FPS experience.  The somewhat satisfying sniping elements are held back by an AI that doesn't know if it's on God mode or stormtrooper mode, while the infantry parts of the game are held back by the fundamentally broken assault rifles that the game gives those characters.
AI can detect you seemingly for no reason as you are in cover, they can sometimes care if you kill their buddies 5 feet away and otherwise not.  At one point I took a break from a mission to shoot birds with an unsilanced rifle, then when I carried on realised there had been a 3 man patrol not 30 feet away that was still in "oblivious" mode.
The feeling of achievement of pulling off a hit with your rifle, taking into account bullet drop due to gravity and wind direction is cheapend somewhat when your enemies can hit you with pinpoint precision using their assault rifles at the same distance.  These are the same assault rifles you will struggle to use, as the kick and spread is extreme to the point of uselessness.
Manual saving is encouraged with this game, the chekpoints aren't always in places you would expect and can indeed just put you into a loop of spawn-die-spawn-die.
At least CI Games paid for some proper voice talent this time round - but the story they are telling is very cliche.
You'll have more fun with Sniper Elite 2 if you want to play a sniper game- I promise you.

These bugs & glitches include but are not limited to;

- The enemies not seeing you when they are supposed to.
- Too many unnecessary cutscenes.
-Too many unnecessary mission objectives that are just f**king annoying after a point.
Some Cons of this game also are;

- In hard difficulty, it feels like all your enemies are veteran snipers who were born with the ability of sniping. They have no problem shooting you with a pistol from 200m. You can make the AI smarter or increase Damage taken or increase wind speed and change environmental factors, but if you are being hit by a pistol bullet from 200m away and almost dying from that shot, then that just makes the game stupid and annoying... Not "difficult".
In short, Sniper: Ghost Warrior is an extremely average game. There is nothing special about it that makes it stand out. If you like sniper games in general and if stupid bugs, glitches and unnecessary things don't bother you, then you can try this game.

It took me around ten hours to complete the campaign. The best part of the experience was interacting with the various characters out of combat and making political decisions. While my choices didn't feel like they had a massive impact on the tactical or real-time combat in the game, the characters were just so much fun to listen to and interact with that it was enjoyable in its own right.
Unfortunately, the RTS portion of the game felt very difficult to get into. While I enjoyed playing as the dragon during the real-time battles, limiting my view point and diverting my attention from building units felt very counter productive, no matter how many casualties I inflicted. Most of this issue seemed to spring from the fact that every unit in the game had powerful active abilties which were incredibly important to their combat effectiveness. If the dragon could activate them, I never figured out the hotkey wizardry. It's possible that the RTS portion of the game could be enjoyable if you're very good at RTS games or invest a great deal of time into it, but I'm just not willing.
In the end, I autoresolved most of the combats, only bringing the dragon out to play in small, even skirmishes in which the AI couldn't just out produce me through superior macro. While there were a handful of fights in which this won me a battle I should have lost, I felt much better off not participating in larger scale conflicts. This left the game as more of a turn-based strategy game in which unit production and tactical movement determined the winner.
Unfortunately, the game doesn't stand up too well when measured from a turn-based metric. It never seemed to feel like unit composition mattered in battle because numbers were so much more important. As a result, the tactical gameplay of the game consisted of me moving a bunch of units around on the map and buying things without caring too much what they were. As long as they could quickly reach my next target of conquest, it didn't seem to matter. This isn't acceptable for any strategy game.
Since I got the game for $5 I don't feel cheated, but I can't recommend it. The politicing and characters in the game really were enjoyable, but the RTS portion of the game was either too difficult or too complicated. The game could have been great if every battle didn't have unit production centers. I would have loved the game if it were just your army with you as a dragon versus an opposing army and dragon. Drop a few capture points on a map to fight over and it would have been golden.

Hitman 2: Silent Assassin provides an estimated duration of ten hours (parameter now average), an in my opinion very addictive, definitely living. Fans would highly recommend it as it is the better of the two chapters on the history of Agent 47 while those new to the saga recommend you try it, maybe at your neighborhood store, to see if the setting menus and commands may be to their liking. If you allow me, a final warning: do not be discouraged, this is a title designed to be extremely difficult, at times slightly frustrating (spend three afternoons trying to accomplish a mission may also get tired!) And then, if you want to play with, arm yourself with a good patience ... good luck, agents 47!

Unlike most Hitman games where you just kill for money, this one has a different and more interesting plot.
47 has 'gone soft' as Diana says, and is fighting his way to save a friend of him who got kidnapped. So basically he's getting back to the killing business in order to save his friend.
For its time the game looks pretty neat, with good character design, decent textures, realistic and big maps for a lot of exploration. Same goes for the animations and sounds, not to mention the music. Its gameplay is a little more challenging than newer Hitman games and it's pretty hard to achieve the rank "Silent Assassin", especially in the harder difficulties (part of me believes that it's also the reason they decided to give the name Silent Assassin to this one). However if you do you get rewarded with unlockable weapons. Yes, you don't have to pay DLC for new weapons but to actually be good at the game. Then again there are multiple ways you can beat a mission so the stealth aspect could be considered optional. If you're mostly into the story and want to progress to save Vittorio, you can always go out guns blazing. So I highly recommend this game to everyone, whether you like stealth or not it's a great game that will keep you busy for a lot of hours.

I'm utterly sad that I never played this game before. It's a great look back on the era of top tier platformers. And with it's sequel coming, what other best time is there to dive in?
Story Quality: Psychonauts introduces you to a funny, dark, and artistic world that stays expanding throughout whatever messed up minds you wander into. The characters all add to the weirdness theme pretty well. Most of their personalities are pretty normal, but the way the style portrays them makes them fit right in. There'll be plenty of plot twists and questions given to the player in every moment as you advance in, and some of the collectables add emotional value to the background stories. I should also mention how every level is entirely different, and never feel watered down for gameplay. The only real problem with the story is that toward the end it honestly felt watered down. Multiple introduced plot points weren't really settled or advanced in. Spoiler examples:
But anyway, it's no 5 star story, but it works to keep the flow going, and is garunteed to put a smile on your face... Or make you cry if you find the extras.
Gameplay: The masterpiece part of the game, I do say. Psychonauts does not only offer smooth gameplay meachanics, but also a level designing that truly lets the player engage in finding solutions. You can be approached by some acrobatic pole spin and jumping... or just use the levitate abiliity to perform a well timed jump instead. Monsters will often have multiple ways to defeat them, like the bombs in Waterloo. And what's best about all this, is that the game doesn't tell you what to do in most situations. You have to really think and find your way to solve a problem, rather than deal with repetitive rock paper scissor type situations. Though if you're stuck on major parts, they do have a hint system to cover your back.. noob ;P
Performance: My pc is no super hyper monster gaming machine, but I had no real issues playing Psychonauts. Though the frame rate dropped on high resolutions, this was easily fixed with option adjustment. I have heard of some players experiencing glitches in the port, but here I had none. I only wish they put the quit to desktop function in-game. Oh, and if you do crash, you'll see some of the developer's charm... xD
Collectables: A very important aspect to platformers, and Psyconauts handles it well enough. The figments felt kinda tedious obtaining, but all the others were rewarding in their own ways, and levels were never too crowded to make completion a chore (except for the flippin' figments...). I'll also warn you that it's an older game before the current age babying, if you plan to 100% this be wary that some items are missable. I advise keeping a guide handy from the start if you want all the achievements in one playthrough. At least keep an eye on the ones tagged as missable.
Price: Worth it at whatever the lovely store page is offering. I got it for 0.99, a complete steal in my opinon. Anyway, it's worth. If it's on a sale for the price of a sandwich, treat yourself to it and just pretend it's a sandwich... A very awesome sandwich. Over and out!

I recommend it for the sincere enjoyment I got from the story and charm, and if you are the type of player who can't play a game without breaks, this is the game for you, because none of the levels play the same. I bought this game only for a single player since I liked it in the European Escalation. However, in this game, it's simply terrible.
The reason why I liked European Escalation was that there were unique missions that were not limited in time (almost all of them). But here every battle is just a skirmish for 20 minutes (so there is no point in stealth) and the one who scores more points by the end of the timer will win. No more missions for several hours with different objectives, which I liked in the first part.
Besides. The main task, too, must be performed for a certain number of turns. Yea, turns. It's a turn-based strategy now, like some Total War game, only without building and unit production.
This is my main problem, because of which I'll probably never start this game again. I don't want to play in rush duel simulator.
Ther is none. No more videos before the mission or after, just a boring text which explains the beginning of the conflict at the start of each campaign and random pop-ups between turns.
Well... I don't think that AI is cheating like in European Escalation, however, it definitely very punishing because it always remembers ideally where your units are, it can simultaneously control all of its units, its reaction speed is always incredibly fast, and to compensate the lack of tactical thinking, it simply spams you with a bunch of units.
There is no point in ambushes also because the AI scans the whole map with reconnaissance units all the time and sends either long-range units or an artillery strike or something against which at the moment you will not be able to respond.
In missions, AI will almost always have a tactical advantage (will have more deployment points). For example, when one of my territories was surrounded by enemy territories on the global map, during the battle, I could not call for reinforcements. But when the same situation was with the AI, for some reason it started on the edge of the map and could call for reinforcements.
I think the devs did it because they can not create an AI with which it would be interesting to play. So, they did not limit its abilities to artificially increase the difficulty, however, AI is still dull and when you know what to expect from it, it becomes not interesting to play.
They are few and they are repeated, which quickly becomes boring.
On account of the multiplayer game I have nothing to say, I'm not interested in it.

I like these choose-your-own-adventure stories in general, but they have been very hit or miss for me depending on how much the writing disconnects from the choices I make. I don't want to give anything away about the story so I will start with an analogy, *not* an actual example. Imagine you are asked by a story to choose your favorite beverage - water, cola, or liquor. You answer water, only to be told you would have preferred liquor and now you are sad because you wanted to get buzzed. I am? I did?
Again, trying not to give anything away about the game, but give an *actual* example of what I mean this time ... on my playthrough, the story severely broke down in the end. It was clear that the later elements of the story were written from the perspective of the character struggling against the crisis unfolding, even if your previous choices made it clear you did not view what was happening as a crisis. In other words, I had to choose the same option about six times in a row to get to the next page so the story could tell me how worried I was again, even though I had just chosen not to be worried. To paraphrase the responses ... "It's terrible, you're distraught, you can't believe this happening. Now is the time to act!" Why? I've told you six times I don't care. Next page please ... "OK, but it's terrible, you're distraught, you can't believe this is happening." I can't? I have repeatedly told you to let it happen. Please just get on with it! "OK, but you view your special item as your one hope to stop this terrible, terrible thing!" No, I don't - get on with it! "OK, but ..."
The result of this defect is that for me, this title wasn't really choose *your* own adventure, more like choose *someone else's* adventure and be told how they feel about it. Therefore, I can't recommend this game based on my experience. I think the reason I don't find this defect in non-text-based games that feature choice is that there is no inner monologue to contradict how you personally feel about the choices. Just something to keep in mind, in case you are thinking of purchasing the game, but would be disappointed by such a disconnect should you deviate from the author's perspective. On the other hand, if you happen to agree with the viewpoint of the author, you would never notice the defect and might really love the story.

This game was amazing, plain and simple. Trying to explain the plot is so difficult because of the interwoven themes and genres that baffles me still about how well it works.
Mechanically, I never felt once like my choices were just tossed off and without meaning, just a number that ultimately turns out the same. Every choice had weight. Some choices were difficult. Some were ultimately very satisfying. All were interesting.
That is something -very- hard to pull off these days, but through masterful writing and an impactful story, they have made it real.
All in all, this game is way more than what I had purchased it for. Not just for the fact that I'm probably going to restart the experience anew right after writing this, but for an experience unlike any story I've seen or heard of before. This is a rare gem, and I thank the creator for it graciously.

First off, this is a text only choose-your-own-adventure, if anyone was unaware. If you value graphics over story or player decisions, this probably isn't the type of game for you.
This is a pretty fantastic entry, which combines compelling storytelling with interesting mechanics and choice that seem to actually matter. I also enjoyed the game testing my own detective skills at a few points, challenging me to solve a mystery with the game only giving me helpful clues for correct choices instead of the direct answer like so many other games do, making it seem challenging without being unfair or obtuse. I felt genuinely immersed when playing this, which seems odd for a cyberpunk-fantasy choose-your-own-adventure, but it was just a very enjoyable experience that I felt a part of.
My main criticism is that some of the decisions, especially the routine ones which you can adjust regularly throughout the game, should have to be confirmed before they are made permanent, as it is easy to make an error if you misclick or misread the option.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good story or enjoys a game where the player's choices actually matter.

Unbelievable experience, one of the best games I have played this year !
You start in front of a computer screen and are shown various short clips of Hannah who may or may not be under investigation for a murder.
The gameplay mechanics are very limited. You unveil more clips by typing in keywords which you can get by listening to former clips ( I wrote down interesting words, phrases and names on a paper while playing ), or you may also just type random words and get lucky.
The story itself is morbide, intense and has a major twist which you could also miss I guess due to what clips you unveil. I wont say any more because the story is really the key element of the game and shall not be spoiled. It is driven by your very own curiosity which makes you also think of yourself. I asked myself a couple of times whether it is "right" to dig so deep in someone elses past, making them open for your judgement.
The experience is veeeery short though. I played it offline yesterday and got to the plot twist after about 80 minutes or so. After this, you of course go and play on and unveil even more of the story, but I felt it was wasted because I already reached the climax, the key element of the game.
The achievements are fairly easy to get as well, although it can get annoying trying to get acces to all videos.
Over all, it is very different from other games and I would recommend this game for everyone who enjoys a good book or movie. It is no game for the typical Call of Duty Kids and may also bore the hell out of you because of the simple mechanics.
Buy it when its on sale due to its short playtime !

As a crime documentary addict, I was excited to play this!  I really enjoyed a lot of the little touches, like the sound of an old harddrive ticking and buzzing as files are retrieved.  While the gameplay is simple (it's more of an interactive video, which is oddly appropriate for the time period the computer console places you in), I think anything more would have been too much.  You aren't *playing* a detective, you *are* the detective, and your moniter becomes a 90s work station.
Some of the videos are very short, and if you search a keyword that is too broad, you can't click through more than the first few in that category.  This is a little bit frustrating, and it's the only thing that really stands out to me as a device to prolong gameplay. Why would I only have access to the first five videos in a search if I really were accessing a police database? Certainly if I was trying to solve a cold case and hit upon a condemning phrase, I should be able to see all the entries at once, right?  Ah, well.
That being said, I didn't think the game led me to any kind of obvious conclusion (at least too quickly).  It was designed to give you some strong suspicions, certainly, but if you are interested in the story and continue to search, it becomes more bizarre and convoluted.  I admit, I like to see mysteries through to the end without jumping to a conclusion, which probably makes me the perfect audience for a game like this.  However, if you really are pretending to be a detective, it would be a little conceited to follow just one line of questioning and assume you know the entire story.  Isn't that what makes a cold case mystery interesting?
So my advice to the prospective buyer would be this: If you are likely to be bored once you think you know the end game, then you might be disappointed as some reviewers have been.  If you like figuring out not only what you think happened, but the story behind it, then this will entertain you!

Just in case City Interactive misspelled every design document they put together for this game, I'll tell them now for next time: sniping was supposed to go into the game, not just the name.
Sniper: Ghost Warrior aspires to be a budget Crysis, but barely reaches the levels of being a discount SOCOM. In that regard the game could be considered a success; it accomplished it's goal of achieving complete mediocrity.
It's boring, ugly, derivative and ultimately isn't worth any of your damn time.

Sniper: Ghost Warrior is an interesting little game. You could see what they were trying to do with it, but they didn't quite get there. To be fair, my first ever Sniper experience was slighty marred by the fact that the game isn't particularly compatible with win10 and the constant freezes, crashes and other little problems meant that my 14hr (twice as long as necessary) playthrough - from training to the end of unfinished business (dlc) - registered as about 25hrs on steam.
Pros: nice enough to look at on max settings;  the killcam never got tiring for me; it does mix up gameplay between sneaky sneaky and run and gun, with a couple of mounted shooting galleries thrown in for good measure.
Cons: gameplay can get repetitive; sometimes (especially prone) the scenery is so in your face that you can't see anything beyond the foliage in front of your face, which ends in tears;  some of the shot/AI behaviour is truly laughable.
TL:DR - fun little game, can get extremely annoying/frustrating at times and no end of problems if playing on anything beyond win7!
Recommended only for patient people.

To be honest, I can't recommend this game. I suppose I shouldn't have expected much from a game that's three bucks, but I've had many games for around the same price that was far more satisfying. The music is rather lacking (I could swear it's just one song, an uninteresting one at that) Visual novels are, at its essence, a story dressed up by the graphics, music, etc. The story of Soul Gambler is, to be blunt, subpar.
There many grammar mistakes that will break your immersion (had you cared enough to really read it carefully). I didn't bother, the writing simply wasn't gripping enough to make the majority of the (unskippable, I might add) story worth rereading. Usually when a story is good, I won't notice the mistakes. Yet here, the problems are so obvious that they are hard to ignore. The writing is also so basic and blend that they couldn't help cover up those grammatical errors.
Another thing I found fault with in this game is the many plot holes littered throughout the story. The rules of the world and the deal the main character makes is never specified. Understandable due to the circumstance, yes, but rather distracting and annoying when new information about the fundamental rules of the universe is still being discovered at the very end of the story. It's one thing for Faust not to know the reason for each character's action, it's quite another for him (and the player) to not know how or why any of the magical things happening works. The story doesn't really flow properly. Due to its shortness, all the plot points are rushed and given flimsy excuses. The romance is a sorry excuse for one if you can even consider it a romance. You are forced to accept Peg as your soulmate, supposedly one of your many, and that's it. It's weak and loses any flavor due to the simple dismissal that your love for her (and vice versa) is due to fate.
Another downside to how short the story is is that none of the characters are remotely developed. All you know of each character is their basic (and very cliche) motivation. And even those are simply stated by each character, there isn't any discovery, any change. While Faust's change (or lack thereof) is understandably in your hands, the rest of the characters has neither the time nor the basis to be developed. The redhead, for one, has far more flushed out character and is interesting than Peg (your plot device of a soulmate). Yet even she falls flat due to the lack of a core or consistency throughout the novel.
There are, however, some things that this game does really well. The artwork is quite nice. It's colorful, interesting and very consistent. It helps carry what is ultimately a boring story. The characters are easily recognizable. The backgrounds are nicely done. The choices you make have major consequences, which was a big plus. There are multiple ways to get through situations and checkpoints, which is quite nice and makes a lot of sense. Despite the linear storyline, you are made to feel (quite rightly) that your choices do matter and that what you do make the story change. Which, of course, still highlights painfully just how short this story is.
Overall
Pro:
Nice art
Interesting premise
Ability to influence story and main character in an obvious and satisfying way
Con:
Flimsy story
Bad grammar
Boring music
Unsatsifying plot
Very very short
Lack of options (no skipping, no lowing sound, etc)

First of all, I should note that I'm reviewing this game purely for its single-player experience. I bought this game for its single-player, and I don't have many friends I can play this game with (I also bought it a long time after it came out), so I have no experience of its multiplayer.
European Escalation was one of my all-time favorite strategy games. I had a blast playing through its campaigns. They were well-crafted, well-balanced, encapsulated all sides of the war, and they even had a nice background story tying the missions together.
AirLand Battle is NOTHING like that. Its single-player campaign is just a joke. There are 4 campaigns you can play, but it is very, very clear that they were meant to be played with their co-op feature. Now, they might be super fun if you play it with a friend, but that wasn't why I bought this game. I bought it to play it by myself in single-player.
What's the problem with campaigns? Well, first of all, there is absolutely no story at all, apart from some snippets that pop-up during the campaign map phase, and they are completely random. Secondly, every match is limited to 20 minutes, which I found extremely annoying. This is a strategy game famous for its hours-taking structure. How am I supposed to win a match in a huge map in just 20 minutes?  Your only options are either set up a defensive position and hope to God that the enemy decides to attack (if they don't have a clear advantage, they don't attack you and just sit ducks in their starting zone), or rush towards the enemy with everything you've got. Thirdly, the AI cheats like crazy during the campaign map phase. You can barely bring in any reinforcements (maybe one division per 2 turns), but the AI keeps sending forces and use strikes as if they cost nothing. This leads us to the last problem; the campaigns are too difficult. Be prepared to fail even the first campaign, advertised as "easy", in your first few tries. The later campaigns get even ridiculously more difficult, even if you set the AI to "Easy."
The game itself is incredible. I'm sure the multiplayer is mind-blowing fun, but as I've said, I have no friends to play this game with (and the multiplayer is almost dead anyway) so I don't care about the online experience. I bought this game for the single-player, and unfortunately, it sucks.
All in all, not recommended for players looking for a solid single-player experience like in European Escalation.

First impressions:
Super Motherload certainly nails the progression aspect of its gameplay. Progressing in the game is very satisfying and the game itself is very fun.
The addition of local co-op was fantastic. Being able to dig twice as fast and all. This is only local, however. Online multiplayer, especially in this day and age, is a must. If you’re going to include local, online should be included as well. Although I do appreciate the addition of local co-op (very few games seem to have it these days), it’s unacceptable to ship a game with only that.
The gameplay itself is very good, mostly due to the immense amount of focus placed on your progression through the game. It became rather addicting, wanting to upgrade that little cart with everything available, and that’s a good thing. Aside from the game’s progression, the gameplay is very simple. Just dig in the ground for ores and other goodies (like fossils!) to get money and upgrade your cart with that money. You’re also able to purchase explosives and other fun tools to help you dig further.
Overall, Super Motherload is a fantastic game. With its great sense of progression, simple gameplay, and charming graphics, it definitely earns my recommendation.
