I have not died once playing this game so far.
the graphics, music and overall presentation is actually stunning, and the controls are really smooth and nice, but it all falls apart on one single mistake; when you're out of fuel, nothing happens.
In the original web browser game, an empty fuel tank resulted in death, which meant that going deeper to find more valuable resources was riskier, but more rewarding for the player. Now, all that happens is that your spaceship/drilling machine just goes a bit slower than usual and you cant mine anymore until you fill your tank again. You could die from taking to much damage by slamming to hard into the walls, but even that suffers from this puzzling game designing choice.
In the original game, an almost empty tank meant time pressure, which resulted in that you had to get faster to the surface in order to not die, while still managing to not kill yourself my slamming into walls as you go faster. Here, that element is completely gone! You can take all the time you want in the world to be as careful as you like, which make everything a slow paced uninteresting grindfest.
Its truly sad, that this one little mistake of leaving this mechanic out just completely breaks an otherwise fantastic remake of the original. As ive already said the graphics are awesome, and hints to a soviet union space rocket type of style and the warm red against the cold green are excellent use of color palette. The soundtrack is also really nice and marries the estethics and story into a great feeling game. I highly suggest that the developers release an update where the empty-tank-death mechanic has been reimplemented, as i see here that im not the only one complaining about it. Couldnt be to hard to do could it?

I came away extremely impressed for a title of this size. The keybinding is complete, with support for various mouse axis, both scrolling directions, mouse 4/5, etc. Visual options are very minimal, missing AA and V-sync toggles (both off by default, available in config files). No real graphical settings other than post processing, including Bloom, DOF, and optional scanline/pixel filters. On insanely unique thing, is that all 3 of those options can be tabbed through using F5-F7 at any time. That's the kind of thing you go out of your way to mod into a game, binding console commands to hotkeys, so it's amazing and crazy to see that kind of feature right out of the box. The game seems to accept forced Adaptive V-sync and runs well at 120FPS with minimal horsepower. It seems to support any res your display is capable of, though I can't confirm multi-display or scaling for 21:9 or wider. FOV is unchangeable and I do wish that was an option. I didn't feel nauseous or anything, but I did feel the perception of depth at times was lacking. Mouse control in the menus functions like a joystick which is really odd and pretty unusable, but it's perfectly fine and responsive with the keyboard.
I jumped into the main game right away, and ended up skipping the tutorial because of the non-standard implementation of it. It pops up and tells you how to turn the camera in front of a little animation of the ship turning, though you have no control of the ship or the transitions of the tutorial pages, and if you click or hit enter, it goes to the control mapping menu, where you hit save and continue and it takes you into the game. It's a really odd way to do things, and I feel it could be vastly improved by simply using arrow keys to switch between each of the tutorial screens, with "Press Enter to Continue" at the bottom. It does this each time you enter any gameplay mode so it's not gone, but it resulted in me going in the first time having no idea what anything did.
Luckily, most of the general controls were intuitive right out of the gate. It's essentially first person shooter controls, with Q and E to roll, and Space to boost. Z/X/C operate a grappling hook you get in the first level, and scrolling up and down controls vertical strafing. Boosting is directional based on your strafing direction which is really nice. So instead of turning the camera up and to the right, and then boosting to go that way, you can strafe right and up, boost to fly in that direction, while still aiming your ship forward. That said, I felt the arrangement could be improved, and the mapping options make that very possible. I used Shift and Space for vertical strafing, the further mouse thumb button for secondary attack, the closer for the grappling hook (click to fire, click to detatch, and hold to reel in), with the right mouse button for boost. It makes it feel a even more like a 3D first person shooter, and grapple on the mouse is much easier to use than having it it below WASD limiting your movement while using it.
Across the two modes, story and score attack, there are 4 different colored ships that seem to fly the same, while having different primary and secondary weapons. Rapidfire+Shotgun, HomingShots+HomingShotgun, SlowLazer+SustainedBeam, etc. The score mode is seemingly endless, with orbs to pick up while being chased by enemies, and it let's you have your choice of any of the 4 ships. The story mode consists of a hub world with 4 gates, and it seems you enter each once to fly around collecting orbs while being attacked in the order it says until a boss appears, and once defeated, back in the hub you get a colored armour (ship type) to then take back into each of the other gates, for essentially 4 runs of each stage.
In the main HUB area, there are clear orbs with a DNA-like spiral in them that pop up some tutorial text when you pass through them. Right after being plopped in that hub it was really difficult to understand what was happening, and those tutorial bubbles were so spread out and in no particular order that they weren't of much use. The average player hopping in like I did, will likely pickup on the controls right away, but the goal or what anything is takes a bit of digging. On one hand it could be tackled in a better way, but on the other side, if the point was to make the player feel like they're in an alien world where they have to learn the rules themselves, it achieved that. I had a level of intrigue specifically because it told me very little. On a similar note though, I do feel the game needs better communication of things to the player. There's a beeping that occurs, and it's hard to tell if it's because your being hit or because you just picked something up. Hit confirmation is along the same lines, and I feel adding a noise or confirmation upon successful hit can be satisfying. I wasn't clear on whether or not I was really even doing damage to the boss in the 3rd gate until I explicitly saw a part break off.
Finally, the controls certainly feel nice, though I feel it could use one thing. A faster response time for turning the ship/aiming. I get it, it's a ship rotating in a 3D environment with momentum and such, but I feel the mechanical satisfaction would improve dramatically with that change. I'd like it for all 4 ships, but at the very least I feel it's needed on the Red colored ship, which really screams for fast precision aiming because of it's slow rate of fire and pinpoint accuracy. You can't really snap-aim to targets very well because of the momentum, and I think it would feel amazing if you could.
Visually I think it looks fine, though not by default. The post processing effects I mentioned above, and as seen in the official screenshots/footage of the game, make it extremely blurry. You could squint and it wouldn't change what you're able to see. After you disable those effects via the menu or F5-F7, the game is far clearer and has a better sense of space, though it's still ever so slightly blurred. The game mid firefight is really quite cluttered so it's hard to tell what's really happening, but it's much more manageable with all the bloom and blurring off. In the very beginning of the story mode you fly through some rectangular tunnels and it uses TV white noise/static effect every few seconds that I found annoying, but it didn't really crop up again after that.
The music and sound effects I felt were suitable, but nothing in particular stood out to me.
The quality of the port is surprisingly high, and the game is much more engaging than I initially suspected from the screenshots/trailer. I'd equate it to some weird little Japanese gem you stumble upon on the PS1, but from an alternate universe where they were making great PC titles instead. I've not finished the game so I can't really speak on the full amount and variety of it's content, but what I have seen will definitely have me back to see, and I'll update this once I know more.

As a crime documentary addict, I was excited to play this!  I really enjoyed a lot of the little touches, like the sound of an old harddrive ticking and buzzing as files are retrieved.  While the gameplay is simple (it's more of an interactive video, which is oddly appropriate for the time period the computer console places you in), I think anything more would have been too much.  You aren't *playing* a detective, you *are* the detective, and your moniter becomes a 90s work station.
Some of the videos are very short, and if you search a keyword that is too broad, you can't click through more than the first few in that category.  This is a little bit frustrating, and it's the only thing that really stands out to me as a device to prolong gameplay. Why would I only have access to the first five videos in a search if I really were accessing a police database? Certainly if I was trying to solve a cold case and hit upon a condemning phrase, I should be able to see all the entries at once, right?  Ah, well.
That being said, I didn't think the game led me to any kind of obvious conclusion (at least too quickly).  It was designed to give you some strong suspicions, certainly, but if you are interested in the story and continue to search, it becomes more bizarre and convoluted.  I admit, I like to see mysteries through to the end without jumping to a conclusion, which probably makes me the perfect audience for a game like this.  However, if you really are pretending to be a detective, it would be a little conceited to follow just one line of questioning and assume you know the entire story.  Isn't that what makes a cold case mystery interesting?
So my advice to the prospective buyer would be this: If you are likely to be bored once you think you know the end game, then you might be disappointed as some reviewers have been.  If you like figuring out not only what you think happened, but the story behind it, then this will entertain you!

OKAY, first of all I'm going to inform you that this game only made a measly 2,000 dollars for it's flex-fund kickstarter on IndieGoGo, so, it's current condition is far beyond probable and in the realm of absolutely expected. However, that doesn't really excuse the little bit of false advertising in the game's description. The game itself, I still recommend.
I've waited so long for a breakneck 6DOF shooter, you don't even know. Freespace Open has a couple of mods that smack of this kind of gameplay, but nobody has
taken up the mantle with serious 6DOF gameplay, as FS is mostly a spaceflight sim. The BSG TC
does have some serious sliding controls, but I'd have to look more into it.
The movement was difficult to master but really rewarding once you got the hang of it. The graphics had some serious eyestrain, but you can turn all that down. The use of minimalistic graphics allows the game to reside in a 400MB package, which is really impressive for most modern games. And the optimization is god-tier, where my old HD5670 can run it at 1080HD fullscreen.
Some of the weapons have a lot to be wanted, but overall the design was stellar. A gunner, a seeker, a seer, and a knight. All of them having a base attack and a really powerful variation on that base attack. Each of the armors makes for a different experience, although it feels like there should be unit shifts for different armors, instead of the same for each venture. Some of the weapons specifically need a buff, like the seeker armor needs a primary fire with a smaller turning radius, as it has trouble hitting targets that you're strafing with, and the secondary fire needs more firepower and a larger lock-on cone.
EDIT2: The HUD needs some work, especially the 1st person HUD. You can't see your weapon status of the light needle (red armor's secondary) nor can you see the fuel in the advanced boosters. Heck, it's hard enough trying to see it while moving around in 3rd person.
The collectible keys as of yet have no purpose besides one, which is a grapple. My only frustration with it, is that you will probably crash into an asteroid with it and you cannot draw in enemies whatsoever, which is stuff. However, it will come in REAL handy when facing off against Argos with the knight/Psi armor.
There are only four sectors, but they're all really good, having a complement of different sub-sections and often the need to go up, down, or alter your baseline orientation to make the most of it. All four are just the right length, too. Their designs and themes are also good. However, I get the feeling like some places don't have any real use, or maybe some of it was destroyed and what's left is still rustily churning away, because the modularity of their constructions allows for this.
The AI is pretty well done, but in some cases you can be completely still and not get hit. Only in the green sector tho; anywhere else you might get swamped. Movement is key when facing off, but some enemies will actually move with you and you can't shake them -  you'll need to take them out. Speed and reflexes are still a big deal. There's a huge variation on fighting styles from the enemies, which is excellent. However, the AI can be dumb as bricks at times, especially in closed-in spaces. The beam-mine things however are always dumb, and are explicitly built as speed traps and to throw you off balance while they zoom past you. This is a good design.
While the game is quite incomplete, what it currently has under its belt is a great starting point, making the game enjoyable from start to finish. I actually binge-played this until about 5am in the morning just to finish it. The end boss wasn't hard enough, IMO, but it didn't feel any different from the rest of the game, which is good - keep moving keep shooting.
However, the Omega armor has a profile a bit too big and the spiny things on the fins are a bit distracting. I don't terribly care for it, but it is faster and does more damage. The first time you complete the game it has the gun armor's weapons; I think you get the other weapon setups for each completion.
It also has triple-chording.
EDIT: It appears from the trailers that there is a lot of cut content. Hopefully these will be published later after getting polished, or are still in the assets and can be brough out through modding. I think they're going to add Steam Workshop support later.

This game is like a hybrid of Forsaken and Rez. If you like games with 6 degrees of freedom (6DoF) then it's definitely worth a look. The controls (I played with a controller) are mostly fine and feel very responsive, the graphics are very stylized and the music is nothing amazing, but very nice to listen to while playing.
The basic game play is each level has 20 jump gate pieces that must be collected and then when you do, you fight a boss. As you collect more and more jump gate pieces, the enemy count increases and they become more hostile and the enemy variety increases too.
The game seems fairly short: There are 4 main levels which you must beat with a specific "armor" (different handling and weapons). After beating a given level with it's default armor, you can then use any armor to beat it. This is actually a requirement; you must beat each of the 4 main levels with each of the 4 main armors. I haven't done that yet, but the game leads me to believe it will unlock a fifth level, boss and armor, though I cannot guarantee it.
Personally I don't mind the length of the game. The levels can get pretty tricky as you collect jump gate pieces (fortunately, the death penalty is minimal), the different armors are fun to pilot and I can see myself replaying the levels even after I beat it fully. There is also a score attack and leaderboards for both modes.
Obviously no game is right for every single person, but I would recommend this game if you like any of the following: Forsaken, Decent, Rez, Zone of the Enders, abstract Tron like graphics, general agile mech action, arcadey space combat games or if you ever wished Space Harrier had sucked you into the console as a kid.

Her Story sets itself apart from other minimal-interaction games by telling an interesting story. The gameplay is extremely minimal: you are operating an old-fashioned computer terminal with video files stored on it in order to review police interview tapes from a murder case. There is no obvious 'goal' or ultimate point to this, at least not from the outset. To elaborate further would be a spoiler.
In order to do advance the story, you need to type in keywords based on the conversation that occurred between the police and the key suspect, For example if a particular person named 'John' was discussed in one of the video files, typing in the keyword would return all videos that mentioned 'John'. The player can then watch the desired video which will in turn yield more information on the murder, which means more potential keywords to search. This makes the storytelling necessarily non-linear, as each player will home in on different approaches to getting at the information. It is difficult to describe this format without playing it for yourself, but if you are intrigued by the idea of 'solving' a mystery in this unconventional way, give it a chance.
The entire story is carried by a single actor who gives quite a good performance. It is therefore reminiscent of old FMV games, but without the campy B-movie feel.
Brilliant storytelling and a unique game

Pros:
- Interesting political decisions
- Well written characters
- Decision tree adds slight replayability
Cons:
- Boring, mediocre campaign
- Poor rts
- poor optimization
The fact that more people don't adore this game makes me sad.

This game creates a good first impression, but crumbles on closer examination. Strategy part is secondary in this game, and for the most part can be either skipped by having overwhelming force (that is easy to get if you use strategy cards to the full potential) and autoresolving, or cheezed with the dragon and mercenaries.
Real game is in decisions that you make, but results of your decisions are not transparent, forcing you to use the guide, which defeats the point.
Your council room decisions are randomly selected, and most of them don't make sense from the story standpoint. All counsellors have at least one or two instances, where they act completely out of character with some ridiculous demand, or by protesting something that they should be in favour of.
Real problem with the game is that story happens between missions. And by story i mean storyline of your chosen wife - the only really good part of the game.  You are forced to choose a wife early in the 2 act. This means that you will have to replay annoying parts of the game over and over, if you want to experience all of the storylines. It progresses at a sluggish pace, forcing you to usually have two full strategy turns between them. And the fact, that results of your decisions not only hard to predict, but you have to play some strategy turns before knowing the result, make it very annoying to reload earlier save, if you are dissatisfied with the result.
My advice - watch storylines on youtube.

This game has gotten some raw reviews lately by people whome have put very little time into this game. Others have voiced legitimate points over the games campiagn mode. This mode is very lacking but shows just a glimpse of what a campaign can really be if they move in a different direction (i.e. Total War). The maps are set up pretty good with great detail in vegetation and the size of the air space your planes fly in is amazing. Model detail for the vehicles and air power are great while the infrantry is mediocre whitch leaves alot to be desired. The difference between models of air craft is neglegable with no difference in aero-nautical and external hardware. They swap out the skins and say it is a different vehicle despite the fact they look the same.
The game play has a slight learning curve with tactics and unit attributes. A combination of Heavy Armor, light Armor, Infrantry to garrison towns, artillery, air power, and the liberal use of scout units (Heli Scouts are the best) is what makes this game frustrating and great at the same time. Most players should start with WG:EE before buying this title unless they want to learn how to deal with a butt ton of heli's, fighter bombers, and air superiority fighters right off the batt. The previous title didn't place as much of an importance on AA platforms as this title did. Combination of 20-30mm AA, Mid-range AA, and the long range AA will ensure that any enemy bogies that fly into your air defence bubble will get wiped out.
The infrantry have been made more potent in towns with the reinforcing of the ideaology that urban warfare for tanks is suicide unless escorted by infrantry. Either Humvee, mechanized, or Heli borne infrantry gives a the player dynamic choices in tactics wether intial push torwards an objectives or flying in reinforcments so that your defensive postion does not collapse. Remember keep your Infrantry to towns and use armor to sweep the edges with heli support. Huge tip, use smoke from atrillery to screen you assault of a town or enemy positions.
Overall I would recommend this game with a dose of patience. Do not go into this game with tactics from Command & Conquer and Total War for you will meet only heartache. Need be look up a guide on the internet, maybe study some modern military tactics, pay attention to the specific stats of weapons platforms, and for the love of god use alot of AA! I cannot stress that enough, deploy alot of AA because you will need it with the game! Of course some tanks wouldn't hurt either.

This is the first of this genre that I have ever played, and I have to say, I really enjoy it. I bought this because it was on sale for like 50 cents or something and had been curious about the genre for a while.
It's sort of an illustrated choose your own adventure. It is exactly as the title implies, you have to make decisions, and for certain decisions, you forfeit part of your soul. Sometimes it works out, other times it doesn't, or so I assume, otherwise this would be a terrible game and story if you said "No" to everything and that was the only way to have something good happen.
From what I gather, it's basically a beautiful Jessica Rabbit looking devil trying to trick you into selling your soul. Unless something good comes from the soul gamble, I kind of fear that the entire game will just be you selling your soul, having bad outcomes and then the end. But I obviously have not complete the game yet, so I'm sure there is a better way to win than just going with the "boring" choice.
It's well drawn, although not my particular taste in art, I cannot deny the artists technical ability. However, the drawings lack soul. They're great drawings, but they don't really feel like ART.
Maybe I'm seeing this through the specs of witnessing a new genre, and it really isn't as good as I think. One thing is for certain, this game has officially hooked my interest in the genre. I'd love to play similar games, however, unfortunately teh only ones I have seen are all anime dating simulators, and while I don't have an issue with anime (I actually quite enjoyed a few of them) I don't want to play a dating simulator. So if anyone reads this, and can recommend a good game in the genre, I'd appreciate it.
Now, the reason I recommend this game? It's cheap. You can relax on your couch or bed (assuming you have a wireless mouse), read the story and click your choices.
However one thing makes no sense, considering you're literally choosing answers from multiple choices, is that there is no controller support. Literally all they would have to do is allow you you to use UP, DOWN, and ONE face button to select your choice. Kind of stupid that they didn't include it.
But I definitely recommend it. For it's low price, it's worth getting a couple of hours of enjoyment. Too many people expect to get 3000 hours out of a video game that costs less than the price of a movie ticket, and that's just silly. So buy it. You could get this for what you'd pay to buy a candy bar.

Pros:
-Writing: Being a Gearbox game, get ready for some fairly typical Gearbox writing a la Borderlands. The characters are unique, funny, expository, and never really shut up. If you like that character, awesome! If not... You can always turn the voices off.
-Characters: Design wise, every Hero looks like they come from a disparate world, with rocket hawks, nihilist AIs, Giant Lumberjacks, Elf ladies, steampunk robots, mushrooms, etc.
-Helix system: Every game you get to choose between two (or three) specific powerups for your skills that give you more options with how you play. I tend to side very strongly with certain powerups over others, but sometimes changing gives you a different way to use your skills.
-Co-op:  A great part about this game is you can choose to run through instances with friends or randos and all work together to achieve something. As someone who prefers Co-op over Competitive, this is appreciated. I like that there is a story, and although the small number of instances makes them somewhat repetitive, there are opportunities for the developers to introduce new chapters. And every instance is different, which is a plus.
-Gamefeel: Everything seems designed around actually having fun while playing the same maps repeatedly, so there are different options for how to get to somewhere, which adds a nice spin on a match if your team decides to take the scenic route.
-SIngleplayer: I can play this game by myself to practice with a hero, and still have fun. SIngleplayer is generally pretty rough, as they don't scale back the enemies enough, but overall it's a nice change of pace to play by yourself and try out some new skills.
Cons:
-Matchmaking: If you want to play competitively, be prepared to wait a good twenty minutes for matchmaking. If you want to play anything besides Incursion, be prepared to wait longer. Further, there is no semblance of balance in matchmaking, so you can be the only lvl 3 in a room of level 80s+, prompting me to ask what's taking matchmaking so damn long.
-Balance: They are constantly tweaking Heroes and skills, but there are still some pretty noticeable balance issues. You will almost NEVER play in a match without an Alani, because she is new, so they want to make her overpowered a bit so people will try her out. After much anticipation, Blizzard's new first person DOTA has come out: Overwatch. It's pretty good.
There are a little less than two dozen heroes for you to choose  from, each having a unique, specific weapon as well as a passive and 2 active abilities. Each also has an ultimate ability with a long cooldown that you unlock and level 5. Yes, that's right, there are levels, and each time you level you can splice your DNA to gain one of two benefits for the rest of the game, and if you play a character enough times, you unlock some third choices on that path as well. For instance, one choice might increase your accuracy and reload, while another would increase your base damage.
Heroes are unlocked through a number of means. The easiest way to unlock most of them is to accomplish specific challenges, like winning 5 games with a hero from 1 faction (like, say, The Horde). If you're not in a rush though, you can also unlock all the heroes by just ranking up enough.
A cool twist on the genre is that you can enter a match with a loadout of three pieces of gear, and you spend points during the match to activate those pieces of gear, so you have to anticipate what you'll need in that match, but you're not bound to buying those things in a specific order. Personally, my favorite loadout is 2 Arcanite Reapers, and a hat made out of 3 hats. Which brings me to another point: there's no crafting, which is cool. Blizzard usually overdoes it on crafting, even in their card games.
Overwatch has both a competitive mode and a co-op mode. The competitive mode is a lot like what you expect, but I'm mostly interested in the co-op. Sometimes you just want to blow things up with some friends, right? In co-op, the game is a lot like what you'd expect from a cooperative FPS, kind of like if Starcraft: Ghost let you play with other people. You go through a level doing TF2-like objectives. Escort the thing, defend the thing, or blow up the things.
The characters are varied, and everyone should be able to find something that suits their style. On the other hand, some characters are better for PvE or PvP, which means the full roster won't see equal play. For instance, the robot sniper, the cowboy, and turret are really good.
People are acting like the game is some new great cultural phenomenon, but it's really not, it's just a pretty good game. I guess if you're the kind of person who puts 2000 hours into the same competitive shooter it might be a godsend, but if you're not that dedicated to single games, but you like FPSes, it's probably worth picking up on sale.

To me, battleborn is definitely underrated when compared to big names such as Overwatch, CS: GO etc etc.
But in all of seriousness, do not compare Battleborn to Overwatch, they maybe both FPS-Moba genre games, but they have so much more differences in it.
Just take some good example is the PVE in battleborn and the helix upgrade for each level. OW doesn't have helix upgrade each level, but they can swap to different characters on the fly when they die to counter a specific match up, and they do not have PVE. I can go on and rant a huge list but nah, I'll just leave the main point here :)
While Battleborn can be played solo/single player (Including a complimentary Prologue, Chapter 1-8), I strongly suggest to go co-op for PVE too. It's fun to play PVE with other players!
There is alot more to be done too, such as completing the lore challenges for each unique character is quite challenging too! Well I guess if it's too easy then there's no point in it right? xD
On the other side, the PVP features 3 modes with 2 maps each:
Capture mode (OUTBACK, TEMPLE): This is just like King of the hill, there are 3 points and objectives to be captured, then defend it from the enemy who will try to claim it back. The team reaches 1000 point wins! It's quite strategic and fast paced too due to switching from offense to defense, and from defense to offense.
Incursion mode (ECHELON, OVERGROWTH <-- most voted map): Have you ever played DotA2 or League of Legends or even Heroes of the Storm? If you played any one of them, Incursion's gameplay is exactly the same in the form of FPS. 5v5, guide your minions to enemy territoy and destroy enemy's sentries to win! To me, Incursion is the most fun game because I play alot of League of Legends.
Meltdown mode (PARADISE, COLDSNAP): In this mode you need to sacrifice your minions to win ): I'm serious! Guide your minions to the minions grinder, to get points. The bigger the minion, the more points you gain. But it ain't gonna be that easy, enemies will try to destroy your minions before it reachers the grinder, so you need to do the same too! First to reach 500 wins. Legitimate a WINnion mode xD
While Gearbox can still give a little bit tweak here and there especially with match-making, other than that this game is pretty fun and worth it. I'd say it improved alot more from the closed and open beta phase.
With the release of the latest DLCs, I'll rate it 7.0/10

Payday: The Heist is a first person shooter game developed by Overkill Software and published by Sony Entertainment. The game was released in October 2011 on PC, after being released on PS3. The game is owned on Steam by over four million players due to its regularity being on sale.
The gameplay is based around completing heists with a party of four people including you. This can be done either in a single player environment, or up to 4 player co-op online. The heists can consist of the classic bank jobs, right the way to the complete extreme of extracting blood from a highly classified patient. You play the role of one of the four main characters in the game, Dallas, Chains, Wolf or Hoxton.  Each member of the team can use a variety of different weapons, you are able to select your load out before jumping into a heist, so once you get to know what is needed to be done on each heist, you can select what to use accordingly. Each of the missions starts off in a stealth style mission, where you have to disable security camera, turning off alarm systems etc. Whether you complete these tasks successfully or not without being seen will determine how the rest of the heist will carry out.  These starting missions are done really well, and you will be fully immersed since most of them have you sneaking around a pitch black building trying to out manoeuvre the guards. A lot of the missions also come with the added obstacle of civilians – these are crucial in any of the heists as you can keep them hostage and use them as bargaining trades should one of your other team mates be captured by the police too.
Whilst you can spend a good portion of the game in stealth and hopefully not being noticed, a good portion of the game will also be spent with you going all guns blazing as you attempt to fend off an almost endless stream of enemy police and SWAT.  The gunplay in Payday really well done. All of the guns feel as powerful as you would expect, and the choice of weapons is pretty big when compared to other FPS games.  Ammo does become a problem with your primary weapon since you’ll be shooting this off constantly at points, but can be easily countered by the abundance of pickups of ammo off dead enemies.
Even though Payday is almost four years old at this point, it is still a really good looking game, especially when you ramp up the resolution to 4k. Originally I thought the game was made using the Source engine due to the familiarities in the graphics with the likes of Half Life 2 and Left 4 Dead, but the game is made using an engine called Diesel (made by GRIN, who are now defunct unfortunately). There are a couple of textures which are very low resolution which is a shame, but I can forgive this a bit given that a lot of the levels are actually fairly big, so this must have been done to reduce the need for loading screens.  The game has a really good ragdoll simulation too, when you are mowing down the enemies, they don’t just die in a normal fall to the floor fashion, each death is individually animated depending on where/how they were shot, which adds to the originality slightly.
Payday is fully voice acted and done really well at that; the game is almost narrated by what seems to be someone behind the scenes instructing your team on what to do next on the heist. You’ll get remarks back from the rest of the team in responses to objectives being completed and you’ll also get a lot of radio chatter when you are in firefights with the police too.
This is a really hard game. The first couple of heists come with the option to play them on easy mode; these must really be the games tutorial since they can be completed without any real problems; yet once you reach the third or fourth mission, the difficulty takes a big ramp up and you’ll actually find yourself either failing missions from not completing objectives, or because you have died or been taken into custody. I had to replay each of the last few stages of the game multiple times before I was able to successfully complete the heists. Even though the ramp in difficulty felt really harsh at the time; I began to enjoy the game even more because of it; because it’s not just as simple as a “get in and out” job, it forces you to plan your every move, and you will tread with caution around every corner because of the unknown ambush that awaits you. The game also has another two difficulty levels to be played on, Hard and overkill mode – these are modes which should not even be considered when playing on single player because you will not stand a chance. I tried the overkill mode out and it is just absolute carnage. I will definitely be asking friends to join in a game to give this mode a proper try out.
Whilst all of the missions have the same key objective, and there is really only one way to complete said objective, it can lead to a little repetitive gameplay. The game does however try to counteract that by adding a little bit of randomness into the stages by shaking things up a bit; such as locations the locations of key civilians that you need to keep hostage, meaning you still have to go searching through the whole building to find them rather than rushing to the one place. Each of the levels has some form of random element to it which is nice to see, since you will be playing the same six or seven heists over and over again.
I have put about twenty hours into Payday: The Heist so far and see no end in sight for it at the moment. There is still a really active multiplayer scene if you want to just find pick up groups with randommers, but I would highly recommend playing this with a bunch of friends on Skype to get the full experience out of it. The added levels of difficulty also adds plenty of replay ability too; meaning you will not run out of interesting content for a long while with this title. The game does have one piece of DLC which includes new weapons and two new heists, which is a worthwhile piece of DLC.
The game is also extremely technically sound too; I was able to play on 4k resolution with all of the graphic options maxed out and I was still able to hit the heights of 160 FPS, so this is one of the best optimized games out there at the moment.  Keyboard and mouse is recommended to play with, given the FPS nature.
Overall, Payday: The Heist is an extremely good game; one that I am surprised it has taken me so long to play, and one that I will certainly be keeping installed on my machine because of the high replay ability factor. The game is also very cheaply priced at £10,99 – but like I said at the start, the game is always going on sale, and most of the time it is for 90% off; at that price, is it an absolute no brainer to pick it up – you may as well pick up the four pack for yourself and friends whilst you are at it.

Divinity: Dragon Commander is like that friend who changed the subculture he was a part of every month back in high school.
The Emperor was assassinated, and his children now war for the empire using amazing new technologies. But the wizard Maxos remembered that his emperor friend had a romp with a giant fire breathing lizard because the Emperor was a total G. You are the outcome of this little relationship, a man who can turn into a dragon, a dragon knight if you will.
Maxos tells you you need to conquer the world, destroy this new technology while also using said technology, and also deal with people that can be so annoying you'd wish you could just throw them off your high powered magic airship called the Raven.
Also you have a jet pack. So there's that.
I'm a casual fan of the series. I managed to get my hands on most of the Divinity series, though I haven't played through Original Sin or Original Sin 2 yet. Though since everyone is raving about OS2, I may as well just swoose right in and review the game in the series nobody cares about! Yaaaaayyyyyyyy!
Dragon Commander is the first game chronologically, taking place even before Original Sin. Most of the gameplay revolves around this risk style game mode where you need to build armies and invade other territories, but there are also a few choose-your-own-adventure style activities while aboard the Raven.
Okay, so now it gets a bit difficult. See, the game is neat, but it's not really all that fun. The campaign mode itself is pretty barebones, and when you go into battle, you can play as yourself, the dragon commander, and personally take command of a battlefield.
The thing is, you can only command on one battlefield per turn, so if there are multiple battles you have to give it to overwhelming force or a luck of the dice. You can also assign a general to command the battle you cant be at for a certain price, but usually you just end up letting the Imperial Army do the fighting and commanding since it doesn't cost anything and they're usually enough.
You have four generals to choose from. The loud Henry who will later go on to voice the Roman General in Total War: Rome II. The proud and uptight Catherine, the “trying too hard to be one of the boys” Scarlet. And Edmund the genius tactician and narcissistic Lizard. That's not an insult, he's an actual lizard person.
I don't like any of them.
Don't get me wrong, there are some fun moments with them, but for the most part they're just annoying. Self centered, arrogant, hostile, surprisingly annoying, and a lot of the times just a piercing sound in your ear. I couldn't even stand Henry all that much even though I think his voice actor, Alistair Parker, did a pretty admirable job as the General voice in Rome II and Blackwall in Dragon Age: Inquisition
But not only are they outright hostile to you through most of the game, but you rarely have an opportunity to tell them off. At a few points of the game you can point out Catherine's hypocracy, but for the most part it just feels like the Dragon Commander is going “Yup, uh huh, alright.” Through most of their discussions.
Then there's the counselors from the five races of Rivellon.
Yorrick the undead, Oberon the Elf, Falstaff the Dwarf, Prospero the Lizard, and Trinculo the Imp.
These people are fairly one dimensional, though I guess it kind of makes sense considering the political satire of the game. Yorrick is very religious, but then again most Undead apparently are, Oberon is a hippy, but his questionable stance on other races sometimes makes itself known, Falstaff likes money, Prospero is the “cold” one
, and Trinculo is my homie.
Every now and then you have to attend a meeting in the throne room of the Raven. Here you talk to the council and discuss politics of your realm. It's kind of interesting, but you never actually see real outcomes of these events, they just kind of tell you what happens every now and then. So basically you just kind of end up picking and choosing political positions depending on what your approval rating is with each respective races. If anyone drops under 50%, then just do something they like the next meeting. No real thought behind it.
Also, you have to choose a bride sometime into the game. But uh...It doesn't change much outside of cards and bonuses you can get with their events.
You know, all things considered, a lot of people like to talk smack to the person that can turn into a giant fire breathing monster and eat them at any moment. I guess you could say they know that you “need” them. But I don't feel like you really do, considering the person doing all the heavy lifting is either me or the Imperial Army.
Maxos is basically your only friend. Just remember that.
Okay, now the combat part.
When I first started playing the RTS stuff, holy hell was it ever a ball buster. There's almost no breathing room, especially when your enemy seems to be able to completely obliterate your entire attack force in just a few seconds with basic units. I'm ashamed to admit I actually had to turn down the  difficulty for a bit until I figured out you can just bring a massive amount of heavy tanks to the fight and then just rush them.
The big feature of the RTS mode is that you can transform into your dragon form and wreak havoc among the enemy ranks. Not only can you just blast them with your breath, but you can also activate a few abilities to do things like cause more damage, heal yourself, or buff your units close to you. You also have a jetpack, which is radical.
But it's all just so weak. The RTS is barebones, the dragon loses it's novelty quickly, the choices you make on the Raven don't really affect anything except for a few approval bars, and your generals are only necessary if you either can't be on the battlefield yourself, or your auto-resolve bar is 50/50 and you don't want to spend any bonus cards.
It's all serviceable, but that's it, just serviceable. The RTS is basic, the political choices don't mean much, and your supporting cast can shove off. It's like they really wanted to make a great game, but then ran out of time.
Should you play Divinity: Dragon Commander?
It's all still pretty neat, but not neat enough to keep you coming back time and time again. I almost wish they went for a more traditional army thing with infantry instead of the whole magic robot route. Maybe larger scale, bigger formations, a morale system so you can just terrorize enemy armies as a dragon? It could be like that kind of okay PS3 game “Lair” except without the framedrops and with a command feature. I think it would be cool, just wailing on fools who think they can fight a dragon.
But anyway, it's not bad, but it's not all that great either. Wait for it to go on the cheap and pick it up for five dollars or something. Or just pick up any other Divinity game. I'm hearing nothing but praise for Original sin and Original Sin 2, and Divinity 2 is still my favorite in the series.

This is a very different and engaging game. The story you are trying to piece together is very intriguing and addictive. You will not stop until you find all of the videos in the game.
Whether it adds up to something greater than the sum of its parts, I'm not so sure.

: The process of gathering the interview snippets and piecing the various narrative threads together has been my favorite gaming experience of the year, so far. Granted, there are very few ludic restraints here, so it really does feel  more like interactive fiction than a game. But honestly, when the whole thing feels so compelling, that seems like a petty concern.
A lot of the credit goes to actress Viva Seifert. Her nuanced performances made the gimmicky testimonal format into a viable medium for the disjointed crime narrative.
: If the actual plot were in a different format -- say a prose story or a feature-length movie -- it would be a boilerplate crime thriller. The more psychological elements would feel like hackneyed cliches. Thankfully, the medium not only hides these flaws, but turns them into a source of potential mindf*ckery and player speculation.
: After my first near-complete playthrough, I may have spent/lost/wasted as much time researching fan theories as I did actually playing the game. There's proverbial wheat out there, for sure, but you have to sift through a lot of chaff to find it.
Of course, none of that is really the dev's fault. And it can only help strengthen the game's value as a cultural product.

Her Story is unlike any other detective game I’ve ever played – and I’ve played quite a few mystery/detective games in my time. This unusual title was created by Sam Barlow (who also created Silent Hill: Shattered Memories), a veteran of the game design world and mastermind of suspense and beautifully told stories.
Throughout the game, your objective is to discover what happened to Simon Smith, Hannah Smith’s (a protagonist’s) husband. The player is presented with a police database full of video clips, none of which are in order though I don’t think this actually has any bearing on whether or not you complete the game successfully.
Read my full review at:

First and foremost, there is no action whatsoever in this game. You are someone going through the videos related to a crime that happened years ago. You use a search engine, like a poor´s man google, to search for videos on this police database. Your objective is to make sense of these videos and create your own theory about what happened.
It is a short game and you will probably be able to see all videos in 4 hours. The videos are mostly interesting, the actress that appears on those videos is a very good actress which is very important as this is kind of FMV 2.0. The videos are supposed to be old therefore they are in 4.3 aspect and simulate VHS however the acting makes it worth it.
If you like games that make you think, I recommend this game. If you like shooting and action, avoid this one. This game is a good FMV game and it is cheap too. It is also a great game to play with a girlfriend or wife. I started playing this game with mine and we had a great time together. Now we are even playing Divinity Original Sin, Enhanced Edition together.

Oh, where to start with this game?
This truly is an RTS with few comparable equals.  Forget everything you learned from RTS games like base building strategies, APMs, and abilities.  In Wargame, your army composition is determined long before the game starts and all units are equipped as theywould have been historically.  There are no upgrades or bases.  It's also a must-have for anyone interested in the Cold War era.  Wargame:  Airland Battle beautifully recreates the fast-paced and incredibly deadly environment of the world war that never happened, but with fewer nukes.
That being said, expect your troops to die.  A lot.  Even though each tank and squad is individually named, don't get attached to them.  Sergeant Voldauer will take a missile through his tank and die.  Sergeant Adams will burn to death in a napalm strike.  And Captain Bond's plane will become a firey comet after that SAM strikes him.  At a scale of this size, individual units are, with few exceptions, very expendable.
You'll also find out that the game is not all just "America, ****yeah!" and "Soviet Union, **** yeah!"  Each nation represented has a distinct feel.  French are very mobile but very fragile (by Wargame standards), Eaast Germans overwhelm their enemies with massive concentrations of slightly older technlogy, West Germans are elite and expensize, assuring that they're often outnumbered, Poland can put lots of versatile helicopters on the field, Sweden has amazingly cost effective units, etc.  Additionally, don't expect to win just because you have the most expensive or coolest statline unit, because everything out there can be killed by something the enemy has (even if it's just a deluge of cluster bombs).
The game, through its system of historical hard counters (SAMs wil wreck aircraft all day long, infantry is the king of towns, ATGMs stop vehicle rushes cold, etc.), highly encourages combined arms tactics. That may be a buzzword, but forces that are severly lacking in a unit type will suffer heavily.  Your tank heavy force will die to airstrikes unless you have AA and/or interceptors and will die from infantry or ATGM ambush if you don't have recce units scouting the terrain they're traversing, for example.
All that being said, the game is incredibly fun to play.  Some of my highlights of playing this game include:
-defeating a numerically superior Warsaw Pact invasion of Scandinavia as NATOby tactically retreating and funneling Pact brigades into killzones where I could surround them and smash them into submission with my concentrated forces
-burn entire forests to the groundwith napalm strikes
-listen to Russian helicopter pilots sing "Ride of the Valkyries" at random
-goading my enemy into sending his best aircraft into the teeth of my air defence screen and racking up kill points from it
-playing a goofy army of nothing but helicopters, airplanes, and infantry in helicopters (imagine Blackhawk Down x50)
-playing a goofy army of T-34-85 tank rush (yes, the WWII tank is in this game)
-storming a Norwegian beach as the USMC
-storming a Swedish beach as Soviet naval infantry
-pummeling an East German armyto death with a Swedish artillery park of 16 155mm cannons
-forcing a battle to a draw by barely hanging on to my last reinforcement point until the time limit while being overrun by T-72s
-chewing up a brigade in constant combat until it had nothing but support weapons and logistical vehicles left
-watching the Russians nuke their own rear areas to attempt to stop my breakthrough
-knocking out tanks with a cannon designed to blow up obstacles like barricades
-HOLDING THE LINE!
-etc.
Overall, this is a very fun game and a must have for history buffs.  Also, check out Wargame: European Escalation (the original!, has more narrative-driven campaingns but fewer factions), Wargame:  Red Dragon (adds Asia-Pacific factions to the game,as well as boats)and their upcoming joint release with Paradox, Steel Division:  Normandy '44 (WWII, very similar game).

FIRST IMPRESSION
Kromaia sets out to do something great but hits some barriers early on.
Visuals:
The game's visual style is simple and good to look at in the beginning, but the screen quickly becomes  cluttered with junk and debris within the first few minutes. This chaos quickly translates into a frustrating game of junk-dodging and eventual disorentiation. If you manage to recover your bearings, you can quickly speed off into the next choatic encounter.
Gameplay:
The controls are clunky at first and there is a fairly unforgiving learning curve. I'm still not there yet, but I'm sure with time I'll eventually get the hang of it and expertly speed off to my death with ease.
Story:
The game focuses more on gameplay than story. If there is a story, I have a feeling it won't be an incredibly deep or engaging.
Overall:
If you're looking for a quick and easy space adventure, look elsewhere. This game's controls take some time to learn and you'll have to master them to move forward. The game quickly becomes chaotic and is a great challenge for someone looking to master flying and shooting your way to victory.

What if Ikaruga, a full 3D space shooter, Rez, danmaku/bullet hell and 2001: A Space Odyssey decided to fuse together? Well, you would get Kromaia.
Actually, scratch that. Kromaia is its own thing. A its core, it's a full 360º degree STG with arcade space shooter elements in the controls. Thus, it has physics-based movement and enemies but shooting mechanics, scoring and overall presentation and style harkening to the shmup/STG genre, complete with bullet patterns, enemy formations ganging on your ship and gigantic bosses.
The presentation oozes mystery, with some cryptic voice in an alien language and all the menus displayed in a symbolic language before you pick each option. This alien feeling is prevalent throughout all the game and is part of what makes Kromaia so unique and intriguing, entrancing. The music only amplifies that feeling, with some pretty damn nice tunes and sound effects that are a bit on the muted side but also help to provide this sort of "calm" destruction feeling as you fly at full speed doing 360º spins and dodging heavy lead.
As you play you will unlock different armors that provide alternate firing modes, ranging from regular scatter fire, guided laser missiles, a melee sword reminiscent of Radiant Silvergun with a shuriken-like shield/strike and a laser cannon to pierce heavens.
On top of that there is an unlockable ship but you have to get all the treasure keys hidden in the 4 stages.
The dynamics of the stage is as follows: you pick up 20 jump gate components and fight a stage boss. Simple as that. Easier said than done.
There is also a true final boss that needs to be unlocked by clearing all 4 stages with all 4 default armors and this is where the game feels like they had to pad things out to squeeze some extra hours. I would've preferred hidden bosses in each stage if I have to re-tread them 4 times. At the very least, this will let you familiarize with the different armors to learn their strengths and weaknesses and then tackle score attack mode.
So, yes, when you think it's all over... Oh, wel, I won't spoil the suprise but, regardless of the repetition, reaching that true final boss (and, thus, completing the game for real) is quite something.
Another interesting thing is that the devs seem to keep working and updating the game now and then, which is always welcomed. In fact, not so long ago they offered a chance to tone done different settings, including one that allows to control the level of the blur in the game, something that for people with severe myopia like me helps a lot since blurry things strain my eyes enormously.
All in all, worth a shot but if you are not a fan of this kind of genre I will suggest to wait a bit for a sale and trying then.

Interesting game for a short while.  TL;DR:  Good game, but it's more like a $5 game than a $20 game.  I suggest waiting for sales before buying.
This review is based on the 1.0K version of the game.  There have been patches since then, so some of this information may be out of date.  The developers release patches and additions periodically.
Content Quantity:
- Only four levels and a "hub" map.  They're big but mostly empty.  It reminds me of like an old DOS game called Echelon.
- Four ships to choose from, three unlocked by beating the first three levels.
- And then you have to beat all other ship+level combinations, too (total of 16 "missions").  The challenge changes since the ships have totally different weapon styles, but it's mostly just repetetive.
- I did two full playthroughs in about 11 hours.  A lot of that was hunting for secrets.  There's not that much content.  You can speedrun each level in 5 minutes if you just dodge enemies and go straight for checkpoints.
Style:
- Graphics remind me of Tron - lots of glowing, solid, colored shapes.  It's typically much easier to see what's going on than what the store screenshots show.
- I love the main theme music (main menu and orange level) and the boss fight music.  The soundtrack is stored in plain .ogg files that you can get out of the game's data folders.
- I enjoyed the timeless, ominous and mysterious feel to the story.
Gameplay:
- Combat isn't very interesting.  You have 6 degree-of-freedom controls, two weapons (primary and secondary) that change per ship, and an afterburner (which works in all directions, not just forwards).
- You have a multi-layered shield bubble.  They have some kind of damage-per-second threshold, after which they pop.  This can be caused by enemy's weapons (which all glow in a specific color that you will know to avoid), or from high speed collisions.  Low-speed collisions typically will not pop a shield unless you're also struck by enemy fire.
- Colliding with things in general SUCKS even if you don't lose a shield, because it will usually cause your ship to rotate erratically, disorienting you.
- There is an unlockable grappling hook which is kind of neat but unusable for any real purpose that I could determine.  It's fun to mess with, though, since it follows the rules of the physics engine - allowing you to pull things or be pulled by things.
- Enemies are predictable, but some are extremely difficult to deal with.
- There is a boss at the end of each level, and all but the stationary one are well designed fights.
- It's similar to a shmup (vertically scrolling shooter/bullet hell) but in full 3D, and instead of attacking from all directions which would be too difficult to deal with, enemies almost always move out in front of you before they attack regardless of which way you turn, making your ability to turn and move in any direction mostly meaningless.  It's not like Descent where enemies would happily shoot you from behind.
- There are afterburner power-ups, shield restoring power-ups, secret collectibles, and that's it.
- There is limited exploration for collectible secrets, but there is almost no point to them.
- There is little to no motivation to kill enemies instead of avoiding them while speedrunning each level to kill the boss at the end.  Enemies are not fast enough to keep up with you and shoot at you at the same time.
- The only things you gain permanently in the game are points and collectible secrets.  Points give you levels, but levels only decrease your secondary weapon cooldown (it's a very minor bonus that you won't notice change between each level).  Getting all collectible secrets give you a fifth ship once you beat the game, but that ship is currently just an upgraded version of the starting ship.
Bugs
- I didn't encounter any major bugs in the game.  It's rock solid.

I am a hardcore strategy games fan and was such disappointed by this title. I think I had some realistic expectations in terms of complexity and overall design (I wasn't expecting a Paradox-like grand strategy game of course!) so my idea was that this game might be something similar to Diplomacy, a political simulator focused on the issue of Global Warming. The first impact with the game wasn't bad: the interfaceis chaotic and badly implemented, although the amount of very detailed infos about the economics of the (too big) areas the planet is divided into (Africa is just split into Northern and Southern) gave me good hopes about how sophisticated the game engine was. Reality game me a slap in the face at the following step though: no matter how many economical, social and environmental variables the games compute... it's nothing more than a card game at its core. The only thing you can do as a player is assigning 'agents' to certain areas of the world; you can then assign a card to any single agent. This card can be a policy, or a task. The policies are very generic, like "Improve the basic education of the population", or "Make the commercial/industrial/agricultural" side of the local economy grow. After having assigned the cards to every agent you deployed, you are just left at ending the turn and look at the consequences of the policies you adopted through the plethora of economic/social/environmental data. That's it. It's so disappointing. I've never seen such an unbalance between the complexity of the game engine (assuming that all those parameters are computed for real, and not just smoke and mirrors) and the limitations given to the player.

There's a lot to like about this game, if only for making people aware of all the things that contribute to climate change, some of the nasty positive feedback, and some of the consequences.  There's lots of colour to the game.
There are a few things I really dislike.  First, most of the information you need to make a decision isn't on the screen where you need to make it.   Should we spend on migrating away from industrial coal?  Well, first you have to go figure out how much coal is being used in industry, proportionally, to find the best place to spend that money.   Should I build facility X?  Well, that depends on what it enables (which is not shown -- you need to remember)
Much worse is that key commodities like coal and oil don't seem to have any price.   I mean, if oil is being produced, Japan is going to be able to buy some of it -- it's the POOREST places that get starved, not the ones farthest away.   And oil shortage = high oil price = new exploration, switching, and biofuels... the global environmental agency shouldn't need to fund more exploration.  Given that price signals (e.g. cap/trade or carbon tax) are a prime method of dealing with GHGs (both in reality and in the game) you'd think the devs would have modeled pricing.
Last but not least -- ten years of 'security assistance' isn't going to suddenly stabilize North Africa.   Give me a break.

TL;DR: Amazing 3D puzzle platformer that puts you in collectible heaven. Characters will make you feel and worlds will blow you away.
Today's new definition of retro: action adventure games with smart aleck protaganists in peculiar settings. Psychonauts is spawn of the golden age of action adventure games, with each brain's area you go through truly feeling like a refreshing unique experience. The camp has very wide grounds that you are encouraged to explore by the immense amount of collectibles the game offers. Collectibles offer experience to level up and gain new psychic powers, often 100s would be in a single area. Collectible tracking and back tracking to previous areas is available so it's easy to return to all the old worlds and 100% the game if you so desired.
Combat is psychic, each enemy has a clear weakness you as a player must uncover, and will be punished whenever you make a mistake. Worst case, you can ask an NPC for guidance and they'll tell you any enemies' weakness, even bosses. There are 8 psychic tools you will be given, and figuring out how to use them effectively is an amazing feeling, especially during puzzles. The difficulty is moderate, you will die every now and then due to small enemies or platforming. But one of the weaknesses of the game are some of its bosses.
Some area bosses are wonderful challenges, often making you use several psychic tools and forcing you to be aware of the boss' patterns. But for some others you will find out their weakness, and it will be over in a jiffy. Bosses having one or two more stages in general would make the game MUCH more entertaining, because dying during a boss battle is rare.
Regardless, this is an amazing game. First impressions will blow you away and you'll come back for those sweet delectible collectibles.
Pros
-Satisfying Puzzles
-Collectible Heaven
-Incredible World/3D Platform Design
-Charming Cast
-Psychic Mind Beams
Cons
-Bosses aren't exciting
-Occasional bug requires reloading

I have too much nostalgia to properly review this game, but I'll do it anyway.
Great game, one of the best, if not, THE best of its genre.
- Fantastic Story, which happens to be very unique and set a theme not really seen before.
- Brilliant Writing, characters, while a bit over-the-top and surreal, always have something to say throughout the game that build upon their character. Almost all characters change throughout the course of the game as a person, some finding love, others making new friends and some even coming into their own and building their self-confidence. Mind you, these are mostly side NPCs where all their dialogue is pretty much optional. Shows the player how much detail the devs went into to make this game great.
- Fitting art style, that manages to blend multiple different locations and themes, like a summer camp, an asylum, a theatre, a French country-side and even a neon lit Spanish city into one game where no texture or color looks out of place.
- The Gimmick of Psychonauts is possibly one of the most interesting and creative ways to design levels like they did, and it never gets boring.
- Gameplay is flawed, where some sections will have you really frustrated with how jumps aren't feeling right or certain abilities are irritating to use, but it never gets too frustrating, and in open areas the gameplay really feels good and it encourages you to jump around and explore.
Overall, it's just a really fun and endearing game that somehow seemed to not get the attention it deserves back when it was released. Thankfully, as you can see on Steam, the game is pretty well regarded among many and I'm excited to see the sequel. That being said, Double Fine and crowd funded projects don't always end well. We'll have to wait and see how they use that 3-4 million that the fans pledged down...

No matter how much they say it isn't, Battleborn is very close to being an FPS MOBA. It's NOT a MOBA, but it's *very* close to being one. Two of the three PvP modes, Incursion and Meltdown, are basically ARAM/2-lane versions of classic MOBA maps.
That said, I like MOBAs, and I love this game--because it brings original game design, humor, and creative character abilities along with the aforementioned never-before-seen FPS almost-MOBA game style.
This game is not at all similar to Overwatch, except that they are both "hero shooter" games (as the genre has begun to be called). I PLAY Overwatch, and it is 100% different in the type of gameplay it offers. Please do not buy this expecting it to be much at all like Overwatch, and do not be scared away from buying it because it "seems" like it might be similar to Overwatch.
Battleborn, simply put, offers a LOT more content; from character lore to in-battle DNA augments, there is simply more depth and scope to Battleborn's gameplay.
There ARE a few negative aspects of Battleborn that should be mentioned, though.
First off, it has needlessly high system requirements. Overwatch has better graphics and runs on my computer at a perfect 60 FPS, yet somehow Battleborn can only run at 30 fps on my computer even at minimum settings? Bad programming.
Additionally, expect some framerate lag during the really big battles, with lots of action on screen.
Also, this game can be very strobe-y. Lots of flashing lights, jerky/sudden movement, and tons of objects on screen can make hard-difficulty co-op gameplay (or even PvP) a literal headache sometimes--as in, I sometimes get an actual IRL headache from playing this game too long because the flashing lights and jerky movement aren't exactly easy on the eyes. However, if you can run Battleborn at 60 FPS or better, this may not be a problem for you.

I like well written political quandries in my games. But, when you are a few hours in and realize the game is going to beat you over the head with a certain narrative over, and over, and over, and over, and over, sometimes, that makes it unbearable.
This game is an unbearable/10, and thats coming from a fan of the majority of this studios games.
Not to mention the combat is trash.

The core concept behind the game is good, however the implementation is severely lacking. The quality in several areas, and sometimes the transparency of what will occur, is extremely lacking. The combat is barebones basic, with minimal strategy elements.
The writing is decent, though the scenarios presented are in a definitive political lens, and I am unsure of how to view that part of the game as a result. I don't really like politics in my games, I can deal with it minimally, but when it goes all in, it kinda sours the experience.
Not the worst game I've played, but the combat is poor. Enemies using anti-air defenses will summarily two shot the dragon, and enemies without air defenses will be two shot by the dragon.
Missiles can track you across map? Literally...the dodge mechanic doesn't work as intended (still taking damage when visually cleared missile, missiles chasing you despite the dodge (even in circles).
I could deal with the majority of that, if it weren't so boring. I essentially won the game within the first 20 minutes, the game is extremely snowball heavy (a single victory at a location where their forces are stacked can allow you an easy victory). Normally I wouldn't rate a game within 3 hours of playing, but in a case like this, the quality of gameplay doesn't significantly increase. It's main element, that is tactical combat, is severely lacking, and the world is rather small.
It uses a risk-esque system for the strategy layer, which isn't that bad. The game (minus the tactical layer) is rather good in fact, but there isn't much to do on the strategic layer beyond have the occasional conversation, usually political-based, with one of your underlings, which is where the issue lies.
You 'research' by spending points on improvements, which add abilities or unlock new units (not really that interesting. There is also the option to 'empower your dragon', allowing you to take a keybar of abilities, which vary in power. The dragon itself is powerful, but instantly dies to missiles, has nothing to do with being bad at dodging, I'm pretty sure missiles don't spin around 8 times in a circle and still collide into you...
It's just not fun or particularly entertaining.
The dragon gameplay itself, and the switch from 'strategy game' to more or less FPS dragon gameplay IS good, and I'd like to see this done in a different game (preferably without the dragon, or other unit being grossly overpowered and therefore having a massive weakness).
I can applaud the attempt, while still criticizing the result. What they did here, if successful, would have revolutionized gaming, and it is moderately impressive for what it turned out, just nowhere near what we expect to be present in a strategy game. They tried to input decision making (politics, usually based on real life :/ ) and tie that in with the strategy layer, which ultimately ties into the tactical layer by how many troops you can provide, etc, along with creating a strategy game, and a third person dragon-shooter thingy on top of that, and the complexity ultimately kills the joy of the game. They tried to do a bit of everything, but instead failed at everything.
5/10

Her Story is a game for the desk jockey. All of the gameplay is summarized as follows; search keywords from live-action video scripts, watch said videos, keep going until the game thinks you’ve watched enough videos. From the collection of videos both cryptic and vague to the poignant and verbose, Her Story hands you the pieces of a story of love, murder and insanity.
Most beautifully, I should say, is the addition of an ‘unreliable narrator’ to such an unexplored genre that is, interactive media. You search these videos by keyword, so most of the time they’re out of order or worse: Completely non-sequitur without its missing context. What appears to be a video of the protagonist (there’s just the one) confessing or slipping on her well-constructed alibi could just be a small piece of something bigger or just a small moment of stress-induced insanity. Is she crazy? Is she just shaken up? The duality of this character slowly weaving  itself together in front of you is also the only one  giving you credible information on the murder you, as the player, are trying to solve.
Where this game really shines is in its use of Engine and GUI. I’m guilty of groaning when I saw the unity logo pop-up at the beginning of the game. While a strong advocate for Unity and user-friendly game engines, I have to admit that my standards dropped a bit in expectations for a game that probably wasn’t going to be as lengthy or beautiful as I hoped. Within seconds, Her Story assured me my time would not be wasted. The GUI/UI background is that of an old tube-monitor from the mid 90’s. A functional and UI that contains a program that runs and feels like a copycat of Windows 95’. As a game dev that’s had to make a similar project, I feel greatly outclassed by the simplicity and credibility of Sam Barlow’s work on the user interface. It’s amazing. If you’re a student in game design or just making user interfaces, I strongly recommend you buy this game at cover price.
The ending left me hollow, sad, pensive and guilty. Without spoiling anything, it’s definitely worth playing this to the end. I understand that these “artsy games” don’t gel with everyone. But to those looking for an unparalleled look into the marriage between two ironclad mediums. Do not miss this game.
