I've been a beta tester for this game ever since November 2013, when the game was in it's Indiegogo campaign.
I can't stress enough how wonderful this game is! The developers are two very different people, yet they've found a way to merge arcade-like shooting and action with mythological-style storytelling. I would describe the game as a bit of a combination of three games:
1. Galaga
2. Descent
3, Shadow of the Colossus
Why? Because it has the waves of bug-like enemies and shooting of Galaga, the six-degrees-of-freedom of Descent, and  grand bosses that factor as the main villains like Shadow of the Colossus did.
You play as a lost soul trapped in a spacecraft, woken up by a mysterious voice and sent on a mission to destroy four ancient gods in the false universes they rule. I like the approach to storytelling they took with the game, since it's unintrusive, but engaging and gives a sense of the scale of where you play.
The art style is also really compelling, if simplistic (but I personally love that kind of style). Colors are carefully placed and silhouettes are easy to read because everything has a distinctive shape.
The gameplay is one of the best parts! Enemies are very smart here, and will always move with you so that they (or you) don't get lost. They'll work together (every enemie has it's own "brain") to perform tactics like flanking, surrounding a goal, and pulling together in formations, possibly just to impress you.
There are some nice choices for ships as well. Between machine-gun fire, homing missiles for new players, lasers for snipers, and (here's my personal favorite) a ninja spaceship! The "ninja" ship actually uses a sword and shurikens to fight off foes, can you argue against that?
My biggest complaint is that there seems to be a few bugs here and there, but those will likely be patched out in the future since the devs care about their game.
The devs are also really great people and passionate about this game. A little support and the game's future will look bright, so please check this game out as soon as you can!

Kromaia exceeded my expectations. This is not a strictly on-rails shooter like Rez, Starfox or Space Harrier. Think all of the above, with the freedom of movement of Descent: Pitch, yaw, strafe in all directions, boost, and barrel roll through a storm of geometry and AI that adapt to you. A 3D compass and level design that rewards your intuition keep you on track. Although the game is listed as third person, the view can be toggled between stationary 3rd as well as 1st person. The controls are intuitive, but also remappable. It's possible to ignore some axes for simpler handling, while experts can enjoy pushing the limits of motion or even customising the thrust physics. The plot is enigmatic and the immense soundtrack fits perfectly, guiding you steadily towards... something... the answer to an unknown question. The boss fights are creative and epic, reminiscent of Star Fox, and playing them with each of the game's 4 ships offers a different challenge (machine gunning the scales off a space snake is straightforward enough, peeling them off point blank with only an energy sword is another matter).
One downside to this game for some might be the length-- completion forces you to replay the same four stages with different ships, which although it provides a unique experience still feels a bit too small for a 20 dollar price tag. However, the score attack mode and editable configs the engine uses may be its saving grace and where the replay value resides, and hopefully official expansions are also a possibility. The boss fights are so good one is left wanting more space gods to conquer.

If you're seeing this, you probably heard about this game being praised as "AN UNDERRATED GEM!" or "A FORGOTTEN MASTERPIECE!" and those two things are lies.
The game starts out promising enough - a fun introductory level, but then it quickly becomes clear it's gonna be slightly slow. The shooting level tutorial has you platform up to shoot some targets. However, enemies are slow to kill and this level teaches you an important lesson - don't even care about the enemies. This becomes especially important later on in a level titled Black Velvetopia where censors (the main enemy) randomly pop out. After the 800th time, I just levitationed past them.
The next level seems like it should be fun, but it ends up slow due to some of the frustrating control choices.
"It must get better here!" You yell out, only to be met with disappointment. You scale your dreamworld, yadda yadda yadda, and head to the beach. You then get to do the worst level in the game - a slow boss fight where every 2 hits you begin a slow chase scene, and a slow world where your slowed to a crawl and get missiles shot at you from every direction.
After clearing that level, you enter The Milkman. You get so far, only to find out that you need to go back and grind 800 Arrowheads (the collectable). Keep in mind at this point, you may have... 50. Don't forget the FUN fact that the only way to quickly get arrowheads involves you slowly walking around a camp with enemies that can randomly pyrokenesis you and take 5 hits to kill! You then next have to do a perfect timing part as you hide behind q door and quickly psyblast somebody. Next one.
You gain access to 3 brand new levels - 2/3 you need to grind to RANK 30 FOR. The only one left is Black Velvetopia - AKA "Wait, did I search this alleyway yet? Oh god dammit more censors."
You finish those, including a boring theater level, and climb the Towers. Not much can be said here.
Finally, you begin the most universially hated part of this game - the Meat Circus. It begins with an annoying and frustrating escort level. A boss where you just run and hit. Grind some rails. Begin a platforming segment where water rises and you must leap from chain fence to chain fence (with terrible hit detection). Annoying boss where you have to run and evade thrown things and flaming swords and throw/hit. Semi-annoying boss which is cheesed by just spamming invisibilty & shield and then spam-clicking.
TL;DR - bad hit detection, annoying levels, annoying bosses, features two moments where you must grind (to pad out game time I assume), and then is all concluded with the worst level in gaming history.

I generally do not enjoy competitive FPS games, but I really enjoy this game and I feel like I got my money's worth out of it.
I find the PvP enjoyable because you don't have to be amazing to win, you just have to understand how the game works. For example, I have terrible accuracy, but I can spend many rounds getting turrets and accelerators going while taking down the enemy turrets and accelerators. If I am feeling quick, I can also focus on the center field shards – making it take longer for the enemy to activate their items. One match I did this so well that even though the other team was technically more skilled at killing our team we were able to win due to my team fighting back and me spamming large minions onto the battlefield.
But if I get tired of the PvP (usually when I get a string of losses), I can always switch over to the campaign maps and either play with a team or by myself. Either way I get levels, credits, and gear that might help with the PvP game.
Speaking of gear, most gear isn't going to make or break your game. Yeah, legendary gear is really nice but it is expensive to activate and if enough shards aren't available in game then you just wasted an item slot. Often times I will go into a match with 3 common items  and have them all activated within the first 10 minutes of the match or campaign map. It won't win the match for the team but that's a slight edge I am getting that a person equipped with 3 legendaries won't be seeing for a while, if at all.
Finally, I like how in PvP that teams have to be made up of unique characters. You won't have 5 Benedicts flying around blasting the enemy team. While some people see this as a problem, I feel it limits the impact of a character being imbalanced (and let's face it, imbalances are going to happen when you have hero classes, or any game that has classes – it's just the nature of the beast. And the more you have the more likely there will be imbalances). When Galilea was a bit overpowered at release, it wasn't a huge deal for me because I knew I'd never compete against a team of 5 Galileas. Furthermore, by requiring unique characters I never feel like I lost a match because everyone wanted to be the “cool” character.
All in all, I really enjoy this game. I do wish a bit more marketing went into it though because there seems to be a lot of misinformation out as to what this game is actually about.  But if it ends up dying quickly, I still feel I got my money's worth.

Having reached the 250 hour mark, I've decided it is high time for a review after having experienced a solid sum of this game.

To start, Battleborn is a mix of content that is rewarding for you to mix PvE and PvP content. While one can purely participate in PvP content, you'll be missing out on some nice pieces of gear which gets used in both forms of content.
PvE:
Currently, we have access to 8 story mode missions and an additional solo Prologue to introduce you to the game.
Each one centers in on the progression of the story against the star-stealing Varelsi and Rendain's Jennerit army.
These missions take place in a variety of different environments, map layouts, and hosts a number of different enemy types.
Most objectives will involve escorting large sentires, who are more than capable of defending themselves at times, or the defense of a stationary objective.
The game's difficulty scales with how many players are on your team, so going in alone will be easier than going in with a 5-man group.
Difficulty can go higher by utilizing Advanced difficulty, which handles enemy damage/health/spawn patterns differently.
There is also Hardcore mode, which removes Extra Lives and making you play cautiously.
5 additional story mode missions will be added overtime through the season pass too.
----------
PvP: Currently we have 3 PvP modes and 2 maps per mode.
Capture: Three points exist on the map to be controlled by the teams, there is limited currency available on these maps and many people will use lower-ranked gear to compensate for this.
Incursion: Each team has two sentries that guard a part of their base. Teams are to push through enemy defenses and destroy the enemy sentry. Getting mercenaries to aid in your push is vital, along with appropriate timing and a good balance of offense/defense. There is often an abundance of currency available and you can use your best gear loadouts.
Meltdown: You must escort your minions to specific areas to sacrifice them, gaining favor with Minrec. This is a balance of protecting your own minions, while destroying the enemy minions before they reach their destination. Two lanes will exist, leading to teams needing to divide their forces appropriately to ensure both lanes are protected. Currency is also abundant here, allowing you to bring good loadouts.
Gearbox has already stated they will be releasing more maps and game modes in the future. They've revealed some concept art for map designs.
5 new heroes are being added over time, these heroes will be available to everyone, but must be unlocked.
We already have one added, Alani.
-------
Balancing:
Gearbox has handled balancing characters with a steady hand. They are careful not to fall into the hole like many other PvP games do, where they overnerf a character and destroy their viability. Instead, Gearbox makes adjustments over time and sees the community reaction, then adjusts further if they feel it is needed. This progressive balancing has made me greatly appreciate their methods, as one of my favorite characters was subject to this balance. Ambra is still as viable as ever and still remains very strong.
So if you're afraid a favorite character of yours will be subject to overzealous nerfs, do not fear. Gearbox has taken the right approach in how to balance.
--------
Matchmaking:
I'm seeing a lot of negativity over this, and I feel like it was unwarranted, because it is something that can and HAS been improved on.
Matchmaking utilizes an invisible ELO rating for players, but did not originally account for Command Rank(which only reflects how -LONG- you have played the game).
This led to people who are command rank 10, who have a somewhat unimpressive ELO getting paired with people of command rank 70 with similar ELO.
While this still sometimes occurs, it is rare that they are not equally skilled.
Matchmaking has seen quite a few improvements so far and it has done well for improving the quality of each match.
Premades now have a priority to be paired with other premades; preventing "pubstomps" from being common place and instead putting you up against a team with equally reliable communication.
Matchmaking itself has improved as well, leading to more equally skilled teams in public matches. This has been great for me, as I commonly queue alone or with a single friend.
------
Characters:
Gearbox did a superb job here, creating a wide array of characters with countless personality, background lore, and playstyles. We have disruptors, support, tanks, brawlers, assassins, rescuers, snipers, and territorials. And with some of these roles being mixed into single characters, this leads to even more unique plays by these Battleborn.
Lore:
Every character has specific lore challenges attached to their character. By finishing off a challenge for their lore, you gain access to tidbits of lore about the character. Each character has a unique audio log to unlock too. By unlocking all lore challenges for a character, you gain access to a piece of gear tailored specifically for that character. They're often quite strong or they change how you play.
Helix:
The helix system is what allows you to further define your build every time you level up. It gives you 2 choices each level, or 3 if you unlock a mutation(done by playing a character often). These choices augment abilities that affect how they can function, ultimately allowing you to fine-tune your role.
Customization:
Currently there are 5+ taunts for every character in the game, some are unlocked through playing the character often, one is always from lore, and the others come from Loot Packs which you can earn or buy for ingame currency.
There are also skins which change up the colors for each character, some are from Loot Packs, most are from playing a character often. While these are just recolors, players have found new skins that are called "Tier 2" by Gearbox. These skins are more unique as they do more than just a simple recolor. Gearbox has also mentioned creating Tier 3 skins, which may change the character appearance greatly.
------
Final thoughts:
Currently, I'm deeply enjoying this game and am happy with my purchase. I paid full price for the Digital Deluxe and would do it again in a heart beat.
My only gripes currently would be quite minimal.
Some players sometimes treat PvP matches like Team Deathmatch, which causes the actual objectives to be ignored. While they may get a fancy K/D ratio, the team will ultimately lose. But this is simply how some people operate, you'll find this behavior in -every- game.
A bit more communication about upcoming changes would be great, especially if they're posted for people to clearly see.
Most people didn't know about the matchmaking improvements, as they weren't posted everywhere for people to see. This could quell some of the doomsayers who assume nothing has changed. As well as let the community know what Gearbox's next step(s) are for everything they're doing.
Overall, I believe this is a great game and recommend anyone who loves Gearbox's humor, wild character design, and gameplay to give this game a shot. It's a solid title that has been overshadowed by competitor marketing and has a great community behind it.
Thanks for reading my review and I hope it helps you make your purchasing decision.

Ridiculously overhyped but still worth your time.
Kotor is your typical Bioware RPG, this time set in the rich Star Wars universe, albeit several millenia before the movies, hence the "old republic" title and here is my minor annoyances with this title begin. The atmosphere is dense and captures everything we like about Star Wars, likeable characters traversing colourful worlds but it never really does anything with the unfamiliar timeframe of the game. Every aspect of the gaming world is exactly like the Star Wars we already know, perfectly interchangeable, the planets are all too familiar and apparently the design of weapons, clothing etc didn't change inbetween Kotor and the movies. The people on Tatooine all live in the same huts like it's some kind of theme park. This may sound like a nitpick but I found the game never delivered on its promise of showing us the old republic, a new fragment in the Star Wars mosaic we know and love. This being said the worlds you are visiting will still get you hooked immediately, it's just a shame Bioware didn't do more with it. I know you have to tread carefully around golden calves but a bit more inspiration instead of trepidation would have been very welcome. Given some of the ridiculous content of the Expanded Universe I don't think Bioware could have screwed it up severely.
Another aspect usually lauded that I found a bit lacking is the overarching storyline about Darth Revan. I don't want to spoil anything here but it doesn't go beyond cartoon badguy territory and in the end it's just a story about another Darth that wants to rule the galaxy and there's a shocking reveal about your character as well. Very safe, very standard. The story did the job alright but it's not as great as people make it out to be and I feel the need to clarify this for people who want to play Kotor and are being promised a shakespearean masterpiece. What story I did actually really enjoy and what I found the great strength of Kotor is the little stories that happen on the planets you visit. They all feel very alive and there's lots to discover and do. This is where I found my main enjoyment as you are given the perfect amount of freedom in how you can play your character. There are generally two extremes in RPG storytelling, either a basic linear progression of a character (which can work beautifully if done right) or complete freedom for the player which has the downside that you aren't playing an actual character with strengths, weaknesses, backstory, motivations because it's just a proxy for you to throw around in a big sandbox. Kotor falls comfortably in the middle. The dark/light graph at the bottom of your character screen does feel a bit outdated though and unfitting for a game where you can play comfortable in moral grey areas.
The pseudo-turnbased combat does its job alright although I've seen it done better. As soon as the lightsabers arrive it gets somewhat tedious but never annoying. I know this is a game about Jedis and Siths but the mindset of the Prequel trilogy that Jedis have to use a lightsaber for everything from light gardening to cutting vegetables is what dragged down Star Wars so much over the last 15 years.
In general a game well worth your time despite some flaws but it's not the second coming of christ that people make it out to be. Kotor is a well made above average RPG and for the current price an absolute steal.

For a game from 2010 I would expect a better graphic department, especially being City Interactive an established game developer with several 3D titles on its record; however, even maxing out the settings the game looks poorly executed, with textures that, at times, seem to come straight out of 1999. The contrast between the good level design, the beautiful scenarios the Chrome Engine 4 creates and the poor texture quality generates a terrible outcome, that not even a breathtaking story and a great sound department can compensate.
After having played for an hour it will appear clear how this game was developed with console players in mind, and eventually ported to PC; the result, as you may imagine, is quite atrocious for a first person shooter.
In the end the gameplay experience is original, but the terrible execution doesn't make this a product worth your time.

Overall I like this game. The game fuses stratigical planning and RTS fairly well with its own unique system. It also had a interesting political/moral desicions that highlight the diffuclty of pleasing different groups within your faction. The dialoge between the you and the main characters you interact with (politicians, your gernerals, and your wife) are all pretty well flushed out. With your generals and wife you also get several story arcs that change based on how you react to situations. These are all good things. However, there are several reasons why this game is only decent/good, not great. The first problem I have is with the RTS sections. While these are avoidable a major part of the game is the RTS sections. While it is true that you can turn into a dragon (which is pretty baller), the meat of the combat you do is just not that fun. All you do is build up units, mesh them together in a ball, and march over to the enemy base after you defeated the piecemeal forces they threw at you. The "grand strategy" phases fair better. You have the option to build troops or different numbers of buildings which strenthen your empire in several ways. A cool, unique concept is the cards system. These cards act as both stratigical and tactical game changers.  From one time mercenary cards that bolster your troops to cards that destroy enemy buildings  this system adds a twist to a fairly old genre. The AI is OK. Like asformentioned on the RTS battles they sometimes just throw half of thier army to be destoryed by yours. On the Larger stratigic map they can annoy you, but I never really felt like I was in danger of losing the game. The final problem I have is the lengh. I was able to complete the game in under 10 hours, and besides seeing different character arcs from your generals (or picking a different wife), gameplay wise, there isnt a lot of replayability. So would I recomend this game? Sure! I had fun with it and it had some cool concepts. I would not reccomend purchasing it at full price. It seems to be a game that nearly always goes on sale and I picked it up for $4. Wait for a sale, then check it out.

This is not uplink. It’s a side grade.
It’s not frantic at all. It’s not that deep and there is barely any lore or content.
However if you want a computer “Hacking” game that isn’t out to overwhelm you this is it. It’s more about how you complete your missions than how fast you can do them as password hacking is always the same no matter the difficulty level.
The interface is significantly more usable than uplink mostly due to the comparative simplicity. It is almost completely one button mouse controlled. It looks nice and retro. You never need to click and drag tiny bars to get things done as the commands are in a drop down menu.
One of the key game element is simply not ever getting a trace on you while on the job. If you try to race the clock you are almost going to lose. Why? The game goes not let you multitask, your computer is decidedly not advanced  which also means it does things slowly one. at. a. time. You are almost always better off disconnecting and aborting the job instead of trying to complete one racing the trace.
Another very nice thing is not having to deal with proxies like Uplink does. You don’t have to string a web of proxies to build up time for your hack. That was easily the most obnoxious part of Uplink. Here you upgrade and buy more proxies to extend your trace timer. If there is ever a sequel or a scriptural one to uplink this has got to be fixed.
The game over isn’t all bad, you get to keep your money in the bank so you can leapfrog from your last attempt getting you to higher levels faster.
However the bad part is it is a little too simple and has nearly no lore. There is no reason to ever hack just for the sake of hacking. There is nothing to read, no bank accounts to pillage(Uplink went wrong way with this allowing you to break the game in 15 minutes), no jokes or call backs. There is a single thread story which surprisingly went in a different direction than I expected but there is no post game content.
However if you want a hacking game that is bordering on relaxing this is it. Once you hack in without setting of a trace you can take all the time in the world. But beware of the lack of long term content. Not a bad game to get on sale.

Foreword:
I would recommend this to anyone that bought it for the same reason as me: a sort of remake of Uplink but with an interface that is readable on a big screen.
If you don't know Uplink, this one will be tough to get started with. If you do, you'll notice that it's basically Uplink but with a better interface and more efficient gameplay.
Gameplay:
You own a Proxy server through which you can connect to target machines and do some hacking: delete a file, steal a file, find a record, delete a mail, reply to a mail, etc. - still pretty much at the beginning of the game.
As you progress you earn money to upgrade your hardware and buy new software in order to do harder, more complicated hacks.
Unlike Uplink, hacks aren't all about time, it's rather whether or not you can do the puzzle in time.
The puzzles aren't too hard but I've seen some that are seemingly not solvable - you can disconnect and reconnect - usually you'll get a different puzzle.
Once you've done a hack, you gotta get rid of evidence, therefore delete logs on the target machine and the routing ones on your proxy. This is a ton simpler than in Uplink where it gets really confusing as to how they even got you.
Flaws:
Like Uplink, jobs become harder over time and if you don't spend your money wisely, you might end up not being able to do a lot of jobs because you lack some device.
However, I've received a patch today and now there are also special missions which come in occasionally which pay really well.
The tutorial is rather lacking. I even got confused as to how the first hack is supposed to work. And I still have no clue what the red stuff is in puzzles. I assumed those are traps of some sort and evade them.
All in all I find it quite addicting but the tutorial is really lacking. And there doesn't seem to be an in-game information library where I could read up on the symbols and what they do during hacks.
That would be pretty cool to have that.
Pros:
The game doesn't instantly kill you when you get caught but your proxy gets taken away. So the money you still had is still there which is nice.
Bottom line:
To me it's fun and addicting but it's a lot of grind as well.

Edit: After a few bugfixes and a full rebalance, now I can fully recommend this game :-)
Very strong Uplink vibe coming out of this one (if you don't know Uplink, you might want to go take a look at it too), so I'll have to compare with it. Main differences:
The balance is pretty good now. It should take about 4~5h for a full playthrough (up to level 8, and completing all story missions) if you know what you're doing, expect some 8h+ on the first run through the game, if you don't get caught first.
Overall, the game is fun to play. There's tension as you hack a new server, and you need to move fast if you get caught, and there's a lot of humor in all the text around the game. The story missions are optional, but most come with some good rewards. You may not want to do them all, but which ones to skip you'll learn after you do them :-)

Agent 47 decides to retire from the killing, and work as a gardener for a church in Italy, until one day, HE NEEDED TO USE THE BATHROOM

Hitman 2 is a direct sequal to the original Hitman, after the events of the original game Agent 47 faked his own death and unofficially resigned from the ICA. For some time he has live a reclusive life as a gardener at a church in Sicily, Italy. Agent 47, tried to make amends to what he has done in the past by donating his blood money to the church and seeking guidence and forgiveness from the priest of the church, Father Vittorio. Despite 47's previous occupation of being an assassin, the good priest knows 47 is good at heart and assurs him that there is a place for him in the next life. Life at the church seem all well until a mysterious group of gun men came and abductted Vittorio. Leaving behind a ransom note for 47 to read, he knows the only way to find his friend is with the help of the ICA. Which means he has to reactivate his membership as a hired assassin once more. The ICA agrees to help 47's search for the priest in exchange for him to carry out orders requested by a client. During Agent 47's travels he will eventually learn that the man who abdupted the priest is someone who holds a serious grudge towards him, The sequal is a big improvement over the original game with not just slightly improved graphics but improved controls for movement and weapon firing. In this game the compass is intact to the screen rather than being an item to buy, the sneaking mode is improved, the map labels enemy locations as well as objective marks, and best of all you are finally able to do mid level saves in case you mess up on the mission! This was also the first hitman game to have the progress of collecting weapons out on the field. Which this leads to players being able to obtain newer weapons to use in later levels as well as being able to used these obtained weapons for previously played levels. Overrall, this is one of the best sequals to be superior towards the original and was the game that helped make Hitman a more well received franchise. A must play game for any third person shooter/stealth game fans.

Better than the first game, I'll give it that! Definitely not on the same level as Blood Money in my opinion, but it was still a relatively good game.
Graphics: Can't say too much about this, given it was released in 2002. I will say that many of the environments looked very plain and were not too pleasing to look at. Most of the levels used the same color palette for the whole level (all white for snow, all yellow for desert, all gray for city) and it just got boring after a while.
Story: Again, can't expect too much from a Hitman game in terms of story. 47 was just as deadpan as always, but it seemed like they actually attempted to create some other characters and give them lines. Unfortunately, the lines were pretty horribly delivered and were downright comical at times, which was an awful contrast to 47's brooding attitude. The story itself seemed pretty straightforward: Rejoin the agency to save a friend, kill this guy, kill that guy, oh now there's this other guy, travel the world killing everybody, finally get your friend back at the end after slaughtering everyone. Like I said, nothing too special.
Level Design: Coming from playing Blood Money, I was expecting some great level design out of these developers. While I praised Blood Money for having large levels, I think this game suffers from levels that are either too large or too small. There might've been 2 or 3 of the 21 levels that were decently sized and required a good amount of planning, but the rest were either so ridiculously big that I got lost constantly, or so small that I finished the level in a good 5 minutes on the first try. There was simply too much variation in the level design, which made it hard to enjoy the game.
Gameplay: Also, I found there was a lot of guesswork to be had in this game. Blood Money did a good job of showing you certain ways to complete the level, or slightly guiding you in the right direction. This game, I found, would throw you in an environment where there was often one easy way to get things done, but that easy way was extremely cryptic and frustrating. And every other way to complete the level is near impossible. Again, just a lot of inconsistencies. Aside from that, it's general Hitman gameplay, which is clunky, but good.
Overall, it's a Hitman game, which I've come to discover is generally a good thing: it usually entails large and complex levels, good sneaking, interesting environments, and entertaining gunplay. This game just barely fell short on just about everything. I still recommend it for anyone who enjoys sneaking games, but I would definitely say that Blood Money beats this game in just about every aspect. Not too bad, 7/10

This game showed me how insufficient Steam's "recommended/not recommended" system really is. Even after spending 26 hours playing this game, I still wasn't sure what to make of it.
Like in Divinity II, the protagonist is a "Dragon Knight", a powerful warrior that can turn into a dragon at will. Divinity: Dragon Commander acts as a sort of prequel to the Divinity series, the paper thin story is set before the other Divinity games.
And unlike other games in the series, Dragon Commander is a strategy game, a TBS actually, although it contains RTS elements.
Being a TBS, the game is turn based. Each turn consists of three different phases: The "RPG phase", the "TBS phase" and the "RTS phase".
The first phase is the "RPG phase". During this phase you find yourself on the "Raven", an airship that acts as your base of operations. This is where you research units and upgrades and make political decisions. Politics are an important part of the game and have an effect on your popularity. There are five different races: Dwarves, Elves, Imps, Lizards and Undead. Each race is represented by an ambassador aboard the Raven. Every once in a while, an ambassador makes a proposal to create new laws or change existing ones. Although you can't please everyone, it's important to appease as many races as possible (which can be rather frustrating), as the decisions you make here often have a direct influence on the next phase.
The second and most important phase is the "TBS phase". Apart from some minor problems, Larian absolutely nailed this part. This is similar to the board game "Risk". It consists of a world map with many small countries that can be conquered. This is where war is waged. During this phase, you can erect buildings. Each country on the map can have one building. Some buildings allow you to build units, others increase your income or generate "cards". Cards can be used to gain bonuses that last at least 1 turn or 1 battle. With cards, you can strengthen your troops, boost your economy or sabotage the enemy, depending on the type of card used.
An important thing to keep in mind during this phase is that the AI has access to more resources than you and is able to build gigantic armies in no time, which often leads to intense battles and makes countries hotly contested. However this is less of a problem than it seems, because the AI sometimes behaves rather stupid, often moving units back and forth for no reason. Moving units into a country that is held by enemy troops will result in a battle at the end of your turn. You can choose if you want to let the computer decide the battle for you or if you want to play the battle. The latter option will lead to the "RTS phase".
The "RTS phase" is entirely optional. Probably designed to be the most fun element of the game, it is actually quite the opposite. There are almost no positive aspects about this phase. The maps are so small that there are barely any tactical options other than mindlessly sending units towards your enemy, and the AI is ruthless, faster and much more efficient than any human player could ever be. Crap really hits the fan when you reach a certain point in the campaign and the enemy units become more powerful than yours. So now you have an AI that works faster and more efficient than you, and now it even has more powerful units! I stopped bothering with the RTS phase at that point, because every battle was destined to be a loss from the start.
The one fun thing about this phase is the dragon. Being a Dragon Knight, you can enter the battlefield in dragon form during the combat phase. While fun, I found the Dragon to be disappointing in terms of power and it isn't as much of a diciding factor in battles I thought it would be. Hell, its main attack is so weak that it takes several shots to kill the weakest unit in the game, even when upgraded to do 33% more damage. The dragon can be a useful tool to support your troops in battle by casting spells, but that's about it.
In the end, Divinity: Dragon Commander is a game that could have been much better than it turned out to be. There's so much wasted potential, it's outright frustrating. Considering its heavy flaws, I was wondering if I should recommend this game or not. But it is an interesting game that can provide lots of fun. If you ignore the RTS part, that is.

“Her Story is the new game from Sam Barlow, creator of Silent Hill: Shattered Memories and Aisle. A woman is interviewed seven times by the police. Search the video database and explore hundreds of authentic clips to discover her story in this groundbreaking narrative game.”
Thrown straight in at the deep end the game wants you to learn yourself how to play and we kind of like that. Of course we didn’t at first check the Readme doc, i mean who does?
We are going to have to keep this one very short because it’ll be way to easy to give clues, hints and spoilers to the story if we don’t.
You are on the hunt through the L.O.G.I.C. database for answers and clues to her story, the story of the women in the videos and what has happened to bring her to the interviews.
- Pay close attention to not only what she is saying but everything you can see within each video clip.
It’s styled to feel as if your looking at a PC monitor from the 90s with it’s Rounded Glare and all the UI within the game is feels like a classic OS.
We took an early break from the main game when we discovered you can play Othello by checking the trash. It wasn’t for long though as we wanted to get right back into the story we were uncovering.
- Play in a windowed mode and open Notepad next to the game. Trust us you’ll need it whilst you listen to all the clues and try to understand who all the characters are. We had hundreds of words and phrases by the time we finished the game. It made it a lot easy and probably one of the reasons we solved the whole puzzle.
Brilliant performance from Viva Seifert, she really sells the persona in the videos and makes the unraveling of the story very engrossing. So much so we couldn’t stop playing till we discovered the true secrets hiding within the interview clips.

First, a little bit about my play experience. I accessed about 80% of the video clips without using exploits, by taking notes and trying to 'piece things together'. Contrary to the claims of the developers and many fans, the end is not open-ended, the "story" is pretty straight forward and just not all that interesting. (though it attempts to be as oooooh Psychological as possible)
Her Story is a great gameplay concept that is squandered by poor writing, an eye-rollingly trite World's Smallest
Piano soundtrack (think -- something in between Max Richter and Ludovico Einaudi) , and the uninteresting narrative fails to make up for the lack of interactivity or choice.
As for "her story", she's got
, and that's all that really need be said. I should have expected no better from someone involved in the Silent Hill series.
The concept of struggling against both a mystery and a fairly believably inept police database was promising though. The wasted opportunities remind me of similar concepts like Indigo Prophecy and Heavy Rain. Still waiting for a game to put the PROCEDURE in Police Procedural better than LA Noire.

I just finished "Her Story" and was pleasently surprised by this experience.  I have purchased a number of 'overwhelmingly positive' games, but few are as deserving of that title as this one.  Though the experience itself was short (I have about 2 hours of gameplay time), it was one that will stick with me far beyond my playtime.
In the game, you play the role of a detective, reviewing old case file clips.  While that itself may not seem to interesting, the game only reveals certain clips based on keywords you type into a search. Type "murder" and you get a maximum of five clips to view, each of which will reveal more about the story and give you ideas for new keywords to try.  When I got stuck, I would try random words to see what they would bring up.  This process allows the story to slowly reveal itself and made me feel very engaged with what was happening.
I highly recommend playing through this experience, especially considering the price of this game.  It is worth much more than I paid for it.

I should also commend the developer for the excellent pricing on this title. I got it for full price and had a fantastic time with it. 10/10 - Definitely recommended to FMV fans and fans of story/naration heavy games.

A very unique mystery game that gives the exact non-linearity and sense of discovery many like in a mystery. I almost felt like I cheated by entering a very magic search term (that I thought up myself - the interviewee hadn't mentioned it) and hearing a very revealing tape. But, as it turned out, I hadn't even found the half of it. And if the game is correct in not yet awarding the "50% database viewed" achievement, there's still lots of little details I don't know about.
Don't be lead to think that the intrigue is simply in finding more random tapes to view, as a mark of completion. There were plenty of times that I was scrambling to find an older tape I had already viewed, as soon as I realized the way that certain puzzle pieces fit together; an old phrase suddenly having a very new meaning, like how in good detective shows, they do a black and white flashback of something said earlier.
The game's total length isn't much more than a few hours; I think it paces itself very well. It has a pretty neat way of concluding, rather than waiting for the player to decide "Eh, I *guess* I've figured out most of it?"

I have had a lot of fun playing this game, and just completed the campaign solo. I am looking forward to the DLC and new maps, and for me, that is a difficult thing to admit.
A lot of reviewers have given this game a bad rap, but likely because of the multiplayer graphical optimization. I like single player and co-op, but the points below are unbiased.
PROs:
- Most FPS are afraid to do asymmetrical class design, which makes games more balanced but less fun.
- I\'m a huge fan of the direction, being an FPS fan and a MOBA fan but not liking the way most MOBA\'s are implemented. I think they just need to optimize the multiplayer\'s performance and i\'d buy a sequel.
- I like that each character plays totally different, and the MOBA-Levelling mechanic is refreshing.
- The multiplayer is fun, with bots or people.
- Single Player performed pretty well on my machine, either at 4k or lower resolutions.
- Unlocking characters is easy, by the time i finished the campaign solo i had 19/25.
- Not as bad as DNF, Aliens: Colonial Marines.
CONs:
- Some characters seem more powerful, but this is mostly due to different skill levels required.
- Netcode is probably the biggest downfall, if it wasnt for that, my score would have been 9.0/10,0
- It is not Overwatch, so there is not as much T&A.
- Obviously more multiplayer maps and modes are needed for longevity. Content and polishing is needed more than new characters, hopefully they keep that in mind.
- Not as good as Borderlands 1 & 2.
I recommend it to people that would like MOBA\'s if it had single-player, fans of Borderlands and want something fresh, or those that want a different style of multiplayer shooters. Or those that have Character-related ADD like myself.
I wouldnt recommend it if you need totally perfectly balanced and optimized multiplayer matches.

An incredibly boring and lifeless protagonist who doesn't seem to have a personality of his own, but likes to make smarmy faces. Maybe the idea was to put your own personality into the character. The cost of course being that you want to have a decent amount of soul by the end of the game. The PROBLEM with this though is that the game doesn't use this mechanic to the fullest. Half the time the offers are completely worthless or literally unobtainable due to the exorbitant prices (which is explained for a price but the story justification doesn't make it better as a game mechanic). The only time I can actually remember selling my soul to be useful in the game was the initial moment where you're offered some extra stat points, which brings up another problem. The stats don't really seem to come into the game all that much. Occasionally they influence things but seldom by any choice, nor do there seem to be any opportunities to increase them (apart from that initial moment of course).
Oh and the game is short but matches the price tag so that's fine.

Not that good, and not really that fun.  Unless you like a challenge.  In which case you'll love Fate of the World, because there are lots of tough challenges.  Your first challenge: learn to play the game.  20 hours in and you're still probably going to feel like you're just blindly choosing options that are too limited and too expensive, and that usually don't really explain how they work either.  This game, and the gameplay, were not well thought out, the learning curve is too steep, and the interface is pretty poor.
But there are a few neat rewards, if you can progress far enough in the game.  Interesting nanotechnology available at high levels to help clean up environmental problems, or quantum computers that you let you suddenly bring in a whole lot more money.
Overall, I recommend the game--IF you enjoy strategy games that have a lot of options that you need to do a lot thinking to sort out.  And if you can stomach all the things I already mentioned.

This is my first playing a Bioware game ever and hearing the popularity of Bioware in recent years of its story and characters I had to check it out, and what better way they manage to create in their early works and my favorite franchise, Star wars!

I will try sum it up as much possible without any major spoilers, the story is average good I’m sorry to say I can’t be wow by the plot which I will explain later in more details, but the main plot is interesting don’t get me wrong. The light vs. dark side I should say is cliché but there are some story telling that is pretty surprisingly interesting picking up half way through the game.
I chose to be light side because I’m always am and got motivated to defeat Malak the antagonist of the game. There are some nice moments where you go “awe” and “what” and that’s good, it shows Bioware was starting to stable themselves as the “capital ship” of 3rd party company.
However, their earliest isn’t much what I expected because the backstory of the old Republic never mention this ever and even talks about the origin of the war. Yes they do talk about the rise of the Sith but just a brief one, I was expected a prequel of the star wars movies about telling the origin of what happen about everything; the war, the rise of Sith, the origin of the Republic everything, but no not a whole lot and both side doesn’t show much color.
The Sith are so generic with their “I’m a snob so that means everyone I look is a weakling” their motivation of doing this to so weak to me, yes they do what Sith do but what they are doing just doesn’t convince me to show sympathy to them or even see them differently. Is just “he’s bad and we’re good.” What about the republic surely they are some goody-two shoes?
Well at first almost but no they can be somewhat corruptive and wrong of their morals too! And that’s what I want from it, the republic side showing its own “both side” but also want the Sith to show “their two faces as well” instead of all being rich snob Nazis.
A final note on this yes they do some moments with the Sith on Korriban but not entirely enough to see them as “they are evil but I can see their side point why they do this horrid things.”
the NPC and partners are interesting as well especially I like that when you got the time you can talk to them and hear some back stories even if you bring one of them along in one certain planet, more dialogue options to choose and you will have a good backstory of the character. Malak I think is a cool villain especially the way he talks plus and robo-jaw that he has is really cool to look at.
Now here comes the problems I have this game and two things are repetitive and cliché for the story aspect side. The NPC of any species just looks the same especially on the human side they have the same texture face model which doesn’t add a lot of emersion seing the same human character twice and even the voice, the alien sort of get a pass but their voice over just doesn't because they reuse the same alien language dialouge many times and it gets tired around the ears.
Yes, I know that Bioware was at their first steps and you could say is budget problem by not hiring more actors and having to change face textures about everything that won’t affect too much on the rating scale, is just a nitpick problem where you try to discover a new world with new species (though in my case I already know the species) but they sound the same you wanted to see many new variation looks/voice as possible. Hopefully in the second game when the game got very popular it will have more.
Alright now the big one and is, which side would you choose, well I should say, none of it matters! Well what I meant was it really doesn’t matter in “morality,” yes of course you still choose your light and dark ending but at endgame, for the rest of the game it really doesn’t matter if you are the lightest person in the world, you can still choose the dark path at the end of the game.
So what gives? What is the objective of those light side dark side points? Is really for gameplay wise in armor and weapons, the force powers I made my main character have some dark powers even some of my light-side partners, which doesn’t really matter if you are good or not you can still equip dark powers or light powers if you are choosing your endings. Another thing about the moral points is just cosmetic option but only in the dark path when your character begins to change color.
So now it sounds like it only effects gameplay and not story telling which blows badly right? Well at first yes, I thought it would be the biggest disappointment ever since no matter if you are the biggest jerk in this galaxy or the nicest one you can switch sides in matter of seconds. Well I should say not entirely in that center problem, because you can still have consequence when doing certain side quest and do evil things and in some planets some characters will pay you back hard, if you are prepare.
No, I think the big point taker has to be your partners’ reaction to the player’s action. Yes they say “you did a wrong thing” but they never “punish” you for it or better yet leave you or stop you even though they are the once that help you do the main’s dirty deed. Most of your partners are from the light side and whatever you do will make them react but not upon action which is really shame.
I expect during some quests or the main “dialogue” choice your friends will abandon you and you will be recruit with more dark players and the story switch to another quest, “conquest” I thought. You can be the biggest jerk without a reason to them and they won’t even leave your side no matter what you did, even by the next set of choice that you made “wrong” you can switch to being nice again and they will forget about your “dirty deeds.”
I find it odd that after everything I do bad they won’t bat an eye of my behavior which just tells me that my choice won’t affect much around me until the very end, but during the whole game experience I thought choosing one side might affect the story telling as two sides, one fight for the good or join the Sith and fight from the republic and you will eventually fight Yoda! (Which I know that isn’t him.)
My main when going dark or light doesn’t give a deeper meaning why he’s doing it, I’m just having that express feeling that “I do it because I’m a bully and want to take things just because,” “I’m good because I’m a goodie two-shoes,” and mind you I’m talking about story wise, the gameplay well that is different because I want the extra status boost.
The side missions some I like but is just another generic “do this because is the right thing to do and do this because you are a jerk” Even the options you choose sounds a bit preachy for me thinking “well duh of course is bad to do this but should I?” There is only one side quest I think is my favorite where it involve no light or dark side points and only pure morality choice which about there I got a moral dilemma and I wish there was more like that but I know if it is it makes the system even more pointless.
The final verdict is a 7/10 a good starting game for Bioware’s time but need improvement on the writing, and moral choice but other than that I did enjoy the game despite some minor flaws the gameplay works flawlessly and I don’t have much of a problem to say, hopefully when I finish star war kotor 2 maybe things will change and improve until then, may the force be with you.

More of a Puzzle Than A Game
Game-wise, the premise is very simple: 1) invest actions into nations with money,  2) invest actions and money to affect change in nations. 3) Try to reach your goals by wise investment and look out for random events.   The first mission shows how easy this is to do with 2 nations. but the second takes out the stops and gives you the world.   You'll be trying to develop and put out fires on a limited budget.   Your only resources are time and actions and already I see how there isn't going to be much replay value once you figure out the missions. So go slow: there aren't many.  Also, even though the game likes to throw precise graphs and numbers at you to show you change, your own actions are clumsy by comparism.  You have no way to apply a finely-tuned strategy or invent something new.  Its always invest money and wait 5 years.
Do not get this game if you have no patience for strategy or hate board games.  Do get this game if you're looking for a unique challenge or want to get perspective on how tough it might be to save the world and keep people happy at the same time.
Have you ever thought you could solve the climate change issue? You may want to give this game a try.

Set in Larian's imaginative and light-hearted Divnity universe, Dragon Commander initially seems to be a heavily flawed RTS, with most skirmishes being too simple and too unbalanced in some way (entirely too easy early on, suddenly extremely difficult later).  Mind you, these sequences aren't completely without fun, as the novelty of blasting through the sky as a dragon wearing a jetpack(!) is a satisfying one during the early hours of the game.  But once that novelty wears off, what are we left with?  Quite an interesting dynasty simulator, as it turns out!  As the emperor, you'll enact new laws and social policy reforms for a variety of issues that have real-world analogues.  Will you cozy up to the various factions in an effort to please everyone, or rule according to your own personal moral code?  Do you marry for love or for political gain?  No matter what you choose, be prepared to face the press and a fickle public.  It's in these segments that Divnity: Dragon Commander really comes into its own, and why it deserves a sale purchase if you're even a little curious about it.

I personally loved this game. Easily my favorite RTS/Strategy game I've played. I'm a sucker for BioWare-style RPG games though, so be warned.
I recommend this game to fans of Strategy, Grand Narrative, and RTS games. If you don't like one of these, this game may not be for you.
Divinity: Dragon Commander is a three layer cake of sorts.
- A dialogue and story-driven political sim plays between battles. This is, in my opinon, the 'main' game. Courting the approval of five nonhuman races is part of this layer. Approval figures are effeced by legislative decisions presented to the player by advisors of each race. I have no idea why human approval figures don't play a role.
- A RISK-like strategic game with an emphasis on postioning and logistics serves as the second 'layer'.
- FInally, an optional tactical fast-paced resource gathering RTS game decides the fate of individual battles. The game's auto-resolutions assume the worst in terms of tactics.
The five races are the (conservative)Dwarves, (ecological)Elves, (scientific)Imps, (pious)Undead, and (liberally-minded)reptilian dragon folk.
This is a very well-written game, but there are a few moments in the campaign where Larian studios' agenda seems forced and apparent.
After the first act, the player character required to marry one of four princesses. This has a strong effect on approval numbers that can be changed by player decisions as it is still early game. This element of romance may annoy or turn-off some. I enjoyed the more personal sub-narrative.

Part RTS, Part RPG. You play a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ prince trying to unite the world against your mad siblings, the war similar to a game of Risk. If you desire to play the individual battles yourself (rather than roll the dice), you can play a (very simple) RTS board, with the ability to use a dragon in 3rd-person perspective to deal damage. Finally, during all this you're dealing in part with the five other races, each deligate a strawman of some of our world's own ideologies.
The Risk is the most fun; the RTS sections are a bit drab if you've ever played another RTS before, (the dragon doesn't make up for it); and the Strawman Simulator discusses issues common of our real world as well (eg gay marriage, marijuana, etc), so it can be hard to move away from your own ideologies on the issues.

The RPG aspects are great fun. Characters, choices, and the story are fully fleshed out. Accompanying music, writing, and  voice acting are strong.
RTS elements are a mixed bag. Sometimes the setup will be hopeless or far too rushed for you to have an impact. At other times you can have a bit of fun trying a variety of tactics. Controls and the camera are a bit awkward. AI either rushes fast and hard or turtles while doing nothing else. It's rather stale in this area.
It's a good game but a bit rough around the edges in certain parts.

I remember hearing about this game a ton when I used to watch G4 and was surprised when I was given a chance to finally play it...for free no less (especially since I didn't buy into the strange
phase others got into).  Needless to say, I was pleasantly surprised, but not blown away.
is a story that takes place in the event of 24 hours, about a kid who runs away from his home to prove to his family that he can be the greatest psychic of all time...to follow his dreams rather than to continue with the family business.  During this time, he discovers that there is a strange incident with the PSI cadets losing their brains.  The story is basically what you would expect from a Saturday morning cartoon with some occassional dark humor thrown in to stir things up.
The graphics take some getting used to, but it's understandable when you take into account that this game was released for the
, which (in my opinion) had a strange style with its experimental games back then.  Though not fantastic, its whimsy can keep you entertained for a fair bit.
I wasn't particularly fond of the musical selections, but the gameplay held my interest.  The levels aren't exactly as "open" as games such as
or
and follow a linear format.  Just get from point A to point B and you should be fine.
I would also like to point out that though this game has some slightly difficult parts, the boss battles are far too easy, making the overall difficulty of this game pretty light.  Nothing that can't be mastered in a few hours, though if you want to get all the figments, you're going to have to get creative as the game doesn't feel properly tested to get these under the intended conditions.  (Like when they're too high to reach and your levitation ball will only go so high...)
The writing isn't particularly special, but it does have its moments.  Most of it honestly felt kind of boring to me, but when there was a joke I enjoyed, I laughed quite a bit about it (namely when it involved
.
Overall,
is a nice adventure game to settle down with for a while.  For $10, it feels like a fair purchase, though I wouldn't expect it to go any lower than 50% off ($5) during a sale.  If you're still wondering about if this game is worth your time, I'd say to give it a shot.  I'll vouch for it.

A very unique mystery game that gives the exact non-linearity and sense of discovery many like in a mystery. I almost felt like I cheated by entering a very magic search term (that I thought up myself - the interviewee hadn't mentioned it) and hearing a very revealing tape. But, as it turned out, I hadn't even found the half of it. And if the game is correct in not yet awarding the "50% database viewed" achievement, there's still lots of little details I don't know about.
Don't be lead to think that the intrigue is simply in finding more random tapes to view, as a mark of completion. There were plenty of times that I was scrambling to find an older tape I had already viewed, as soon as I realized the way that certain puzzle pieces fit together; an old phrase suddenly having a very new meaning, like how in good detective shows, they do a black and white flashback of something said earlier.
The game's total length isn't much more than a few hours; I think it paces itself very well. It has a pretty neat way of concluding, rather than waiting for the player to decide "Eh, I *guess* I've figured out most of it?"

Short: Excellent different game, FMV story exploration. Get it.
Longer: (no spoilers)
After playing it in full, I understand the buzz around it. It's almost of a choose-your-adventure type game, but in full video form. You have access to a bank of 271 clips of police interviews of this woman whose husband has been murdered. You can't just browse sequentially; you must enter search terms and see what comes up from the transcripts. This makes you organically discover what happened in different threads, in an order that will be unique to you.
Elements of the story are open to interpretation, if you lookup online you'll see almost thesis length discussions. The whole thing did stick with me many days after playing it and I have to give huge props to both the writing for giving your breadcrumbs to continue on, and the acting for keeping you fascinated and interested even if in the end you have no input on the story itself -- they journey is discovering the story and organizing it in your head yourself.

Not worth it IMO, the game is good don't get me wrong but its just frustrating. Its a lot like Evolve or League of Legends in the sense that if you're rolling with a good team then its a fun experience, but when you're playing with randoms its infuriating.
Battleborn is a team based game and a lengthy one at that. So when you que up for a game you're investing somewhere between 30 - 40 minutes of your day to that one match.
My main gripes with the game so far for the most part are no fault of the game of its own but at the same time something that will cause you to have a bad experience.
#1 Typical FPS community in a non traditional FPS game
As I mentioned the game is a lengthy Class Based, objective based shooter. Its very much like a MOBA except its an FPS. But the fact that its an FPS made it attract the FPS community which for the most part for some reason flat out REFUSE to communicate and work as a team. You get the typical problems in every class based FPS game where everyone either wants to be the Sniper since they think they\'re friggin Chris Kyle or everyone wants to be the Assault class because they\'re some kind of warhero and in the end you get an extremely unbalanced and mismatched team. In addition to this, no one talks. Like at all. Out of all the games I\'ve played I can count by hand the number of games where the team was actually interactive and communicating and working with each other. For the most part your fellow team mates will be playing in their own little world and view you as nothing more than a sentient AI.
#2 The game is had a terrible launch and is dying
For some reason whoever was in charge of scheduling the release date of this game decided it would be an awesome idea to release it around the same time as Overwatch came out. Not only that but even though these two games have been very heavily compared to each other Battleborn released with a full $60 price tag vs Overwatches $40
So not surprisingly, the player base it had during the Beta for the most part jumped ship and went to play Overwatch.
Now you have a diminishing player base who are getting more and more agitated by ironically the effects of the diminishing player base. I\'m serious it took me maybe a good 10-15 mins to write all this and the whole time I\'ve been qued up waiting to find a game.
Battleborn is completely underrated and is filled with amazing, fast paced, and stategic combat.

So, Payday 2 feels too casual or you just hate its irrational weapon balance? Welcome to the roots!
So, here, like in PD2, we have:
- Our favorite specials:
-- Dozers: simple Dooo.... Wait, WHAT?! HE'S SPRINTIIIIIIING!!!
-- Cloakers: nothing to worry about in the silence of the night... AAAHHH!!! Get away from me! GET AAAWAAAY!!! HELP!!!
-- Tazers: just Ta-a-a-a-a-azzzzzzze-e-e-e-erzzzzz!!! ZZZ! ZZZZ!!! *on the ground, no ammo*
-- Snipers: yes, those little black dots far away out there! You mean which red lazers? Naah, that couldn't be so easy, could it?
- Difficulty levels:
-- Easy: or is it?
-- Normal: no, you really should start with easy!
-- Hard: oh, yes, you, courageous one! Heard of loud Death Wish yet?
-- Overkill: would you like your a$$ served you on a plate rare or well-burnt?
-- 145+: well, oh well!.. Now you will die! ...and die! ...and die...
And, unlike PD2:
- The FPS are great, but the network code is soooo sloooow.
- There's no wrong "bound-to-fail" setup - you can make any one work, even with a "wrong" weapon.
- Skill-trees, that you gradually unlock - feature by feature, no skipping, but you'll eventually get them all for every tree (don't forget about that <Tab + 1...4> button combination during heists).
- You have no "gray screen" for the last down before custody, but you can tell it is by the health you get back (with every down on lower difficulty levels it decreases: 75% -> 50% -> 25% -> go get your medbag heal NOW!).
- No First Aid Kits, so either you go down and hope your buddies will get you up (no Inspire either!), or screw your team's medical supplies (and get kicked for being selfish!)!
- Fast-paced raw hardcore experience, where you can only win with skill and team effort on anything harder than Normal.
- Yeah, no weapon skins!
Give this one a chance! It might just be your thing!

Summary:
+ The fantasy designs are pleasing to the eye and something I wish I could dive more into.
/  If you are looking for a good game to be your first RTS, you might want to consider something else.
- The political system is pretty poor and almost uninspiring.
So, let me state something really important up front: before playing this game I had never played Risk nor had I played any real-time strategy games with the closest thing being Advance Wars (which was a turn-based strategy,) but I had a love for politics at the time. And I've heard from another critic that this game is actually pretty easy, so I figured this might be a great "baby's first real-time strategy game."
Oh no, it wasn't. Sadly, I don't think I can get into any real details as to why it was not a fun first RTS on the account that I'm not experienced in the genre. What I did get hung up a lot though is that I couldn't quite figure out what certain units beat other units. Sure, there was an optional tutorial I took, but it felt like I've missed a lot of stuff. And I have no clue about the Risk-like over world as I did better in a real game of Risk than with Dragon Commander. So if you are like me with no experience in RTS, I would advise something else.
And then there is the politics. In case you haven't noticed, this is set in a fantasy world. You actually play as a character who can shapeshift between a human and a dragon (hence the name.) And the fantasy aspects are actually enjoyable with at least 6 various races, with a few going beyond the standard Tolkien races, and each having different quirks and interests such as the skeletons being very religious because it was the gods who brought them back to life and goblins having a love for inventing and discovering. So we have a world where we could have some pretty interesting view points on different subjects.
But instead, we get stereotypes of different political stances. Going from left to right as they are at the table: a religious fundie, a liberal, a big business owner, a libertarian, and a scientist who seems to believe that the ends justify the means (okay, so the last one is a bit more interesting.) Now pick a political topic: you know where everyone stands and it is shallow. No one ever has an opinion that goes against their stereotype. The dwarf will never say, "You know what, the brewery industry makes a lot of money, even in war, so I think we can shoulder a bit more taxation to help rebuild cities." Nor will the elf state, "This addictive substance is harmful to society and, while it goes against my belief of personal freedoms, I believe that it should be outlawed." That's it. There's no upset, no one is quite unsure, and no one seems capable of admitting that their opponents do have a ground. This is a fantasy story with you actually playing as a dragon, and they have one of the most boring politics.
And the cherry on top of the politics is that the responses never use any of the fantasy elements for something a bit more interesting. At no point does someone bring up the subject of doing something like providing berserk weapons or something. "Oh they will help our fighters for sure." "But wait! The side effects are really harsh, we can't do this!" Or maybe we should draft those who are magically inclined. "Yes! They will make our standing army much better!" "No, we can't! It should be their choice to fight for us or not!" I just made those two things up, but instead the game has you discussing about stuff like legalizing (fantasy) marijuana, national healthcare, and taxes. Even worse is the game seems to be unaware of the fantasy elements. No, liberal elf, I would not advise ignoring the talking skeleton who's best explanation of why he and his kind exists is because the gods have decided to give them a second chance at life. And I know the gods exists and can be angry because I have apparently crossed them off before. So if you want to legalize gay marriage, either explain why said skeletons are alive or pull out your religious documents and start debating the skeleton guy on his turf. Because you are talking to a dragon on a fly fortress, not some guy in a building painted all white.
Weird mix that is not that fun in the end.

I'm one of the unlucky people who did not play this game back when it came out. Back in the day, I didn't even know it existed, which is a shame. This game is truly something else. By combining a 3D platformer collectathon with graphic adventure elements in a psychedelic setting full of quirky characters, Psychonauts made its way into my heart faster than I could ever imagine.
The first thing I'd like to mention is something I never say about 3D platformers ever: the story is great. Most 3D platformers go for a simple, straight-forward story whose unique purpose is to motivate the gameplay, but not Psychonauts. The story starts with our main character, Rasputin, fleeing his abusive circus owning father's grasp to become a psychonaut (a psychic military agent) in a psychic training summer camp. After a motivating speech about how the camp allows people to be appreciated for talents that got them shunned in the outside world, we get ourselves a bed at the sleeping quarters and can unofficially join the lessons. The lessons involve entering the teachers' subconscious minds, consisting of crazy sceneries full of perils and challenges, in order to obtain precious merit badges. It doesn't take long before really strange things (even for psychic camp standards) start happening, and Razz decides to investigate them with his camp buddies.
The characters which support this story are all unique and cool. Each of them has a weird, quirky personality and their own set of psychic talents. The dialogs and interactions between characters are pretty well written, and some characters have really deep, emotional stories behind them that we need to figure out. The camp is a dynamic place, rife with opportunities to learn more about the characters, their lives and their camp experience. At the end of each lesson, the characters move to different places within the camp to do different things, allowing the player to discover more stuff about them.
The graphics are all around one of the game's strongest suits. Instead of trying for a boring realistic style, the game goes for a borderline acid trip of quirky character designs, stylistic sceneries and funny looking monsters and enemies. Every character's personality is very well reflected in their quirky design, not a single character looking too much like a regular human, but all of them looking very cool.
The sceneries tend to be crazy and awesome. The most "sane" scenery, so to say, is the camp itself, looking appropriately like a summer camp in the mountains, but with quite a few crazy things around that you wouldn't see in one. The sceneries inside people's minds tend to be way more bizarre, reflecting a person's thoughts, memories and personality in crazy ways.
The music that accompanies all that is also excellent, full of crazy satisfying tunes that always fit the mood the game's trying to reflect. At times, you'll have a crazy war theme, or a dance party theme, or many other themes, all of which are pretty fun and well composed.
Which brings us to gameplay. It is mostly pretty good, but not perfect. Let me get the bad stuff out of the way first: the platforming and camera controls are awkward and stiff, and the combat is pretty basic. Everything else is great, though.
Let me start by talking about the camp grounds themselves. They serve as kind of a "hub world" for different lessons and missions (as well as the place where the story related events take place) but they also contain tons of secrets and collectibles hidden all over them, rewarding exploration and curiosity every step of the way. The collectibles to be found in the camp grounds are things like psi cards and challenge markers (which you can gather to obtain new psychic skills and upgrade existing ones), arrowheads (to be used as currency at the main lodge) as well as scavenger hunt items. Obtaining them usually requires discovering where the object is and finding a way to get to it, but some involve more ingenuity, requiring you to make good use of your psychic powers (for instance, to become invisible and avoid startling an animal). There are also some graphic adventure elements in the camp, in which you need to use an item or skill at the right place (or person) in order to progress, either to discover a secret or to advance the plot itself.
The real challenge, however, lies inside people's minds, where the "levels" themselves take place. The levels follow a more linear style, full of enemies and obstacles, but that doesn't mean there aren't plenty of collectibles to discover and investigate. For instance, you may want to sort out people's "emotional baggage" (represented literally by crying purses and suitcases), or try to find all figments of imagination, or vacuum out some mental cobwebs, or discover some memories sealed away in mental vaults. While most of those tokens are easy to find due to the more linear nature of these levels when compared to the camp, some of them will require more exploration and ingenuity. In general, these subconscious levels are pretty fun and cool, and I'm betting Persona itself got some of its ideas from this game.
The kinds of enemies you find inside people's minds range from bizarre monsters that probably represent inner fears, to "censors", small men in suits that represents a person's mental filter, and a plethora of others, as well as the occasional boss. Battling is pretty straight forward, with some options given to you, like burning enemies with pyrokinesis, throwing objects at them with telekinesis, punching them, zapping them with psi waves, or becoming invisible and passing by them. The mechanics themselves are pretty primitive, with a simple lock on mechanic that allows you to shoot foes without a chance of missing, and slightly awkward controls that encourage mindless spamming at times due to a near inability to react quickly and dextrously to situations. The boss battles are usually frustrating, but they're hardly ever too long, thankfully. Now, just to clarify, the combat is not bad (as in, it didn't bore me nor anger me), it's just kind of mindless and spammy.
Overall, in spite of the flaws, I'd say this game has pretty good gameplay. Even the most awkward parts are still relatively fun, and the exploration element is strong and awesome. Also, every new ability you acquire tends to be really, really satisfying to use, especially when it allows you to get to a place you previously could not in order to get a formerly inaccessible collectible.
That about wraps it up. If you're looking for an awesomely quirky platformer full of personality that rewards exploration right from the get-go, has a good story and great characters, and really feels like an adventure, this is for you. Do keep in mind, however, that this game is over a decade old by now, meaning that some mechanical and technical issues are to be expected.

Music    7 of 10
