My net feelings about this game are 100% positive, but I can't really ignore some of the negatives coming out of the other reviews. I can tell you right off the bat to disregard anyone whose primary argument is go play Overwatch. None of the reviews I've read like that had anything useful to say, just biased hate and buyer's remorse.
At the time of writing this I have 32 hours in the game and have only been playing the PvE story content. This does mean I've repeated the missions many times over but I've honestly found them all to be quite replayable/enjoyable.  Including the prologue and the finale there's 8 of these missions that easily take 40-50 minutes each. You can unlock most things in the game through these missions with the only major exceptions being lore and achivements related to fighting other players in a PvP environment. Additionally, achievements that require match victories can actually be done by beating missions too.
I've found pretty much all the characters to be quite memorable without even having played them all; whether or not they're enjoyable is another matter. There's a couple whose personalities I just can't stand (Bouldur, Benedict) but beyond that their ability sets and histories are actually unique. Unlocking lore and skins/taunts for characters you enjoy is very satisfying and it simply adds to the game universe, and if you enjoy hoarding lore en masse then you'll easily get your money's worth out of this game several times over.
Now, for the negatives, such as optimization issues in the game. I can tell you right now if you have an AMD graphics card you'll want to disable PhysX as soon as possible and then just try to find settings that help your performance. While I don't know how bad performance is in the smaller multiplayer maps I do know that at least a couple of the PvE missions are suffering from some serious optimization issues in a couple sections of the mission, and sometimes regardless of the missions you're in you may just have some rampant effects crushing your fps as the game in general doesn't seem to play  nicely with AMD GPUs. Don't get too discouraged though, bout 95% of my experience has been perfectly smooth gameplay, but the 5% is pretty noticeable when your frames are crippled.
I've heard a lot of people complaining about PvP matchmaking being imbalanced and some frustrations with certain Battleborn being overpowered. I think the offenders were nerfed recently, but I can't speak much on this as I have yet to try versus. That being said, I got this game to escape from the expectations of hardcore competitive play that I usually expect to see in games like League of Legends. It could be that its imbalanced enough to not be fun, but when I get on to play this game I get on to play a specific character because I enjoy their abilities and their personality. I've heard some pretty funny statements and interactions come out the few times I've had my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me in the PvE missions, so my outlook is I look forward to hearing the full compliment of my character's voice lines when I start playing PvP. I'm just looking to have some casual fun and I think this game is in a prime position to allow just that without riding the esports hype train that other games do.
Lastly it seems Gearbox just gets a lot of hate in general. I'll be honest, I don't know♥♥♥♥♥♥about this or why this is. I've absolutely loved the Borderlands series and I pre-ordered the deluxe edition of this game with no regrets. I know some major complaints are the $20 off sale in the 2K store that occurred 2 weeks after the game released, but I imagine that was mostly to try to compete with Overwatch's release. A number of players feel ripped off because they payed for it at full price, and while I can appreciate the sentiment, I also feel those players had no business buying the game in the first place. When I spend money on a game, when I pre-ordered Battleborn, I did so with the intention of not giving two ♥♥♥♥♥ if it went on sale the next day. I wanted to spend that money on the game to support its developers in addition to getting access to the most content because I think its worth it. Objectively anyone could argue whether or not its worth the value, I've penny pinched on plenty of games by waiting for sales, but when I find a game that really looks fun and I have the money I will pay full price and more for it. And I still think Battleborn is worth that full price, there's a fair bit of DLC that seems to be planned for release down the road that can be secured with the deluxe edition or buy the season pass separately.
Beyond these points I can't argue much else. Most of the other negative reviews out there are valid (except if they're calling it dead already, that's just unfair) and if they turn you off from the game then don't spend the money on it. I think, like borderlands, this is a game that's only going to get better with time as more content becomes available. I look forward to seeing where the story goes and what future of the games PvP content is, and even if it suffers at present I definitely seeing it experiencing several population spikes as future content is released and sales for the game become available through Steam.
Also if you do nothing else there's a pretty badass animation that occurs right before the prologue mission in the game. Look it up on youtube "Battleborn Prologue Animation." It got me and friends super hype to play the game and on its own the animation is pretty great.

Battleborn was almost a sort of impulse buy for me.  I enjoyed the lore that the Borderlands games set up, despite not playing them, and while I wanted to save money by buying the cheaper Borderlands games, it was at that very moment that Battleborn was released.  I found some people who were enjoying the game, and the promise of PVE was what sold it for me, hands down.  Other games such as Team Fortress 2 tend to require you to have many, many people to play with, with either queues or servers that have random, ever changing rules.  Even the PVE in those games tend to require upwards of 5-7 people to complete, especially for those who were just playing to have fun.
As such, Battleborn quickly became a favorite for me.  I play PVP when I'm in a team of three or four friends, and when I'm playing alone, I queue up for PVE.  On normal difficulty in PVE, I can group up with only one or two random people, and even without communication, I've learned how each map works enough to get through without too much trouble.  It's become incredibly fun for me, despite me only having an hour or two a day to play on weekdays.  The PVE stories might not be the most amazing novels in the world, but Gearbox has dialed back the memes and brought us a slightly darker story that seems lighter from the fact that every character is a little crazy fun in their own way.  Every one of the 25 characters has two or three dimensions to them, usually displayed through their "lore" that is unlocked mostly through just playing the game.  Some are harder to get than others, but it is really much fun to do them as a goal to work towards as you play, rather than focusing solely on collecting them as quickly as possible.
There are three different PVP modes to play, and while the "Incursion", that is, the MOBA style mode, is the most popular, there are two others that can be played as well.  There's the "Capture" mode that is similar to more WoW/FF14 style PVP, that is, holding land and defending it from attackers.  Then there's Meltdown, which I've found to be fairly unique among Multiplayer PVP.  It's all about destroying your enemy's LoL-style minion waves while protecting your own.  The more robot minions you save (and then subsequently sacrifice to robot junkyard god Minrec) the faster you win.  It's really fast paced and tons of fun, if not a little crazy and hard to do without proper communication.
While there's lots of fun things to do and the replayability is high (with both PVP and PVE to keep you occupied), there's always bad things to every game.  Despite the game touting 25 characters that don't cost anything, only about 7 are available straight out the gate, and the characters you play in the prologue aren't even part of this initial team.  The game claims that there's a character for every type of player, but if you prefer to be a tanky melee character, you're stuck playing a tanky ranged or squishy melee until the character you need opens up to you.  Technically this isn't so bad; just playing through the entire PVE storyline should net you enough characters to find your niche pretty well, if not completely so.  It only took me about a week to unlock all but six characters, and my two mains are already among them.
Overall, I find that Battleborn is money well spent, even with the retail price tag.  If you're a little stingy compared to me (Who is probably not going to buy another game at all this year), then just wait until a sale!  Please try this game out; saving stars have never been more tense or more hysterical!

There are level 100 player who still do not play objectives in the game or cannot play with specific battleborns. The only problems with this is that people already give up when they see a high rank level in the enemy team. This is the problem. Not the matchmaking. Gearbox should make the command ranks invisible. It does not matter for the matchmaking or the matches. Even with a command level of 100 it may be my first time playing a battleborn or even with command level 5 this might be a battleborn I feel familiar with, because it uses game mechanics I prefer in other games as well.
That being said, what draws me to Battleborn mostly? I am a huge Dawngate fan. Yes, that is the MOBA that was killed by EA, because it did not make enough money in the Beta (sic!). Battleborn feels a little like it to me. Some of it’s modes got MOBA elements, but first and foremost: Battleborn has got awesome and unique character background and lore.
Battleborn got me immersed into the universe and it does it all within the game. I do not have to rely on out of game ressources. Battleborn has single player campagin which narrates the story and the setting. All characters got lore challenges to unlock tidbits of background on them. This feels more natural and more satisfying to me than in other games. Yet they also have a comic on their website which made me squeal, because Dawngate had an extra comic series as well. So it reminds me a lot of it.
While playing Battleborn everything in the game feels like I get to play the lore as well. For Battleborn the setting fits with all the things you are playing in game. All those characters from different factions are even supposed to fight sometimes on the own team. So all the bickering and remarks in game feel natural. This is why the immersion in Battleborn works so well. Battleborn hit me on the spot of immersion way better because of all this.
I like how the game merges the lore and the game modes. This is done pretty well and I love this postmodern apocalypse. It is rich with self-conscious irony and there are so many things which make me chuckle and after about 40 hours of gameplay I still discover some minor things which make me smile. This game feels like there was put a lot of heart and soul into it and I appreciate it for exactly this. This is a game which wants to be fun and does not take itself to serious in some moments, but in other immerses you into a pretty fun apocalypse with interesting characters.
And what about the combat? It is fun. I like FPS and this game does it pretty well. Each character feels so different to the point that I still do not know how to play some of them. This is one of the challenges of the game and I like that it takes this risk. You have to invest some time to learn those characters and some of them are not easy. Although you can pick some easier characters as well. But I have to admit that those are the least interesting to me. There is so much depth hidden in all the helix options, in the gear system and all those buildables.
It is not an easy game to get into, but once you give it a chance and invest that first few hours it is so rewarding and fun - at least to me.

An incredibly fun and unique game. I've truly enjoyed playing it, and will continue to keep playing. It gets far more criticism than it deserves.
Cons:
- Optimization. Unfortunately, you are going to need newer hardware to play this game. Gearbox has stated that they are working on this.
- On-screen effects. It can be a little disorienting at times. However, it's not nearly as bad once you get used to it. Gearbox has stated that they are working on this.
- Lack of variety in campaign. I do find the story fun in multiplayer, but it could certainly use more variety. Single player is a little boring for sure.
- Player numbers. *THIS IS AN ISSUE IF YOU ARE OUTSIDE OF THE US OR EU* As of right now (May 29th), there are thousands of people playing. I live in the US, and I've never had an issue finding a match or teammates for the campaign. Match queues have been very quick.
- No good tutorial for multiplayer in the game. If you want to be competent in multiplayer, you'll have to do a little research. Luckily, the game does allow you to practice against teams of bots. I highly recommend practice before jumping into online matches.
Neutral:
- It's a complex game. Make no mistake, this is a MOBA (most multiplayer modes at least). If you go into it playing team deathmatch, you are going to have a bad time. That being said, it's deep and rewarding once you know the rules. It also manages to be fast paced and very fun. I personally love this aspect of the game.
- Grindy. If you want lots of gear, expect to play the campaign a lot. You also have to level up to unlock many of the various characters in the game. Some may love it, others hate it.
- It's new. There are some balance issues and bugs. Some characters are strong and a few are weak. This is to be expected, and gearbox releases new patches (hotfixes) weekly. Right now, I feel that the balance is actually pretty decent.
Pros:
- Fun. Battleborn is a game that doesn't take itself that seriously. You won't find a long-winded ultra-tense MOBA here. While the game is deep, it still manages to be hectic and super fun. It's a rare combination.
- Character design. The characters in this game are awesome. I've played most of them, and they all have unique and interesting skill sets. Whatever playstyle you enjoy, you'll find a character that suits you.
- New content and frequent updates. Gearbox devs are active in the community and listen to feedback. At this time, there are at least four new characters coming in future updates. One has already arrived (Alani).
- Unique. Battleborn's charm and gameplay are refreshing. I am not a fan of MOBAs in general. However, I feel that Battleborn hits the right mix of FPS and MOBA elements. I loved Monday Night Combat. This game scratches that itch.
- Graphics. The environments in the game look great.
- Multiplayer. So far, I've had a lot of fun in multiplayer. You get occassional quitters (early surrender) and toxic players, but that is any multiplayer game.
Overall:
I highly recommend it. Check out some Youtube videos or streamers on Twitch. If it looks like fun, buy it! Just make sure you have a good enough machine to run it on.

What would you sell your soul for? That's the question posed to Faust, the protagonist of Soul Gambler. If you're looking for a game with a fair amount of replay value, an interesting story, and a good comicbook art style, I highly recommend this game. For the price asked, you'll absolutely get your money's worth.

I was pretty disappointed with Soul Gambler. It looks impressive up front--it has a nice graphical style, a neat concept, and throws a stat screen at you to make you feel like it'll have some RPGish elements. But like the worst of David Cage or Telltale, what ends up happening is a strictly railroaded plot where very few decisions have any major impact beyond, at most, a stat going up or down. The ending/s is based on a single ending choice combined, possibly, with a single stat value. Outside of that, there's little variation from scene to scene, with major story beats happening no matter how hard you try to derail the plot to something else. Add to that the dull, sometimes poorly translated narration and dialogue and the fact that there's no dialogue-skip option for subsequent playthroughs, and it adds up to a pretty disappointed visual novel experience.

Her Story is an experience far away from the mean, presenting a 90s OS computer screen with a limited program full of clips of a woman talking about the disappearance and possible murder of her husband. With a few simple design rules it creates a brilliant and intricate nonlinear narrative that branches in whatever direction strikes you. Whatever the woman says you may search to dive deeper and see just what more she has to offer on the subject.
This procedure simulates the detective role more realistically than I have ever felt in a video game. I felt like a real sleuth with some of my techniques, noting inconsistencies and ever-so-slight details that made me reconsider previously understood information.

Backstory:
I grew up playing strategy games such as Command & Conquer and Starcraft, but after a while I grew tired of the arcade-y gather resources, build a base, spam a unit, upgrade, repeat archetype. I came to want a game with some more strategy than spamming a good unit. So, I told my friends the kind of game I was thinking, no base building, units that don't have unlimited fuel and ammo, and more sophisticated combat than 'this does more damage than this' and they said, "you mean Wargame?" Thus, I bought the game.
Getting into the Game:
First off, there is the singleplayer, which is basically skirmishes with the nigh mindless AI. It's not much, even with a campaign of sorts, but it isn't a bad place to get used to the game and test things like new decks before you start playing multiplayer as the AI does know how to defend itself and keep the pressure on you. Next up is the multiplayer; unfortunately, with as few players as this game often has, most players will be either very good pros who've been playing this game a long time or almost completely new players to the game giving it a test. So, chances are unless you find someone willing to help you (whom I have seen a lot of; the community is typically fairly friendly), you'll have a lot of games were your allies can't pull their weight or your enemies have super-sneaky infantry and fire-support for them in every bush you don't want them to, making getting used to the game in multiplayer a difficult but not insurmountable challenge for the unseasoned.
Gameplay:
The first thing that sets Wargame apart from most RTS games is the realistic attempt at mechanics.  Units are often very specialized for countering certain other units, and there are often counters for those units. I could go into great depths on the handling of the units and the importance of anti-armor ability, high-explosives, range, accuracy, stealth, supply vehicles, command vehicles, capturing sectors, radar AA, anti-radar planes, bombers, fighters, helicopters, manpad infantry, anti-tank guided missiles, artillery, recon, maintaining a good screen against enemy attack, and so on, but that belongs in a manual. For now, I'll leave it at large numbers of units not being a good stratagy, because an intelligent enemy can simply pick your guys off out of range and sight with ease. Positioning, recon, and being ready to kill whatever comes your way are typically what win the game.
Decks:
The replacement of base building and research in contemporary games is the building of decks. You can create a deck in the deck editor to your liking (balanced approaches typically work best, but unique strategies have their place) and use it in any match that isn't campaign, and start with every unit you will be able to use that match at your disposal, only limited by the deployment points gained from capturing sectors with command vehicles. Do not be discouraged by the sheer choice of units: you can limit your selection by country, date, and general combat philosophy (mechanized, motorized, marine, airborne, armored, etc.)
Vs. Red Dragon
Of due note is this game's sequel, Red Dragon. If you find the need for a lot of variety and a large playerbase, you might want Red Dragon instead. However, Red Dragon, while it adds more content, is broken in gameplay compared to Airland Battle. Simply put, Red Dragon is what happens when you put late 1990s top-shelf equipment in a game modelling the late 1980s; it isn't a perfect fit, and game balancing suffers.
Pros
+Solid gameplay. Nations are well balanced, while still being diverse in technologic advancement
+Sweden. Sweden, a neutral, often forgotten country in warfare, has a lot of great strengths and perplexing weaknesses
+Intelligence, preparation, and careful management over nigh-mindless spamming. Chance for good, in-depth strategy to develope over what often becomes stack-wiping battles
+Diversity. Plenty of ways to win and get a sneaky one-up on your enemy
Cons
+Aging graphics. Not bad by any means, but certainly not the shiniest toy on the block
+Few people. Everyone pretty much has no idea what they're doing or knows the game like the back of their hand

Invisible walls: the game
There's some fun to be had here, especially in multiplayer, but I can only recommend this one for a bargain price. The graphics are rather pretty and the game runs well on older PCs too but the actual game contained in the engine isn't that interesting. Level design is incredibly linear and punishes every urge to explore with plenty of invisible walls and telescope-vision enemies, that often spot you from a huge distance if you stray from the tiny path offered by the developers. The sniping itself is a lot of fun at times and adjustable to your comfort level, despite the AI but regular gunplay which unfortunately occurs too is a drag and discourages further playing.
The story is of little help to keep you invested - even by the low standards of military shooters it's unengaging and keeps jumping back and forth between "characters" which I set in quotation marks because we never learn anything about the characters we are playing. I don't think I can even recall the name of the main character. Your main incentive as mr. soldier man is the voice in your head telling you to pop heads of south american baddies and after a while you kind of feel sympathy for the guys, since you, as the good guy, just show up with no authority, wreck their stuff and kill all their friends. It's somewhat feasible they might be the bad guys and it doesn't reach as far into the uncomfortable territory of the hyper-jingoistic splinter cell games but the story only has some shred of redeeming value if at the end it turns out you were part of a psychological experiment to determine how far you'd go if an authority figure tells you to.
In conclusion, Sniper: Ghost Warrior isn't deep enough as a stealth game and not fluid enough as an fps, marred by restrictive level design and a tedious single player campaign, however the multiplayer can be incredibly fun if you're not confronted by expert players. There aren't that many maps and modes but I enjoyed it more than any other generic fps in recent memory. There's a lot of room for improvement and the game is not a trainwreck by any means, but still I can't recommend it, unless you love multiplayer and you can get it really cheap.

I think most of the negative reviews come from bad experiences pre- and early launch. A lot of the bugs and issues have been fixed now, so I can definetely recommend this game. It may not be the best fishing simulator, but it is still an enjoyable game.
A few positive points:
- An in-game shop with a very extensive set of possibilities for your tackle boxes: reels, rods, lines, hooks, baits...
- Several fish species: multiple carp species, catfish, bream, roach...
- different bed types: silt, gravel and weed. You have to keep this in mind when choosing your hooks and bait.
- Enjoyable and relaxing ambient sound.
- The thrill to keep fishing to get to the top of the leaderboards, and/or set a personal best. There's also your profile with statistics and fish species and bosses you have already/not caught. Each lake has its own unique bosses.
- There are also online tournaments, tutorials, AI competitions and minigames which all reward in-game currency and xp.
Negative points:
- A few graphical bugs.
- The time to wait for a fish to bite is sometimes too long.
- Some players find casting too hard. I find it easy (after a bit of practice).
In general this is a very good game, but for some people this may be too expensive because you can get bored soon.

Once upon a time, I decided to recommend this game over the sequel. After spending 600 hours playing PD2, I can safely say that it is WAY better than PDTH. There's no reason to even own this game anymore, aside from the soundtrack. The heists from PDTH were even ported to the second game. All you're left with here is an old game with barely any players.
For this review, I'll be talking about the more important things in the game, and I will not be going in depth when it comes to gameplay mechanics such as the leveling system and gunplay, since them being good or bad is subjective and a matter of personal opinion.
I'll leave a TL;DR right here, but I would seriously recommend you read the entire review.
TL;DR:
All you'll ever find are either noobs that know NOTHING about the game, joining Overkill lobbies thinking they can win, or an Eastern-European player that uses the entire team as bait, so he can get away and win on his own. There is no teamwork in this game. Every game will take one of those routes. You either fail because the team was being brought down by multiple people, or you (and maybe even your other 2 teammates) spend more than half of the match in custody because the tryhard, M308 using "pro", left everyone to die and wondered off on his own.
The AI in the series is notorious for being terrible. I can confirm that's the case. The bots tend to stay in the open, only to get lit up by hordes of police officers. When one of them goes down, the other tries to help him and ends up dying as well. This is managable on the lower difficulties, but playing on Overkill and above with bots is the worst thing you can do.
Unlike PD2, this game does not have any kind of boosts or bonuses for the AI, essentially making them useless for solo.
The balancing in this game is leagues above PD2's, but that is to be expected from a game that only has 13 weapons total. Most of the time, you won't even use the other 10, since pretty much the only Overkill and Overkill 145+ viable weapons are the M308, Bronco, and GL40. You CAN use the other weapons, but you'll most likely be told to change them, or just downright kicked from the match.
I'll talk about the ingame items available to the player. The deployables consist of the Doctor Bag, Ammo Bag, Sentry Gun, and Trip Mines. They all serve a purpose, but the mines and sentry aren't that good on higher difficulties. The sentry is just a distraction. The trip mines aren't that useful unless you plan on camping out somewhere, but everything they do, a coordinated team can do it better.
There are 4 pieces of equipment available to the player.
The top three are useless. Extra ammo is the only thing you'll ever use, so there goes that. Now let's move on to the Crew Bonuses.
Six of those bonuses are useless. The only ones that are worth using are Big Game Hunters and Agressor, since you get a damage bonus and extra ammo for your team. Coordinated teams tend to run 2 BGH's and 2 Agressors so everyone in the crew gets the same bonus, since the bonus only applies to your teammates and not to you.
There are 8 heists in this game. Two of them are from the Wolf Pack DLC, those being Counterfeit and Undercover. The missions in the game range from your typical loud and exiciting bank robbery, to sneaking around a skyscraper avoiding guards and gunfire, and even going as far as stealing a virus from Mercy Hospital. The heists in this game are great. The atmosphere, and the overall design of the maps is amazing.
The performance in this game is way better than PD2's since the game is older, even on low end computers. If your PC has trouble running this game, I'd recommend this guide to make it work:
On high end computers, everything should be flawless.
The voice acting in this game is GREAT. The way the crew talks to each other really gives you a feeling that they're in sync, like true professionals. The playable character are also great. You got Dallas, Hoxton, Chains, and Wolf. They're all special in their own ways, although Chains could have been a bit better, especially with the voice acting. One of the best things this game has to offer, is the voice acting and the characters.
Unfortunately, great voice acting and likeable characters isn't everything. The game has too many flaws for me to recommend it, the maps (with the exception of No Mercy) are in the sequel, and PD2 is overall the better game. If this wasn't the case, there wouldn't be many people playing it. RAID WW2 tried to go back to the roots, by taking a lot from PDTH. Needless to say that the game failed. I really tried to enjoy this game, but I couldn't bring myself to spend 500 hours like I did with the sequel. If you're sure that you want the game, I suggest picking it up during a sale. And try to get someone to play with you, so you don't have to deal with cancerous players and newbies.

Witch It Review
TL:DR Witch it offers a unique twist on the Prop Hunt genre that was popularized due to the G-Mod game mode. Absolutely a blast with friends and even if you don’t have some, finding people to play with shouldn’t be that hard.
A more In-depth review:
Witch it is a game of hide and seek in a similar vein to the Prop hunt game mode found in G-mod. While being an early access game (as of writing this review) it offers a fair amount of polish and game play that is accessible and extremely fun to play.
A round of “Witch It” involves the server being split into 2 teams; Hunters and Witches. Witches Hide, and Hunters…hunt. Both sides have access to 2 broad categories of powers to aid them; Movement and a special tool or spell. Witches start off the round by finding a prop to transform or possess while the hunters are locked inside of a room for a set time while this is going on.
As mentioned earlier each side has access to various abilities where up to 2 may be chosen to be used from a pool of so far 5 abilities at the beginning of the round. Such abilities include a Witch detecting Chicken, yeah you heard me- the hunter has a badass chicken that can detect witches. Witches possess abilities that can confuse or trick a hunter such as the ability to control a decoy prop.
Victory is determined like any other game of hide and seek, if every witch is neutralized then Hunters win, and of course if even one Witch survives the Witches win.
Content wise the game features customizable aesthetics for each side, over 200 props to disguise as and half a dozen maps or so  to play on as of this moment. While no game play is locked off, there is an in game purchase (no doubt more to come) where you can get a costume set for the witch. I would like to add that this isn’t actually very intrusive at all and you won’t see it plastered on the splash screen or main menu begging you to buy it, it’s clearly an optional thing should you want to show more support to the devs; Most aesthetics can be unlocked by playing the game and leveling up (GOOD ON YOU DEVS!).
In terms of graphics it’s  very pixel like in appearance but all the maps have a charm and theme to them that I quite enjoy them, all feeling quite unique as well. As an early access title it also runs great I’m pushing above 120 FPS on max settings; but my rig isn’t a slouch either. I wouldn’t see an issue on older or less capable hardware.
I’ve only every encountered one bug in Witch I wasn’t able to use my abilities (pun whole heartedly intended).
The only glaring weakness to this game is that it has a bit of a small player base, and it is multiplayer only. With that being said I have had no trouble finding full or mostly full servers (NA region atleast) and with it being featured on the steam 2017 winter sale with a price of $11 CAD, its player base can only grow.
To the Devs if you’re reading this:
I absolutely adore this game and wish you all the best with your continued development. Consider more map variety/themes and adding some more abilities would be very fun and appreciated.

So, you think you fix the world? In this game, Planet Earth is a puzzle (that you're probably not going to be able to solve first time!)
Different regions of the world have varying virtues and vices. Stable regions won’t mind having their long-term energy consumption tampered with, but you will need to balance this out with short-term environmental solutions to keep the sceptics happy. Or perhaps you would rather make the Earth uninhabitable? Well there is an unlockable scenario where you can do just that!
What keeps bringing me back to this game is the tiny margin for error. Perhaps you’ll lose control over a region a few turns before your time is up, causing it to fart out just enough toxic gas to lose the game. So you go back to your last save and make a special effort to keep that region happy.
You'll either love or hate this game. But if you're a fan of thinking games like Civilisation, Fate of the World is for you, too.

Objectively this game has the basics of a good pvp moba, but it seems that Gearbox doesn't quite understand how to balance this type of game. Matchmaking regularly pair up low level players with players well over lvl 50. Not only does this create an unbalanced choice of characters, some of which are locked away behind level capped doors, but it also allows the higher level players to access better upgrades that lower level players can't hope to obtain. The games start off with everyone knowing full well the outcome. This leads to match dodging the likes of which I have never seen. Players will abandon a team without a second though if they see anyone below level 40. It's next to impossible to get a match going. In the off chance that you do get in a match, you get to sit through an inevitable 20 minutes slog as the opposing team increases their power gap to the point where one opponent can't engage an entire team by himself and win.
Add on a incredibly dull story mode which consists of killing waves of enemies while listening to some witty dialogue and you have Battleborn. This game is terrible for anyone who hasn't been playing religiously since launch day. I like Gearbox titles, but this is a huge letdown.

It is a good game...when playing campaign but after that it really stops there. The narratives, dialogues and the style of it is all good. However the multiplayer is very poor. The matchmaking is always uneven, the maps are the same and Echelon hardly see any play.
The melee characters are quite favored here, they have the dmg and the hp at the same time as they recieve the killing blow quite often. Gearbox seems to just released this as to have something compete with Overwatch or/and trying to experiment on a PvP that might result in a PvP varient for upcoming Borderlands 3. I want to like this game because Gearbox gave me hours of fun on Borderlands 2, but I just can't.
Did I stress enough about how poor the matchmaking is?

Update:
While updates to Battleborn did slightly improve performance, it wasn't until I upgraded to a GTX 1060 before I could actually enjoy playing the game. Now the game runs fine with everything maxed out at 1080p (steady 50 fps with VSYNC on), but it still doesn't look that great and the cutscenes and animations still feel like they're from an indie game. Co-op missions are good fun with a friend, but the game has failed to get me hooked on any level. It feels like all of this has already been done better before, which is why I still can't give this game a recommendation. If you're looking for a fun single player or co-op experience, try Borderlands 2 instead if you already haven't. If you're looking for team based fps action with MOBA elements, Overwatch is the better choice. Battleborn of course offers both aspects in one package and isn't really a bad game as such, so wait for a decent sale and get it with a group of friends and it might just be worth it.

Just finished playing the prologue and already a lot of the game screams "unfinished":
-The installer tried to install an older .NET onto my computer and gave all sorts of warnings when it finally realized that it couldn't replace the current version with an older one.
-The game started in 640x480 resolution, which gave a pretty hideous first impression.
-Navigating the menus was impossible with the mouse when running the game for the first time. Clicking on menu options only worked sporadically and often the option below or above the one that the pointer was over would be selected.
-Alt-tabbing to and from the game doesn't work. I alt-tabbed to the desktop but found myself unable to alt-tab back into the game. Since the game was still running somewhere in the background, I couldn't restart the game so instead had to reastart the whole computer.
-The game is not properly optimized. I'm running the game on 1176x664 with everything set as low as it goes, and still I'm constantly dipping below 20 fps whenever there are enemies on screen. I know my GPU is a big bottleneck on my system, but I can run Borderlands 2 and Killing Floor 2 at 1080p and higher settings with higher fps. Both look a lot better than Battleborn and both are easily playable. While I'm not very picky when it comes to fps values, Battleborn just feels too sluggish to be any fun.
-The cartoon cut scenes occasionally look like they're from a cheap children's cartoon ie. poorly animated and drawn. Furthermore, you can't skip them.
So, the first impression is that the game is still unfinished and that's even before I've had the chance to experience how well the characters are balanced and how good the content is. Needless to say, I was expecting a lot more from Gearbox. Not recommended at its current state.

-16 GB of RAM
-Samsung 850 EVO SSD 500 GB
-Windows 8.1
-NVIDIA GTX 650 1 GB (I know)
I'm upgrading my GPU in the near future, which should take care of the fps issue. Hopefully Gearbox has ironed out some of the other wrinkles by then. In the meantimen, I'm tempted to give Overwatch a chance...

Hitman 2: Silent Assassin is the second game in the Hitman series. It follows the journey of a contract killer named 47 as he travels around the world, eliminating his target in order to save one of his few friends.
Hitman 2 is one of the few game that manage to do a disguise-based stealth right, with tons of disguises you are able to use all over the game. However, that does not make the game easier, as the AI in this game are capable of seeing through your disguise if you even act one bit suspicious (and some of them are even capable of seeing it from far away, as the ninja's from the Japan level can attest. Dem Psychic ninja). This makes sure that the game can be intense as well as satisfying when you do manage to beat the level with Silent Assassin rating.
This game also allows one to take multiple way to eliminate 47's targets. From disguising his way to the target, or going in with guns blazing high, there will be many ways one can do in this game, ensuring its replayability value.

For a quick version of this review:
Battleborn is a very deep and strategic game including PvP with in-match character growth via their helix, long times to kill, mechanics that punish death, and a focus on PvE and tower defense amide the PvP.
The PvE includes 8 missions that contain a mix of escort, protect the objective, and 'raid' (as in enemies to mini-boss to enemies to boss) mechanics.
In public match making for PvE people vote on a random selection of four missions.
There is progression system that includes unlocking characters and extra options on their helix tree.
The five characters being added in the future and all future PvP related material can be accessed for free (but if you own the season pass you just skip the step of unlocking the characters).
The major issues with this game are that it has optimization issues and when you first start out and the system doesn't have any data on you, you may end up in some one-sided matches.
Personally I really like the game and feel like I got my full 60 dollars worth.
Now for some extra details for those still reading:
I definitely recommend this game, but at the same time I do not recommend it to everyone. In the PvP, this is not a typical team based FPS, and whatever you have learned in other FPS likely will not carry over into this game. It definitely has a learning curve, even for somebody like me who had a taste of it before buying during the open beta. As a team based FPS with MOBA inspired elements (the game is not a full MOBA itself) Battleborn is all about choosing your battles, staying with team mates, avoiding death at all costs (death is punished in this game with increasingly longer respawn timers), and always remaining aware of the AI controlled minions (ignore these little guys and you will lose every game even if have been steam rolling the enemy team in kills).
The game comes with both a PvP mode and a PvE campaign. For me personally this is very nice because if I get tired of competitive PvP matches, I just switch over to the PvE and have fun blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up for a while (while making sure to keep an eye on the objectives of course, these missions to have some challenge to them).
The missions of the PvP are not made to be played in a specific order besides doing the first 7 before the final mission against Rendain (In normal difficulty this is a seperate mission, but in advanced it gets mixed into the usual voting selection mentioned above) and as a result they do not have an over arching story but rather just the story of the mission itself.
Also I should mention that the PvE missions are VERY full of Gearbox style humor, so just be prepared for that. They basically went full on silly and ridiculous for the writing on this one.
While some people are turned off by progression systems, I personally find them a fun little bit of extra challenge, but I will say that for any worrying, unlocking the characters is not hard at all. And in case you do somehow have trouble, every character has two methods they can be unlocked by, the second being profile level. So even the characters who can be unlock by completely the advanced story mode and such can alternatively just be unlocked by inceasing your command rank which happens no matter what you play.
The progression system, aside from unlocking characters, is also involved in unlocking "mutations" for each character's helix tree. All this means is that as you play a character, you unlock extra options to pick from as you level your character up each game (at the start of every PvE or PvP match you are at level 1). These mutations are often very useful, but they often won't redefine how you play a character but instead just give you another very useful option when playing. Also there will still likely be plenty of situations where you will choose one of the original two choices rather than the new mutation.
Another important topic to touch on is the gear system. As you play you will eventually begin to collect gear which can be activated in matches with the in-match currency of shards. This gear will provide stat bonuses to your character, and later legendary quality gear can even give special unique effects. However the power of a gear piece is always balanced by the number of shards you must gather and then spend in order to activate it. In fact, walking into PvP with a loadout full of three legendary pieces of gear is often a very bad idea because you likely won't be able to collect enough shards before the match ends to even activate all of them (additionally you will likely also avoid using the buildables situated throughout each map which tend to be very important to victory). Additionally, it is impossible to activate pricier gear right off the bat in PvP because giant shards don't spawn until a few minutes in (and even then you have the enemy team to compete with when it comes to breaking and gathering them).
I do feel like I should touch on some issues you have likely seen in other reviews and let you know which ones are no longer an issue as of the time of this review. First of all, the incursion mode exploit involving snipers on the map Overgrowth is no more. Second, the 5 minute prologue cutscene can be skipped if you do not wish to watch it. Third, after her third wave of nerfs, Galilea is no longer overpowered and can no longer 1v1 everyone and win (and in case you did not hear Ambra ceased being a problem quite some ago).
I will admit that the game can certainly still use more optimization, though they are gradually working on and improving that. And finally the match making is not completely unbalanced, though when you are first starting out and the system does not have any data on you, yes it can tend to put you in somewhat onesided matches. But I can personally say that this definitely changes once you have a collection of matches completed, as I very rarely find myself in matches that feel one-sided in terms of player skill.

Honestly, the only major flaw in Battleborn is its release timing. Overwatch is sucking out all the air in the room right now, with its hype, marketing, and accessibility. Because of this, people are looking for ways to validate Battleborn's not doing well that aren't simply "Overwatch", so they're finding and over-emphasizing Battleborn's flaws.
I can' almost guarantee that if Battleborn were released at any other time, it would have immediately done better and the general consensus about the game would be more positive.
TL;DR: Don't buy into the anti-hype! Battleborn is excelent and lively! And this is coming from someone who also loves Overwatch to death, so no bias here. The two games are different enough to exist in the same space, but superficially similar enough to be competing for the same people's attention. I can see Battleborn growing and growing over time as the space opens up a bit.

Exceedingly clever "discovery" game that is just the right amount of creepy. As I put together what happened I found myself wondering exactly how deep the rabbit hole goes (and occasionally wondering what is WRONG with these people). It is a brief game -- I'd concluded the story probably 3 hours in. The additional 2 hours were spent milking every piece of info out of the game I could before I wandered off into spoiler territory.
In terms of 'gameplay' it is basically a game of trying to use a limited search engine to discover data (in the form of video clips). There isn't much to it besides that, other than keeping track of info (like other players I found a pen and a bit of paper handy - used it to keep track of search terms that came to mind watching the videos), and reading between the lines with the 'evidence' presented in the videos.
I would qualify it as a game as there is a challenge (thinking of the right search terms, using the search engine correctly (make sure to carefully read the readme-s in game) and a goal (uncovering all of the information, figuring out as much of the story as is possible). But it is very, very story/discovery heavy.
Highly recommended.

I don't consider this to be a "throwback" or "homage" or anything of that kind. Her Story is a completely new, unique and untapped method of interactive storytelling that I found absolutely fascinating. This title is definitely not for everyone, but it has been a long time (if ever) that I have been to engrossed in a story. By its very nature Her Story makes you care about what is happening. Caring about, understanding and absorbing the story IS the gameplay since it is the only way to progress. I found this an incredible breath of fresh air after decades of "hint" buttons superfluous story that may as well be ignored.
This title, with such minimalist pseudo-gameplay has, in my opinion, been the first to chart new territory of storytelling in an interactive medium since Spec Ops: The Line and Telltale's The Walking Dead, both back in 2012. And where those titles hesitantly tease and hint at new territory, this one dives into it face first to either sink or swim.

A good game.
It could have been great, if not for some of the control designs (made with consoles in mind) and the plethoria of technical issues. Review is based on one very recent light-side playthrough (game crashes far too often to warrant a fun second playthrough), what with the star wars hype and the new movie and all.
Story is quite good (even though i did not really like the major plot twist) and has a lot of typical Star Wars settings, minus the family drama from the movies. Game is set at the height of the galactic republic, a long time before the events of the movies, where Jedis are more common. You get to visit and explore different planets, and you can travel from one to the next as you see fit once you get your own means of transport after the first planet.
Dialogues are quite well written, but sometimes it is not so obvious which dialogue options mean light side, dark side is very obvious most of the time tho. And the voice acting is absolutely top notch for the main companions.
Graphics are very dated, as you would expect from a game released in 2003, but they are still far from eye-cancer inducing. There are a few mini games (swoop racing, card playing, manning turret on your ship) that offer a change of pace, and there are some puzzles that even require some basic cognitive skills to solve. And, of course, there is the choice of dark side or light side, and it is possible to go balanced too (sadly there only is dark side/light side restricted gear, no grey jedi gear). Also the choice does not really lock you out of the force powers from the opposite spectrum, it just makes them more expensive to cast.
Difficulty: if you plan your character ahead (game uses a d20 system very much like AD&D), the game is very easy on "normal".
So far, so fun, sadly there are some things that detriment from the experience this game could have been:
Technical issues:
Oh my. This game requires a small amount of tinkering with the settings to even get it to start without crashing, and even then it likes to crash A LOT upon saving, corrupting the savegame. I used flawless widescreen to get the resolution up to todays standards, and that may have contributed to game stability issues.
Video sequences are another possible source of crashes, and while some people claim disabling videos does not take away from the gameplay experience, in my opinion it very decidedly does.
Bugs:
There is a chance for your character to be unable to move after almost any action like fighting or looting (can be worked around by saving and loading again). Super annoying.
You can lock yourself out of quests, especially companion quests, unless you do them in a specific order.
If you do not cancel out of video sequences while flying from one planet to another, the game will fail to capture your mouse at all from then on, and the only possible course of action is quicksave (cannot do a normal save for some reason without mouse), exit game, restart and load save.
Game controls:
VERY clunky. Obviously made with consoles in mind. You can control only one character (out of your team of up to three) at a time, though you can switch between them. Sadly, the other characters sometimes instantly forget what you told them to do (their "follow player character" script overwrites the orders you gave while controlling them) and they also have a mind of their own when it comes to when to follow you or when to run in the opposite direction you are going in to attack enemies. This makes a certain part of the game where there are constantly spawning enemies a lot more annoying than it should be.
Animations can lock your player character in place for several seconds after they finished.
Characters wait for the start of the next "round" to even walk up to the enemy when they are told to engage them in melee, but are out of range.
Also, more of a design decision, but i'll list it anyway here: the pazaak minigame has you always at a disadvantage which makes this minigame very save-scummy.
If you can live with those issues (and it is certainly possible to have a fun experience despite them), then go ahead any play it.

This visual novel has an interesting idea and characters, but it also justifies its low price with simple art and exposition dump dialogues that sometimes try too hard to keep the vague mystical elements shrouded.
The story of Faust is one of most intriguing pieces of literature – no wonder it influenced many people since its creation. Soul Gambler is another spin on this old tale, this time taking the visual novel format in a comic-like skin.
Our Faust is an accountant stuck in a seemingly dead-end job, whose life is turned upside down when he signs the infernal contract that lets him sacrifice parts of his soul in exchange for wishes. Also, his story leads into a large, centuries-old conspiracy instead of an internal struggle with his own demons.
The writing is a bit hit and miss. The dialogues are often plot dumps and the pacing is hectic even for a visual novel, but it does a damn fine job with characterisation: Faust remains a relatable, everyday character even in the most extreme situations.
The art style tries to follows the Hergé-like clear lines school of drawing, with mild success. Faust and his temptress are portrayed well, but the rest of the cast lack emotions and feel lifeless, and the often empty backgrounds didn’t help a lot. Still, it is among the better art we can see in the cheap VN category.

The Hitman series is a piece of history.  I think this game was the fruition of the stealth/action genre, and its effective implementation have inspired dozens of other games, including Assasin's Creed. Hitman 2 is my favorite, not because it's the best, but because it was one of the first PC games I fell in love with. The atmospheric mood, soundtrack, and art stylization really drew me in and have greatly influenced what I look for in the medium. While the gameplay has dated, the effective combination of other aspects have kept it consistently in my top 20, even a decade later.
Gameplay: 5
In a post Assasin's Creed world, it has definitely dated.  At the time, however, the controls and AI were stellar.

Story: 6
Nothing revolutionary, but it serves to draw together the wide variety of locations presented in the game.
Art: 9
The mood and atmospheres are incredible. No other game at the time captured the diversity of worlds so well with so little graphically, justifying literally hundreds of hours of slow sneaking - without ever feeling dry or boring.  This combined with the music makes it a classic.
Music: 9
Jesper Kyd is a master. At a time when most games featured popish midi synth, he had his soundtrack was performed by the Budapest Symphony Orchestra.
Should you play this?
If you haven't played this before, you likely won't be impressed. But if you like classic games and want to see a bit of history, enjoy it for the fantastic environmental moods the game creators were able to capture. For those of you who enjoyed it 10 years ago, you'll appreciate a replay.

I started off not wanting to get this game, but the open beta changed my opinion to give it a try. I logged at least 50+ hours into the open beta and this satisfied me so I purchased the game.
If you are not a fan of MOBAs, Gearbox, Borderlands, FPSs or anything of that nature, do not get this game, otherwise you will end up writing a negative review because you did not look into the game.
Moving on now:
Pros:
-Uniqueness of characters
Each character has a unique playing style that can be easily seen throughout the battlefield and in-game. You can also have a different "feel" for each character since the first person view of each character is different with what weapon they hold, what stance they have and what they see (just look at Toby's view). Also, the characters have unique personalities which sometimes can be rather difficult with a large cast of playable characters.
-Aesthetic of the game is good
The game holds the tried and true typical Gearbox aesthetic, explosions, cool guns, cartoonish art style, etc. which really does not create a sense of reality, which goes hand in hand with the humor and silliness that Gearbox has shown us thus far with games such as Borderlands.
-Gameplay
Gameplay feels smooth and nice. Even though there are a multitude of playable characters, I have not found one character I do not have fun with. Movement is good for a FPS, the shooting feels nice, and getting around all missions and maps feels smooth, not complaints here.
Cons:
Horribly unbalanced matchmaking:
With all the games I have played, I have found certain characters to be too weak and too strong which makes the matchmaking not pleasant at times. Also, with the imbalanced teams, meaning 5 level 100s pitted against newer people to the game, it is hardly fair. I remember in the open beta there was a ranked queue for matchmaking, I really wish Gearbox would bring that back.
-Short campaign:
The campaign is a little short (which they are adding more missions with DLC) but it is replayable in my eyes since there is a lot of special dialogue with characters plus 25+ characters to play the game with. So it's perfectly fine with me.
Heated topics and debates I have seen in the reviews:
-Locked Characters at start:
I know some people are ticked they just paid money for this game and there are locked characters, however I do not see an issue with this since that is the way to progress and become better at the game. Personally, I do like how characters are locked so I have a sense of accomplishment earning said characters and I can try them out as I go. Of course I do see that I could do that anyway by just going down the list of characters.
-Comparing it to Overwatch:
People, stop doing this. The games are two different games entirely, one is a MOBAFPS, and the other is an FPS like Team Fortress 2. They cannot be considered better than the other since they cannot be compared based upon different genres. Personally, I do like both games, both are really good.
-Price drop after this past weekend:
People who complain about this should note that they did have access to the game 3 weeks earlier than people who bought it on sale now. Also, this trend is increasing because it is a good marketing move in order to get people to purchase the game. Since this trend is apparent, people should wait to buy games rather than complaining about the price drop itself.
-Free content: Gearbox clearly labeled that the free content would be multiplayer maps and characters (since the characters can be purchased with in-game money),"46,000 credits is such a huge price though" what are you buying with those credits anyway? Loot packs that you can get with leveling up or playing the story? Just play the game, save up your credits and not complain, otherwise buy the DLC and get even more skins and taunts along with another story mission and a hero key good for ANY Battleborn.
TL;DR
This game is nowhere near perfect, but I do recommend it to everyone who enjoys MOBAFPSs, Monday Night Combat, or Borderlands. It has some really cool characters, great asthetics, and fun gameplay. Although the matchmaking is a little frustrating at times I'm sure Gearbox is working to make it all the better with patches to come.

So, I owned this game back on CD until that one broke, and when it appeared on Steam, it didn't take me long to make the decision to re-acquire it.
This game is one of the classics and my personal favorite of the series (maybe, mabye tied with
).
Don't expect HD graphics as the game
fairly old, but they still hold up and the gameplay makes well up for it.
The game mostly gives you free reign over how you deal with your missions, wether you go in guns blazing or infiltrate the building disguised as the milkman, take out your target and leave without anyone ever knowing better; the only consequence being a distinct shift in your overall mission ratings (though wether or not a

What you have to know is that if you play it quiet, you play it slow. Sadly, I have to start off by saying my time in the military playing with the toys that this game has for units has somewhat colored my experience with this game...  There are quirks about this as a military veteran and wargamer that drive me up the wall (AV-8 Harriers losing eyes on the target they are inbound for when a friendly ground unit is destroyed for example, never mind that the Harrier is inbound and should be 'eyes on' the target already before attacking).  However, EVERY WARGAME I PLAY HAS THESE PROBLEMS.  That is the nature of the wargame, to include the ones we played in the military to prepare for actual wars.
This game is darn close to what you can expect from a tactical simulation in the 'real world' training environment.  If you get too focused in one area of the battlefield, you will get flanked and bombed from another.  This chaos in a consumer RTS is priceless and should be embraced.  I don't know how many times I've won a scenario and gone 'huh?!' in much the way I'd respond to ENDEX (end of excercise) in the miltary.  Frankly, this is a credit to the developers.  Scenarios can be frustrating hard compared to other RTS wargames out there because of this.  Once you get into the flow of how things work in this game, you'll find yourself enjoying it and likely getting better and some of the other lesser RTS games out there.
While there are times I wish the units acted more like real units with the cabilities of their real counterparts, the above described chaos makes this well worth it.
Developers:
Do some more homework on how Close Air Support aircraft work.  Just because a friendly ground unit is destroyed doesn't mean that the aircraft magically can't see its target anymore.  Quite the contrary, when an aircraft is inbound onto a target, that unit should stay visible to it, even if others get lost in the blur (fog of war for fixed wing aircraft especially faster movers like the F-16 and MiG-27).  A-10 and SU-25 pilots are less likely to lose their targets, and in fact should be able to spot targets better than others, this is the nature of the attack pilot.  I'm hoping some of these issues are because of lack of processing power and AI limits....
Morale seems a bit too finicky.  I've seen units in plenty of firefights continue on better than units in this game.  It never ceases to amaze me how in RTS games with morale, units break so easy (or conversely, not at all in others).
Going back to the aircraft, loiter time for some of these aircraft is agonizingly so small, it negates much of the realism I see in other parts of the game.  Even short duration fast movers hang out much longer than the short 30 seconds you get with some of the games airframes.
Perhaps a future scenario set can include units that are limited to the TO&E of actual units.  You get a battalion of this, and that is it for the scenario.  Support is what your brigade/division/corps allocates.  Command points aren't bad though, the cost of units is pretty reasonable to keep the forces limited and close to actual NATO/WARPAC levels in the region.
I will likely play this a lot over the next few years.  Good job, and I highly recommend this to any serious wargamer or anyone burned out with base building RTS games that get too much of a grind to them.

It doesn't means that there is nothing interesting. The story can be fun, somewhat immersive, long enough, and you get to see the main characters' opinions and personalities evolve through time. In summary, I'd recommend it for the combat mode, the gameplay, the animation, the aesthetics, but not for the rpg elements.

Waited ages for the price of this game to come down, been keeping my eye on it for months because it looked like a really great game. It's basically 3 mini games in one, you have the risk style battle map, the animated and voiced interactions with your retinue onboard your flagship, which is meant to serve as the political/diplomacy portion. And then ofcourse the actual meat and potatoes of the game, the RTS style gameplay.
1)Strategy map.
Way too simplistic, felt very empty and lacked purpose. AI moves were predictable. I don't like the card system either, for example there is a card to commit genocide in a region of your choice. It just feels all too easy, would of been better to have raider units, which you must create and then transport to the region. But no, you just plonk down a card and suddenly the job is done.
2)Ship interactions (household and military retinue)
Fully voiced and looks ok. But feels more like a slide show presentation sometimes, for example, you could be talking to one of your aids, then pick one of the limited dialog options and your aid will suddenly change stance or move location slighty instead of it being a seamless animation, it feels each bit was stiched together haphazardly.
3)RTS battle game
Probably the bit I was looking forward to the most, and the bit that disapointed me the most. The UI is clunky and way too large, it obstructs a large part of the screen. The actual fights are super easy, once you get to grips with buildings and managing your recruits, it very quickly becomes a snore fest. And the novelty of being a dragon in battle wears off after the first 5 minutes when you come to realise that being a dragon just made the game even easier.
It might be worth playing for the story, if you like that sort of thing. But if you're looking for a totalwar style game with dragons, then this is probably going to leave you with buyer's remorse.

This is a game literally everyone needs to play. Unless you don't like fun. You
like fun, don't you?
The game itself is an odd blend of politics, Risk, and a classic RTS game. You play each turn by first exploring your ship, settling political issues that crop up, upgrading your units and/or dragon, as well as talking with your queen when she has the time. The characters you have to interact with are all quite unique and interesting. While they're not exactly complex beings (most of them have a few core personality traits they stick to relentlessly), your own choices in the politics and personal situations you are called to decide upon can have a marked effect on their personality by the end of the game. (I'm looking at you Edmund!!)
The next parts of a turn is where Risk comes into play. You build units and move them between the various territories inked out on, quite frankly, lovely maps. There's not a
to say about this portion of the game. It's very fluid and the game makes sure you don't spend a ton of time here. A few of my peeves actually come from this section of the game. The camera jerks you around between areas when showing your opponent's moves and zooms in inapproriately, keeping you from seeing everything that is happening. Thankfully, you'll have plenty of time to review the board on your next turn, but it's still jarring.
Finally, you get to the RTS section of a turn. This can be a ton of fun as this is where you'll have the chance to direct the units you brought into the map, build even more units using a pool of resources everyone must fight over, and most importantly of all, turn into a freaking dragon. Unless it's before the first few minutes have elapsed, or you don't have a certain amount of resources. Okay, so the dragon aspect of the game that gets pushed so hard isn't invulnerable or all-mighty, but honestly I liked that. You have to work with both troops and your dragon, especially as the difficulty cranks up.
Everything meshes together to become a lot of fun to play with an excellent replay value to boot. Even the single player campaign can be replayed several times before you see everything. Those political and personal matters that I mentioned you having to deal with are randomized. Even making difference choices on the same decisions can dramatically change your tactics.
Okay, TLDR bullet point time.
Overall score: 8/10
Pros:
- Awesome political system that directly imacts your overall strategy.
- Colorful and fun characters to interact with.
- Game AI unafraid to teach you a lesson if you get arrogant.
- Enough variety of units to allow you to decide your own tactics.
- Completely replayable, even the single player campaign.
- Hot keys allow you to continue controlling and building your army even in Dragon Mode.
- Simply inspired Voice Acting for each and every character.
Cons:
- Naval units as a whole are a bit of an afterthought.
- You can certainly feel that a few features were cut from the game. (Looking at you Imp Princess and Orc Race!)
- Surprisingly short single player campaign.

I don't consider this to be a "throwback" or "homage" or anything of that kind. Her Story is a completely new, unique and untapped method of interactive storytelling that I found absolutely fascinating. This title is definitely not for everyone, but it has been a long time (if ever) that I have been to engrossed in a story. By its very nature Her Story makes you care about what is happening. Caring about, understanding and absorbing the story IS the gameplay since it is the only way to progress. I found this an incredible breath of fresh air after decades of "hint" buttons superfluous story that may as well be ignored.
This title, with such minimalist pseudo-gameplay has, in my opinion, been the first to chart new territory of storytelling in an interactive medium since Spec Ops: The Line and Telltale's The Walking Dead, both back in 2012. And where those titles hesitantly tease and hint at new territory, this one dives into it face first to either sink or swim.

Recommended with reservations.
Her Story sends you digging through archived police interviews to get to the bottom of a murder and the bizarre story behind it. The game itself takes the form of wrestling with dated software and its extremely limited ability to present disorganized, decontextualized short clips of video ranging from about 3 to 90 seconds. They're at least transcribed so word searches will check against the transcripts, but without meaningful tags, organization by chronology or subject, or any way to easily remove red herrings from your painfully limited search results. So the real "game" of Her Story is understanding your interviews, putting them into context, seizing on hints for further search terms, and coming up with your own.
But there's a problem. This is a game that lives and dies by its deliberately hobbled search mechanics, but a glaring oversight by the developers makes it possible to power through everything in chronological order without ever scratching your noggin. And it's a trick simple enough that I thought of it within the first few minutes. You have to consciously avoid using it if you want the story to unravel in roughly the direction the developers intended.
One last warning: This isn't some classic detective whodunnit. There's some mystery and ambiguity to it all, but the real object is to find out "what happened here," not to collar the bad guy. And if the Steam forums are any indiciation, any idiot can come to a conclusion about what happened, even if it's not backed by evidence or even basic common sense. With no moment of truth, no public accusation, and no grand reveal, Joe Dumbass's "a dragon did it at the behest of the Freemasons" theory gets treated just as valid as your well-reasoned, evidence-backed analysis.
All that said, Her Story tells a pretty good tale with some wonderful acting, and it's a delightful experience to have the oldschool frustration of computer research become a set of game mechanics. Pick it up on a sale.

This game is a blast to play with friends or solo and is an absolute steal when the game is on sale. There are two main games modes: Hide and seek and mobification. Both game modes are mostly the same, except in mobification once you're found found as a witch you will then become a hunter so you'll always be playing. Teams are split into hiders (witches) and hunters and there are fewer hunters than hiders at the start of the game. Hiders are able to transform into any prop in the map and then either stay hidden or avoid the hunters. After a 25 second timer for witches to hide, hunters are then given 4 minutes to find all the witches on the map through the use of skills, melee dmg, or throwing potatoes. Each hunter/witch has the choice of two skills chosen at the beginning of each round, one movement and one utility skill, which adds more depth and skill to the game. There are quite a few maps already available so far but there needs to be more. I would like to see a new game mode, because the only other one (Hunt-a-hag) doesn't really measure up to other modes because it doesn't utilize props at all. Hopefully there will be a tutorial eventually for new players and the game could use better stat tracking, and a better scoreboard at the end of each game with more information.

Firstly the closest I have ever come to actually fishing, is this game! I knew nothing of fishing or it's intricacies until I ventured onto this game. My Husband and Son have been plaing this game for a while, and to be honest, it is great viewing as well as playing.
But I wanted to have a go myself and see just what all the fishy fun was about. Cue my guy, Wilhelm. Wilhelm is going great guns. He has 3 rods; Kenny 'Fishing' Powers, Ray Bream-ero and Doug Heffer-Carp. The delight in pulling in a fish that takes a while to land is thrilling and just so satifying. An Acheivement that is as unexpected as it is awesome.
So about the game; well, go through the tutorial or Acadamy to learn the basics- if you know nothing as I did then this is the  place where your fishy education begins. Then feel free to go and complete the challenges you have unlocked, or free fishing and just enjoy the game's beautiful ambience. The graphics, the fish detail, the weather, the sounds within this game are just fantastic. Immersive and peaceful. The gentle plopping of fish as they leap out of the water, or the sound of the wind as it begins to rise (shadow detail also shows the tree shadows moving in the wind) or the pitter patter of rain. I just simply love playing.
There are levels to go up, a skill tree for tackle and bait. Earning Tackle Points as you catch fish, complete challenges and finish tournaments (the latter has either a live daily match or in game AI tournaments) means that you can develop your fisher-person to be the best in every field or go for one particular area of expertise.
There is nothing quite like landing your first big carp, or first fish, but the ultimate (next to Boss Fish) is catching a HUGE Catfish!!!!
Notes on gameplay: -
* Have patience. Learn the tension gradients that are applicable to your tackle- losing a fish that you have spent 5 minutes reeling in only for it to get away can be gutting. Learn your rod's capability
* Equip your net at 4yrds or less to get the instant land- anything above 4 and you wont be able to manouvre the net to catch the fish.
* Screenshots are addictive- But awesome to show off those catches that made you feel proud. Please do take a peek at mine if you would like to see the look of the fish.
* Character choice is limited- but there is no need to have a full on customisation option when all you see mostly is the back of your character.
* Learn about the rigs, the best bait for that rig and go fishing where the fish you want to catch hang out.
* Read the Boss Fish Menu and descriptions they are awesome
* Don't be disheartened Rome wasn't built in a day and neither is the best tacklebox- take your time and have fun with the game.
* Make as many fish related puns as you can- this is a source of never ending amusment. Life is but a Bream :-)
* Slow life down for an hour! Take the small joy of a days fishing and be at peace. No traffic, no bosses moaning, no stress- just one rod at a time, one fishy at a time
Enjoy and 'Carp-i' Diem ;-P

Fate of the World is an educational strategy game that places you in charge of many global policies to try to save the world from ecologocial disaster. It's pretty fun to play, and certainly far better than you'd expect from edu-tainment. You basically have to balance the political, economical, and social problems of individual nations with the fight against long-term solutions to global climate change.
This game is hard. Very hard. The first mission's no problem, but I'm still trying to figure out the second one after three failures. The main problem is that you aren't given enough information to tell what affects what, or how you're supposed to react to certain problems. One false move in 2030 will leave India devastated in 2070, and you don't know what it was most of the time.
It's worth giving this game a try if you can pick it up cheap. It's fun to play around with and see what you can do, but don't expect to finish this one without a lot of out-of-game research.

I'd give this game a qualified recommendation.  Soul Gambler is a visual novel with some decision tree choices.  While the choices are few, it does give SG some replayability if you want to see all the options.  The premise is interesting.  You play an "everyman" who is stuck in a boring job and social life.  Early in the game you are approached by a mysterious woman who offers you a deal to make your life more interesting.  Suffice it to say you don't have much choice, and from there you are presented with a series of scenarios where you can choose to expend a portion of your soul in order to influence the outcome favorably.  You don't have unlimited soul "points", and this is where the gambling part comes in.  You can elect to spend the points or not, but there are consequences either way.  The goal of the game is to uncover the true identity of the old lady and figure out why you were selected for the "deal".
The graphics are very clean and cartoonish, but not in a silly way.  The game takes itself seriously for the most part, and some of the decisions you make have serious consequences.  The sound is good, and for the most part the dialogue is well done.
As I mentioned there is some replayability in that you can re-load a save to see what the other choices bring.  This is definitely one of the better visual novels I have experienced in that I actually finished it (it's not overly long).  The ending seemed a bit abrupt, but it does have an actual conclusion.  If you enjoy visual novels with some meaningful choices then you may enjoy Soul Gambler.
