This game is bloody genius! You play as an 7 year old boy named "Lucius" who was born in room 666 at the St. Benedict Memorial Hospital on the 6th of June, 1966. Lucius is possessed by the Devil. But you live in a ordinary family where all you do is slowly kill every single person in the house without anyone finding out in very unique ways. Like for example locking someone up in a Meat Locker with freezing temperatures until they slowly die. You also have supernatural abilites like Telekinesis, Mind Control, Mine Erase and Combustion. However, in the sequel, Lucius II: The Prophecy, Lucius has several other unique abilites, such as turning invisible and causing blindness on others. While Telekinesis, Mind Control, and Combustion remain present, the player must gain levels by killing the staff and patients to unlock and upgrade them.
As the opening suggests, Lucius has been possessed by a demonic entity since birth, but this only becomes apparent after his sixth birthday party, when Lucifer suggests that he locks a maid in the cooler and freeze her to death. Learning of his unholy affiliation on the 6th of June 1972, Lucius embarks on a year-long campaign of sacrificing each and everyone of the Dante household to his spiritual progenitor, Lucifer. Starting with staff and moving to family, Lucius accomplishes this covert genocide by planning "accidents" and using his supernatural powers for furthering Lucifer's influence and instating pandemonium. At the end of the game, Lucius' power increases and sets the manson ablaze before battling two priests and his father, leaving only Lucius alive and tricking the detective McGuffin into believing that his father was the killer.
True to his father's nature, Lucius is not very comfortable around crosses, which sap his entire energy and render him unable to use his powers. However, this can be prevented when he/the player turns the cross upside down. His name is partly based on his father's name, Lucifer. His character is believed to be based on Damien from the from the Omen series, who is also a murderous child Antichrist whose birth has suggested to also have been June 6th, 1966.
Due to his quiet nature, little is known about Lucius's personality before his awakening into the Antichrist. However, Lucius is portrayed to have an above average intelligence in sciense, as is evidenced by learning biology at just 6 years old, yet he seems to be only average when it comes to mathematics. Lucius is revealed to be quite witty through his journal entires, often making clever, and sometimes humorous, remarks about the deaths of certain subjects. Lucius is very creative and efficient in his methods and doesn't waste his time on the sadistic torture of his subjects while trying to complete his objectives, in the way that his half-brother Isaac did. Demonstrating a very calm demeanor through the entireety of these events, Lucius is never shown to be in a state of panic, fear or rage. He proves to be very determined to answer his calling, as is displayed by his attempts to kill a nun while stripped of his powers. His own parents seem to be quite reserved in their affection, possibly because his mother went through atrocious pain while giving birth to him and his presistent silence coupled with vacant stares gives everybody uneasy feelings, including his own father.
10/10 Epic game! 100% Recommended! You can pick up the game for a relatively cheap price :)

From the mastermind behind the unique psychological thriller "Silent Hill: Shattered Memories" comes a new point-and-click murder mystery experience unlike any other.
"Her Story" puts you directly into the seat of a homicide detective tasked with piecing together the truth behind a husband's death back in 1994. Your mission is to scavenge through the police database and uncover all the facts (e.g. killer(s), motive(s), method(s), etc.) by watching several live-action clips of interviews with the widow.
Sounds simple, right? Well, here's the tricky part. Due to a Y2K technical error, the clips have been scattered all over the database and you can only load up to five at a time depending on the search keywords you use. So, in order to get the full story, you need to use different keywords for different leads. For example, if you look up a few clips in which the widow says "car" and then you hear her say "baby" in one of them, try looking up the word "baby" and you'll find a whole new set of clips.
So, the game gives you the freedom to unravel the whole story at your own pace. You can either cut to the chase and search for the culprit(s) or you can get to know the characters (most of them only mentioned and unseen) and uncover the events leading up to the murder. This strengthens the suspension of disbelief by making you feel like a real detective hunting for every last clue you can find! This is my favourite aspect of the game because most murder mystery games I've played in the past (e.g. Ace Attorney, Heavy Rain, etc.) don't give you this much freedom.
With regards to the core gameplay and presentation, it's very simplistic (being a point-and-click game and all) but authentic to the old mid-90s computers which I believe helps maintain the suspension of disbelief. Plus, the subtle music in the desktop changes depending on which clips you watch thus matching their respective moods. I feel that this all intensifies the enigmatic atmosphere surrounding the story.
If there was one thing I had to complain about this game, it would be its short length and minimal replayability. Since this is an FMV point-and-click adventure game, I can't say that I didn't see it coming. Still, I found that it's possible to gather enough clues to identify the killer within two hours of my first "playthrough." Regardless, I came back to play the next day and watch clips about the characters' backgrounds in case I might uncover any new secrets.
So, all in all, I would describe "Her Story" as an immersive psychological puzzle game which succeeds in putting you right in the seat of a detective piecing together the truth behind a murder. Due to its simplistic point-and-click nature, I wouldn't recommend this to hardcore gamers who prefer gameplay over story. But, if you loved "Silent Hill: Shattered Memories," then I bet you're bound to love "Her Story" too!

A Murder Mystery that is a very unique in many ways. It is nice to see some games that take chances and are confident enough to pull off a game like this. For me certain aspects remind me of Tex Murphy (One of the only good fmv games back in the day) and the old Police Quest games. While not quite as much gameplay as those other games, the vibe and atmosphere is there, along with a good performance by the leading lady. It might not have the level of depth or different gameplay mechanics as some of those other games, but it still is very enjoyable.
Some might cry that this is not really a game and what not, but for me it is very much a game and a wonderful, unique and engrossing experience. I hope we get many more of these types of games in the future. Yes you sit at a computer and search for videos, but it is so much more than that. You really feel like someone who is going back to do some research of some old murder mystery. At times I wasn't sure if she was guilty or if she was innocent, being truthful or lying, that really says alot about the acting done by the main character in this.
You have to listen in this game and pay attention, put on your detective cap as you watch, listen and search for things on this computer that might help you. For the games price it is a must try, especially if you like mystery or muder mystery,etc..  Did you hear her mention someone new? Type that name into the computer to see any other videos recorded with that word used in it. Get in that chair, turn on this old computer from the mid 90s and get to work Detective!
On one side this game is unlike anything we have really ever had, but on the flip side it reminds me a ton of things I liked in the past (Tex Murphy, Twin Peaks, Police Quest, detective shows,etc..). Excited to see where the developers go next with this, I hope this is the start of a series or the first a large collection of smaller games. Maybe with a new murder mystery each time? Add in some more variety in gameplay and the possibilities are endless.

Her Story is an incredibly fascinating game that really gets the brain gears turning. Within seconds of starting up the game and trawling through the hundreds of clips, you begin thinking like a real detective and are rewarded with "A-Ha!" moments.
Her Story is a unique game that uses full motion video clips of a police interview seeking to unravel the case of a missing husband. As the police detective going through the clips, you type in simple or complex keyword searches and are presented with clips that contain those keywords. As you watch through each clip, you begin to piece together the story of what happened and who these characters really are.
It is a spellbinding game, and one of the most uniquely fun indie games to be released for a while. Check out my video playthrough of the first 20 minutes or so below to get a better sense of how the game plays.

It's a really excellent game. The acting really makes or breaks it in an FMV like this, and Viva Seifert is absolutely stellar. Do your utmost to avoid spoilers as 90% of the joy of this game is in the discovery. I learned a fairly important plot point extremely early in the game, but it wasn't actually a bad thing, as I then got to work backwards and piece everything together around that large reveal. Once I realized how many small clues were embedded in the videos themselves, it became utterly delightful.

Nice way to spend a rainy afternoon. After that you won't need to return to the game unless you want to 'collect' every video clip.  Worth the small amount of money.  I found the personality of the woman a bit annoying but realised in the end that she's probably right for the role.  If you like this type of game you might also want to check out Cloud Chamber which is similar but more interesting due to the crowd-source colaboration aspect and discussions.

The game does a great job laying out the who, what, when, where and why.  What you are left with is a story that's ambiguous, dark and captivating enough to have you thinking about it for several days after its over. Some of the major plot reveals are down right chilling.
If you enjoy a good story, playing detective and maybe a bit of armchair psychiatrist, Her Story is a must play.

The Monster Inside describes itself as a 'film noir style, audio-visual novella', is free on Steam and takes around 30 minutes to complete with full achievements.
This game is also black and white, with a basic art style (almost like the objects are untextured) and a typical film noir soundtrack of saxophone and piano that fit the theme of the game. It quickly becomes clear that you are a detective and have been asked to look into a missing person and murder case. There is some really nice writing, that even manages to compliment the overall darkness with some comic undertones. Lines like "my head hit the pillow like it owed someone money" made me laugh without feeling out of place.
Things start off well and I was following and enjoying the story up until about chapter 5/7. At this point things got weird.
It was such an out of place plot twist that I struggled to take the game seriously after discovering it and kinda just chuckled my way through the remainder of the game. It's a shame as it could have been good and I was genuinely enjoying it but when things get strange that quickly with no context it's just silly and comes across as poor design/writing.

Soul Gambler is a really fun and short visual novel which is a modern retelling of Faust.
The novel follows on Faust. He works a boring job and has a mundane life, but all of that changes when he sells his soul to a witch for wishes. Each wish takes away apart of his soul and you have to find a way to get rid of the witch so you get to keep your soul.
The novel is  a very interesting retelling of Faust, which I don't really remember much off, since the last time I read it was back in High School.
The novel is also quite interesting in general, since you can choose perk points at the start of the game and those help you out in other parts in the game, like seduction, brute force and intelligence to trick people.
The art style is also really well done, it's just fun to look around the environments, just because how awesome everything looks.
The multiple outcomes are also quite nice as it adds more replay value and I can see myself coming back to this game in the future to replay and get another endings I haven't got yet.
A single run of the game will last you 1 hour, but as stated before there are multiple endings and from what I understand there are 5 endings so that's 5+ hours of content and for the price that's quite a deal.
There are a few negatives like some sloppy writing and the horrible soundtrack.
I enjoyed my time with Soul Gambler and if you can get this game I highly suggest trying it out, cause it's quite awesome.
Final Rating:
7/10 - Good

You are alone on a remote island and need to explore the land and collect the plants needed to synthesize a cure.
The best thing about the game is the mapping system.  It's still much easier to find your location in this game than in real life, but the triangulation system adds a distinct flavor to this game.  Really the majority of the gameplay is chaining triangulations to uncover more and more of the map. Traversal of the terrain is challenging with cliffs posing a large hazard and a night that is realistically dark.  There is an creature that occasionally hunts you but its more of a harassment than a threat.
It's a 10 hour game with a strong focus and a nice distinctive set of mechanics.  I'd recommend it for people looking for a calm, tight, different game.

I love how this game has the layer of shooters on top of the customization of MOBAs.
You can't really think of it as one or the other, as you require the finesse of the first and the patience of the second.
The helix system is a little clunky, slowing down the battle as you need to find a safe spot to choose your next perk, but I like how it greatly changes how you play the game. I can gear a healer towards a DPS build or maximize it as a support depending on how I want to play a match.
I also really like the way it paints a picture of the world through the context. You get a sense that this is a crew of losers and rejects based on their designs and animations. It makes me think "What if Masters of The Universe was based off of your old doodles from middle school."
What's really cool though is how subtle and expressive the characters dialogue can be. I found out a lot about Atticus, the rebel thrall, and Toby, the heavily armed penguin just based on their flavor dialogue during the fights. If Atticus fights other thralls during the story mode, he'll bemoan his actions and try to justify them as he kills his own people by the score. Toby, if he gets into a fight with Benedict, will reveal that he used to serve under him and resents him for it.
It strikes an amazing balance between character and gameplay that you don't see enough of.
My main gripe would have to be that there is too much space between spawn and the minion spawn. It takes a bit too long to get back to the fight sometimes.

Loved this one. You're piecing together a story about some woman by going through a database on a pretty old pc. The presentation of the pc is fantastic, with some really cool details and quirks. You investigate the story by watching small clips where the girl is being interrogated.
All clips are already in the pc, you just have to get them to show. You can search through everything she said in the fragment, but it only shows the first 5 fragments chronologically. So while "the" is a word used in most fragments, it will only show the 5 earliest fragments. This means that more specific keywords will reveal more recent clips, creating a very alinear progression. This means that if you play it too well, you might figure out the story way too earlier, which can impact your experience somewhat. I think it's quite brave of Sam Barlow to choose this design, and I'd love to see more experiments like it!
The story itself is very mysterious, but also very fun and fulfilling. I figured it out using good ol' pen and paper, which gives you that real detective feel!

Hitman 2 Silent Assassin is a game that one approaches with much anticipation. The original Hitman was a true classic and any follow up to that would have to be something extraordinary in order to meet the expectations.
As Silent Assassin starts out 47 has retired and now lives a quiet life, tending the gardens in a Sicilian monastery. This all changes rather dramatically of course as your friend and mentor is kidnapped and you are forced to once again, take on the role of a professional hitman.
The story in general leaves much to be desired and the extremely subpar voice acting does not to help it. The grating sound of foreign accents that might as well have all been done by the same American voice actor often takes you out of the game and it is a shame that the developers couldn't have sprung for a couple of authentic sounds along the way. The high quality soundtrack and some passable ambiance makes up for some of this shortfall but not all of it unfortunately.
In terms of gameplay nothing much has changed. You travel from mission to mission, picking your starting gear and then going about killing a preset target in whichever manner you find to be the most efficient. Silent Assassin introduces a new rating system at the end of each mission that rewards you based on performance. Unfortunately the highest rating you can receive is usually only given out for executing a mission in a very specific way and this makes it very counterintuitive to the otherwise very open-ended missions.
The mission areas are much bigger this time around and while this sometimes allow for more creative thinking in solving the missions it also tends to slow down the game's pace, particularly in missions where running might attract the attention of nearby guards.
The developers seems to have paid attention to some of the fan feedback of the original and Silent Assassin has now been given a save game system. Depending on your difficulty level you are given a certain number of saves each mission and while this is still a far cry from what really should be standard in PC games it is also a huge leap forwards from the complete lack of in-mission saves in the original. A number of new camera angles are also available to you at popular request.
Graphically Hitman is still a beautiful game, not quite as big of a step forward as one might have wanted, looking at what else is out there, but still good enough that it adds to the experience rather than detract from it.
All in all Hitman 2 Silent Assassin is a good game, even a good sequel, but in many ways it is also a bit of a letdown. It doesn't do much to advance the franchise instead sticking with what worked in the original and mostly rehashing what was already there. If you liked the original Hitman then you are going to like Silent Assassin. Just don't expect it to do anything new or exciting.

Aside from a couple of early weak "move to the other end of the map" missions in Japan, and an obligatory (although nowhere near as the first game's) final action level, this is Hitman hitting its stride. The Monster Inside is a short Visual Novel developped by Random Seed Games and totally free to play on Steam or directly in your browser.
Jack, a detective that used to work in the police force, is dragged into an unusual murder and disappearance investigation as a mysterious woman rushes in his office. The game is linear and takes only 10 to 20 minutes to complete, but it's well spent time if you're looking for a brief and interesting narrative experience.
What I enjoyed the most in this game was definitely the noir art style coupled with the "old detective movie style" music, creating an appropriate and intriguing atmosphere together.
Sadly there isn't any real challenge or investigation ; except for some dialogue choices, you can only follow and read the story divided in 7 chapters. Every time you finish a chapter, you'll unlock the associated achievement automatically.
A simple and short mystery Visual Novel - there's nothing more to expect from it, but I'll recommended it nonetheless because it's a pleasant surprise coming from a free game ; I wouldn't mind playing more similar games honestly.

...is a film-noir text-based story. Jack, a private investigator with a dark past, is approached by a woman that sets him on a case to investigate a series of murders.
There is little to say, as this isn't really a game at all, more like a short story or chronical. Your character is the narrator, and you progress through a few dialog choices, going from a short scene to another. As you read the story, you have a simple and lightly-animated image of the location.
One word to describe your experience is atmospheric. While simple, the monochrome images are accompanied by gorgeous music that puts you in the right mood.
I suppose achievement hunters can probably see this as an easy opportunity to make a few points.
You can't make mistakes or make a wrong move, nothing will challenge you intellectually or morally. It's linear, has no branching path, and by Chapter 5 it's all very predictable. There won't be any reason to give this a second playthrough, unless you just want to listen to the music playing while reading an actual book.
Probably my shortest review. On paper,
wouldn't be more than a one-page column in a collection of short stories. However, it's free and won't take much of your time. Go ahead, take 15-20 minutes and give it a try. If you didn't like your experience, you didn't waste much.

Psychonauts gets so many things right. Its premise and story, its art style, its humour - all fantastic, and people have talked about these things a million times, so it seems pointless for me to do so. The problem is, I just don't find it very fun. I wanted to like it so much, and over the years I've started the game so many times, but never got further than a few hours in. Today, I've finally pushed through the game, further than I've ever got before, and I've come to accept how I really feel, which is that I don't really like it.
It's hampered by bad level design (in a gameplay sense), stiff controls (yes I'm using a gamepad), a clumsy targeting system, and awkwardly-designed boss fights. Parts of it have just aged poorly, other parts were never very good, and yet some moments are pure genius which just makes the rest of the game all the more disappointing. I would love this game, if it wasn't for the whole "game" part of the game. When people praise Psychonauts, they talk about the characters, the world, the story; most people aren't praising the gameplay, and that's something you should keep in mind if you're new to it. The gameplay itself is, at best, average for a platformer from 2005, and subpar when played today.

I liked it because:
- There is no combat.
- You're mostly just exploring a beautiful island (in immersive first-person view).
- The mapping technique was unique and challenging.
- The character movements are realistic of someone who is sick: you're a little sluggish and it's easy to get hurt. (Once I actually said "Whew!" out loud after climbing up a steep hill. This was a big part of the immersion for me.)
- Plot was interesting and drove me forward. Though it's not in your face - you have to look for it.
- It's fun to replay once you know what's going on. (1st playthrough took me about 20 hours; 2nd playthrough I attempted a speedrun in about 2 hours.)
You may NOT like it because:
- There is no combat.
- You're mostly just exploring a beautiful island.
- Mapping technique is a little hard to learn (but once you "get" it, it's fine).
- Character movements can be clunky.
- You have to search for notes and clues to learn the story.

This was the second indie game I ever got really interested in, (after Sangfroid). It's a real shame it took me so long to get to it, because now that I have, I am not impressed.
Visuals are ok, and I'm not usually picky about them. Tension was non-existant during the first hour or so... the monster they hype up in the trailers doesn't even make a scripted appearance to help build said tension. It might've been out there, it might not, but after an hour of play I would have expected something after how much time is spent hyping it up in the trailer.
Game details are obtuse... couldn't figure out the triangulation mechanics, but that's also fine. Things don't always need to be spelled out to you and if you're willing to spend hours with a product you can definitely learn. All in all, the setup was one for a game that could have been savoured, rather than rushing to get to the good bits.
However, I'm not savouring anything because of the SECOND. WORST. FIRST. PERSON. CONTROLS. EVER. The only controls that I've experienced that are worse are from Datura for PS4.
Movement is arduous at best, ridiculously floaty at worst. Running is the only way to get anywhere in decent time, but watch out that you don't go down hill for any reason, because you will trip, you will fall, and then you're stuck hiking back to a bed to sleep off the resulting fever... yes, a fever from falling. Climbing up anywhere is equally painful, where a slope you would have no problem scaling in real life is impossible, and you keep sliding down. Yes, you could argue this was done for realism, but there's a fine line between realism and unfun.
Hard pass, if you want something similar go play the Forest, Minecraft, Don't Starve, or 7 Days to Die. They all have survival elements, crafting, roughly equivalent graphics, and you're being hunted by enemies that actually show up in the first hour, all without making you want to grind your teeth to dust as you try to move through the world.

Note: This was my first visual novel game ever so my review does not focus on how it compares to other visual novels  but rather more on my personal exprience with this piece as a standalone.
I got it in a special bundle that was going very very cheaply and thought, "Why not? I've never really tried visual novels and it's only a couple extra rands in cost". I didn't know what to expect but was pleasantly surprised. I enjoyed playing through it, mainly because it was a very relaxing experience; I didn't have to agonise over minutiae that one usually needs to stress over when playing other genres. All I did was sit back and enjoy the story. Unlike most times when I play games, I was not pressured into playing the best or correct playthrough; I just played freely, without fear of getting stuck with the bad/insufficient ending.The story itself was intriguing though not notably complex; the ending was a nice twist. I felt satisfied at the end. There was pleasant ambient background noise that made it feel very immersive, although there was an irritating blank/mute space in audio whenever the ambient or music track looped over. I would love to hear more immersive background sound like that in other genres to be frank. I found the artwork competent, but not necessarily spectacular, although I am quite glad it was not the usual animefied style - seriously guys, what the hell; every visual novel seems animefied. Why?!
All in all, I would recommend the game. It is a competent effort that was a fun and relaxing way to pass time, and very much worth the price

3€ isn't that much... but rethink for a while if you want to buy it.
super short, bland story, not impressive, albeit has pretty pictures.
First: it's super short. I spent like 20-30 minutes and get the story to the end. Saying that I was disappointed is like saying nothing. Really, I walk my dog (in both meanings) longer than completing "Soul Gambler". It should be longer, a little at least.
Second: you cannot skip dialogues. So if you want to have 100% achievements - once again, rethink, because you'll end with 3 hours of clicking. And while clicking isn't that bad in clicker games... well, other visual novels rather have that option - guess why? So the player won't get stuck with the lines he read already few times.
Third: the story is lame. Seriously. I'm a big fan of Faustian myth - starting from the short stories from 15 century to Goethe's masterpiece and then to contemporary literature and movies that cover many interpretations of the same story of Faust. And to be clear: I don't expect the game (that cheap at least) to have complex, wonderful plot just like writers decades ago. But I expect it to have at least decent story, decent writing and characters that will have my heart. In the end, it's a visual novel and that genre is ALL ABOUT STORY. And this one is... bland. It just takes few trite motives connected to word "devil", mix it without understanding and voila! You have a pact, some of 666 here and there, ridiculous rituals and bam! you're done with the story, leave it idle for cards.
Fourth:  the ending. Except being lame and devil-may-care, it's basically always the same. Minor things changes depending on your choices, but you will always see the same scenes, the same dialogues, nothing will surprise you. So, if you're looking for the game where you can create a story from beginning till the end and where CHOICES MATTER, sorry, but it's not the game you're looking for.
To be honest, I really wanted to like this game. I appreciated the artwork, especially of the "dark reality", but for me pretty pictures aren't satisfying enough.

This game is simply awesome Gearbox has a genius for hybridizing genres when on-form. Take Borderlands as an example. It might have been the cel-shaded carnage and left-field sense of humour that first hooked you, but the clever mash-up of FPS and Diablo-style dungeon crawler elements was what kept you coming back for months on end. Battleborn, then, might not be quite as crazy as it sounds. Part team-based shooter, part co-op blaster, part MOBA. It takes a mix and match approach to genres then splashes on a Borderlands aesthetic with gags to match. What’s not to love? You need to give this one a try..

All right so Battleborn is a MOBA with single-player campaign as well. Multiplayer in PVE aspects are highly encouraged as shown through lore challenges and in-game interactions. Getting into the good and bad of Battleborn:
The Good:
Obviously this is a Gearbox title with their art style and humor. If you are a fan of the Borderlands series games you will fit right in with the jokes and crazy character designs. As you play through PvE there are random dialogue options that play so generally back to back maps will actually have different conversations, to a certain degree. These conversations also change based on the heroes in the party at the time, as they will also comment on the situations. For PvP when spotting an enemy player your character will generally have something to say. For example Oscar Mike when seeing an enemy Montana will something along the lines of "Mutant Lumberjack Spotted." The atmosphere of the game is quite fun and the diversity of characters is great. Leveling system is also fun. In a single storymode you will generally get to at least lvl 9, but mostly 10 (which is the max). The Helix system allows you pick one of two augments to your skills/attacks. Also with enough playtime as a certain character you will increase their character rank and unlock Mutations which give you a third choice on certain skills. The community is generally helpful as there are some challenges, more on that below, where you have to play with certain other Battleborn, and generally if you ask someone will help. There are tons of other great things you will find in the game if you just scratch the surface.
The  Bad
Lore challenges. I am not saying Lore challenges in general are bad. Completing certain tasks allows you to learn more about the character you are controlling and delve deeper into this games story. The problem arises when you have to do PvP specific challenges. More specifically kill certain characters X amount of times. This creates tension as you que again and again only to find the enemy team does not have the player you wish to kill on it. By the off chance they have the character on it you have to deliver the final blow. Assists do not count. Also certain characters are so rare to find now. Take Ambra for example. Part of Galilea's lore is to kill Ambra 25 times. At first this was not hard as Ambra was a common damage/healer hybrid, however, with the addition of Alani (damage/healer hybrid), who also has to kill Ambra 25 times, Ambra has become quite rare. There are several reasons for this but will not dive into them now as there is a character limit on reviews. The problem that does occur here is that you are trying to kill one enemy player instead of trying to win the match so you get tunnel visioned as you weigh your teamates victory against your lore that you are desperately trying to complete. Specific challenges like this do not further cooperative matches but rather destroy them. On the other hand other characters' lore challenges are really easy and can be done solo or group PvE, which honestly all should have the option to do solo or at least in PvE.
Another sad reality is these "free Battleborn" are not free. After each match you get around, let's say 600 credits, I know you can get more but you can also get less. For Alani and the planned release of Peddles or whatever "Snake Guy" I will call him, you can either use a Hero key, if you have the season pass, or unlock them for like 42,500 credits. There is no problem with grinding, I get that. I have played multiple MMOs. I am no stranger to hours upon hours of farming. However, with a stunted playerbase making such a steep price for another character sucks for newcomers.
Matchmaking: I, personally, have not had a real problem with ques however pitting newcomers against seasoned vets of the game does suck. Many a match I have had a full team of high levels and the enemy teams highest commander rank is 16. Now does this mean we will win? No, however, we would be a disgrace if we lost. It just means my team has had tons of playtime with characters, unlocking powerful mutations and having good sets of gear to activate. Also high levels, lvl 40+, have access to all hereos but a lvl 4 only has access to starter characters. Now apparently there is a fix for this coming out, sometime, but until then matches generally go one of two ways. You get wrecked, or you completly wreck the other team. Which is why there is a decline in Solo que because you want to win so you do premades.
As for the declining player population, I think the game is just in a rough patch for the time being. So long as fixes get implemented, and way better advertising, the game still has a chance to flourish. For the price drop well......You win some, you lose some. It sucks but that is how the real world works. No one is going to give you a cookie just because you payed full price and then there was a price drop, generally anyway.
Overall, I recommend Battleborn because it is a fun game, and would like to see more newcomers. The advertising for this title was lacking as it should have shown more of the Gearbox humor in it. Battleborn just desperately needs a little polishing to match-making and character lore and I think Gearbox fans will enjoy it.
I know there is a declining player count for this game but if changes are made it could easily come out of this rough patch. Besides the game has not been out all that long yet so only time and Gearbox's actions will tell.

**********************I recommend this game if you can get it for $35 on sale (or cheaper)***********************************
I have Battleborn for my XBox One, & for PC so I'll try to compare the two as well. First off I give this game a 7/10. The Campaign is sparce in story & each level is linear. However each level is grindy & challenging solo. Group play is adjusted, but slightly easier. The MOBA aspect of the game is cool, but in 1st person view can be very annoying when thinking of Battleborn as a true "MOBA" - rather, its a FPS with MOBA-like elements. Each of the characters are unique & fun. However, you need to unlock the characters as you progress through the story or gain achievements/unlocks by gameplay. Currently I have 21 playable characters.
The game has unlocks much like Hearthstone from Blizzard. You unlock items that you can equip (3 items total) in a "loadout" for gameplay. The items range from grey (common/lame) green (uncommon/semi-lame) blue (rare/good boost) and purple (epic/great boosts). You can get these items from replaying levels, PvP, or buying "packs" off of the online store - list like Hearthstone and/or other MOBA / RPG - esque games. This gives a "reason" for the regrinding of levels. Each character also gains levels, so you level up the characters you like. The development team has already stated they're working on releasing more free content/levels/characters, with priority going to season subscribers which is the standard model at this point. So expect to see some new levels and balancing. However, don't expect to see sweet new gear & skinz for your character unless you buy packs or get a season pass.
PROS:
1. Good PvP and group PvP synergy
2. The story is difficult enough in solo to keep you engaged
3. Replaying through the campaign with friends or public players ups replay value
4. Grinding up character levels & loot gives new reason to revisit levels
5. The commentary & crap talk from characters & badguys is humorous & not rehashed
6. Plenty of characters with completely different skills keeps the game refreshing
7. More free competitive maps and characters are coming, so if you like PvP you will be taken care of
8. The PC community seems small but way better (imo) than on xbox live. Less trolls, better players
CONS:
1. Those expecting rich in detail story & content will be dissapointed. This is NOT borderlands.
2. Even with cartoon style graphics, high settings & shading will require a decent graphics card. No intel HD scrubs.
3. You have to be logged into their servers for EVERYTHING, even to play solo player campaign mode - which is stupid
4. Your internet connection will determine if you're enjoying your gameplay or want to go on a violent RL rampage
5. Your internet connection will effect your solo campaign gameplay
6. The game seems about 75%ish finished, with the last 25%+ content being released in the future or with season pass
7. The levels are linear without alternate routes, making it very boring fast if you're a solo player without friends or willing to play with public players
8. Free loot packs requires an arbitrary secondary "sHIFT" account to redeem codes, which is strange/ confusing to some
9. Some characters need serious balancing to use solo play. You WILL get destroyed playing solo with some. However, once you play in group play, those characters really shine & bring synergy. Don't expect every toon to be solo playable
10. $59.99 is way too much for what it came with at launch. Get it on sale while its $35 & wait till more content comes out if you're a strategic/cautious buyer.

As a RTS/strategy/visual novel hybrid, It's basically three thematically related games grafted to each other.  What you get out of it seems like it's strongly influenced by how deeply you delve into the RTS section.  I found the singleplayer campaign is also a bit short at 9 hours, which, while taken at a veeery leasurely pace, also intentionally excluded most of the RTS battles that would have massively padded it).
Visual Novel (Shipboard diplomacy sections)
I suppose the first thing I should say is the game's politics are VERY 2014 American-centric.  Thinly veiled medical MJ, sexual orientation issues, and social justice themes abound.  I could almost 1:1 match the races to poltical factions in US poltics as seen from a cynical 20-something.  It's so blatent that it's almost immersion breaking.  At one point you will be required to choose a wife for your arranged marriage.  Each prospective bride has a mildly branching story arc that ends in one of two conclusions, and these are somewhat better written, although not by much,  The same goes for each of your four generals, General Dudebro, General Racist Snob, General Femanazi, and General Badgirl.  While the generals all start out varying shades of unlikable, their character arcs are not quite as hamfisted as the fantasy UN.  Voice acting is competent throughout though rarely standout.  Visual Novel sections are also where you buy your RTS upgrades.
Strategy (World map sections)
This is the part of the game I spent the most time with.  A region map is broken up into territories where you can station units.  Each territory can have a building on it, either a factory to produce units, a mine to increase its income, or one of the other structures to give you advantage cards.  In practice, I found the mines and taverns (they give you coupon cards for free, one-battle units) to be overwhelmingly the most useful.  Minor balance issues aside, it all looked and played very competently, if extremely easy on normal.  I lingered on act 1 and act 2 to see more visual novel development when the enemy was hopelessly outmanned and maneuvered and accidentily carried the per-turn advantages of money and research forward with no penalty.  Thus Act 3 was a steamroll that never faltered and was never close.  I think the biggest problems were that the AI wasn't aggressive enough.  It allowed me to almost without exception choose my battles and only fight when I had an overwhelming advantage.  Add to that copious mercenary cards from my many taverns, and I should have bumped the difficulty to hard at least.  I feel like there should have been a hand of cards limit to avoid stockpiling.
Real Time Strategy (Burninating all the people, in their thatched roof cottages!)
It's odd that the heart of the game was almost completely optional!  When a territory is contested you are presented with the option to auto-resolve it or start a RTS battle.  Any general other than the Dragon Knight auto resolves, but if you choose youself as the general, you start battle.  Then starts a pretty conventional RTS.  Bases are only constructed on pre-designated locations and only by your infantry.  You have two resources, recruits and money.  Money is required for buildings and both are required for each unit contructed.  Summoning yourself (a large dragon with a jetpack) requires recruits (I jokingly suggest you eat them to transform).  While you are flying around as a dragon, you can't issue commands and your army will only follow preissued orders.  It's all very competently done, but I never got the feeling of being an unstoppable dragon.  Mostly you pick away at units until you soak up too much damage and have to flee without having accomplished much.  Wooh...
Overall, it looks like the singleplayer campaign was barely more than an extended tutorial for multiplayer. If I can find a friend with it, I might even try my hand at multiplayer.  Still, I had fun with it and will probably play it again.   I just can't help but wish they had streamlined the VN parts or required RTS more forcefully.  As it is, the three gameplay modes don't really mesh all that well and prevent the game from being truly great.
A compilation of a bunch of games, all of which are fine, but none of which are great.. and are all made weaker by their proximity to each other.  Lame setting.

Witch It is a hide-and-seek game with very similar gameplay to the popular Garry’s Mod game mode “PropHunt”. Though the game is still in Early Access, it is very well polished with a surprising level of player activity for a smaller game, meaning if you had any doubts as to whether you’d actually be able to find games (as some multiplayer games can often be very inactive), rest assured that this game will not leave you in a searching queue for hours on end.
The game’s six maps are all very attractive despite a fairly basic art style and most importantly, perfectly designed for the game. With the way this game works, attention to detail is extremely important as to create maps that make it easy for the witches to hide without making it impossible for the hunters to find them. With that in mind, I do think that the maps they created have made the game very well balanced, where the hunters and witches both win a fairly equal number of times. The maps have also been fairly good for their new “Hunt a Hag” game mode too, as running around the map on top of buildings usually feels smooth, which again goes to show how well the maps were made.
6/10 Points

I loved Prop Hunt in TF2.  This is a standalone prophunt, with its own tweaks and nuances.  For those who havent played, there are two teams.  One team disguises as props on the map (books, pillows, giant cheese wheels) while the other team hunts them.  A very silly game of hide-and-go-seek, with a few special powers on both sides thrown in.  Its a relaxing and goofy game, not a competitive one.
As of writing this, the game is in early access but has received frequent updates for balance, new mechanics, and for seasonal events with new maps and added cosmetic content.  There are two main modes with potential for more in the works.  I've played this game for about 30 hours and scarcely encounted any meaningful bugs, which is a great sign.  Controls feel responsive, are rebindable, and the aesthetics and sound are very pleasing and silly.
If there is any complaint its that the userbase is low... but you only need one modestly populated server to play in (and there are usually a few more) as even at 300ms ping on a cross-continent server the game is completely playable.  I've never had issues where I couldnt find a game, just sometimes only one game mode is represented on populated servers sometimes.  However, if you join an empty server (and with a few friends to help get the numbers up) you can often get people to join on you.  Games are usually best with more than 8 players.
Overall its a good game, I'd recommend it.  If you're worried about playability in the future due to population loss, having a few friends to play with will always help.

While the game doesn't have strong replayability value due to its low amount of unique mechanics, I can definitely say I had a blast playing it through the entire singleplayer campaign.
The battles were fun to lead & satisfying to win, managing to destroy enemy troops as a dragon is fun as♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and the game's art design is wonderful. My main problem was the lack of difficulty here - the battles usually come down to who brings a larger amount of tougher units, which I think are a bit unbalanced too - despite having various abilities, it's clear that a slightly pricier battleship is gazillion times more powerful than the other, lighter ship. It's rather difficult to win fights unless you create a giant army and use that for combat. "Dragon OP, plz nerf", the enemies would say. I think the game would be better if at some point strong anti-dragon enemies were introduced. The game also features a card system - through the game you can get various cards that can help you in battle (boosting your units, damaging enemy units, mercenaries to fight for you), help your empire grow (boost to gold for one turn) or hurt the other empire (destroy his buildings).
The cherry on top of this dragon commanding cake, for me, was the political system and stories of characters on board of the ship - the generals.
First, the political system - a future emperor not only has to worry about leading his units, but he also has to think of the future of his nation. Representatives of five different races live on board of your ship and will hold meetings during which you have to agree  or disagree on some of their ideas, a lot of which are valid in modern times as well - things like taxation of the church or gay rights. All races have different opinions on the issues. The system isn't big at all (quite small, in fact), but I found the issues to be rather interesting and I enjoyed pondering about my choices as I tried to keep up good relations between all the races, especially Elves and Dwarves, who usually have opposite views of discussed problems. Even though I had three races on 30%-40% approval at some point, I have to say bringing them all the way up gets easier as you progress. Your rewards are small - maintaining high relations with a specific race makes it easier to lead battles on their grounds and as a treat you can gain (or lose) bonus gold, science, motivation.
Characters of the four generals serving you, which I mentioned up above, are written well and I find all of them likable, even the character of a snobby lizard who definitely wasn't meant to be liked at all. Occasionally they will ask you for help regarding political issues or situations that may affect your relationship with them, with whole races or bring small advantages / disadvantages.
While the game might not be worth picking it up for its full price, I can definitely recommend it whenever it's on sale.

so this game did not end up doing very well in sales when it was originally released and its not very hard to see exactly why. I just played and finished this game for the first time and its a hard sell. Honestly had I not gotten this for free I would be wondering if this was worth my money right now.
On the positive side this game boasts a very unique art style that has managed to stand the test of time perhaps purely because you most likely will never find a game that looks anything like this game. The writing and characters are top notch, this being no surprise coming from the old Lucasarts Team that brought us adventure game classics like Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle, and Grim Fandango. Every character is memorable, well written, beautifully voice acted, and has little details that give them a huge amount of personality. The Comedy almost never misses a step and the story is engaging all the way through. The level design is beyond creative and clever filled with platforming, puzzles and enemies to fight. Each world takes place in the mind of a character in the overworld that captures their personality and later even the psychological problems some characters face like bipolar disorder. The Game is filled with tons of collectibles that can keep you busy for hours.
Where this game falls apart however is on a mechanical level. This game can be very demanding of the player, while you can certainly meet the challenge that's only if the game allows you to. This game has some terrible controlls, I played with Keyboard and Mouse so people using console controllers might not run into any of the problems I did. I've seen our main Character "Raz" refuse to grab ledges, poles, ropes, and climbable surfaces constantly, there are sections of the game where you can be expected to double jump off a flagpole onto another platform but the game will simply refuse to perform the second jump nearly 80% of the time. "where is my bleach?" or "why is Napoleon Bonaparte missing most of his face?" I don't know about everyone but my game was filled with tons of graphical glitches. Now Double Fine hasn't had the best track record for its steam releases, the game is prone to crashes, not booting up sometimes, and graphical bugs. I basically went the whole game with Foliage blinking in and out of existence until Raz was litterally touching it. I had facial features never render themselves into the game, even Raz's head would appear as a floating set of goggles and  pair of eyeballs constantly throughout the game. Much less of the Hitman: Codename 47 feel.  You can get through almost every level with round-the-corner shooting, even if it's not the way the game is meant to be played.  This game has its frustrating moments, as well as its diabolically clever ones.  7/10

Silent Assassin isn't just the subtitle of this game - it's also the whole theme. Hitman 2 takes the social stealth element introduced by the first game to the next level - enemies who are familiar with a particular disguise are capable of seeing through it if you get too close to them or behave suspiciously, making your choice of disguise tactical. This makes levels far more tense and tactically complex, requiring more thought and planning on the part of the player to carry out hits in a clean way. The game also emphasizes cleanliness more - you get an end-of-mission rating that breaks down your activity, and if you get a perfect score (Silent assassin), you can get bonus weapons for use down the line. Whereas Codename 47 had several levels that encouraged combat on the part of the player, Silent Assassin has pushed the series far more clearly towards stealth and subtlety - and when the bullets do start flying, it's far more satisfying this time around. This game is still somewhat frustrating, but not nearly as much as the original - it's more polished in nearly every way, and the story is presented in a distinctly movie-like fashion, which suits it perfectly. Like it's predecessor, this game has a lot going on for those willing to put up with the occasional bad level or frustration - but not nearly as much as before. Also, this time there are mid-mission saves.

I didn't enjoy this game at first. I put it down and finally came back to it years later. Again I had issues coming to terms with elements of the game.  The movement felts sluggish. The cartography system felt obtuse. But these elements serve a purpose that makes Miasmata a very positive experience on the whole.  The movement system is one you learn to use. It only feels sluggish in that any other movement system is very forgiving, whereas Miasmata's can be punishing.  As a sick man in an unwelcoming landscape, rather than contending with terrorists or zombies, your struggle is you against the land.  A misstep can mean doom if you're scaling a steep hill to get a better vantage point on your surrondings.  Likewise, carelessly skirting a cliff or running down uneven terrain can send you painfully tumbling.  However, once you learn how to move, it becomes second nature and you find yourself discovering safe pathways through the rough wilderness.  The cartography system, similarly, does not hold your hand and guide you through the game.  Instead it is a tool that you use to guide yourself using landmarks.  The game rewards you generously for taking the initiative to explore by planning your trip around keeping known landmarks in sight and discovering new ones to expand your records of the island.
Miasmata is a very refreshing game if you're tired of hand-holding open world games and want an experience of exploration unrivaled by anything in recent memory.

Miasmata is rare gem that I somehow found under the rubble. The game is no where near perfect, as some of the landscape graphics may show. But don't let this unique survival game slip past you for such a low price.

A few years ago, Steam began an ambitious and promising new program called Steam Greenlight, a place where aspiring developers could, for a small fee and compliance with a few simple instructions, post information, screenshots, video, and updates about their game projects for Steam users to vote on. Those that reached a certain number of votes would, when development had finished, be released on the Steam platform.
I remember I was looking at colleges when I saw the program for the first time. An important task, yes. But I realized how important the program was and how the landscape of independent development was changing. Greenlight would allow developers with the best ideas to be easily published by a major company, something relatively unheard of before even in my lifetime. I quickly stopped what I was doing and browsed through the first wave of hopefuls, casting my votes.
Miasmata was one of the first games I voted for. The game oozed potential all over the Greenlight page. For a two-man development team, the environment looked great and a fun place to explore. Gameplay looked fun and different, and the idea of interacting with the mysterious creature intrigued me. I was happy when the game was Greenlit and it became the first Greenlight game I purchased.
While I am pleased at having been a small part of this game’s release I, unfortunately, still stand by the conviction I had when I voted for this game years ago: it still oozes potential. But after a release, that no longer becomes a good thing to say about a game. As a beta, Miasmata would be a hit. As a game right now, it is more a missed opportunity.
The only area in which Miasmata thoroughly succeeds is in the sky effects and day-night cycle. I have yet to see any other game, independent or AAA, match them. Watching the sun rise and set, and the sky change from day to night, is stunningly beautiful and mesmerizing. Watching storm clouds march towards you is both ominous and entrancing. In all of this, the light compliments, accentuates, and stages(and hides flaws in) the environment well. Shutterbugs, fair warning: you will be snapping screenshots like crazy. For a few years, my own screenshots from Miasmata were the desktop backgrounds on my rig. The music is also very well done and I enjoy listening to it while I work.
Miasmata also does pretty well in the overall feeling of exploration. The idea of setting out on a journey through a completely unmapped environment, and uncovering the map yourself, is thrilling (though I found the process of triangulation, albeit realistic, quite a pain). Collecting/analyzing plants and synthesizing medicines is also strangely interesting, probably because it’s so different from anything else I’ve done in games before.
Said journey is often so engrossing that it’s very easy to forget that you’re not alone on the island. The creature (inspired by one of the developer’s cats) does not make frequent appearances (about once every 3 days), so every encounter is memorable and sometimes fatal. One of my favorite memories of playing Miasmata involves one such unexpected appearance. During my first month of college, I was playing the game while listening to an (optional) recorded lecture when the creature suddenly appeared. Giving him the slip was such a terrifying experience I had to rewind the lecture 20 minutes.
Though moments like these are fun and memorable, they are also jarring, especially in an experience clearly more concerned about exploration. It almost brings up a discussion of identity crises, as there is little explanation (that I was able to find anyway) about what the creature is supposed to be or represent, except a way to occasionally terrorize the player and make them forget about what plant they were looking for. Would it be better if there was more explanation or analyzing of the creature? For that matter, what about making the rest of the plot more meaningful (the madman supposedly on the island, and the civil unrest where the protagonist came from)? Could Miasmata still be a game without the creature? Would it have been better with more emphasis on survival (fighting the creature, hunting for food, not just finding water, permanently deteriorating health to stem a sense of urgency to synthesize the cure? Etc.) My answer would be a yes to all of those—if everything else worked well.
Strip all that away, and the rest of Miasmata suffers from a myriad of technical and artistic problems. As an individual with a degree in computer animation, this is both extremely disturbing but also fascinating—It’s like seeing everything I’ve been taught to avoid brought to life. If you do decide to take on this journey, be prepared to see stretched/wonky textures, broken trees, awkward animations (the final scene of the game is hilariously bad, as are the drinking animations), a funny typo at the end of the game, glitched/broken achievements, being able to pick up more than one item in one hand, and odd framerate drops. For the more the more CAD inclined, there is faceting in the animal models, texture seams visible in the arms/wrists, aliasing on the larger water surfaces, and intersecting geometry. Also be prepared to take your own notes on what plants do what, as the notebook is hopelessly disorganized and, later in the game, as more plants are analyzed, is missing information.
I know that, to date, this is one of my harshest reviews. I am aware that I sound demanding. I am also aware that I sound ungrateful to the hard work that the two brothers at IonFX put into making this project, and to the dedicated work of Steam member DarkStarSword in creating fixes for some of the above-mentioned problems when IonFX abandoned it. But my reason for being so critical is because Miasmata deserves to be great. It deserves to be fixed. It deserves the love that DarkStarSword has given it—seriously, hats off to you, sir; a job well done and one that I hope you continue. He has proven that not only does the game deserve to be fixed but that it can be.
At the end of the day, there would be too much of that oozing potential wasted to just say “yeah, I recommend this game for certain people, it was ok.” No, I do not recommend this game. Not yet. Because this is not the greatest it can be. Not by a long shot. But with people like DarkStarSword, it will get as close as it can to that ideal.
It’s only a matter of time.

Besiege is one of those games that makes me wish I could give a "meh" score on Steam. As a physics-oriented building tool, it's great. As a game, it's kind of anemic.
Let's start with the good. Besiege is a medieval-themed game in which you construct siege engines in order to fulfill certain objectives. The physics in this game feel nice and crunchy, and it never gets old to watch your creations tear themselves apart. The visual style of the game is also very good, with a deliberately "simple" style that is deceptively detailed. Most of the levels have unique assets, which makes them memorable to play. There are also many mods available, if that's your thing.
However, as a game, it leaves much to be desired. The levels are preposterously easy to figure out, and the game seems to be unaware of the things that are possible with its own mechanics. For example, I made a crane in an early level and named it "first crane", expecting to make better, more complex cranes for later challenges. But for every level that requires me to lift something, my first, ♥♥♥♥♥♥, crane is enough. There is very little challenge to the levels, and I've beaten too many levels with creations thrown together in five minutes. The game is also a system hog, and older computers need not apply, especially if you intend to use mods.
In the end, I would say the strength of Besiege is that it isn't like other build-a-thon games in that it has progression and a strong theme. But that is also immediately its weakest part, making Besiege one of those games that depends very much on whether or not the player can entertain themselves with it. If you already love building games, you will love Besiege. If you are looking for a fun puzzler, you'll be done in two afternoons, tops.
Besiege is also an Early Access game, and my worry is that the developer will focus more on the sandbox building component than the puzzle component. For now, my judgement is a tentative "recommend", but only because it's cheap when on sale, which is when you should get it.

Somehow, my "recommendation" of this game was deleted. Maybe it was an accident, maybe not. Seeing as that I cannot be bothered to rewrite it, I'll be terse:
The story and music for this game are great. Unfortunately, those are the only praiseworthy things in this game.
About 85% of the game is comprised of VERY boring driving sections where NOTHING happens. If you break a traffic law like speeding or running over someone, you have to evade the police or pull over. You get a game over for serious crimes. You can evade somewhat easily because the AI is dumb. You would think this would work to your benefit in gunfights, but no. Friendly AI charges♥♥♥♥♥first into gunfire while enemy AI has aimbots. The controls are terrible and are obviously a result of a lazy console porting. The game stresses car chases, but they are not developed enough for any strategy, like shooting out tires, to be of any use.
The worst part about the car chases? They can be COMPLETELY NEGATED if you drive backwards. Apparently, the AI is so awestruck that you are able to maneuver in reverse, that it stares at you in amazement.
EDIT:
Some kind reviewers have pointed out that this game was actually released for PC first, and that this is a PC to console port. I admit my mistake, but I feel that this does not help the game at all, and actually strengthens my view that that the controls were absolutely awful.
I have also been called out on the fact that I complained about how tedious I find the driving segments which comprise most of the game. Furthermore, getting speeding tickets due to speeding is actually a criminal offence in the real world, and adds to the "realism" of this game. To this, I have no answer. If you find the thought of living out real life through a digital interface interesting, by all means, do what you must to achieve this. I would feel awful if I kept you from enjoying yourself while getting the most out of life by playing a nearly two-decade old game featuring endless boring driving sequences spaced out with segments of clumsy shoot-and-cover mechanics.

Divinity: Dragon Commander is a great game. I absolutley loved each moment I had with the game. Even when I was being beaten back harshly by the AI on my attempt to start the game on the hardest difficulty, it brought a smile to my face to know that a game is attempting to be challenging nowadays. Thus, please note: This game is hard at the beginning. You start off with two territories, a few armies, and face an enemy that has much more resouces and territory than you do. All the while, you have to juggle the political field with counselors that present problems, choose a wife, and manage your generals. There's also a neat bit where you have to balance gaining resources with losing most of your population. There are three main aspects to the game: Risk, RTS, and Diplomacy.
This game does a fantastic turn-based war map, on par with the old-fashioned Risk board game. It's literally presented as a board game, as you move unit pieces around a map on the bridge of your ship. Everything seems balanced here, as different units constitute different percentages of winning. Assigning generals to the battle will help the battle's odds, but the true varying factor is, indeed, you.
Yes, you can personally oversee each battle on your own. In the battle, you switch back and forth from commanding your armies to turning into a dragon and fighting them yourself. A timer begins each map (which is rather annoying), in which you must build up the largest force possible to counter the enemy until you can intervene and help your troops on the ground. The RTS feels SOOOO much like Starcraft 2, and fans will probably like it as much as I did. I did not feel that the dragon controls were awkard, and easily commanded my armies as a dragon. Of course, once the battle is done, you must return to the ships, where you are expected to be a diplomat.
After each battle, matters arise on your ship. Whether one of your generals is fighting for feminism, gay rights, or censorship, you must attend and solve the situation. After that, counselors from Elves, Imps, Undead, Dwarves, and Lizards will constantly fight over issues such as weapon restrictions, violent media, and religious worship. After that, YOU GET TO CHOOSE A WIFE. EACH ONE IS INTERESTING! JUST DON'T CHOOSE THE LIZARD WIFE! Each wife brings forth unique quests and storylines, which further enhance the depth of the universe. One battles with family matters, another with the traditions of her people, and another experiments with ethics and medicine. It's all very interesting and a joy.
Divinity: Dragon Commander is a great game that has fantastic RTS, Diplomacy, and War-Map gameplay. The only complaint that I have about it is how unequal the counselors are. Every choice seems to be everyone vs. the undead and dwarves. Therefore, if you are conservitave, this game will villify you on 3/5 races. This game actually seems like a great advertisment for liberal beliefs. However, I still loved it, and didn't take it too seriously.
9/10

Lucius is a game even thought it is some bugs, below average graphics and a very limited soundtrack with tracks often looping... I still like this game... well kind of.
Story: Lucius is set in the 1970s where you play a 7 year old boy Lucius who's dad is a powerful and rich politician who they all lived in a large manor. The twist is that Lucius is the spawn of the devil who's being ordered by Lucifer himself to kill all of the people in the manor to extract it to him. For those who are familar with horror film is that it is basicly The Omen: The game but without the well-done twist and add in excessive gore and some nudity and you get Lucius. Yeah the game is not subtle about the satanic references for example Lucius is born on  June 1966 ( 6/66). The Voice acting at least the English speaking version  is not that bad with some actors who in certain scenes convictingly give out emotions to their performance and while their are other actors that are pretty hammy and keep chewing the scenery. So the story in itself is all-right but clearly not the main focus.
Gameplay: Lucius is a third-person point and click adventure game. While i'm sure some people who saw YouTubers playing this thought it played like Hitman, trust me it doesn't and i'll explain in the a second. You explore Dante Manor in order to pick up items in the enviroment  to use as tools to the victim's demise. Lucius while may be the anti-christ, he's still a 7 year old boy so he can't just be like Agent 47 and just choke and shoot people. Lucius must often use stealth and do puzzles in order to create death-traps for the target to be killed by. There pretty varied from poisoning to straight up decapitation. There's one glaring problem with that, why? Because the game is extremely linear. You can only kill people in one specfic way: Finding items to solve a puzzle to see a cutscene of the target being killed in often gory fashion. that's it. It would've been so bad if the game ever tell you what to so most of the time. I swear, one time I have spent 30 mintues to find one item that is on the other side of the manor that's hidden in the enviroment. The supposed "hints" are often to vague and only be triggered if you find the item in the first place. So in the end i have to open a tab to a walkthrough of the game just so i know what to do. I just wish there would be more options for the player to kill the targets to add some  replay valve it and give players more hints.
Presentation: Well the graphics is not so good. but in this case as the developers, Shiver games is a tiny Indie studio with a small budget compared to others, so i let it slide. But it is weird how the adult characters looked fine, Lucius' character model look less of a young boy rather than a little alien. I don't know his face just doesn't look right. teh soundtract while the complain of being looped is annoying at times I admit the tracks are well composed to add the atmosphere of dread and suprisingly spoooky with the loud whsipering and the creepy organ music. But there is some bugs that irrated me such as being stuck into the enviroment and having to reload a save to continue and some wired graphic bugs in the cutscenes but don't worry this isn't doesn't make the game unplayable but soemthing to be mention.
Conculsion: So in the end while Lucius has many, many flaws that can affect my enjoyment of the game at times especially those horrible stealth sections. I do seem to like the game warts and all becuase of it unique concept and strange execution. You don't often see games like these days that's isn't afraid to be odd and strange that make it unique rather than just another bland forgettable shooter or rogue-like etc.
For those who are interested, It is really best to buy the game at sale as it often just cost over a pound  and for others even if you unsure, you don't have much to lose.

The Monster Inside is essentially a visual novel, in that it's all reading with a few interactive elements. It's not a bad experience, if yet very short; up until the last chapter I would say that the writing is pretty damn good, with good pacing (given that it's so short, it's a pretty brisk pace, but the writing keeps up with it) and it is all very faithful to the noir style of monologue/dialogue. The music also helps a lot to set the mood, and the environments serve their purpose pretty well.
However, I will say that the last chapter is a bit of a nosedive. Without spoiling it, it just seems a bit rushed and where the rest of the story has some elegant foreshadowing, the payoff fails to connect. Even the quality of the writing suffers in the end, as if the writer suddenly didn't know what to do with their material and threw together something last minute. It's a bit of a shame, since the rest of the writing does have a lot of promise. As such, it sadly fails to be a fulfilling story, in my opinion: a near miss is still a miss, I'm afraid.
If you really like noir, I would say that this is worth spending half an hour on. For everyone else, it should probably be a pass.

Miasmata is an open world, survival, adventure game where you must craft medicines to cure a disease that is slowing killing you.  There are other medicines that you can create to help you on your journey but beware, for the interior of the island lurks a creature that is hell bent on killing you before the plague does.  Unfortunately, that's where many of the plants grow that can aid your condition.
Pros:
- Highly detailed world
- Passage of time
- The island is very diverse in it's topography
- Mapping the island is fun (at lease for me it was)
- Various plants, many with medicinal properties
- Many notes and pictures to find that will give you clues to plant locations
- You get to play scientist
- There is no place on the island where you can't go
- Numerous unique buildings, ruins, tents, dot the landscape, several with notes so you want to visit them all
Cons:
- The game is not well optimized
- It is very VERY easy to get lost if you leave the path and you will leave the path... many times
- The creature seems to show up at the most inconvenient times (but then again, it's more of a pet peeve then a con)
Besides fashioning medicines, one of the most entertaining activities for me was mapping the island.  I've always had a interest in cartography.  If you want to map the entire island, you have to be clever on where you stand and find two known points of reference, especially when it comes to mapping the interior.
At the time of this review, Miasmata was selling for $14.99.  Well worth it in my opinion.

This game opens with a very interesting premise, you have a disease and you must cure yourself.  The landmass you find yourself on has lots of materials to turn into possible cures, but you need to discover it all yourself.
The crafting mechanic is slightly obtuse, but is somewhat novel in combining plants and other found ingredients together to create healing and other potions.  The map for this game is very unique, you don't get an auto-map like most games, you have to discover and then plot your points using 3 waypoints, so that you can use cartography to map where precisely something is on the map.  It does this for you of course, but it is an interesting and new take on in-game maps.  The fighting mechanic is sorely lacking though.  When you finally come upon your first fight, you will most likely die, and then wonder how you are supposed to prevent yourself from dying.  The game gives you no help here, and largely I guess you are supposed to just run and hide, although rocks and other refuse can help you avoid animals.
Nothing fancy here, the environment is much like many other games, there is a lot of detail in the chemical lab and the grass looks neat.  But nothing here wowed me beyond the panoramic views you can see from vantage points.
Nothing fancy here, the music doesn't take away from the experience and largely gives you a nice time.
I enjoyed playing the game until animals started going after me, at that point I lost interest because I didn't know the game even had combat, was woefully unprepared and just died.  Overall though it was a positive experience until I died.

Like a lot of recent reviews, I'm of a mixed mind on this. I'd like to give this a thumbs up because it's an interesting concept, but the overall execution is just not strong enough to merit it.
For the first hour of playtime I was tense because I knew coming into the game that apparently there is a creature on the island that will hunt you down and kill you. I kept expecting to hear it skulking along behind me in the distance, and a few times spooked myself because I had stopped hitting W but still kept hearing footsteps crunching the leaves—which was just me, staggering along I guess. But eventually I gave up on ever actually encountering any real conflict (other than tripping and giving myself a fever or slipsliding into the bay to nearly drowned).
Really, the control scheme's wonkiness is why I can't recommend the game, not the overall lack of conflict. The controls are this strange combination of stiff and mushy, incredibly accurate at times and utterly non-responsive at others. I'd find myself trying to turn my character only to move forward instead; I'd have to stop moving a good ten feet from the edge of a cliff because I wasn't exactly sure how far forward I might stumble after I released W. I get that the character is supposed to be weak from plague but if that's what they were going for with the "can't climb a speedbump-sized hill but careful you're running full-tilt at that cliff and will take three seconds to stop!" movement scheme, then it's just not going to work for a game.
I think this is a solid alpha for a game, and since I got it on sale for 80% off ($3) it wasn't a horrible purchase, but it's definitely not worth the regular $15 price tag. Give it another 4-6 months' worth of updates and an overhaul of the control scheme, and then it might be fair to ask that much for it.
