TL;DR, get this game if you like to see the beauty of destruction.
At this point, I'm already bored. This game still lacks a lot. Currently, there's only two islands that you can conquer, and it serves as some kind of a learn-and-challenge part of the game. You started off with simple task, finish it, then do it with more obstacles, and so on. But the challenge itself is still so lacking. The fact that there's a bunch of "all-stage machine" is enough to tell just how simple the challenges are. The building functions are still basic, you can only attach stuff, see how it works, if it fail, you fix it, if it works, you add things. But you can't really do much unless you do it outside the game and edit the models yourself.
And I recommend it. This game has its own beauty. You know that urge to destroy things, even the ones you made yourself? You can do it a lot in here. You don't feel like making things on your own? You have a lot to pick in the Workshop. You don't have to worry about losing the machines because you can just reset the stage again and destroy it again. Wouldn't it be boring? Well, yes, I said it at the very beginning that I'm bored. But as a stress relief, this is beautiful. Fly things, blew it up mid-air, on high speed, and see the shrapnels flying around hitting stuff. Or simply give a crack on a wing and let it rattle so much until it meets its misery. The exact same machine on exact same situation will give different results. You can have a catapult, throw a bomb on a tower, reset the stage, throw it again, and the shrapnels are enough to tell you it's not the same result. And my favorite feature? The speed control. You can do a really slow motion and see how every shrapnel shatter and hit the poor soldiers. Yeah, this game is pretty fun.

Mafia is mind numbingly difficult.  Sometimes you have to rely on pure luck to succeed.  This is all good however, because when you do finally succeed it produces a true sense of accomplishment.  At no point in this game does red jam get thrown on your face when you get shot, just so you can hide behind a sandbag and magically regenerate. If you like difficult games, or 1930's American crime, this game is a must for you.

I'll open this review by saying something quickly: Tattletail does not run very well. Others have this problem as well, you can get less than 14 FPS while playing. While it sounds bad, it's still playable and not a game-ruining issue.
Now that that is out of the way, on with the review!
So, everybody and their dog has heard of F.N.A.F (and don't worry, I won't compare it to it that much), Tattletail also utilises jumpscares as its primary source of scare, along with REALLY UNECESSARILY SCARY NOISES. Tattletail is spooky, fast and very unforgiving, especially with what you might expect. You play as a child, who like all of us, really REALLY wanted to open his / her presents, just days before Christmas. So, you sneak down to the basement, despite hearing a
of things you shouldn't hear from the basement. And what's down there making all that noise?
You guessed it. Tattletail. He's the hot new toy hitting shelves just in time for Christmas! He eats real food, and goes through your fridge like it's full of chicken nuggets, but the sexy cutie Furby-like guy needs some serious styling as well, so be sure to keep him brushed! Don't forget his batteries (Not included) also need charging, or else he'll be no fun! He also likes to invite some "friends" over for a "party" sometimes.
This is a very short game, like FNAF, but it has a quirky charm to it: You have to take care of Tattletail. He is so frigging loud as well. Like, on par with that meme where Bart Simpson shouts "testing" into 50 megaphones all lined up. Tattletail is a cutie though, so you can kind of forgive him for being a loud fuzzy fuzzball.
I really don't want to say more, because this is a short game and you should find out for yourself, but I will say this:
Expect surprises, spooks, and cutie fuzzy friends in this delightful indie horror!

An excellent combination of rts, rpg, and turn-based strategy games. Political choices and personal interactions influence the wider world, leaving behind a legacy from your character. Auto-resolve allows you to delegate the responsibilities of battle to your army, or to your extremely skilled generals. Alternatively, you may lead your forces personally in one battle per round, inspiring and protecting your troops, demoralizing and demolishing your enemies, all in your resplendent draconic glory.
Politics allows you to gain greater advantages in your territories, while giving an idea of what actual political decisions are like, as someone will always dislike you for the decision you make.
While the game could also be called an rpg for the storyline that centers on your character, roleplay takes a backseat to  battle and expansion. However, for what the game is, the roleplay is nicely done, allowing you to flesh out your character's likes, dislikes, and opinions through political decisions and character interactions. The relationships between you and your spouse can be particularly rewarding.
All in all, this isn't a game for players expecting a hardcore version of any of the genres it's composed of, but an excellent choice for anyone who enjoys a variety in their games...and those with fantasies of ruling a vast empire with an iron fist.

Divinity: Dragon Commander is an RTS/RPG hybrid game developed by Larian studios, the fellows who created Divine Divinity and Divinity II: The Dragon Knight Saga before going on to create the well received Divinity: Original Sin.
At heart, Dragon Commander is an RTS game - you gather resources, make buildings, build units, and go roll over your enemy's stuff.
The game may appear simple, but Larian studios decided to add a lot of risky mechanics to spice up their game. This RTS throws in a twist, one loyal to the game's name: playing as the Dragon Commander, you have the ability to drop onto the battle field
, flying around the battle field in third person and raining down fire on your opponents. This is possibly one of the only RTS games where you have the ability to summon a super unit you control so directly.
The execution of the Dragon Commander mechanic is mixed. It's an unfathomably cool idea, and having access to the dragon makes for a very fun 'super' button to push. On the other hand, actually commanding your army is more difficult in this stage - making army selections can't be done with the mouse anymore and casting unit spells becomes a bit of a headache, never mind selecting buildings and creating units out of them. Another side effect is, since the Dragon is partially controlled by the WASD keys, units will not have spells or fuctions bound to those 4 keys, making it less comfortable for those RTS players who like playing with a 'grid' setup (where abilities are hotkeyed according to where they are on the menu).
As a pure RTS, the game is weak. The maps do not have wide varieties of objectives, the units are awkward to control, and the mini-map doesn't do much to help navigate. All units supposedly have strengths over others, but there are some which are clearly universaly better than others. One bonus though: free camera control, including the ability to zoom, turn, and even look upwards, a rarity in RTS games!
However, despite the RTS portion of the game being weak, there is an added element which adds depth when playing the story mode: the RPG/political side of the game. Earning favor with races means that any time you hold an RTS battle in a country primarily populated with that race you will have a higher maximum army count, as well as more production from that country when you win. It is very possible that if you fail to ever compromise with a race's demands you will enter fights with a max army size a fraction of your opponent's, upon which your only hope of winning the fight is to rush them. The fact that the roleplay element of the game affects the gameplay element is a very tasteful touch which helps put importance to the political debacles presented.
Sure, the politics side of the game is not executed in the best way possible and some of the decisions you are presented are obviously better than others, but it's still interesting. You are often presented with decisions such as whether you want to install a public healthcare system, tax the church system, add regulations to limit freedom of the press, etc. Most of the decisions are very tongue-in-cheek versions of current real life issues, and the choices made affect resources and gameplay. Interestingly enough, most of the more 'good' choices end up making the game harder, so compromising with the councillors you do not like is sometimes a necessity in order to have reasonable approval ratings in regions where fights are likely to occur. There are dozens upon dozens of choices to make, decisions branch out into relevant new choices, the characters have a wide variety of personalities, the voice acting is believable, and there is an enormous amount of dialogue that will simply not be seen in a single playthrough. This is all completely optional: everything can be skipped, clicked through, or ignored to get back to the RTS portion, though I wish more games had these kinds of options.
All in all, the game is a bit of a power fantasy - except unlike games which turn you into a super-powered being who can screw the lives of evey person in sight (GTA, AC, TES, etc), you get the added perk of being able to screw with the lives of every person
of sight too, and they can't do a thing about it because you're the Dragon Commander/Emperor with incendiary respiration. However, despite having so many glitches and design flaws, and despite the game's concept precluding it from being taken seriously by RTS enthusiasts, at the end of the day the game is just fun. It does a lot of things that no other game of its kind has tried, and though it has not done it in the best way possible, it's the kind of game that makes one hope for a more polished and refined second attempt. As a serious game it has failed, but as a fun romp it has succeeded.

Witch It is an online prop hunt game where witches - you know witch long hooked nose, pointed hat, laugh like a mailed fist scraping down a blackboard, broomstick - try to hide from hunters by turning into any of the props lying around. They can also fly, and cast spells to confuse the hunters. Witches are vegiphobes (who knew?) and loose health if a hunter hits them with a potato, no health - no witch.
The hunters - and what fine figures of manhood they aren’t - are armed with the above potato, a witch finding chicken, grappling hook, anti-magic garlic and a few other gizmos. Both sides select 2 of their skills at the start (a recent change) and you earn more skills by gaining xp points at the end of a round.
The maps range from complex, a manor house with inside and outside, to a simple ice-scape and are all full of items that a witch can use to disguise herself.
It's early access so some things – like selecting graphic detail – don't work yet but the basic game is there and is huge fun. The devs recently added magic dust which players can collect for more xp to try and tempt witches out of their hiding places rather than just sitting there disguised as a book, apple , outside toilet or whatever. Both sides can collect this.
The rounds are short, around 3 minutes, but it does mean you can spend a long time dead if your witch is discovered right at the start. Depending on the server mode, any dead witches become spectators and can zoom around the map watching the action, or join the hunters side. If you join  a match halfway through you do so as a spectator. I once saw a witch player follow behind a hunter for most of a  round without the hunter turning around once.
Some people complain the hunters chicken is overpowered, but it just sits there saying there’s a witch somewhere in range without pointing at their exact location and most of the time the witches will win the rounds... i think this is one of my favorite games now. schafer has done wrong but this is not it. the man undeniably had/has talent. both this game and grim fandango have pixar-quality world building, taking an absurd concept and both treating it as such to have as much fun with it as possible while also grounding it in the context of a more realistic world. it helps you buy into the characters and setting, feeling like a resident of the world because you can more directly understand how it works because it's so fully realized, but also it never loses its fantastical whimsy which makes it believable escapism. writing like this is a reflection of how the world works while still seeing it with wonder. it's a really optimistic look that finds discovery amidst familiar human things. hopefully that makes sense, i'm tired. anyway i always see this game recommended with the caveat of it having bland/bad gameplay but i think that's far too harsh. it's obvious you recommend this game primarily for the story, but if you like 3D platformers in any general sense it's hard to imagine where psychonauts doesn't succeed where a general genre standard like banjo-kazooie does. the game controls fine, the camera is more cooperative than the previous era like you would expect, there's frequent collision issues, but nothing game-breaking. collecting stuff has good feedback and is even upgraded to having some direct connection to the character development, which also includes the world design. this game is a great mix of implied narrative and direct narrative. so many defined details and also a lot of room for you to add your own interpretation. people often like games like banjo-kazooie not for their mechanical depth but because of the constant positive feedback as you explore this fun, charming world, and psychonauts comparatively has so much more meat to it than most of the genre when it comes to that and does not fail on the gameplay part (though is clearly not a mario 64/sunshine/odyssey etc). so in that regard the "weakest" part of the game is still "good". the rest is amazing, and the game's story doesn't burn out the way the latter half of grim fandango does. this will possibly be schafer's greatest contribution to gaming, and hopefully it doesn't get lost in the villainization of both schafer and the style of gameplay.

Any game that makes me take four full pages of notes to put together what is going on I think counts as a good game.
This is one of the few (though this number is growing) games that I consider perfectly mesh gameplay and story together.
Just as films are a visual medium games are an active medium; the best films tell their stories through visuals rather than simply tell the viewer and in a similar fashion the best games tell their story through gameplay.
For those who believe that games must have obvious winstates or combat or running or all the generic gameplay tropes just don't bother buying this. But for people who believe that games should be viewed on the same level as books or movies I absolutely recomend this.
However although I do immedietly recomend this game for doing what more games should I do still have a few criticisms: As you start to put together the games story the useful keyword searches start becoming fewer and farther between, eventually leading to me putting in any word I could think of hoping to find something new. Also the story feels a bit cliche, however the manner in which it is presented somewhat makes up for this.

The gameplay is really immersive and engaging. Puzzling all the pieces together and slowly forming a picture about what happened is fun. I wish there were some additional gameplay elements like some kind of data base to check facts, a notepad to write down thoughts, or a (fake) webbrowser to check some fictional websites about things.
The plot itself though is pretty ludicrous and your enjoyment will depend heavily on how much you can suspend your disbelief. Since the presentation is so hyperrealistic, I had a hard time buying into some of the revelations.
Ultimately I like the concept of the game more than the actual game itself. I still recommend it, though if you haven't, play Gone Home first.

Miasmata is survival geocaching. You're a plague-stricken scientist who must create a cure by finding specific plants on a remote island, via the use of exploration, maps, clues and cartography.
The central gameplay mechanic is unique and very appealing to me. I've always wanted a game that did this and I'm happy to say that it does this part extremely well.
The terrain is nicely detailed and there's plenty of little animals on the island, which really bring it to life. I thoroughly enjoyed exploring the island, discovering the plants and uncovering the story.
Consequently I am recommending this game, but it is important to say that there are a lot of problems. This is far from a polished game. Notable things are:
* The game crashed twice and then crashed again during the end. Somewhat anti-climatic, but at least it worked after restarting the game.
* After closing the map/journal the game would very frequently ignore my mouse movements. Meaning I would have to open and close the map/journal again. This got extremely frustrating. The map and journal are well designed, but the bug put me off using them as much as I wanted to.
* The character can somehow climb up very steep terrain, but will also fall on easily navigable terrain. It doesn't make a lot of sense.
* Many floating trees.
* Can't pick up two of the same plant.
* During animations the colour of objects can change, which is a bit immersion breaking.
* Creating a duplicate of an item you already own will just overwrite that item, with no warning or explanation.
* Terrain was constantly popping in and redrawing, even just a couple of metres in front of me.
* The terrain diversity is quite limited, which is further worsened by the colour draining. The unique terrain features that do exist are memorable and make the island seem more alive, but the amount of them is very small. It would have been nice to have a waterfall, clearing, cave, tunnel, proper cliff, massive tree, etc.
My final issue with the game is subjective, so I'm not including it in the list. I didn't care for the creature at all. I felt that it was an unnecessary feature that added very little to the game and became an annoyance very quickly. It appears very early in the game and will happily stand there in the middle of the path, so there's no suspense or mystery. The game's description says the creature will stalk you for miles, which sounds amazing, but I didn't see any proof of that happening. If someone said it randomly appeared in a random location near you, I'd have no evidence against that.

Miasmata is not really a bad game, it has potential, but it is not one I would recommend anyone to play. It feels unfinished, like it is lacking some essential key aspects for making it a really good experience. The graphics, the story and the gameplay are all quite lacklustre. There are no puzzles, no character interactions and essentially no combat.
I finished the game, but I cannot say why, other than pure stubbornness.  The graphics are not too bad, but not exactly gorgeous (and view distance is pretty awful), which is a problem. The game consists almost exclusively of exploration, but there really isn't that much to explore. Sure, the island is big, but you don't really get those "wow, what an awesome place" experiences. You see an interesting looking ruin in the distance and you run there... and there is nothing to see. That's the experience you will have all the time, in between running through relatively bland vegetation.
Similarly, the story is okay, with notes scattered around to give some idea of both who the people on the island were and the place they were coming from. But as you don't meet any people and the main character never speaks, there is a very empty feeling. I did not find all the notes, but the ones I did offered a pretty lacklustre story that evoked more "Oh... okay then" rather than "Wow, I wanna find all the notes and figure out what is going on.". I found myself looking for the notes mostly to find maps of the area and directions to the cure ingredients. And its good that they are there, but it doesn't make them very interesting. Getting the ingredients also doesn't require any special ability or thought-process. It's all spelled out in the notes, you just have to walk to the right place. There are no puzzles in the game.
So what about the gameplay? Well, there is very little. The game is actually very easy, I only died once... because the creature hit me through a wall. And it really is THE creature, because there is only one enemy type in the entire game. The only other enemy is the controls. You have to be careful of how you run as you are very likely to fall over, even at small inclinations. And you slide like you're wearing rollerskates. And falling will give you fever so you must make medicine. But that only serves to slow you down. If you don't run too fast and you avoid the creature (which is not very hard) you will be fine. And once you realise that, the tension kinda disappears. There is nothing to fear on this island but boredom.
So overall, I did not hate my time with Miasmata, but the only really memorable part was the frustration from the controls. I would not play it again and I would not recommend it to anyone else.

This is my ultimate sleeper game. You wake up on a mysterious island with blood on your hands. At first, it's an ambulation simulator.  Walk around, pick flowers and orientate yourself to your surroundings. Just like your gran on a day-trip to a botanic garden,except your gran isn't being chased by an ethereal demon, trying to escape from a lost island, and synthesising drugs to survive.
As your character progresses, they pick up the basics of ethno-botany, cartography and organic chemistry. You develop a deep appreciation of regular hydration and the plot gets weirder and weirder by the minute. Armed only with a feeble throwing arm, a selection of rotting fruit and the occasional burning twig, you uncover the mystery behind your disease.

I couldn't let the story go. I dug deeper and deeper. I got to the ending and thought this game is a worthy successor to the literary novel. Hyperbole aside, this game is intriguing, deeply satisfying and introduced me to a narrative driven experience that is a well-crafted alternative to the alpha-wave twitch. Miasmata has a highly  enjoyable discovery/survival game mechanic with an excellent soundscape. Your own heartbeat never sounded so terrifying.
It still astounds me  that it was made by only two people. It needs a sequel.

A great horror-survival-exploration game that's worthy of attention.
You begin the game stranded on a beach, exiled because of a contagious disease...
That's it, then it's basically up to you to explore, find clues and try to stay alive in hope of finding a cure.
Quick Summary:
This game is a great example of an exploration game where you need to make sure you have enough water to stay alive and where, at night, losing your source of light is the worst thing ever, while avoiding an unknown creature and trying to find a cure for your condition by searching the local plantlife for ingredients.
It is an immersive, tense and beautiful experience that I highly recomment to everyone interested.
+
Atmosphere:
Man does this game nail everything I like about atmosphere and ambiance.
It is stunning and mysterious at day and yet absolutley terrifying and pitch-black at night,
and the ambient sounds really makes the environment come alive.
Sound:
While the game has almost no music, it more than makes up for it by the afromented
ambient sounds which range from flowing water to tweeting birds.
+-
Graphics:
Alright, let's face it: the character model looks kinda bad, as does a few other things;
the water from the pitcher comes to mind...
The fauna however looks absolutley stunning, and you could (and probably will) get lost in
the islands locales whether merely trying to get a better view or to find new plants to
experiment on.
Gameplay:
Gameplay isn't exactly what you would call exiting and is a matter of taste.
Do you like picking up random plant life, checking them for new components, combining
medicine, triangulating your position trying to explore the island while keeping yourself from
dehydrating or getting sick-er as well as being scared because darkness is falling then
getting lost for days on end?
Also, there is a creature on the island that is far from friendly...
Personally, I love it, it is a tense experience, but it might not be everyone's cup of tea, but
on the other hand, if any or all of these sound appealing to you I highly recommend this
game.

Bought it on the Steam Sale in Oct 2015. I think everyone ought to try this game. It's got so many interesting features, ranging from the Strategic Cards, Dragon Abilities, tech trees to diplomatic relations. Definitely worth trying.
1. Interesting Game
It is both familiar and refreshing to see the Dragon Commander's characters. The standard Tolkien lineup of human, dwarf, elf, dragon and undead lets you expect certain stereotypes of the races. However, the slight tweaks and nuances of the races do make the game more interesting. E.g. The technical Imps (instead of goblins), the religious Undead (instead of a holy Ecclesiarch) and the business-like Dwarves (instead of a helmet and pickaxe rune monger).
2. Strategic Map and Combat Map
Kudos to Larian Studios. I love the Strategic Overview and the Combat Map. The difference between macro and micro is so distinct, yet the game plays so smoothly. On the Strategic Map, the little chess pieces that you load onto the transports are so beautiful.
3. Character Interactions
Too few to count but it is pretty interesting to hear the conversations and complaints.
4. The Raven
I love the command ship. So cool. I wish I could interact with some interesting parts of the ship. E.g. The main batteries / canons, buying a cloaking module for the ship, watching the crew have conversations and gossip.
5. Interaction Choices
I was hoping for a 4 choice table whenever a tough decision has to be made. It would be arranged in a square with 2 options on top and 2 options below. Some options might even be greyed out due to one not fulfilling certain conditions.
6. Political Intrigue
A bit more juicy please. So far, I get the very dry and stale decisions which can be decided with a "flip-a-coin" contest.
7. Combat Map
Love the scroll out view. Reminds me of Supreme Commander. Love not having to do Bob-the-Builder
1. Jetpack Dragon
There is a Chinese saying "Drawing legs on a snake". It is a proverb of two boys who competed to draw a snake. One was so good at art, he drew a complete snake in matter of seconds. However, in his arrogance, he added legs to the snake. This, of course, lost him the competition.
2. Dragon Cards
I do not like having to bind the Dragon Card Skill from the list of skills to the 0-9 keys, if there is excess space. It should be default. Imagine if you missed binding the key, you would have wasted a Dragon card for no reason.
3. Ships & Land Masses
There are some maps where you have 2 water bodies split by a land mass. This causes the reinforcements that you bring in to be stuck on the wrong side of the land mass, preventing you from hitting the enemy base. I think the name of the map might have been 2v2 Dragon Pass (I might be wrong on this). I know that naval units are hard to balance with the water body maps but I think you can solve it with water teleportation / Dragon transport.
4. Campaign Act I
It is odd but I think that prolonging Act I is more beneficial to the player than cutting it short. If you end Act I too fast, you won't have enough research to bring over to Act II. Thus, it's actually beenficial to conquer the whole map in Act I and drag it on until you complete enough dragon/unit research.
5. Combat Map
The view and orientation are horrible. The minimap and the orientation do not move in tandem. E.g. You move forward and the minimap moves right.
6. Units
It's kind of boring attacking the same units that you have. I can see that both sides have a
1. Trooper
2. Grenadier
3. Warlock
4. Shaman
5. Hunter
6. Zeppelin
7. Imp Fighter
8. Transport
9. Ironclad
10. Dreadnaught
11. Devastator
12. Bombing Balloon
13. Armour
More asymmetry please. Add more unique units to the list? I was expecting each faction to add 13 unique units to each side, at the very least. That way, you would get 39 different units, not counting unique buildings. There's a defunct game called Naval Warfare that you could take the units from.
7. No Tutorial
You have to guess that you right click on the map in order to build units. You have to guess that it's a turn based game and you end your turn by clicking on the hourglass.
8. Unintuitive Keys
Q for Auto-attack? Why not A?
1. Racial Superweapons / Superpowers
For example, if you became extremely friendly with the Imps, you could create a super Imp Air Fortress. If you became extremely friendly with the Elves, you could get use rare Land Magic of the Elves.
2. Overcoming the Limitations of Water
Screw physics, you already have a jetpack dragon. Here's a list.
a. Airship Dreadnaughts
They used to be limited by water, now they fly.
b. Giant Air Transports for Ships
Now you can move ships from one water body to another, even across mountains. You could even use the Dragon.
c. Ship Teleportation
The Hunter can already teleport. Why not teleport the ships? If this reduces the uniqueness of the Hunter, how about a whirlpool effect, just like Heroes of Might and Magic?
3. Enemy Generals
You have 4. Maybe you can capture / convince more to your side?
4. Arguments between the Diplomats and the Generals
How would that pan out?
5. Unit Backstory
I know that this might sound strange but it helps to flesh out the story but engaging with a story character that signifies a certain unit. E.g. Admiral Stukov from Starcraft (Battlecruiser), Sarah Kerrigan from Starcraft (Ghost)
6. Certain Major Strategic Locations for the Campaign
Every location on the strategic map is more or less the same, save for the Capital. Perhaps, Larian could include some areas where there are certain special buildings or quests? These maps would then have a special map designed just for campaign purposes. The current method of using a multiplayer map isn't as exciting.
7. Co-Op Campaign
This game can be played with friends vs AI. Could you add that function in?
8. Multiplayer Allies
As far as I understand, there is no such option available. Each player takes their own position.

Divinity: Dragon Commander allows you to play in one of three ways, Campaign Mode, Custom Campaign, and Skirmish. You can select one of three dragons, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. Visually the game looks both beautiful and amazing. It has a very modern look with great colors and attention to detail. Much like the total war series, Divinity: Dragon Commander uses a combination of Turn based strategy, and real-time strategy. Players can research abilities, talk to NPC's, and such, much like you would in an RPG. You then move on to the turn-based portion of play where you can select your units, move, construct, etc; Finally, when it comes to actual battles, you can use real-time strategy, or allow the battle to auto-resolve.
As far as the story for Divinity: Dragon Commander, it takes place long before the other games in the series, making it a prequel. The story seems interesting as you must go to war to destroy demonic technology. The RPG portion of the game is static however, and does not allow you to move around in first person, which is a downer, because it looks fantastic. All in all it is an interesting game, combining a lot of different elements, with a decent story and beautiful visuals.

It's an odd blend of game genres, and I'm not sure how many people it will honestly appeal to, because I'm sure most people will either find turn-based strategy and dialogue trees boring or the hectic third-person bullet-dodging RTS too frantic, but for anyone who likes being jerked between slow and fast, this is a game with a decent variety of game on offer.
Unfortunately, like many "kitchen sink genre" games, the strength of the game has to come from its collective whole, because its individual components don't quite stand up on their own.
The turn-based strategy game is clunky and board game-y without any of the more free-wheeling rules that make actual strategy board games more interesting.  You buy troops and mash them into other units to claim land you use to buy more troops or research points to unlock more troops you can buy.  You can go into RTS mode to win one battle per turn that would otherwise be hopeless, because the turn strategy game is raw dice rolls with what existing units you had on the map, while, once in RTS mode, your constructed units swiftly outnumber whatever units you had on the board game section, rendering being outnumbered by anything but the most ludicrous margins a minor temporary inconvenience.
The "political decisions" part of the game is like playing through South Park parodies of different political groups, but without any jokes, and being told to take them all seriously because you need them all to like you.  They're paper-thin cardboard cutouts of different interests with zero charm, and some of the voice acting is terrible.  I'm convinced whoever wrote the man-hating Catherine's dialogue was a man who hasn't spoken to a real woman in at least 10 years, because she both goes on endlessly about how inferior men are, but then also makes a constant stream of biggus dickus jokes while doing it.
. It's like Wizardchan wrote the character just to talk about "how dumb feminazis are, amirite?" The imp (amoral scientists) ambassador has lines expressing disgust or rage or sorrow, but can't manage any tone other than a sedated mirth.  The undead (religious) factions talk about how mercy or compassion are the sole providence of the gods, and how caring about your subjects or trying to better your realm is a sin, basically making religion always evil all the time.  These are the most egregious cases, but generally, the game wants you to hate all its characters equally besides maybe the upgrade characters, which in turn means you have little investment in any of it.  It's terrible, because it deals with real, serious issues, but then ham-acts the setups and consequences so badly and basically demands you go for stat benefits, not your own moral compass.
Your political choices rarely have the sorts of impact you'd expect other than who likes or dislikes you, and it seems these choices are geared mostly towards just making sure you keep everyone mostly on-board with you, because you suffer combat penalties (including "support" penalties that deny the ability to build units) conquering new territory if you enraged the race that dwells in those territories.
Also, humans apparently don't exist anywhere but on your ship, because they don't hold any land.
The RTS section has barely over a dozen units, your bases are built on pre-defined locations, even turrets, no worker units exist, and buildings have no upgrades or tiers. (This is so strategic mode units matter more - all units available from the start of battle.) It lacks some features from games like Supreme Commander that I really miss when I'm in dragon mode, like the ability to simply tell my factories to just keep producing specific units in a specific proportion forever, instead of having to keep popping out of dragon mode to babysit my factory because I worked through the build queue.
The tech tree makes this worse, early-game.  The air and sea units unlock later than ground units, so for a while, your only air unit is the zepplin support unit, then an interceptor unit who can only be used to shoot down other interceptors and zepplins, (which can be shot down just fine by the ground units,) and only in the mid-late game, when bombers exist, does controlling the skies actually start mattering.
The ability to fly down onto the gamefield would make some sense as a way to entice players who traditionally aren't RTS playres if and only if you really could win without worrying about the RTS components so much, but that's rather deliberately not the case.  The RTS portions of the game lack the previously-mentioned scriptability of a game like Supreme Commander, forcing micromanagement babysitting that mean that you wind up having to constantly dodge missiles, shoot at enemies, drop buffs on allies, order troop movements, keep an eye out for enemy flanking attacks or cloaked enemies, and babysit factory build queues all at the same time, and it's massively overwhelming.  You ultimately have no way of controlling your army from dragon mode except by hitting the "select all" button and generally mashing them all into one big mob that you clumsily lob at the enemy while trying to support as best you can manage.  I frequently find myself with no clue exactly how many of my units I even have left while trying to stand my ground against ceaseless waves of enemy forces.
Simply not using dragon mode, on the other hand, is generally not an option.  It's just way too overpowered
to use it, especially early-game against things like troopers, which your dragon can easily shred with impunity.  Whereas shaman support units have a shield that can block 50% of damage, your dragon can drop one that lasts longer, blocks 75% of damage, and has a cooldown short enough that you can drop it on two units.  In fact, if you just buff your own troops, they're basically invincible between a shield buff reducing damage, a buff that makes them shoot faster, a buff that ups damage, a buff that makes them move faster, a passive buff that gives regeneration to every friendly nearby, and to top it all off, a skill that turns your fireballs into healing bolts that you can use to basically ensure none of your units ever drop below max health for more than a fraction of a second.
On the other hand, if you're in dragon mode, all the active abilities of units like shamans and warlocks tend to be wastes of research points, because you can't activate them in dragon mode, and would be far too busy to individually select specific units even if you had the button to do so.
Also, the dragon is surprisingly fragile against concentrated anti-air defenses like a half-dozen ironclads, and you can easily wind up in a situation where you have utterly lost control of the sea in such situations.
The end result is that battle becomes a confusing brawl where you frequently drop out of strategic situational awareness to focus upon personal conflict, only to dart back out to try to reassess what just happened while you were away. (Oh, look, a transport dropped off some troops in that minor side-base and captured it, now you have to take it back!) It makes for slippery gameplay where you never quite feel in control, and are mostly just trying to tread water, keeping an eye on everything you need to be aware of, using all your powers as they cool down, even while you're unquestionably winning.
And this is single player... Add in another player who's also a dragon and can duel you on even terms, and you have a recipe for completely ignoring the rest of the battle.
The result is a giant chaotic mess, but it can certainly be an amusing chaotic mess.  I just wish it featured more tools to actually help players, like AI settings that let you tell units to use special abilities on their own.

This review is a "compare & contrast" with another popular fishing title released around the same time, Fishing Planet. I like both and think they're both quality titles, but they do different things well and will satisfy different tastes. This review is meant to help you decide which one you might prefer. I wrote a similar review for FP, and will update both when FP comes out of early access.
DTG's Euro Fishing really nails the old adage "There's more to fishing than the fish." The different lakes have a real sense of place, and they're all beautiful locations that are a pleasure to be in. This is helped by the ability to actually walk around each location and fish from different areas. Being able to explore and discover your own favorite spots adds a lot to the feeling of authenticity. While Fishing Planet may have a greater diversity in locations and environments, only a few tiny areas in each place are open to you.
After landing each fish, DTG's Euro Fishing gives you a little photo-op with your catch. This might sound silly, but it actually adds a lot to the game by providing a sense of closure to each catch and a sense of personality to the fish. It's why Euro Fishing is one of only 2 games I ever bother to screencap (the other being Kerbal Space Program).
The fish themselves are well done, and thanks to the photo-ops you get some time to really look at them. Fishing Planet's fish look good, but not nearly this good (and w/o a good photo-op moment, you never get a clear look at them anyways).
You can play multiplayer matches with other people on the same lake. FP, while ostensibly an MMO, is so highly instanced its multiplayer is basically a chatroom added to a single-player game. That said, both communities are very friendly and helpful, and FP's multiplayer features haven't been fully implemented yet.
This is a blessing and a curse. Casting is an actual skill to master in DTG's Euro Fishing, which makes it satisfying when done well and frustrating when it impedes you from catching fish. Landing the perfect cast to catch a unique fish you know is hiding in *that* weed bed feels like an accomplishment. Casting your rig into your foot over and over again for 10 minutes gets aggravating. FP's casting is much easier, but is nothing more than a power meter.
Most areas have a number of unique named fish. Since IRL people fish stocked, managed lakes where you must release your catch, some fish gain names and reputations (one famous carp even received a burial from anglers after it died of old age). These unique fish are well-implemented, and catching one is a fun accomplishment. They go a long way toward adding personality to each location. FP's unique fish don't have nearly this much to them, and seem to be just very large specimens of the species.
All of the locations in DTG's Euro Fishing are stocked lakes. While you can walk around and explore them all, they all lend themselves to the same kind of fishing. Compare that with FP, which has a much greater diversity of location types.
DTG's Euro Fishing currently has one kind of fishing: ledgering. This is a rather sedentary form of catching fish, where a weight holds your line to the lake bed and you wait for a fish to pick up your hook & bait. Float fishing will be added in a future free DLC, but currently you only get to do one kind of fishing: ledgering for carp & coarse fish. Fishing Planet supports both float and spin fishing. Spin fishing in particular is a much more active method of angling, and FP even recognizes different techniques and styles of presenting the lure.
Lake fishing for carp & other coarse fish is the focus of DTG's Euro Fishing. No trout, no pike, no crappie, no bass, no salmon etc.
Euro Fishing's selection of gear is pretty small, and the descriptions do a mediocre job of explaining what it all does. Fishing Planet has a dizzying amount of gear, which supports its greater variety of target fish, locations and fishing styles.
Netting & landing fish is barely functioning at the moment. It beats FP's landing mechanic (it has none), but it won't take much for FP to release something far superior.
A fishing game really needs better water. It doesn't cripple the game, but it doesn't compare well to the water in Fishing Planet. Considering how much time you spend staring at it, I'd have hoped for something more convincing.
Euro Fishing's tutorial is mediocre, but it actually has one (which is more than can be said for FP). However, it does has a really helpful series of videos to help those completely new to coarse fishing. Unfortunately, the lack of a wiki will hamper those who want to dive deep into the game. This is a similar issue with FP, which lacks a real tutorial but has a great WIP wiki.

This is not going to show as an "Early Access review" but as far as I'm concerned it should be. DTG pushed the release on this (Nov 2), perhaps to try and counter Fishing Planet.
It was a mistake because the bugs and problems with this are numerous.
Some of the glaringly obvious:-
- Fish that SLIDE sideways, they don't swim at all. Sure, their tails wag but that's the model, not the AI. They almost teleport they move so fast sometimes. Even the biggest fish around the 40kg mark, bounce and slide around like a Smartie in a blender. I've written script for fish and rotating them "naturally" is a pretty simple task. Adding proper inertia and momentum is a little trickier but certainly doable too.
- The casting is not bad (with practise) but a 50m cast, to the opposite side of a lake, which looks to be 150-200m away, is up on the bank. 2 winds of the reel and you're back in the middle of the lake at 30m or so. In some cases you can't even see where your gear is until you bring it back to under 30m.
- Reel winding is shocking. A 5:1 reel, with zero tension, should be bringing in close to a metre of line per turn. You can literally turn the handle 50 times and get back a metre of line. I made this observation in the forums and was told it's an "audio" problem because I mentioned I should at least be hearing the clutch slipping. Did they answer about not being able to wind in with zero tension or that my reel acts like it's  1:25 ratio?  Not even mentioned.
- Fish snap off, for no reason, in some places on some maps. Can't even be bothered reporting it.
- The fish "fight" is only really differentiated by time. A BIG fish in RL can and will run for 10's of metres non-stop, sheer power. Smaller fish dart and dance. Some of these 40kg monsters swim like a Goldfish and you get frustratingly stuck with a bouncing yo-yo fish, 7m out and 5m deep, going nowhere. Some smaller fish, where your breaking strain is 3 times that of fish, simply "lock up" 10m out and just pull against the line. You cannot wind them in, you have to pump and wind like it's a 10kg carp.
- 15lb Touchdown line is borked. Unlimited drag. Max it to 100% and skulldrag your fish straight in. I mentioned this is a pretty serious exploit because XP and TP (the currency) is linked to catches. There are also live tournaments against real players and anyone NOT fishing 15lb will lose - obviously. Answer from devs. "It's up to you if you use it or not".
- Tournament scores do not update in RT, in some cases not at all.
- "Boss" fish are able to be caught one after another. I caught 5 in a row, from the same location, using the same gear, line, bait. everything.
- My favourite. You can catch a "Boss" fish (all independently named) on Rod #1 and while you're taking it off the hook, Rod #2 goes off and presto..... same Boss fish. I've caught 3 in a row on this, others have caught the same Boss 5 times in a row.
- FPS is capped at 30fps. Yes folks. UE4 engine, PC game, CAPPED at 30fps.
- AMD users are suffering all kinds of glitching, gamma, flickering and crashes. Devs say it's AMD and/or Epic (UE4). Anyone who playes the multitude of UE4 games out there (Ark is one of the most popular) knows that AMD cards are NOT suffering this across the board.
- VERY short gameplay. In 40 hours, much of it playing the broken tournaments, I am nearly maxed out and own almost everything.
- The gear. Some of it is so similar (or lacking in gameplay neccessity) that it makes accumulation pointless. BUT, you need to buy item #1 to be able to buy item #2 so... accumulate you do.
Look. I've had enough of this, I've annoyed myself, sounding all whiney and sooky. I could go on but just the attitudes of devs to problems you officially document is pretty poor. A whole lot of pseudo-surprise, "we'll look into it", "our testing didn't do that"  etc... all the while telling you they're working on more content, and given it's Dovetail Games, it'll be mostly DLC.
For now. IF it's on special it might be worth a look because they MAY address these issues. $20 for 40 hours is probably not too bad so I'll not complain too much more.
IF this had been an Early Access title my review would be completely different and my tolerance for errors would be much, much higher. But when you release broken titles... Shame.
5/10

This game is basically a knock-off versions of Furbies, but their Mama is possessed by Satan, who was captured by your mother in a vase.
When you break the vase, you awake Mama, and the horror begins.
The game's first two nights are simple, and teach you what to do:
On the first night:
-You learn about the ''Sound'' mechanic in this game;
-You learn the position of the fridge and the brush;
-You learn you need to feed and groom (Not reffering to the Outlast: Whistleblower one) the Tattletail.
On the second night you learn:
-About the recharger;
-About Mama;
-About the existance of a flashlight (Sadly it's a shake one).
The game is incredibly good, inflicting horror through the eerie sounds when you're hunted by Mama, and when she gets you, the jumpscare will be ten times as efficient.

Whilst the map itself is small, it still is pretty good.

Who doesn't like snipers? Well, maybe the poor guys that have to patrol those deserted open streets and jungles. Ever since I played the "All Ghillied Up" and "One Shot One Kill" mission in Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, snipers have always kept a special place in my heart. They are portrayed as coldblooded, skilled experts, trained to kill with precision. And while the sniper has sadly lost some of his respect, especially in video games (thanks for that one, codkiddies, hope the noscopes were worth it) they  are still treated with a lot of respect in most media (give the movie "Shooter" and the Sniper series a try if you're interested in more one shot one kill gunporn). So back when I found out about this game, I was kind of interested in it. But just like Metro 2033, it's not until quite some years after releasedate in 2010 that I finally bought a copy for just one key and tried it out. And boy, does this review hurt to write. Because not only did I want the game to be good, I even enjoyed it sometimes. Yes, you read that one correctly. Quite a few aspects in Sniper: Ghost Warrior are a lot of fun. The sniping mechanics are pretty sweet and so is the bullet cam (arguments about whether or not a gory cam like Sniper Elite's is better belong in the comments). The graphics are fairly pretty and the tropical island setting seems to be a nice homage to the previously mentioned Sniper series (first one is set in South-America). The story, while nothing spectacular, does the job: dictatorship overthrew the democratic government and we can't go in all guns blazing, so you go and snipe things out for us (kind of like in that movie again..). And hey, there are some jokes, there's some cool stuff, all that. Voice-acting is solid, but I'd appreciate it if the enemy soldiers would stop talking about each others' sisters so much, or what brand of tobacco they prefer. But there are some big problems with the game, too. Firstly, the AI is just strange, as in the bad kind of strange: sometimes they're nothing but brainless tangos with legs, just waiting for a bullet through the brain, sometimes they seem to have binoculars for eyes and can spot you when you can't even see them. The AI is very accurate with their weapons, which is not that much of a bad thing in a stealth game (you shouldn't remain alive long if you'd happen to be spotted), if it weren't for the fact that you sometimes have to go "all guns blazing".
That's right! Forget your stealthy ghilliesuits, scope breathing and breath holding fetish, we've got ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and forced assault rifle segments to play! Although I must admit some of these missions aren't so bad if you're still allowed to keep your distance and can pick them off before they even notice you. Sadly, the game felt like targetting the CoD audience and thus you sometimes play as Ranger McAssaultrifle to use your M4 that seems to have more recoil than any other fire arm in the game, even sniper rifles.
There are so many weird and downright awful things about this game but I won't waste too much of your time anymore. I cannot recommend the game, I'm sorry, except if you really want to play a sniper focused game that is played in first person and you can get this game for cheap (one key is a reasonable price, two is the maximum amount I'd pay). Despite all the previous stuff I mentioned, I enjoyed Ghost Warrior a lot sometimes. The fairly open levels work wonderful in a jungle or island setting and you sometimes feel like a real ghost warrior in some of the better stealth missions. But the lazyl AI programming, bad decisions in game design (giving an USAS shotgun more range and less recoil than an assault rifle? Really?) and bugs or glitches you'll encounter sometimes keep me from recommending me this one to a lot of people. If you want to give it a try, feel free to do so, but be warned: there's a lot of ugy besides the wonderful sniping mechanics. That said, I am looking forward to giving the sequel a try, although that one seems to have received mixed ratings as well.

This game is a very good rts that requires quite a bit of tactical play as well as strategy and unlike more traditional rts games this game focuses more on tactics than actions-per-minute or unit spamming.
Before each battle you must select a deck of units which you can customise to suit your play style. Initially it is a bit overwhelming because of the sheer amount of units to choose from so it's best to start with any custom deck and fine tune it after every battle as you learn more. Eventually you could have different decks to suit different strategies and maps. It's a lot of fun creating a deck, previewing the units and checking out their stats.
The graphics and effects are amazing but during a battle you probably won't get much chance to see them in all their glory. However if you win a good game make sure to play back the replay and you can view the action up close and personal.
Multiplayer seems to be where this game is at it's best and although a lot of the player base seems to have moved onto it's successor Red Dragon you can still get a game in most times. There are also single player campaigns and a skirmish play mode too. Overall I would recommend this game.

Live action video in a game is nothing new; Many developers in the past have experimented with this medium to try and enhance the gameplay. Often these come off as corny or just plain bad but, Her Story is a game that mangaes to make it feel real. Settle in and listen to her mind boggling account of the events that would lead to murder.
Her Story starts with a message telling you that you are an authenticated guest of the police department, and you have access to these specific case files using the crime database. At your fingertips are tapes; interviews with the wife of the deceased. Short videos appear on the screen that you watch one by one in hopes of adding more information to the story. The videos are between 10 seconds and a minute, with differing information, date stamps, and Her appearance changes from video to video. This can all seem somewhat confusing at first but, after time feels natural; like your really reviewing old case files.
The database will only show you 5 videos at a time so you cannot just flip through and watch them all at once. Instead you have to search different key terms in the database to get videos refering to them. Say you type in murder, the database will give you the first 5 videos where she says the word murder. Players will need to pay close attention, and even rewatch videos to get info that could lead to their next search. She often drops names, workplaces, local areas and other things that become vital in your search efforts. This all helps to make players feel emersed in the gameplay and it works with little flaw.
As you dive deeper into the narrative, you start to make sudden realizations about her story. Pieces begin to connect and the story lines up. Many theories are already swirling in players heads as they slowly but surely narrow it to one connecting timeline. The story has so many nooks and crannies that doubt still lies in everything eliminated; and the story is told in a way as to be intentionally confusing. This is one wild ride that is hard to find in other mediums. Her Story plays more like an interactive movie; where the viewers can enjoy it at their own pace, as well as exploring her story with little restriction. Players are free to uncover different parts of the story at very different times depending on which key terms they search. Player's truely feel like the investigating detectives, the accused seems very guilty, and the whole world comes together and feels real.
The gameplay is quite simplistic; You are placed at a 90's computer screen and free to click around at things on the desktop. There are different things to read and see on the desktop, but none more important than the criminal database. The oversimplified colour schemes of a 90's desktop are a throwback to most players youth; and you can even see some flourescent lights reflecting in the monitor. Littles cosmetic things in the game do make you feel as though your sitting in front of a Police computer.
Her Story is fine to play by yourself but, I would definitely recommend putting this on a TV and playing with friends. You can get even more of a feel of a group of detectives trying to crack a case. Everyone bounces theories off each other, and the whole story felt easier to keep up with when discussing it together. Like I said this somewhat feels like and interactive movie, and therefor deserves a bigger audience. Much of our group was at logger heads over the story, as many of the theories brought forth held water. A contributing fact to the games ability to emmerse people in the story. This suspense story has you guessing, even after the end.
Her Story is game for aspiring detectives. It really feels authentic and natural the way you search through the case files, and blank blankys acting makes the world feel very real. Live action footage can be difficult to pull off in video games but, Her Story has managed to find a method where the game wouldn't work with anything but; Any other artstyle applied to this game would feel to much like a video game, and not enough like the detective simulation Her Story is.
This game is an automatic recommend for people to experience. Whether your playing alone or with friends, the story is fantastic and the emersion will keep you there. Her Story for now at least, truely is one of a kind.
Hats off to all involved, genuinely ingenious in conception and execution.

First, this game will not be for everyone.  It's a horror/suspense game with FPS type controls.  The main driver throughout the game is that you suffer from fevers.  To combat these fevers, you must craft medicine from plants you collect on the island.  Your in game character is no superman. It is very hard to believe that only two people are responsible for the creation of this game. The result of a two-man team work looks astounding: vast forests and plains of the island are teeming with life, sun is shining through the leaves, day is slowly turning into night, dying in a wonderfully beautiful sunset.
Our protagonist arrives to the island in hopes of getting cured of the plague. A small research group has been working here for quite some time, and it seems they’ve been successful in finding the cure. But as we soon find out, the scientists are all dead and the research outposts stand empty. It is now up to us to explore the island, find out what happened to its inhabitants and finally create the cure for the plague. And oddly enough, we are still not alone on the island…
The game is very atmospheric – just let it pull you in and enjoy the challenges it presents. You are going to hunt for flowers and mushrooms, climb the hills and explore the ravines, map the island using a compass and landmarks and run away screaming when the mysterious Creature arrives.
The main problem of Miasmata is at the same time its main attraction. It is a budget game. Miasmata lacks content, excitement and diversity – the Creature’s constant presence helps at first, but as the game progresses the constant stalking stops being as frightening and becomes somewhat tedious. And when you remove the Creature from the equation, Miasmata has surprisingly little to offer – the plot is straightforward and almost non-existant, there are no sub-quests, just pure plant hunting and island mapping. However, the game’s hardcore nature and the fresh approach to the genre is going to keep you interested long enough to be able to survive and find the damn cure.

Battleborn is a Multiplayer, Co-op FPS game that is REALLY fun. Gearbox dida good job yet again. The game is filled with different characters, each with a different backstory, and skill set, and its just a overall fun game.
- Before I start talking about the game itself, I want to clear some things up. I am NOT comparing Battleborn to Overwatch, simply because they are nothing alike. Besides the graphics, and the fact that they're both FPS's, they are two TOTALLY different games. So, keep that in mind as you are reading this review, that I will NOT be comparing the two games. I'm also not saying that Overwatch is bad, either, so dont start thinking that.
In Battleborn, you are, well, the Battleborn, and your job is to stop Rendain and the Jennerits from rebuilding the Heliophage, and destroying the last star, Solus. In some ways, this game is very similar to the Borderlands games, which I absolutly LOVED. The campaign can be difficult at times, and may require you to go and do the campaign online. Now, the campaign isn't that long: only 8 missions. However, each mission can take up to about 30 mins, so your time and money isn't being wasted. Each mission has the chance to unlock a new character. Characters can be obtained 1 of 3 ways: by completing a challenge, by reaching a certain rank, or beating a mission that unlocks said character.
Now, let's move on to the PvP aspect of the game. There are 3 different modes of PvP: Capture, witch is your standard capture area and hold it for a certain amount of time, Incursion, which is just destroy the enemies base, and Meltdown, but it's basically, you have to sacrifice your minions to a god, which is actually unique.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game. i recommend it to everyone. It truely won't disapoint you. May our battle, never end.

EDIT: With the extremely low player base, the fact that updates are really only coming once a month on a game that still needs so much work, as well as the ludicrous new in game currency for a $60 dollar title... I can't really recommend it. I wish I could, I really do, but GBX/2K or whoever is to blame shot this game in the face, and it does not seem like they'll fix it ever.
The game REQUIRES about a 10 hour time investment until it "clicks" and you start to see the bigger picture. It really is an extremely addicting game and a crazy amount of fun, and it's a shame that it is getting overlooked.
Yet, the game is far from perfect. Having some strange/bad design choices (mostly in terms of UI) and is still missing some much needed things (post game lobbies, better character selector menu, abuse reporting, tutorials for game modes/characters) that a MOBA should have. The lack of polish on certain things such as El Dragon's body slam, or the UI make the game look and feel like it is in beta.
The screen clutter problem and balance issues are extremely overstated, visual effects can be a little overwhelming at first but it grows on you.  Contrary to what people say, the game has plenty of content, and the character design ranges from good to utterly fantastic.
I never thought the humor in the Borderlands series was very good, and as BB is a Gearbox game the humor ranges from pretty funny to cringe city. I do find the humor to overall be much better than the Borderlands games.
If you liked Monday Night Combat, you'll love it. If you like MOBAS and FPSs, you'll probably like it.
Obligatory Overwatch comparison: They are not really comparable and both are fantastic. But I will mention that Overwatch IS a more polished game in terms of design and shooting mechanics. Battleborn offers a deeper gameplay experience with progression and single player. Battleborns games are much longer and more methodical, everything (including minions) takes much longer to kill. If you like instant gratification shooters with the kill/die/respawn formula, Battleborn is probably not your cup of tea.

Pros:
Pretty fun, fast paced, action packed shooter game
Very reminiscent of the Borderlands series
Decent story mode that has good replayability
Large character roster with good progression
Cons:
Not well optimized for most computers
PvP balancing is non existant
ENORMOUS price drop 2 weeks after launch, with zero benefits for the existing playerbase
Overall, I would say this is worth buying since it is a good game. However, out of principle, I can not recommend any game from a company that will cut the price tag by nearly 50% 2 weeks after release, and then give no compensation to the existing playerbase. Had I known this game would be $20 less if I waited a week, I wouldn't have bought it. Bad company decisions.

The game has MOBA like pvp, 3 modes, 2 maps each, with gear and buildables.
A story mode with 8 levels each allowing gear and credit collection while getting xp for yourself and characters.
Each of the 26 characters can level up to 15 and every level will give you something either for the character or as a loot pack. They also have 5 lore challenges each to work towards unlocking to get more info on the characters. They each have a helix as well that allows 1 of 2-3 skill augments each level that last for the match up to level 10.
I reccomend this game as all the issues are being addressed. Gearbox has put out an update each week since its launch to tweak balances and modes.

The mechanics are great, and each of the 8 stages plays out like a mini-dungeon run featuring either point defense/horde, escort, or just great boss fights.  The MOBA-style in-mission leveling and variety of characters keeps each run feeling fresh, and the advanced difficulty runs are just challenging enough to keep things interesting.

Overall a great game and a steal on sale.

My reviews tend to focus on game mechanics and flaws, but this game is so mechanically simple that it's hard to even discuss. The game exists as a series of video clips that are short snippets of conversation. Every word in each video can be searched upon, and the game is basically a manner of performing searches to find more videos and get more of the story.
There is a well-thought-out mechanic in the game to prevent you from simply searching on "a" or "the" and getting all the videos. When you run a search, you are only allowed to view the first 5 videos that match the search, so searching for very common words will only allow you to watch the very early videos in the process.
Many videos contain potential threads to search on, and depending on which ones you choose to follow first, you can take a wildly different path through the available videos, which allow you to slowly piece together the story as you go.
Beyond that there's not much to discuss other than the story. Since I'm not here to spoil it for you, I'll only say that I found it enjoyable, if a little cliche at points. I don't even feel comfortable describing what specific cliches I found mildly off-putting, because even knowing that much could potentially be a big spoiler. I think hearing this story told traditionally would be only mildly interesting, but coming to it in this fashion really added a lot to it.
This is barely a game, but if you're up for an interesting interactive story that clocks in at around the length of a feature film, Her Story is a solid choice, and is priced smartly at $6.

This game is a mixed bag, but it's a good game over all.
It can be broken down into 3 parts: Politics, RTS, and Risk-like Strategy game.
The politics part is pretty straight forward. You make choices on touchy subjects and risk alienating some races while getting the support of others. The characters are really unique and the story lines that you can follow are very entertaining, and definitely one of the highlights of the games. All the characters are memorable and have amazing voice acting. And you get to pick a wife.
Also during this part of the game is a chance to unlock upgrades for your dragon. The upgrades turn you from overpowered dragon that destroys everything into an invincible god that demolishes anything it looks at. It also has upgrades for your RTS units but who cares about those when you can destroy everything yourself.

The strategy part has your maneuvering your forces along a map as you try to defeat the enemy in a large scale campaign. You decide where to move, depending on what political infuences you have in the area and how your opponent advances, and which units to build with your limited resources. You also get cards which can give you an advantage in individual fights.
Also for the less RTS-inclined, you can skip the battles and just get an outcome for each fight. This is nice if you absolutely hate the RTS part, but you learn not to do that when your dragon character is part of the fight since you can easily turn a 1% chance of victory into 100% since the dragon is overpowered.
Each action counts and you have to think about where you have to send each squad. You'll quickly learn just how overpowered your dragon character is and will have to decide what the best place to send him is, more than any other factor.
The RTS part is the most disappointing part of the game. I know a lot of people are interested in this game because of it. but it doesn't live up to the expectations, at least not as an RTS.
If you try to play this game like a proper RTS commanding your units, you will get destroyed every single time by the AI. It is extremely difficult to outplay the AI this way, and almost never works. However, once you understand how to use your dragon powers, you only need your units to capture each area. Your dragon will destroy everything every time. It is so broken in this mode, that you will stop sending commands to your units except to send them all the way to enemy's base, and you decimate all the enemy's units while they get there.
This is the least interesting part of the game since it's completely unbalanced. That said, it's always fun to blow stuff up so it's still fun in it's own way. It's just not a good RTS.
(because you can blow stuff up as a dragon mostly)
Overall the game is fun to play. I haven't had a chance to play it online since I mainly just wanted to play the campaign, and I enjoyed it thoroughly. The story is not the most amazing thing ever, but the characters more than make up for it. I think this game tried to do too much and was therefore mediocre at everything. Perhaps for a future installation they'll fix the shortcomings and make an amazing game.
This is the perfect game for anyone who likes dragons, blowing stuff up, and humourous characters.
You will not like this game if you are looking for a serious, balanced RTS or strategy game.

Owning every Larian develeoped game in steam I guess I can present myself a some sort of fan. I praise Divinity II: Dragon Knight Saga and Original Sin is IMO one of the best co-op titles in steam. Even so, Dragon Commander is difficult to like as it is also difficult to hate. It mixes so many different elements and genres together (more or less successfully) and was produced so harriedly that devs must have had some compromises.
Majorly gameplay is quite much adapted from 'Total war' series combaining real-time - and turn-based strategy.The game puts player into the boots of Dragon Commander, a powerful dragonbreed, and on each turn on a world map player builds units and constructions and moves his armies to invade new areas. When player and enemy have units at the same area in the end of the turn the blood will spill. In these conflicts player deals with the enemy in real-time combat and gameplay reminds the popular rts -series. Optionally, commander can let the AI sort out the battle by paying a reward one of the generals who increase the precent of success or let the army in the location fight without support.
Most of my playtime I spent on battlefields personally commanding troops and the rts gameplay has its pros and cons.
Starting with the pros. There is various available land -, sea - and air units and each of them have certain special abilities. The resources are collected automatically by constructing settlements on predefined places, that add some hecticism forcing player to act quickly. The genuine feature is ability to assist your troops not just by commanding but to turning a dragon when gameplay transforms into third-person-shooter game. There is also various talents to choose from: some of them are attribute increasing buffs for your units but there is also some heavy weaponry which can blast dozens of enemies at once.
And then to the cons. The biggest thing is the lack of maps, which begin inescapably to repeat themself before finishing the game. Secondly, battles are easy to win with most simple strategies and here is a typical scenario: Build units-take a defensive position if outnumbered-destroy enemy assault-build more units-take control of the nearest resource buildings-hire more units-take a defensive position-destroy the enemy assault-take all your units and march into their capital.
I never felt couraged to use more sophisticated tactic because I never needed one. I didn't have any use for transport ships for an example.
Among these conquests and war planning there is quite much to do and to decide in a political court also. The population of Rivellon's world is inhabited with 5 different species: Dwarves, Elfs, Imps, Lizards and Undead. As you might guess the values and preferences of these folk differ a lot from each other and it is impossible to please them all. The race which you are bowing may grant populations support on battles fought on their lands whereas the breed you are abandoning may degrace their support. Depending on case, the secondary effect of choice is how much money you make or how much units you can hire on each turn.
Amusing thing is that you'll also earn a liberty to choose a wife between 4 exotic races - I chose undead Ophelia. Ehmm, I don't consider myself a necrophilic person - I did it for the empire. (lol)
All these events and scandals happening outside of the battles are fun to follow. Some politcal crisis are brilliant improvising our own modern cases and the some decisions have impact how your generals relate to you as war goes by.
However, dealing with all this politc jumbo is not as hard as I first imagined. I always had at least the 50% support of each race and all I needed to do was to be victoriuos in battlefields and to take a side of a majority in cases. The nightmares of crisises and political challenges faded away just too easily that partly ruined the good idea.
All in all Dragon Commander deserves good rating.  Dragon Commander is a sum of many compromises and might lose a part of its potential after promising start but on the other hand it has some wonderful moments. Engaging as a dragon for your troops' support in battles was something that you don't see everyday and it was always fun to watch and hear how others were reacting when undead wanted to legalize Necromatism for an example. On its full price I can't recommend it, but on sale a fan of light strategy should give it a try.

And getting to know the land is, of course, really helpful when you're trying to get about, especially at speed. This game may not be for the impatient, or those who need their hand held and told where to go and what to do all the time, or who like to feel in control over everything, but if it was, it wouldn't be so rewarding for the rest of us.
Not a game. An experience you`ll remember for life.
