I was lucky enough to get into the open beta and try this game out before paying or else I'm not sure if I would have picked it up. Especially with all these negative reviews, but don't let naysayers disuade you away from this gem.  The game has two distinct play modes featuring a PvE co-op or solo campaign mode that includes a regular mode, hardcore difficulty (1 death) Advanced  difficulty and also a Hardcore Advanced. The campaign includes I believe 8 or so levels to indulge in. Each of which is roughly 30-60 minutes to complete. Items also drop in the campaign from "bosses" which can be used in the campaign or also used in the PvP which is the second gamemode. The multiplayer PvP has three game modes with two maps for each mode. Modes are essentially a "territory" mode where you hold zones to gain points. "Incursion" which is your MOBA gamemode more or less where you push your AI controlled bots to destroy the other teams "sentries" to win. The last mode is "Meltdown" Which is simliar to Incursion, but your goal is to push your AI minions to a mutual point on the map where they suicide for points while stopping the other team's minions. While playing in any of these modes you select from a pool of 25+ heroes to play as. Each hero has their own basic attacks or abilities (left click/right click) then three unique abilities (Q,E, and F keys) When starting each new match you level your hero from 1 to a max of level 10. As you play each hero you also level them up to unlock new ability choices in your "helix." Your helix allows you to choose between 2-3 choices as you level up within the match. I would further elloborate but I feel as those it gets more confusing to explain and easier to understand if you play instead. The game both PvE and PvP is loaded with that Borderlands esque humor and will keep you entertained for hours. A lot of the negative reviews I've read nitpick one thing or two. Yeah this game isn't perfect by any means, but I've found it to be well worth the money so far.

I don't write many reviews, but there seem to be a lot of misconceptions out there about what Battleborn is out there (especially with the inevitable Overwatch comparisons), and overall I think the game's getting much worse reviews than it deserves, so I thought I'd write my thoughts on the game in the hopes that it will help some people better understand what the game is and maybe convince them to buy it.
Overall, the core idea of Battleborn is to combine aspects of MOBAs (such as LoL or Dota) with team-based shooters (such as Team Fortress 2, Overwatch, or Left 4 Dead).  While Overwatch's core gameplay is pure team-based shooter and the MOBA-inspiration comes only from it having a large cast of heroes with abilities with cooldowns and ultimates, Battelborn combines MOBAs and shooters at many different levels.
Battleborn has both competitive and coop modes.  Neither of these feel like an afterthought, to me.  This coop campaign isn't a glorified tutorial like some competitive-focused games, and the competitive mode isn't tacked on like in some campaign-focused shooters.  Both feel, at least to me, like fully-featured, well-developed modes.
Like most MOBAs, Battleborn has a large cast of characters (characters need to be unlocked, but none require spending money - the 25 release characters are unlocked through challenges or leveling up your account, and DLC characters can be ulocked with in-game currency if you don't want to buy the season pass).  Characters have varied playstyles, including both ranged and melee characters, and level up over the course of a match like in MOBAs.  As you level up, you customize your character by picking between two or three helix upgrades each level.  These are fairly similar to the talent system in Heroes of th Storm.  Characters also unlock an ultimate ability at level 5.
Personally, I've really enjoyed Battleborn's characters.  The playstyles very a ton, and most of them have been very fun to play.  The helix system doesn't seem to have a ton of depth, but it's still fun to have some customization.  While some helix choices seem like no-brainers, I have seen debates or varies opinions about diferent helix builds for some characters, so there definitely are some meaningful choices or opportunities to customize a character according to your own playstyle.
Now, more detail about the modes:
Battleborn's coop mode features 8 missions (with 5 more planned as DLC, for $5 each or $20 total if you buy the season pass).  They take around half an hour to an hour to beat, so there isn't a huge amount of raw content, but the replayability is good.  The missions are designed to be played for high score, there are two difficulties, and, of course, the large number of playable characters.
Some missions simply require you to get to the end and kill a boss, while others require you to defend points or escort a robot.  The defense and escort missions can be fun, but it can also be frustrating if you lose towards the end of the mission because the robot you were escorting decided to move on while you were killing enemies.  If the point or robot you are defending is destroyed, you instantly fail the mission and have to restart, no matter how many extra lives you have left, which is rather frustrating.
The writing in the coop missions is also fun.  There is a story here.  It's not an incredibly compelling story, but it's fun to at least have a story in the game, as opposed to most multiplayer games where you basically have to read about the plot online.  The writing is quite funny, though, and has the same sense of humor as the Borderlands series.  If the Borderlands games made you lauch, chances are Battleborn will too.
Overall, the coop can be frustrating, but I've enjoyed it so far.  I haven't played enough of it to say how long it will last, or whether it's worth the price on its own if you have no interest in competitive, but I can say that I've found it fun.
Battleborn has three competitive modes.  The three modes play very differently - there's a lot more variety here than in Overwatch, in my opinion, where you're always trying to attack or defend some objective and the main difference is whether it's moving or not.  In Battleborn, the three competitive modes are all completely different from a strategic standpoint.
Incursion and Meltdown are the more MOBA-like modes.  Incursion plays kind of like a one-lane MOBA, requiring your to push a single lane of minions to destroy the enemy sentry robots.  Meltdown has two lanes, but no senties - instead, you get points whenever your minions reach a grinder at the other ened of the lane.  Both modes emphasize focusing on objectives and minions, similar to a MOBA - kills aren't the goal, just a means to an end, allowing you to get a level advantage and buying time to push wit your minions while the enemy respawns.  On the other hand, the maps are much smaller than traditional MOBA maps, and unlike in MOBAs, there isn't really a laneing phase - you're skirmishing and pushing for objetives right from level 1.
Overall, these two modes successfully combine a lot of what I like about shooters and MOBAs.  They have the more complex, strategic objectives of a MOBA, as opposed to the simpler goals of getting kills or capturing points that most FPSs have, but they still have the constant, fast-paced action that most shooters provide.
The third mode is Capture, which plays more like a traditional shooter.  There are three capture points, and each one generate points for your team as long as you hold it.  No minions, and the only side objectives are some "jungle" camps that can be cleared for experience.  Capture mode doesn't seem as deep as  deep as the other two, but it's nice when I want to play a mode that's a bit faster and simpler.
I've really been enjoying Battleborn.  I don't know if it'll have the staying power of other online games I've gotten into in the past, but I'm glad I bought it and I plan to keep playing it.  It has some frustrations, but I've found both the coop and competitive modes very fun.
+ Lots of content.  Lots of chaacters, both competitive and coop modes, and the three competitive modes feel very different, not just variations of the same basic gameplay
+ Competitive modes combine MOBAs and team-based shooters very successfully, creating a very unique game
+ Diverse and fun cast of characters
+ Lots of challenges (including 5 "lore challenges" for eac character) give plenty of objectives to strive for
+ Coop missions have good replay value, between the large cast of characters, ability to go for high score, and multiple difficulties
+ Funny writing
+ Actively supported by Gearbox so far, with regular balance updates and new content planned (including free characters and competitive maps and modes)
- Performance issues.  I get some major framerate drops, and other people have had similar experiences.  It's not unplayable, but it's enough to be a problem.
- Defense or escort coop missions can be frustrating
- Coop mission difficulty varies a lot with how many players.  Tends to be harder to win with more players, but easier to get a good score if you do win
- Competitive modes can be frustrating if your team ignores the minions and just focuses on getting kills
- Sometimes competitive games can get really chaotic and it can be hard to tell what's going on, especially when wading into the middle of the fight as a melee character
- No ranked mode yet (but they're working on it)
It's a fun time for co-op play. Fun PvP too. I wouldn't bother with it solo though.

Battleborn is my favorite game of 2016 so far.  I don't generally play FPS games, but the art style, MOBA components, and interest from my friend group sold me on this game.  This game has a similar blend of charm and humor that made the Borderlands titles so strong.  It has some quirks, but the Gearbox team has been vigilant on listening to community feedback and addressing concerns thus far.  For example, major geometry and design changes have been made to the MOBA-style Incursion map "Overgrowth" that fixed cheesy sniper strats.  GB has been quick on balance changes as well, and we've seen a few god tier characters brought into line without being ruined and sent into garbage tier (Ambra, Galilea, Miko).
Character design is good, sound design (especially dialog) is enjoyable, and the game plays quite well.  Playing in a 2-5 player group is highly recommended.  The game is not free, which means you won't be nickled and dimed for skins, taunts, or new characters; everything is unlockable just by playing.  Characters that are still in development will also be available for free, which is nice.  This could have easily been a F2P title, but I'm glad that they didn't go this route.
The game could definitely use improvements to matchmaking.  People complain about facing against high level players, but my rag-tag group of scrubs has beaten higher level groups before, it's not always a stomp.  A high level just means you've played more, and has almost nothing to do with matchmaking.  The game has some sort of MMR system, but it is hidden, which is probably for the best.  Apparently, ranked play is in development, but a couple months off.
This is a bold game, and I'm happy to see titles like this get made and released despite the extreme competition available in the FPS and MOBA spaces.  This game is both, so it inevitably is compared to juggernauts like League of Legends and TF2/Overwatch.  I think that BB and Overwatch can peacefully co-exist, and TF2/Overwatch players that also like MOBAs will probably also like this game.

You race through an obstacle couse with some challenges (like doing a whole combo for the full length of the level or collecting all the collectables in the level), you have a nitro to give yourself a speedboost and to some arial tricks with and you can do some simple stunts to fill you nitro meter up again. You can race in various vehicles: a minekart/buggy, motorcycle, mono-wheel and a jetpack, each with their own handling (althoug the 4 wheeled and 2 wheeled vehicles feel a bit similar in my oppinion).
Don't get fooled by the multiplayer aspect of this game. They are probaly referring to the leaderboards. There is actually some form of multi-player gameplay, but it's just bad (and only local, not via LAN or the internet) and I strongly recommend ignoring it exists or is mentioned on the store page. Neither should you get fooled by the 'many characters' in the game: they are just skins (and some with some voiceovers) and the game does not always remember which one you used the last time. And sadly, the ghosts are not available in the skin you've played with: they are just orbs of magical stuff in various colors.
There is also a level editor and it seems easy to use. I haven't really bothered with it too much, because it's not really my kind of thing. But for people into challenging games and wanting to create a challenge for other people to enjoy: this is it! One thing though: the dev's decided that it was a good idea to force the level editor tutorials down your throught in order to get 100% completion. A decision I frown upon...
Nevertheless, I really enjoyed myself with this game. And I think a lot of other people can do to.

psychonauts is somewhat like if you combined the basic play styles of action-platformers and adventure games with a tim burton-esque aesthetic and the polish that 2005-era 3d could afford. even 12 years later, it still looks and feels fantastic, with fluid platforming, tight level design, and some of the most genuinely funny dialogue i've ever heard or read in a video game.
beyond that, one aspect of the game that really appealed to me, and which makes it stand out more than anything else to me, is the theming of the levels. aside from the two hub areas, every level in the game takes place inside the mind of one of the cast and characters, and is intended to represent their personality, their past life, and their current mental state. the first is of a relatively sane man with a reverence for the military, and thus his mind is full of training exercizes somewhat similar to what a real military would have. (which also fits, given it is literally the game's tutorial level.) meanwhile, a character much later suffers from chronic paranoia and, potentially, multiple-personality disorder, and thus his level revolves around a conspiracy in a town with nonsense geometry, and a variety of government agents in fairly poor disguises, among other things. notably, the hardest level in the game is entirely centered on the traumatic memories of two characters.
the game also has a wonderful soundtrack, which doesn't get enough credit for how diverse it is. it can be tranquil, atmospheric, catchy, and/or chaotic at any one moment and still sound great.
if for some ungodly reason you have yet to play psychonauts, please, do it now. i firmly believe it to be the best game ever made, and given its age, it should theoretically be able to run well on a toaster.

This game has overwhemlingly positive reviews, and pops up on top 10's for people a fair amount, but let's say you played the story through and you don't like the game. I had exactly this problem, and I thought for a minute that it was some people letting nostaligia goggles (hah) get the best of them. The Bosses are cheap, the story is short, and being surrounded by little guys is a pain.
Then I looked at my file and how much I was missing, and the enjoyment I HAD gotten out of the game, in spite of not having gone out of my way for anything yet because I was hoping it would let me interact with everything and everyone after the story was completed. Unfortunately, there wasn't, but I felt like I was missing something, so I took the plunge and started over after watching a speedrun.
If you're having problems with combat or gameplay like me, consider these things:
1.) Dodging is your best friend. It has almost no cooldown, and Raz's hitbox is surprisingly fine tuned for a game from the PS2 era. It's also his second fastest ground movement method. Traverse uphill faster, and put space between you and the enemy so you have time to get your powers to work.
2.) Don't look up anything up if you can help it. It adds to the satisfaction when you can get it on your own.
3.) Debating if you want to look something up because you're just that stuck? Take a minute to enjoy whatever idle animation Raz is set to use at the time (it changes depending on the level and sometimes held items), and the soundtrack.
4.) Pay attention when characters are talking because the writing is so good in this game. It's funny, deals with dark issues (such as mental illness, of course), and hand-holds in the same script while never once being disrespectful to the player and the problems they might have.
The real beauty of it was what I thought was it's ultimate downfall: the decision to not allow me to play after the story. That's right, when they say POINT OF NO RETURN, save your game on a separate file because they mean it, darling.
The point is that you collecting things while the story is going on is part of the beauty of it. No matter when you decide to do something, there is always a logical write-in that makes it possible. It's structured to be not structured at all. It's open, and also linear. It's a masterpiece that will never get the attention it truely deserves, even with the recently ended free event.

I'm not a big fan of survival games but I am utterly fascinated by Miasmata. The main draw for me is that you never have a persistent map that shows your location, instead you have find your location by triangulating with known landmarks, which encourages caution in exploration and always checking your bearings. If you think you can just go running into the woods haphazardly think again because the game will punish you with one or a combination of three mechanics:
The first mechanic is realistic terrain traversal and falling mechanics. Your character builds momentum as they go down gradients and you can't just stop on a dime, which is particularly dangerous if you're right next to a cliff. Falling is also realistic, as your character will take damage, drop items, and get stunned from heights that one would expect to get hurt from in real life.
The second is the creature, the single enemy in the game that persistently follows you, the idea of which always keeps you on edge, I actually found it quite frightening.You can't kill it, the game purposely leaves weapons lying around to prove this point, and you can't flat out outrun it. It makes you think twice about going out at night, and you'll always keep in mind where is the nearest body of water.
The third is simply getting lost. As I've mentioned before since there is no persistent map it is very easy to lose track of where you are and to just start going around in circles aimlessly in the woods. The game purposesly gives you a limited amount of inventory slots, and you'll die out quick if you don't know where you're going.
Given the love the developers have put into this three game and the unique mechanics, it is well worth the $15 they're asking for.

One of the most memorable PC experiences I've had. It's not tightly polished, it's fairly simplistic, and it's slow - but it's immersive, challenging, and different than anything I've played.
GAMEPLAY: Using a standard FPS control scheme, you explore an island searching for the cure to a disease which afflicts you. Symptoms manifest themselves in the form of fatigue (you will drown faster while swimming and lose your footing easier when climbing), suffer from blurry vision, and eventually die. You must stave off these effects by crafting medicines out of plants found on the island, of which there are many types, and you have to collect and research each one to see what it does. You also have to drink water, which you can find in ponds, pitchers in cabins, or in your canteen. Dehydration causes onset of the symptoms above. Strangely, and somewhat jarringly, you don't have to eat at all.
Perhaps the most unique aspect of this game is the navigational aspect. You will find small snippets of maps, but most of the mapping will have to be done manually in the form of triangulation - pinpointing your location in relation to two landmarks (statues, cabins, and tents). It's the largest factor in determining your route, as you will be forced to stay within sight of landmarks. It creates a feeling of helplessness and empowerment simultaneously - you will be walking blind with little clue where to go, until you add a little bit more to your map, which is a great feeling every time.
Your compass is a vital suplement to the map, as it's easy to become lost. The game doesn't handhold, and when you lose your path, there's little recourse except to take your best guess as to where to go. This is most dangerous when falling, as the screen blurs, you become turned around, and drop whatever items you were carrying. It has the potential to be fatal, especially when in uncharted territory.
Another useful tool is your watch, which you must use to ensure you aren't caught in the jungle at night - visibility is extremely limited, to the point where it is almost entirely pointless to travel at night. This is another large factor in determining your travel schedule, as you will want to be in a safe place before nightfall.
Of course, there's another danger on the island in the form of a monster that stalks the island, against which you are defenceless. It has the potential to throw off your plans, as getting away from it will be paramount - sometimes necessitating flight into unmarked territory.
VISUALS: The game looks very nice. It goes for a realistic style, which looks great for the environment elements - rocks, water, etc. Living creatures look a little stinted, but by no means bad, and certainly not immersion breaking. Reaching the coastline and looking out onto the water is one of the most beautiful parts of this game. While most of the game takes place in nature, there are a few man-made elements that stand out visually - ruins in the jungle, for instance.
AUDIO: Serves the game extremely well. There's a soft ambient soundtrack that underlines the experience, making exploring the island strangely calming, despite the need for survival. Sound effects are great too - perhaps the most memorable being the pulsing and ringing that occurs when taking a fall. A sound you will quickly identify is the pounding of the character's heart when the monster approaches, its intensity indicating the creature's proximity. It's a very quiet game, but each sound serves to add a little something to the experience.
STORY: The focus is on survival and escaping the island, but there's a tale to be uncovered about the protagonist's past, as well as that of the island - who had been exploring the island and why, and how they came to disappear. It comes off mostly as context for the gameplay, which isn't a bad thing, especially considering the story is satisfying to uncover in all of its little bits and pieces, conveyed almost entirely by optional notes.
This game is a slow burn, and has challenges unlike those I've seen in other games. Which is why I enjoyed it so thoroughly - it's a chance to explore a beautiful island on your own, and craft strategies for survival. It's hard to say, exactly, what type of demographic I'd recommend this game to - perhaps horror fans looking for a new angle, or those who like exploration games - but I know that I would for sure, as I had a great time with this game.

You start off stranded on an island, infected with the plaque and in search of the cure for the plaque. Luckily you are on an island on which the cure for the plaque was researched.
As sick as you are your bodies’ condition isn't good at all. You can't run very far without getting out of breath, swimming is beyond question and falling down a hill becomes a regular thing. After a while (or after falling down) your condition gets even worse and you start having fever. But fortunately there is plenty of plants and herbs that can be manufactured to a temporary medicament against the fever.
Besides the fever medicament you may also make temporary as well as permanent body enhancement medicaments, which allow you to run faster, to run a greater distance and even to swim.
Recipes for the different meds just as parts of the story behind the research team are found all over the island on certain campsites.
As you progress through the island searching for the cure you can't miss the beast, a creature which sole purpose it is to obstruct you. As soon as it hits you your fever worsens and after the second hit you lose you consciousness. There are several possibilities to escape from the beast and you have to escape from it not being able to harm or even killing it.
Another major part of the game is to triangulate your position and map the island. Without triangulating it is very hard to find your way to different parts of the island so triangulate as often as possible. If you can't find any known landmark and need to know where you are, you can drink a tonic you are able to mix to get temporary the ability to know where you are on the map.
By finishing the game you might get behind the story of the island, the research team and yourself.

Great combat (Think Borderlands with 25 playable characters and 3 actives each), charming yet familiar art-style, great soundtrack and phenomenal voice work, Battleborn takes a lot of what I hated in Borderlands 2 and does the right thing; throws it in the trash.
This feels like going back to Borderlands 1, I've played around 6 hours at the time of this review and I have laughed a lot. Lots of running gags, as well as quick witty one-liners that will either hit you straight away, or have you laughing 20 seconds after you heard 'em. The writing would be one of my favourite things about this game, if the gameplay and voice work/characterisation wasn't so damn good too.
Seriously, the amount of effort put into the characters is crazy. They have SO many lines for so many situations, often calling other Battleborn by name, either friend or foe. I don't think I've run into one character who isn't likable, but I have run in a good number who are downright lovable.
But I think my absolute favourite thing has to be the gameplay overall. I love progression systems, and although I know they're not everyone's cup of tea, I love it when you can progress the same character(s) over different game modes, Rainbow Six Vegas coming to mind for this. The multiplayer is very fun, and I didn't even buy the game for the multiplayer, in fact I wasn't going to bother with it at all, but I hopped in a game after (failing) the first proper story mission and I've been hooked all damn day, it doesn't seem to get boring like other shooters, or even other mobas. The Co-Op is difficult. Like, sometimes it can be very difficult, I guess it just depends who you are playing with but the game does a great job at keeping you on your toes.
I just hope more people will get to play this game and have as much fun as I'm having, especially when living in the shadow of the giant Overwatch, which had its beta while this game launched.
Do note this game is not without flaws, performance is a bit weak as usual for Gearbox PC ports, the servers have been iffy all day, especially matchmaking, and I hear AMD GPUs are having massive problems with the game at the moment, hopefully drivers and/or Gearbox fix this.
As other reviews have mentioned, Matchmaking is very poor. This is something GB have acknowledged and are well on the way to fixing, but seriously, it's bad. That's the only thing I dislike about this game.
As I said, the game isn't flawless, but it's pretty damn close.

Larian's problem is that they're too unfocused and it makes them often lose sight of the project they're working on. They seem to get bored and then begin other projects to leave unfinished. Then some of those projects get mooshed into one game. I don't think they've made a fully realised game since the original Divinity.
So, how does that apply here?
First of all, let's consider that the original concept for this game was actually very different than what we ended up with. There's a lot of evidence to support this.
1.) Their Kickstarter described a game devoted to dragons and aerial combat. It was to be an apology to those dragon fans who'd bought Divinity II for how badly they were screwed over and let down. Furthermore, the media (such as trailers and screenshots) released at the time depicted proper aerial combat, along with unique art assets for enemy forces, enemy flying bases, and flying base combat that never made it into the final game. It gave the idea of an aerial combat MOBA with dragons, which was a brilliantly original idea to be sure.
2.) The concept art for the game shows dragon forms for the various characters who were kludged into your crew as generals. They were supposed to be leading their own forces, as the generals of the diplomats you're dealing with.
3.) The AI behaves like a MOBA. It hangs around out in the middle of nowhere just to give you something to fight (jungling), and when it's not doing that it strictly follows preset paths in big blobs. This isn't even remotely like how an RTS AI is supposed to work, and it doesn't play like any RTS I've ever experienced. It definitely acts like a MOBA in which you were supposed to play a champion (dragon). Yet the end result of the switchover to RTS makes the dragon pointless (I'll come back to this later).
Thus I believe at one point Larian were distracted from creating the game they wanted to make by starting a number of side projects. Such as the 'Risk clone,' the 'card game,' and 'diplomacy.' I've used quotations because it is to laugh to actually consider them to be such (I'll come back to that later, though).
And each of these projects ended up grossly unfinished, with some having barely any work done on them at all.
Of course, once Larian was done being distracted by experimental shinies, they realised that all of these ambitious projects could never be realised. This included the dragon aerial combat MOBA depicted in their Kickstarter. What to do? They didn't have the assets necessary to actually create their MOBA now, so they ham-fisted whatever they had together and called it done.
Worse than that? They even lost sight of what they were actually making: A game about ruddy dragons! It's a game called 'Dragon Commander' where you don't ever see any dragons -- including your own!
Yet this is what Larian is known for. Losing focus, lazily slapping together something, then merrily dropping it into the market hoping that people will be stupid enough to just buy it sight unseen. They did the exact same thing with Divinity II. THis is what they do.
That, and they just make so many promises that they never, ever keep. How is their reputation not utterly destroyed by this point?
Really, all they had to do was make an aerial combat game about dragons. Instead, they've ended up with what feels like a compilation of bad shareware/home computer games from the '90s, all slapped together into one package that they've very optimistically overpriced. And anyone who's played budget games from that era knows what I mean -- lazily made, unfinished, shallow, uninspired, aggravating, and borderline unplayable cash-ins. That's Larian to a tee, but I gave them the benefit of the doubt. That's on me. I was stupid. Never again.
You might think that's an unfair comparison, but let's look at what Dragon Commander actually is, shall we?
It's a shallow, binary, yes/no, choose your own adventure sort of affair. It lacks subtlety, nuance, and imagination. It's funny at times, but that's the only virtue it has. Instead of being able to posit your own ideas, instead of debating and politicking to change a proposed bill, you become the voting public embodied in one, tyrannical instance. I didn't want any of that. If you're going to offer me diplomacy, offer me diplomacy! What we got was tyranny.
If you're looking for this sort of thing, I'd recommend looking elsewhere. Any Choose Your Own Adventure book does it better. Try Lone Wolf, or Fighting Fantasy, or even the entirely free Choice of Dragon, which is written much more eloquently and humorously than Dragon Commander could hope to be.
Uninspired.
It's a completely one-dimensional affair about the basic micromanagement of units and resources. There's no real strategy involved either beyond brute-forcing your way through the map. This isn't even Risk, it's too oversimplified and one-dimensional for that.
Lazy.
You have to micromanage everything so if you take your eyes off your units for a moment they're probably going to be doing something painfully stupid (thanks AI). And the enemy forces progress so quickly that they gain weapons and units that can quickly destroy your dragon whilst resisting any damage it could otherwise do, thus rendering the presence of the dragon completely redundant.
Pointless.
The cards don't really have much of an affect on anything. You can completely ignore them and still easily beat the game. They're almost entirely cosmetic, essentially only tickling your resources or units, hardly altering them in any meaningful way.
Crap.
The only viable strategy is to create a lot of units and send them in one giant blob to your enemy's base, which results in an immediate victory as the AI is flummoxed by this tactic. I'd hardly call that strategy. Strategy involves... well, strategy!
It feels like the enemy AI was expecting to have a dragon of its own protecting it, which is also suggested by skirmish mode where you pick a dragon type for your AI enemies but they never actually use it. I believe Larian has even admitted to dropping the ball on this one.
So, ultimately...
It's a pretty game, yes. But it's all style and absolutely no substance at all. When you play the game, it really does feel like a bad shareware compilation. It leaves an unpleasant aftertaste in your mouth. You'll feel entirely ripped off by the price they're rather optimistically asking for it.
It's got the depth of toilet paper, and the general design ineptitude of a bad movie tie-in. It's not fun to play, unless your idea of fun is driving a nail into one of your eyeballs. Yes, at first, it'll wow you with its graphical flair, but that's all it has. And that's not worth the entry price. Not remotely. Dragon Commander is a game that looks good until you actually play it.
I find myself wishing they'd stuck with the original idea, which was brilliantly unique and could've ended up being one of the best dragon games on the market. As it is, the amount of 'dragon' in Dragon Commander makes it entirely disingenuous to even call it such. It feels like false advertising to me. A bit of a con, if you will.
If you're buying this because you're looking for a dragon game? Trust a fellow dragon fan -- save your money. I know that us dragon fans have been longing for a game for us, but this isn't it. This is just an effort to take advantage of us by selling us a shareware compilation disguised as a dragon game. That's the most uncool thing anyone could do, really. And I certainly won't be buying from Larian in the future. I've learned my lesson.

Heavy on exploration. Light on gameplay. This is not a game for everyone.
Miasmata is one of those modern indie games that, in my opinion, is striving to be an artsy like experience than what is traditionally considered a game by the average joe. And just like those games with similar aspirations, the gameplay is diminshed so the player can be wowed by the "experience".
And that's why I was on the fence when deciding to recommend this because I couldn't help but feel that this game could've been grander if the developers spent more time on the gameplay aspect. However, it's hard to overlook what effort they did put in the environment/sound effects and I think it paid off.
Miasmata is beautiful to explore. Realistic looking and massive in size along with its varied topography, it's almost like hiking in a national park.  But, it has a dark character and history to it as well that will become apparent if you decide to play it.
I only recommend this game to those who love exploring natural, beautious environments (and finding flowers for a cure) because that's what 90 percent of this game is. On the other hand, if you're the type of person who needs something constantly happening in the game, then you'll probably be bored with this one.

Miasmata is made with humble graphics and an eye (or four eyes) for technology. It executes mapping and movement shockingly well, both concepts working in unison with the fundamental idea of player disempowerment.
The character trips, stumbles and gains momentum on an incline. Traversing the environment feels realistic within reason, and the quickest way to a point ahead is not always a straight line.
Cartography is tedious and the nature compelling enough that the player is likely to wander off the beaten path and fall into two possible scenarios: inside, safe or outside, lost. Loss of direction evokes glimpses of freedom rarely experienced in a video game.
The systems can be time-consuming to grasp and the solution to the mystery surrounding the player is scattered and abstruse. But why should things be easy to understand?

WARNING: LONG REVIEW
Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic (KOTOR) is easily one of the best games I have ever decided to play, especially for Star Wars games. I beat this game in a little over 41 hours, which for an RPG is quite nice, not extensive though. However, the game is very replayable, and between some of the hilarious dialogue options, you will want to come back and play again. Other than the obvious fact you may have been on the light side, now you want to be on the dark side, or vise versa. I've never been a huge fan of RPG's, but considering how many people say they love this game, I gave it a try, plus it was only 2$ for the Holidays. That alone made the game a steal, definitely worth 10 dollars either way. The storyline or plot is very compelling, and there are some major plot twists which had actually surprised me. The game did not give away too many secrets right away, and that made working to find them out after many hours totally worth it. Some things about the gameplay overall, the game is 50% clicking, and 50% walking as you have to walk everywhere. Besides the fact after you beat a quest you have to backtrack  quite far, unless you are in an area which allows you to teleport back to your ship. The scenery is quite nice though and has a good amount of detail surprisingly. Areas have a good amount of MPCs as well, so you don't feel like you are always in a ghost town. The appearances of your character are linear, but overall not dissapoiting, plus there are many different armors to wear. The graphics are low res, but that doesn't take away from the gameplay at all, and you will definitely have a great experience.  Lightsabers dueling is my favorite part of the game, even if it takes a couple hours to get to that point from the start, but easily what makes the game the game. The real reason I truly enjoy this game though, you feel as though you're actaully playing as your character because, you actually put your personality into him/her. The choices you decide will actually make you question morality, and wether or not you have done the right thing. The dark side is quite tempting at some points, you will wonder if being a part of the light is worth it. I give this game a 9/10, but absolutely recommend everyone to play it. The reason I say 9/10 is that, some mechanics while playing can get clunky or you will become stuck for whatever reason, and some important RPG aspects of the game are linear. My biggest complaint for this game would be, you can't keep playing as your character once you have beaten the game. It's over and that means starting a whole new character, but hey that might be something people enjoy. Enough about those flaws though because this game is one a of a kind. Play this game if you enjoy RPGs, play this game if you love Star Wars, play this game if you like lightsaber dueling, JUST PLAY THIS DAMN GAME. KOTOR is truly incredible, and one of the most amazing games I have ever played.
Always remember this though:
There is no emotion: there is peace. There is no ignorance: there is knowledge. There is no passion: there is serenity. There is no chaos: there is harmony. Lastly but not least, There is no death: there is THE FORCE.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic:
Pros:
- Amazing (and suprisingly quick) turn based fighting.
- Some difficult moral descisions to be made here.
- Some very well written and developed characters (notably Bastila, Malak and Carth)
- Brilliant story and worlds
Cons:
- Slightly short in comparison to most other rpgs (I finished my first playthrough in 26 hours)
- Some slight bugs and the occasional crash (This is more because of the fact that I was using windows 10 on this.)
- No option to continue playing after the main quest
- Some enemies can be unfairly balanced and difficult (Rancors and Terentatek on Korriban. If you buy this game, go to Korriban last or one of the fights will prove to be phenominally difficult)
Verdict:
All in all a brilliant RPG. However, it is slightly on the shorter side of things. That being said, the story is very well done and the pacing is very solid. I feel though that the option to continue playing after finishing the main quest was slightly annoying (That and saying goodbye to some of your companions) Would reccomend for any RPG fan!

A very nice effort from Larian which would have been even better if they'd just spent a bit more time on making the parts fit together. I love the blend of RTS/TBS with dragon combat and political chat'em'up. The RTS segments feel like a dumbed-down version of Supreme Commander - it looks like whoever has the most units wins at first, but it's entirely possible to beat terrible odds using clever tactics and some units (Juggernauts) are massively overpowered, which lets you exploit the mechanics to great effect. Dragon combat is satisfying without being so effective as to completely dominate every battle. Unfortunately the AI is prone to abusing the cheap spellcaster units and there is no effective counter. I had to auto-resolve some battles where my army was superior on paper, because I could not win otherwise.
This brings me to the greatest single weakness of the game - the way battles are resolved on the strategy map. You can only personally manage one battle per turn, which is fair - that's what your generals are for. But then, despite having four of them, you can only use one per turn. Are the rest of them drunk at the bar, or what? Furthermore, the effect of using a general is paying a flat fee for a slightly increased chance-to-win, nothing else. They don't gain levels, their dialogue doesn't change and there's no risk of them dying if they fail. Essentially, all four generals could have been replaced, strategy-wise, with a once-per-turn bonus of 10-20%. A terrible waste of an otherwise very promising feature.
This would not have been so bad if auto-resolve (when neither you nor a general is available) was anywhere close to realistic, but it doesn't take the actual map or unit composition into consideration at all. Units with NO anti-air capability will have a non-zero chance of defeating flyers, ships may greatly influence the outcome of auto-resolve whereas the actual map is laid out so that you can't use ships offensively. In effect, auto-resolve ends up being used when you have no choice because you're out of battles for that turn, or to get out of having to deal with broken mechanics (like mass spellcasters).
Continuing with the strategy part of the game, I love the board game setup with the cards to make things a bit more unpredictable, but it's unfortunately *much* too easy. Playing on Normal (I shudder to think what Casual mode is like!) I was easily able to build up such a strong economy in chapter two that by the finale, I was maxed out on research and could simply buy enough units to steamroll the enemy throughout. The AI never attacks you where you don't expect and will often willfully engage in battles it has <10% chance of winning, wasting units.
It must sound like I'm not recommending this game but I actually greatly enjoyed most of the RTS battles, the population mechanic (where you can only build so many units in a match) and the fixed building sites make for more dynamic and fast-paced gameplay than most RTS:es, turtling it out in your base is simply not an option although it may be a viable short-term strategy. The maps are well-designed and the visuals are good. Nice bright colors make your units stand out in the detailed terrain, and when zooming out the units are represented by simple icons (another thing that is brilliant, and reminds me of SupCom).
Adding to the enjoyment is the part in-between battles, where you manage the politics of your empire. The dialogues are humorous, the characters quirky and interesting - it's always a treat to find out what they're going to suggest. Weighing your personal views against what would be the most strategically sound decision for your empire makes for a different type of challenge - I am sure many players will already have a principled stand on an issue like women's rights, but what do you do when giving both sexes the same pay will put a significant strain on your war economy? For the record, I ended up playing liberal/capitalist, meaning I sided with the elves and dwarves most of the time, made the feminists happy-ish and I still ended up with approval over 75% with everyone. So there you go.
You'll notice I've spent almost none of this review talking about the story. That's because there really isn't one. You will see bits of one in barely-animated cutscenes and you can listen to some dreary exposition from Maxos the Wizard if you so desire, but it's laid on paper-thin and has nothing to do with gameplay. In fact - it seems to have been written completely separate from the game itself! At one point, Maxos tells you in horror that the powerful demon he had been using to power your flagship has broken free. Yet the ship is still running just fine and the demon's still down there, business as usual! Another time, you're asked whether you want to start allowing women to serve in your army. But at that point you already have TWO female generals and some of your combat vehicles are very obviously piloted by women! Best to simply ignore the story completely unless you want to be bothered by contradictions.
In summary, I recommend this game if you are in the mood for heaps of casual RTS action with a sprinkle of very enjoyable dragon combat and some political intrigue to keep things interesting. If you prefer your RTS complex and your story deep, look elsewhere. For the 17 hours it took me to play through, I consider my money well spent.

Before I start, this is going to be a generally subjective review
Overview:
BattleBorn is a decent game with some good gameplay mechanics. Story mode brings back the classic days of working together to beat an ingame mission. Some of the other multiplayer modes introduce some refreshing mechanics to make the game more interesting.
Pros:
-Heroes o' plenty
There are lots of heroes to choose from (and from what I heard on the grapevine, more coming down the pipeline) all with their unique abilities and unique personalities.
-An FPS inspired MOBA
I feel like that sums up the gameplay on this game, most (although not all) of the gameplay, especially multiplayer has mechanics and systems similar to that of the likes of Dota and LoL whilst making it feel like a natural FPS.
-Pretty
I really like the look of the graphics in this game, I've always had a thing for cartoony and slightly cell shaded graphics that are in this game, it really makes it stand out from other games trying to achieve the same thing.
-Controls and feel
the FPS mechanics (If you're playing a character with a gun) feel natural, if you've played FPS games before, you should have no trouble adapting to this games style of play.
Cons (oh boy):
-Forgettable
This is something that might not apply to some of the BattleBorn gamers out there but I feel that the characters, story and gameplay is very forgettable. I didn't feel like I connected to any of the characters, although all unique in looks I feel like the devs through in a bunch of characters with little to no explanation on them. The gameplay is either too strewn out, or not explained enough. you'll have long sequences of boring filler story and plot, and then other times, you'll have the littlest of explanation to what is currently going on.
-Immersion
Another possibly subjective con, and this is gonna sound dumb but. It feels too much like a game, personally, I think of games as another reality to escape to, a different story, a new world. I was not immersed in the story or game at all, excluding the cutscenes, the characters aren't humanized. This will become more noticeable in gameplay.
-Worst possible time to release this game
If you're reading this, you probably haven't played Overwatch, don't own it, or you genuinely want to play this game. Don't get me wrong, this game is unique in it's own perspective. But if you play Overwatch, and then play this. They both have similar styles of play despite the obvious difference in gameplay mechanics. But Overwatch feels like it's everything that this game should've been.
-Little marketing
I bought this game 2 days after release, but due to exams, didn't play it until 2 days later where I finished my exams. At the end of the exams, I told all my mates about BattleBorn and how excited I am to play it. Not a single one of them ever even knew the game existed, and they were the kinda people to keep up-to-date on future titles.
-WHY ARE ALL THE CHARACTERS LOCKED???
I still haven't figured this out yet, but WHY ARE NEARLY ALL THE CHARACTERS LOCKED??? I get it, the devs want some kind of mission/progression to unlock those characters bringing on the sense of achievement, and it is a rewarding feeling! BUT IN A MOBA STYLE GAME??? What I liked most about Moba style games is the heroes, so many to choose from, so many styles of play. But it kinda forces you to choose from a small number of heroes that you might not even like
Conclusion:
If you can forgive all the cons above, and you like games like Smite, then this could be for you, it's that kinda game where (if you like it) you can clock thousands of hours into it without getting bored. Unfortunately for me, I bought this game on♥♥♥♥♥so I can't refund it on steam
The only real issue for me is that there's not enough people playing this, there are some things that must be adressed but it is so much damn fun

Psychonauts is a masterpiece. Psychonauts is a one-of-a-kind game full of all kinds of wacky characters, über-creative levels, subtle dark humor, innovative gameplay mechanics, responsive controls, and mature themes under all those bright colors (the Memory Reels are quite tragic and sad, mirroring the losses and hardships we've all faced). I consider Psychonauts to be one of the finest games ever made, and I guarantee that no matter what type of gamer you are, there's something for you in Psychonauts.
Where to start? With the heart of game: the characters. Psychonauts has a wide variety of memorable characters that are amazingly fleshed out and perfectly designed. They're an eclectic mix of witty, serious, nutty, psychotic, and all around goofy, and that's what makes the game so original. Nowadays, games are all about realism and I'm afraid developers have forgotten that games are supposed to be a fun escape, not a chore. The characters in Psychonauts showcase more creativity than 20 other games combined. The main character of Raz is likable and funny, really giving the game heart. His design is clever (I love the goggles/leather pilot helmet combo) and his voice actor (Richard Horvitz) does a fantastic job. The supporting characters are what really elevate the game from great to amazing. Each is wonderfully designed with their own personalities and quirks. There are too many to list, but my personal favorites include camp mentor Ford Cruller, who has multiple personalities and reminds me of Doc Brown from Back To The Future; the portly Coach Oleander, who is scarred by both his abusive father and the horrors of war; and Boyd Cooper, a tweaky milkman with paranoid delusions about the government and double agents. Even the very minor characters have personalities and deliver funny quips.
Along with each of these eccentric and memorable characters comes a completely original and beautifully designed level that reflects the character's current mental state. Again, there are too many to list, but the standouts are a trippy black-lit Spanish villa being terrorized by a giant pink bull, a minature metropolis populated entirely by talking lungfish, and Boyd's government conspiracy level (which is one of the coolest levels in any game, ever). There's not one repeated idea throughtout the 10+ levels either. It is this uniqueness that is Psychonauts' biggest strength, never making the game feel boring or forced; it all flows naturally and seamlessly. A rather deep and complex story ties all the levels together, so if you're one of those people who complains there are no longer any games with compelling stories, here's a game that will pleasantly surprise you.
Now a game can be the most original thing around, but if the gameplay stinks it renders all that creativity moot. Luckily Psychonauts excels in the gameplay as well! Being a psychonaut, you have an impressive arsenal of psychic powers at your disposal. You can use levitation, pyrokinesis, telekinesis, and clairvoyance, among others to your full advantage. Don't feel like fighting that enemy? Set them on fire and then levitate to a safe location until they're dead, or pick them up with your mind and throw them off a cliff. The powers are fun to use and easy to wield, thanks to the excellent controls. Each level has a different theme, with a new gameplay element central to beating the level. For instance, in the government conspiracy level, you must collect ordinary household items that disguise you as double agent performing a certain task in the eyes of the bad guys. If you're holding a plunger, they see you as a plumber and you can pass by undetected into the sewers. Every level also encourages you to use your powers in a way you wouldn't have thought to use them, like using clairvoyance on a crow feather to spy on enemies from the crow's point of view. In short, the gameplay is excellent.
If you love collecting things like I do, than this game will definitely satisfy your appetite. There are thousands of items to collect, all of which upgrade your psychic powers, actually giving you a reason to collect them instead of just for 100% completion. There are figments (as in figments of your imagination), mental cobwebs (which clutter your brain), memory vaults (for those repressed memories), emotional baggage (which is actually baggage, like a suitcase or storage trunk), scavenger hunt items, stolen brains and loads more. I had so much fun collecting these items, some of which are very cleverly hidden.
The music, sound effects, and voice acting is superb. The music, composed by Tim Schafer regular Peter McConnell is great and compliments each level nicely. The sound effects are top-notch, each with its own memorable sound - I love the sounds the enemy censors make. Each character's voice perfectly suits their design, even the minor ones. The voice acting is professionally done and doesn't feel phoned in by anyone. I was highly amused to hear the voice of Earl Boen (Dr. Silberman from The Terminator and Terminator 2: Judgment Day) as a boss character.
So is there anything wrong with Psychonauts? No, nothing that takes away from the extraordinary gaming experience. I only have a few minor nitpicks: There are long load times, but this is understandable considering the intricacy and amount of stuff going on in each area. The targeting system and camera could use some tweaking. Sometimes I couldn't get a lock on an enemy or the camera would cause me to miss a platform I was jumping to. Finally, and this is strictly my opinion, at the end of the game Raz removes his helmet and we get to see his ridiculous hair-do. Talk about hat hair...let's just say he should never take off the helmet! However, none of these tarnish Psychonauts' brilliant shine.
All in all, Psychonauts is one of the best games ever made, of this or any generation. Everyone, no matter what your age or gaming experience, should give this masterpiece a try. You won't regret it!

I suspect a few people, by now, have wondered why such a self-professed "horror nut" as myself has a few games in his Steam library with names like, well, "Shiny The Firefly", to name but one example. The slightly embarrassing answer - though only VERY slightly (I'm pretty shameless) - is that I also have something of a penchant for "cute" and "child-like" things.
Now USUALLY these "child-like" things will also need to be a tad on the spooky and/or violent side - Among the Sleep, Limbo and Little Inferno all spring to mind as personal faves - and therefore have a kind of cross-over, however tenuous, with my more usual tastes. And extremist though I may be, I think I may have actually crossed a bit of a personal line with the game I'm currently reviewing...which is to say...I think that Shiny The Firefly may be just a tad TOO light-hearted and child-like for Yours Truly to handle, even on the most whimsical of days.
You want "cute"? This game has it in spades. Chuck a "sickeningly" in front of that word, and we're getting even closer to the truth. In fact, I'm starting to harbour the vaguest of suspicions that Shiny The Firefly may NOT actually be aimed at 40-year-old man-children such as myself, but rather - inconceivable as this may sound - may even be squarely and solely aimed at KIDS. And I don't even mean "big kids" like myself. I mean, y'know..."kid" kids. Ones under ten years of age, let's say.

All of which might be well and good if I actually HAD any kids of my own, or even nieces or nephews or whatnot. But seeing how bereft I am of ALL of the above, I possibly have no excuse to have ever bought this game; much less an excuse to be playing it ALL BY MYSELF.
Don't get me wrong...this game is actually pretty good. A tad pedantic at times where the controls are concerned - it's perhaps more suited to a tablet and a touch-screen interface than it is to PC and mouse - but certainly by-and-largely "competent". Nothing much wrong with it, basically. Except that IT'S ABOUT A MALE FIREFLY WHO HAS TO GO AROUND "COLLECTING" HIS BABIES.
Is the Universe trying to send me a message here? Have I somehow failed in my God-given task of reproducing my worthless self, and now I have to be digitally derided for my sins?! How did I even end up with a game called Shiny The Freaking Firefly in my Steam library?!? Oh, waitaminute...that's right...I probably bought it cheap in a sale, just out of curiosity, and to further my admittedly paltry ambition of edumacating myself in as wide a variety of gaming styles as possible.
Well, let's consider this mission a success, then: I have now, officially, played a game just a tad too painfully "cute" for my stomach to bear. Damn you, Shiny, you loveable rascal, you!

Took me a little while to understand the mapping part of the game. You basically have to identify at least two man made structures (Building, statue, beacon) to pinpoint where you are on the map then find other unknown structures that are also in view and they then become known. You can now use those identified structures as map elements. Don't wander too far, try to keep these map markers in view and keep checking the map to add more pieces to it.
The concoctions you can make are temporary ones or permanent ones. You can carry only one of each temporary type so don't bother making two basic medicines, just make one basic and one enhanced. The weapons seem practically useless so far, there is a beast that stalks you, attacking with knife or axe doesn't seem to bother it at all. Ducking into cover doesn't seem to help much but getting behind hard cover like a tree does.
You have to drink quite often but fresh water is plentiful, yet in seven game days I haven't eaten anything so the finds of bananas and apples lying around don't seem to matter.
Climbing even the gentlest of slopes can be difficult and it is super easy to go tumbling off and falling. Try hitting reverse when sliding down a hill to slow your descent, that helps. Save by lighting anything (beacon, candle, fire, lantern) or by sleeping and keep an eye on the time, right mouse button brings up a compass and wrist watch, when it gets dark...it gets REALLY dark! You can get lost very quickly at night or go falling off a cliff, we forget living as we do in towns and cities that street lighting however dim is still there, in this game there's you holding a piddling little lighter unless you find brush to use as a torch until it fizzles out a minute later.
I am enjoying it immensely, yes it feels a little clumsy at times and low budget but the night time without a torch and no where near a camp confusion is very real, and then there's the beast tracking you, when you see it coming for you and you run, panic just sets in, fighting it doesn't do anything, just have to run or hide.

Witch It is a game very similar to Prop Hunt from GMod if you've ever played or seen gameplay of that. You have two teams: The Hiders (aka Witches) and The Seekers (aka Hunters). The Witches have the uncanny ability to transform themselves into objects found around the map, henceforth called "props" and it is the Hunter's job to find them. It is the Witch's job to simply not be found, or barring that, to avoid being killed before the time runs out.
To aid them in their mission, Witches and Hunters are given unique abilities. Currently, with the latest patch, they both have 4. Not sure how in depth of the specifics of the gameplay I should get in a review, but each ability changes how you play the game, whether you choose Flight on a Witch to hide somewhere high above the hunters, or Mushroom Clouds in order to invert their controls should they find you.
Currently, there are 3 game modes: Hide & Seek (a classic), Mobification (where caught Witches become Hunters), and Hunt a Hag (a work in progress where Hunters only have a melee attack, and Witches cannot transform). Each one offers a different way to play the game, but everyone has their favorites.
In this sort of game, playing with friends is best in my opinion. Especially if you do so over a voice chat such as Discord or Skype. Luckily, even if you have no friends who wish to play Witch It with you, Barrel Roll Games have a public Discord server in which they actively participate. As of July 7, 2017 there are at least 3000 members in it! The community is extremely helpful (if a little trolling at times) and constantly look forward to new players.
If you're looking for a game with which to chill out, have a few laughs, and occasionally freak out at getting almost getting caught, then Witch It is a great game to check out. All in all, a solid game with a great playerbase. I'm looking forward to seeing it grow!

This is helped by the large world to explore with plenty of things to turn the player away from quests, including gathering ingredients for potions or killing enemies for the ever valuable experience. There's no denying the problems of Two Worlds, along with it obviously being made to appeal to the Oblivion/Gothic 3 craze of the time. But there's more beneath the surface than its reputation gives.

Overall, it is a fun, if flawed, game. Where the game shines is in its political mechanics. As the dragon commander, you make decisions that shape your empire and the personalities of your generals. Every character is well written and has excellent voice acting.
The combat, unfortunately, is a bit half baked. It just isn't all that unique and suffers from some poor design decisions. You can't build a base freely, and micro managing your units is fiddly. I found myself autoresolving most of the battles because I simply got bored with the combat.
With all that said, I still recommend the game. The decision making mechanics are fun to role play with and the voice acting is so well done it raises the game above its poor rts components.

Everything except the combat in this game is really nice. I actually like the strategic game board more than most other games I've played, and the dialogue and characters all have voice acting and at least some amount of characterization, which is pretty nice.
The actually battles, which unfortunetly are a large part of the game, have a user interface ad overall setup that is frankly unpleasant to deal with and not fun at all.
Here are a brief list of the pros:
-The dragon transformation works well and playing in dragon form is pretty fun. The transition between normal rts mode and dragon mode is mostly seamless. Given that this is a major differentiator between this and other games I do have to give some props.
-The unit effects are pretty nice. General graphics are good.
The cons (mostly interface related):
-Scrolling is a pain, because the map orientation doesn't change with the camera rotation. You can't use the minimap because up becomes down, sideways, and every direction in between, and it is almost impossible to keep track of what else is going on when units that look like they are coming from below your base are actually up and to the left.
-The above minimap issues make it very difficult to form strategies and think about what is going on, because unit and base positions are so difficult to keep in mind.
-Units that are moving towards enemies will not fight back unless explicitly told to. This is actually pretty common among strategy games, and it wouldn't be a problem except that there is no obvious visual indicator to say that a unit is attacking or just moving near an enemy. It is possible to lose whole armies because you clicked near an enemy instead of on them. Attack moving is a partial solution, but unit attack ranges are so long that parts of your army can get caught attacking non-critical targets on the way to a fight.
-Unit movement is slow and feels clumsy. I guess it is more "realistic," but not my cup of tea.
-Controlling your units in dragon form becomes even more difficult. With certain hotkeys it is possible to control your nearby units, but it feels really clumsy and there are no visual indicators to tell when units are moving or not. It is difficult to check on your units in dragon form because your camera is restrained to your moving first person view.
-Probably the worst part of the dragon form controls is that you cannot produce new units while in dragon form. You are forced to either create long queues of units to make (which you often don't have the resources for) or switch between being a dragon and scrolling back to your base to issue more commands (using the mouse because the minimap is impossible).
-Somewhat minor, but the hotkeys are a little strange. Q is the attack hotkey, not A, etc.
-Obviously the AI has none of these problems. This creates frustrating situations where the AI is attacking on two or more fronts and you can't even issue commands to your units because the controls are so clumsy.
All these may seem minor but they really build up. It's a shame because the game is almost really good, but it just isn't fun because of all the issues in the actual implementation. I might try to play the game a little more, try to figure out the controls and see if that helps any, but I doubt it. Let me start this review by saying that I REALLY want to recommend this game. Really.
As far as RTS games go, this Wargame Airland Battle has done a lot of things very right, and I’ll start by talking about these.
Firstly the ability to zoom from the full scope of the map right down to see individual men running across a field really gives you a great perspective. You sit with your 12 tanks, 8 armoured personnel carriers, 4 mobile AA units, 4 tank destroyers, 40 mixed AA/AT infantry and recon team and think 'yeah, this is a nice army.' you set them up in nice defensive positions to await the rush of enemy units, maybe you even set down some artillery to cover them. Then you zoom out to see where the enemy is at and notice how rapidly the map swallows your 'nice' army until you can barely see them; little coloured specks in an otherwise insignificant woodland in a corner of the battlefield. It’s really absolutely brilliant and I love it.
Another great feature is the persistent units; units you lose in one battle stay lost for the next. If your super powerful expensive helo gets shot down, you can’t call him in again, which gives you a real attachment to your units and makes you think twice before sending your recon and choppers on what’s probably a suicide run.
I also love the unit resupply mechanics, all units have ammo and fuel which need to be maintained. leaving an AA squad out in some far flung corner of the map just to be a♥♥♥♥♥♥to your opponent only works until they’ve used their 8 missiles, after that they really are useless until you can resupply them. the resupply mechanic hasn’t been overthought though, all units can repair, collect fuel and any kind of ammo just by being in the resupply radius of a unit or building, there’s no micromanaging the carrying of 8000 different kinds of ammunition to the front lines *ahem* Men Of War *ahem*.
Sadly this brings us to the negative points. Campaigns consist of a Risk board game style army movement that feels unnecessary with powers such as nukes and reinforcements that leave little impact on the actual 'board'. I was told by one mission to nuke an enemy sector before attacking it, I braced myself for the horror of what I was about to do. I was told it would be done within 24 hours (1 turn) of my order, so I gave the order and waited. And waited. And waited. Did it happen? Is it on route? If I attack now will I nuke my own men in a minute? No indication was given whatsoever that this horrific deed had been done, and it’s in touches like this that Wargame falls down.
When playing a battle you are given no obvious objective, no indication of what to do, just to deploy your units here. Then the battle happens, you kill some stuff and suddenly, without any warning, the battle screen disappears and you’re told you won a major victory. Did I? I don’t feel like I did. I had no idea what I was supposed to be doing.
It seems the battles consist of just killing the enemy units faster than they kill yours, until you've killed enough that the battle ends. Whilst this is fine (ish) for multiplayer, from a solo or co-op campaign, I really want more. Just little touches like being told to hold a sector whilst VIPs evacuate or to secure a supply route, just something. it even boils down to the same main objective - hold here whilst the enemy throws units at you, but the simple addition of some kind of objective makes the whole experience more tangible and less just like a punching match.
Lastly the units, whilst very varied, are gone into in far too much detail. You’re told exactly which weapon each unit uses, whether that’s a strela-2 or RPG-7, AK, RPK, or a bajillion others that I can't name off the top of my head, it’s not necessary. I wouldn’t mind though if the game told you what kind of vehicle/squad it is, but instead you're told that it has a KONKURS, and that it has 2 AP power and 6 HE power (totally making that up, but you get the idea), the game neglects to tell you however whether this is an anti-tank launcher, an anti-air launcher, some kind of unguided rocket, a recoilless rifle, etc. etc. you can make guesses by its rate of fire and total ammo count, but I’ve been surprised on more than one occasion, and I would say I have a fair knowledge of modern firearms.
Basically it gets very anal about the units you have available, but fails to tell you how good they are against other unit types.
All in all then I really can't recommend this game, it provides a great platform for strategy gaming, but give you no direction or variation in your attempts to do so. The game is also impossibly difficult at times, totally without warning.
Here’s my overall rating then -
+ Lovely graphics
+ Some great mechanics
+ Wide unit variety
- No direction given to player
- Some not so great mechanics
- No mission variety
- Sporadic difficulty jumps
6/10
There’s better RTS games on the market, maybe Red Dragon improves upon these points.

I got this game free from Humble Bundle, and am writing this review right after I finished the game.
I'm not really amazing at reviews, so I guess I'll just shortly list out the pros and cons.
PROS:
- Amazing and fun gameplay
- Great and satisfying storyline (took me 12 hours to beat without too much collecting around)
- Superb characters and atmosphere
- The age of the game doesn't show a lot unless you're trying to inspect every detail.
- Semi-open world feels great and alive
- Lots of collectibles
- Wide variety of ways to approach things with your psychic powers
- Parkour mechanics that are up-to-par with many modern games' systems.
- Extremely creative levels
- Interesting, fresh, unique multi-stage boss fights
- Variety of enemy types
- All of the above all mix together so, so well, you really can't say you aren't having fun.
CONS:
- Gameplay and parkour can feel clunky on rare occasions, leading to frustration.
- Small amount of glitches that can cost you a part of your life in some cases.
- The inablity to unequip items. In the game there is an item called the Cobweb Duster which performs its action by you pressing the interact/use button, which means you can't talk to NPCs or use map objects while you're holding it. If you don't have any other items to equip, you'll have to use one of 2 other items that are always in your inventory which trigger animations that will take at least 10 seconds.
- Aforementioned Cobweb Duster needs to be bought with the game's currency to progress the story and to collect Arrowheads, you'll need to run around for 10 minutes collecting them. (tip: buy the drowsing rod. It'll set you back 50 but you can net from 30 to 200 arrowheads at once)
- The inablity to free roam the Camp after beating the game.
So, that's about it for now. As you can see the pros are plentiful while the cons are nitpicky and won't really affect your gameplay for too long. If you aren't sure, yes yes yes I 100% recommend the game. It's a one-of-a-kind experience with a lot of replayability for 10 bucks, or even less during the sales. Put it on your wishlist if you don't own it yet. And get it as soon as you can.

I wouldn't buy into this DLC sales platform. It was semi-working as a beta, but in 2017 it is pretty much broken on its best day.
The issues are NUMEROUS, the gameplay is inconsistent, and to add insult to injury they have rapid-fire released 2 paid DLCs for what is an objectively broken game! If it were my game, I'd feel like a crook trying to get dev funding on the back of a broken game, but that's me.
To the point:
- Fights are awful since removing the netting mechanic. Ever since all you really need to do is reel in with low-ish drag so your line never snaps and wait for it to tire so you can reel it in all the way  and press the net button. Even then sometimes it'll get close and the tension will skyrocket for no good reason annnd you lose the fish anyhow.
- This game is very poorly optimized. For how it looks in a given setting it should not be so resource-hungry and laggy.
These are the 2 biggest ongoing issues for months and months now. At this point it just looks like they're either trying to fund the development needed to fix this broken game (with new DLC), or are trying to make as much cash as they can off of the game before everyone writes it off forever and it dies.
Anyhow, I feel like an idiot for endorsing this game and feel like I got suckered by that video of the team talking about how they wanted to make the best fishing game. It's a damn shame, because as you'll see below, the game had extreme potential at one point.
Do not buy unless you can get it VERY cheap and don't mind gambling on its future. I just can't see this game recovering after a few years of spinning its wheels and sinking.
With Phase 6, I think it's even clearer than before that this game is going to turn out to be something good. It started out as a very solid, albeit bare, fishing game, but with every update features are added, and mechanics are dialed in some more. The team seems to be listening intently and working hard to put out as much win in every update as they possibly can.
This update brings a working multiplayer mode, which consists of the training lake (only) and up to 4 (iirc) other people fishing. There is a (half-working atm) chat function that lets players on a lake share tips and brag about big catches, which is very cool (if I see someone landing many fish, I tend to ask what bait they're using). Using chat while on a peg is problematic, though, due to the hotkeys for keyboard controls not being disabled while focus is on the chat box. My whole peg has been closed many times because I tried to chat, heh. The chat box also has a bad habit of ignoring sentences. Other than that, multiplayer is definitely working and enjoyable.
The quality of the fishing experience gets better with every update (imo), and the team behind it stay on the forums, getting feedback and making changes based on what they see and hear. Force feedback on a 360 controller is much improved, and the controls, for the most part, make sense.
