I played this game on the 360 back in 2008. The game came out in 2007 on consoles in America, and it's 10 years old now.
Two Worlds is a very mixed bag. It's more like a tarnished gem, actually. There's so many aspects of this game that are great, and for every good point there's one or two steps back.
The world. It's huge, and it's not just empty space. There was an achievement on the 360, to discover every single location in the game. I never even got close to that and I played this game a lot. Lots of unique little areas that I'm pretty sure only a handful of people will ever see, due to the unpopularity of this game. There are tons of varied environments, as well. Snowy mountaintops, rocky foothills, fertile river valleys, deserts, bamboo forests, beaches, corrupted forests, etc. etc.
The magic system. The second game expanded on this to great affect, but the magic system in Two Worlds is pretty unique. You have an amulet, with three slots. You find cards out in your travels that hold spells. There are 5 schools of magic total, Fire, Water, Air, Earth, and Necromancy. Each school has it's own unique, and sometimes overpowered, spells at your disposal. On top of this there are modifier cards to amplify their affects and reduce their mana cost, and when you find duplicate cards, they'll increase the power of your spell up to a certain amount.
The gear system. I haven't seen a game do something like this since. In Two Worlds, when you have duplicate pieces of gear, you can combine them with each other to create a single stronger piece. You can do this with weapons, armor, quivers, and rings. This allows you to find gear that's your favorite and actually let it grow with you. This is nice because there are hundreds of sets of armor and arms to choose from at any point in the game.
The character design. This isn't so much for actual characters, but for the monsters you find in the game. There are tons of unique, interesting monsters throughout the land of Antaloor. Even the less interesting ones are varied, from different species of wolves, wyverns, reapers, to varied models for zombies, ghouls, orcs, groms... the list could go on and on.
The soundtrack. Simply put, the music of Two Worlds is excellent. It fits the setting perfectly and I listen to it outside of playing the game regularly.
The voice acting. I'm not entirely sure if this should be labelled bad, because I'm not entirely sure this wasn't intentional, but the voice acting is like listening to a high school classroom re-enact a Shakespeare play. A lot of the dialogue can get somewhat humorous at times, especially with how
the voice acting can get at times, but more often than not it'll just be off-putting. Especially in the Asian-themed city of Ashos.
The story. It's generic fantasy bullsh*t. The game would be better off if it just dropped you in without the main story at all. Though the game does do a good job of making you feel like a son of a b*tch with the main quest. You can wipe out two whole cities while completing it, one city is mandatory and the other you have a more stealthy approach to, so you don't have to commit genocide just to get a jewel. Caught me by surprise the first time I played it. Other than that, I don't reccomend pursuing the main storyline unless you really, really want to.
The combat. It's just button-mashing. Press a button to attack, press a button to dodge, rinse, repeat. This is not unique to Two Worlds, though. Even the Elder Scrolls boils down to just rolling your face over the keyboard til something's dead.
The performance. It is worlds better than it is on the 360, but the game can get choppy in places and the graphics aren't as crisp as they could be. Lots of pop-in as well. This hurts the otherwise great open-world aspect of the game.
Alchemy. This one skill breaks the game. Level it to 10, find ingredients with a 'permanent' modifier, and you can brew and drink yourself to godhood.
Overall, Two Worlds is a decent game. It has some really great parts, some really bad parts, but at the end of the day, I'd say it's worth the purchase on sale. Not at $10.

Battleborn is to MOBAs (League of Legends) what Borderlands was to ARPG's (Diablo).
Saying it's just League Legends with guns is completely disingenuous though, as Battleborn really shines with its zany writing and gorgeous 2d animated effects. There's a full campaign that you can do solo, with friends, or with matchmaking. The writing is more Monty Python than Citizen Kane, so if you don't like juvenile humour then you should probably avoid. Good thing I still find fart jokes hilarious.
The multiplayer is as addictive as the best of them, and it has a lot of skills to master as you move up the ranks. Gear, unlockables, skins etc. are all great surface details, and the real depth comes from how the characters interact during the match to snag a victory.
Downsides: As of 5/23/16, matchmaking is broken and you'll probably get your face wrecked the first 20 games or so. Ick. I'm still enjoying it, but I did play the beta so I'm not losing too poorly to the 200hr+ hobbyists.

Battleborn is a really interesting mix of MOBA and PVE first-person action.
The campaign (multiplayer or solo) is well-written and each mission takes anywhere between 25-45 minutes. It is a blast to play through with friends, but can be quite a drag alone. In addition, you can play each level on an advanced or hardcore mode, which adds more challenge.
The online multiplayer has three game modes. The first is a standard capture-the-area mode, and is purely PVP. The other two are unique blends of minion pushing and objectives. Incursion is simply pushing a single lane to destroy your opponents sentries (towers). Meltdown, which is my favorite, is guiding minions to sacrifice while destroying your opponents minions (and hopefully them).
The game has, as I've mentioned previously, really good writing; I have laughed out loud a large amount of times. In addition to all that, each part of the game is embedded with a "tower defense" type build system, where you can build turrets, accelerators, and healing stations through shards you pick up while playing. The character design is also really well done, and each of the 25 heroes feel special in a way. The movement is fluid and solid, and you really do feel like a giant machinegun toting lumberjack, a hardened and sassy dwarf, or an insane four armed alien.
I would highly recommend anyone who is a fan of first-person games and MOBAs or online co-op play. It takes awhile to get good at the game and can be discouraging, but it is really fun once you understand what you are doing.

I recommend this only to the extent that you pay no more than $15 for it. This game has high production values and is very polished, but it is a very very short game. There just isn't enough content. I beat the single player campaign in 12 hours on my first try on normal. There are a couple game mechanics quirks that you can exploit to make the game a breeze once you learn them.
There seems to be a push to have you play multiplayer but this isn't a popular enough game to really find others to play with. The RTS controls are mostly primitive, and dragon form doesn't really last long enough (and isn't really effective enough) compared with RTS controls to really be a big part.
That said, I still give it a thumbs up because the dialogue is witty, the voice acting is well done, the world is refreshing, and there are innovations here that I enjoy. It just all ended too soon. I have a general rule - each dollar of a game should last me at least 1 hour, so a $40 game should give me at least 40 hrs of enjoyment to be worth the price. This game is therefore a "thumbs up" at about $10-15, but not a good value after that. I will try the custom maps and maybe change my review, but given that the best part of this game is not empire management and combat, but the characters and politics engine, it really is a better fit as a single player, story-driven game.

Even though I only have about 21 hours in experience in Wargame Airland Battle, (As of the time I'm typing this) I can see that this is a very great game and a very good one for RTS lovers. It has a, "Total War: 1985" feeling to it, as it shares a lot of characteristics with total war, but with a higher learning curve. And not just some, "Oh, new game. Better see what to do," its like dumping all of your experience in other games to adapt to this one. It is a very confusing game at first, and a lot would not get into the game at all. But for some RTS lovers, like me, it would be a strategical fiasco of combat. With so many units, and with soooo many stats for the units, its a very balanced game. You got tanks, that can be countered by airplanes, which could be countered by AA, which could be countered by infantry, which could be countered by helicopter, which could be countered by AA, which is countered by tanks. You get the gist. It has a very big, rock, paper, scissors, feel to it as you play. In the end, great game.

I really enjoyed this game, it took me 18 hours to make the cure and I am even somewhat sad that this journey is nearly over and I rarely get such a feeling when I finished a video game. In any case the game is a unique experience AND a niche game, so its not for everyone plus it has its faults (clipping issues, mapping can be tedious especially in the beginning and some objects like tends just vanish if they are farther away but can still be used as a point for triangulation if you know where they are, some graphics and textures don't look like they belong in because the rest of the environment is so well made and looks really beautiful) but those are only minor issues and didn't spoil my enjoyment in any serious way.

Miasmata lives from its immersive atmosphere when I came home from a trip I made my medicine, studied my journal and map and planed the next tour for tomorrow before I sat down on the edge off a cliff and watched the sunset or the cloudburst over the sea and just enjoyed the world around me.The game for me like for some others was a "slow starter", I didn't really like the first 1-2 hours very much, maybe because I already knew the beginning from lets plays or because I felt so lost without clear cut instructions other than to make the cure and no way to tell were the ♥♥♥♥ I am right now, but as time flew by and I made progress I got slowly sucked into the world of Miasmata. Music plays sparingly but its very soothing and fitting in such situations when you just barely escaped the creature and reached a new safe haven or watch the sun go down from your shack before taking some well earned rest.
The creature while not particularly smart or scary looking definitely gave me some memorable moments and is really the last thing you want to bump into when you spend your last 15 min mapping and trying to reach an outpost before night sets in. One day I ventured out found two new plants, got a lot of mapping done and forgot about the time so I didn't make it back to my base before nightfall. I got tired of waiting and my water was running out so I decided I will just try to slowly stumble forward through the darkness when suddenly I hear my heart beat. I turned around running as fast as I can before falling down a ridge landing in some bushes. Instinctively I ducked down and in the next moment the silhouette of the creature appeared on the ridge of the hill wandering around before running off.Needless to say I spend the rest of the night cowering in fetal position under my bush praying that Milo doesn't come back. I lost my plants but I survived that night, without water and a fever I dragged myself to a near outpost in the next morning and from that moment on I made sure to always make it home in time. Thats just one example, I had a few more thrilling moments but I will keep those to myself. And just to give you an idea I met the beast around 10-15 times in my 18h of playtime and that was just the right amount to keep it somewhat special.
After playing it 76/100 as a neutral rating seems about right when you consider all the minor flaws it has and that it could have been even better with a bit more polish, but my personal rating would be closer to a 90/100 and I would definitely buy it again even at full price.

Soul Gambler is a queer visual novel game. It grabs an interesting idea and develops it, creating an enjoyable story and experience all around. The idea is that, by making a certain pact, you can sell tiny bits of your soul in order to fulfil certain desires one might have. Ence the name, Soul Gambler. However, by decreasing your soul, the person will feel less and less human, and by reaching 0% he or she will simply become empty inside, unmoving and depressed.
Choice making also affects the outcome of several actions, something that makes the player want to replay the game a few more times. This is positive due to the low playtime this title offers. Also, the background music could be better. Sometimes it doesn't actually fit what's happening throughout the game.
The story of Faust and his misadventures with soul gambling are compelling and I ended up completing my first playthrough in one sitting.
The art design utilized in this title is satisfying and I have no complains about it. Overall, I have no complains about Soul Gambler, besides the short playtime, which is balanced by the high replayability value.

Albeit a bit short (little under an hour), the story is interesting, the presentation very good, and the story having enough branches that you'll probably play it a second and probably third time. More would just be for the 5 endings (and thus 5 ending achievements).
Having said that, I was pleasantly surprised how good this game was, and there's no reason you shouldn't pick it up now with Face It (That I haven't played nor own) for just a dollar. Go check it out!

Nice little game for under a dollar. Sell part of your soul to gain advantages in life, but suffer consequences as a result. SImple idea, but presented in a fun way.

Cons: the dialogue is sometimes aweful(though to the point of almost being amusing,) a lot of grammer problems(some almost seem like it was lost in translation, not sure if this game originated in the US or not,) short(though for the price I paid was the perfect length.)
Its on sale all the time, so wait for the next one and pick it up.

Reminding more a book than a game Soul Gambler is these titles called visual novels, where options are limited in reading plus decision making which has effects in the story.
So, while the gameplay in Soul Gambler might be thin it is the story which this is should be played for. I won't get into details but the tale is about mystery and romance and the manuscript is quite pleasant. This is not a child feature though because there is some drugs and murders included.
The chances to affect in tale are various and it should take 5 or 6 times to see every possible dialogue and event. The diversity of storyline is achived with the decision crossroads and four different attributes chosen in a beginning.  Although 'all roads lead to Rome' - the choices made aren't remarkable. No matter how you played your cards you are more or less chained to follow the main agenda.
The graphically well drown Soul Gambler might not be the long lasting joy taking only 1 hour to complete, but the decision points add some re-play value for as long as player is not annoyed of already seen events.
In my opinion Soul Gambler is good for its price and great when on sale. A good title in evergrowing family of visual-novels.

Eventually I tried to brute-force the database, and discovered a simple exploit that allows the player to play all of the videos in chronological order from start to finish. I watched them all, and the story was so bizarre that it lost any sense of drama I had at the beginning.
It was a clever idea that needed better execution.

I got this game free from Humble Bundle, and am writing this review right after I finished the game.
I'm not really amazing at reviews, so I guess I'll just shortly list out the pros and cons.
PROS:
- Amazing and fun gameplay
- Great and satisfying storyline (took me 12 hours to beat without too much collecting around)
- Superb characters and atmosphere
- The age of the game doesn't show a lot unless you're trying to inspect every detail.
- Semi-open world feels great and alive
- Lots of collectibles
- Wide variety of ways to approach things with your psychic powers
- Parkour mechanics that are up-to-par with many modern games' systems.
- Extremely creative levels
- Interesting, fresh, unique multi-stage boss fights
- Variety of enemy types
- All of the above all mix together so, so well, you really can't say you aren't having fun.
CONS:
- Gameplay and parkour can feel clunky on rare occasions, leading to frustration.
- Small amount of glitches that can cost you a part of your life in some cases.
- The inablity to unequip items. In the game there is an item called the Cobweb Duster which performs its action by you pressing the interact/use button, which means you can't talk to NPCs or use map objects while you're holding it. If you don't have any other items to equip, you'll have to use one of 2 other items that are always in your inventory which trigger animations that will take at least 10 seconds.
- Aforementioned Cobweb Duster needs to be bought with the game's currency to progress the story and to collect Arrowheads, you'll need to run around for 10 minutes collecting them. (tip: buy the drowsing rod. It'll set you back 50 but you can net from 30 to 200 arrowheads at once)
- The inablity to free roam the Camp after beating the game.
So, that's about it for now. As you can see the pros are plentiful while the cons are nitpicky and won't really affect your gameplay for too long. If you aren't sure, yes yes yes I 100% recommend the game. It's a one-of-a-kind experience with a lot of replayability for 10 bucks, or even less during the sales. Put it on your wishlist if you don't own it yet. And get it as soon as you can.

This is the first game I bought and played when I aquired my first computer(I didn´t have steam back then, good thing because then you would know how many hours i actually put into this game...). I was quite young, and was absolutely amazed by the medieval fantasy world of "Two Worlds". No matter where my young self went, i was flabbergasted by how the world painted a beautiful landscape, played a blood-boiling soundtrack, made cool weapons and the open world feeling was a first for me. I played this ALOT. Like, ALOT ALOT. Like, ALOT ALOT ALOT ALOT. You get the point...
I absolutely loved it.
As I grew up, I started playing other games. After a while, I was introduced more and more to the internet
(Sidenote: I remember activating my game with a telephone code...). On the internet you can get a whole lot of opinions on all kinds of things. Such as opinions on "Two Worlds". It seemed as though no matter where I went, players and critics all said the same thing. TWO WORLDS SUCKS.
I couldn´t disagree more! Did we really play the same game? Did they not experience the glory of shooting magic and summoning monsters from the tip of your fingers, riding your horse through vast grass plains and the narrow paths in forests? Had they been exploring all the different types of landscapes that the game had to offer?
Furious, I started Two Worlds in order to prove them wrong. Immediately my ears were caressed by the main menu music. I listened to the whole song before even starting a new game. Bliss, bliss! I began a new journey! I was thrilled to be playing Two Worlds again!
After clearning the tomb of filthy skeletons, I noticed... different things about the game. The framerate was poor, the screen resolution was messy and the animations seemed helter-skelter. The voice acting seemed weird, but it was just the introduction. But alas, i knew this even from when I first started playing the game! With this in mind, I made my way into town after picking the skeletons clean of loot.
Upon my arrival I talked with most of the townsfolk. As I didn´t speak nor understand english when I was young, I was in for a treat. The style of speaking in old english caught me off-guard, and made me slightly jump in my seat. After more and more dialogues, I started bursting into laughter! I was delighted as I continued my journey.
Suddenly when exploring, I remembered the reviews. I remembered how I was going on about the landscape, the cool weapons, the magic and yadda yadda. Those things actually still seemed great! Despite the poor resolution, framerate and other technical issues, I still found the world to be absolutely stunning!
After playing for quite a while, basking in the radiant rays of the sun, riding my horse wherever i pleased and killing monsters, I found myself to revel in the medieval fantasy world. But... I also started to see things more clearly. The things that the players and critics was saying alike Two Worlds was true. Two Worlds has a bunch of problems. Most forthcoming and noticeable are the technical ones.
Despite this, I still found myself appreciating the game! The comical old english, the enemies falling like ragdolls the instant they died, the entirety of the world was worthy of praise. The gorgeous enviroment, magic and freedom to explore was magnificent. I found out why I liked this game so much, and it can be summed up in one word. Immersion.
I truly feel immersion in this game. I tend to forget that I am playing, until my stomach starts to growl or i notice how the clock claims that it is three o clock in the night... Stupid clock... I am overjoyed to have found this game in a game store when I was a kid despite its popularity. Naturally, the feeling of nostalgia had a big part to play in this. ;)
This is a fantastic game, despite all its flaws. I nominated this game for the "No Apologies" award, as I see this as somewhat of a guilty pleasure game for me. ;) But no apologies! I will play this game with my head held up high with the corny appeal of this game! Keep on playing folks!
To finish, I hold a grand salute to all the ones who had a part in the making of Two Worlds.
Two Worlds will always have a special place in my heart.

Two Worlds, my first experience with this game was back in 2009 maybe? That was on the original XBOX 360 and boy did it SUCK to play on console. The frame drops, stutter, and lag spikes combined made it tough to continue playing especially as you progressed and your save game got bloated. Which is the primary reason this game got such a bad reputation!
However, the story asides from the terrible (but great in a comical sense) voice acting as well as the lore; this game was quite enthralling! In fact it is what made me play through the entire game from start to finish a few times over and to then purchase it on PC years later!
Now on PC, assuming you have a decent PC. For example something like a Quad Core chip from ~2008 8GB of RAM and a GTX 470 at least. This game is absolutely a pleasure to play, all the aforementioned issues with lag and stuttering and such are 95% gone.
Meaning you get to focus on the quite interesting and surprisingly expansive lore of this game! The open world design while feeling a little bit empty sometimes is usually quite lively with creatures NPCs etc... some interesting quests and storylines but most of all what I always loved about this game was the customizability you have in regards to abilities and magic!
From a Game Developer's perspective these systems are the most fun part of the game. They allow to you really customize your weapons, and magic in a real way. Weapons can be combined with special components to make them stronger, you can essentially choose any weapon you like, become attached to it and not be punished for it! You can upgrade the weapon as you progress through the game without limits and have it be just as good as other weapons you'd find much later (with few exceptions).
The magic system is even more fun allowing you to literally craft spells by choosing an element, and applying different card effects to the chosen element like a summoning effect which will make it summon a creature, a projectile effect to make ranged magic attacks, AoE effects to make spells that do things in an area around you, time effects to make buffs and debuffs! It was really quite neat and is also expanded upon in the sequel "Two Worlds II"!
So while this game may not hold up to todays standards. It definitely has some very interesting mechanics and some well thought out lore, stories and just is an interesting title as a whole.
Definitely would recommend this game. However, definitely check it some videos on it's gameplay and such to see if it is worth putting the time into for YOU. It's very dated now, and won't hold a candle to a lot of other options today so do some research before you jump in and are disappointed.

Battleborn is a really interesting mix of MOBA and PVE first-person action.
The campaign (multiplayer or solo) is well-written and each mission takes anywhere between 25-45 minutes. It is a blast to play through with friends, but can be quite a drag alone. In addition, you can play each level on an advanced or hardcore mode, which adds more challenge.
The online multiplayer has three game modes. The first is a standard capture-the-area mode, and is purely PVP. The other two are unique blends of minion pushing and objectives. Incursion is simply pushing a single lane to destroy your opponents sentries (towers). Meltdown, which is my favorite, is guiding minions to sacrifice while destroying your opponents minions (and hopefully them).
The game has, as I've mentioned previously, really good writing; I have laughed out loud a large amount of times. In addition to all that, each part of the game is embedded with a "tower defense" type build system, where you can build turrets, accelerators, and healing stations through shards you pick up while playing. The character design is also really well done, and each of the 25 heroes feel special in a way. The movement is fluid and solid, and you really do feel like a giant machinegun toting lumberjack, a hardened and sassy dwarf, or an insane four armed alien.
I would highly recommend anyone who is a fan of first-person games and MOBAs or online co-op play. It takes awhile to get good at the game and can be discouraging, but it is really fun once you understand what you are doing.

Despite the games many infuriating flaws I still find myself coming back to play. Over and over.
Yes, matchmaking is finicky. Yes, players can currently cheese one of the incursion maps (which I have never witnessed myself thus far). Yes some heroes are a downright pita to be matched up against (early days yet to be able to give an opinion on balance updates - unlike some players I can understand we can't have a patch every other day). And yes, there urgently needs to be a way to report toxic players.
But it is fun. It's got a great single player and co-operative campaign, which may seem short at 8 missions but I've found the replayability is there and I really don't mind doing this for gear upgrades. The recent addition of Advanced matchmaking has been a godsend and I've been lucky with the PUGS I've played with. Except on The Saboteur. That mission is cancer.
Like Borderlands before it, the games oozes character. The campaign is full of the Borderlands standard of humour we've come to know and love but I think what really stands out is the characterisation of the games heroes. I've found myself doing the Lore challenges not just for the hero specific legendary gear attached but... gasp... the lore. Oscar Mike being a personal favourite.
Multiplayer wise, I've come to prefer Incursion. The games most moba-like game mode. And while I've experienced the same issues as others being matched against higher level premades I have not had any issues waiting for matches. The longest waits being on the 2-3 minute side. Hero balance is an ongoing thing and it's quite early to comment specifically on how well Gearbox is doing with this, other than there has been some balance tweaks in hotfixes already and they have shown an interest in hearing what the players have to say.  I've not as much been infuriated by certain characters being overpowered but moreso with certain premade compositions (read as: I need friends and to not play alone). Obviously being moba-like, communication and co-ordination is key and a helpful pug can turn the tide against higher level premades. Sometimes. Kinda.
Performance wise I've had some hiccups on certain missions and maps. I am however playing on a low to mid range rig and with most settings at medium and AA and Physx off I've had a steady experience with fps and no other performance issues preventing me from playing and enjoying the game.
I do hope the game offers a demo or free weekend at some point as there are (and rightfully so) a lot of mixed views on this game the best way to decide if it is for you is to test the waters for yourself.
Personally, I'm having fun and while I can see why some aren't I'm deciding to keep the faith in GBX. At least for now.

Of all the games that I have played, the game that probably did the best at challenging my ethics was Divinity: Dragon Commander.  Admittedly, the gameplay is lackluster in both the strategy and combat phases; it was not long before I habitually skipped tactical battle for auto-resolution.  But where Divinity: Dragon Commander really shines is in the diplomacy phase – the phase of each turn where you take a step back from world conquest to deal with management of your empire through the enacting of laws and policies.  Your empire has racial factions, each with their own dominant political, social and religious sensibilities.  Sure, their representatives are largely caricatures of modern political stances, but they still manage to bring arguments to the table that push you to evaluate your choices.
Every decision will have consequences – in the very least, they will alter how favorably each faction views you, and can have other (sometimes quite unexpected) impacts as well.  Displease the dwarves too often, and you might find your royal coffers running on empty.  Make the imps happy enough, and they’ll offer up the opportunity to gain a fantastic and horrible new bomb… if only you’ll allow them to mine in the one place where the mystical material they need can be found (despite, you know, the whole “sacred elven burial site” nonsense).  Divinity: Dragon Commander was surprisingly good at making me examine if and when I would embrace practicality or expediency over my personal sense of right and wrong.
The diplomacy phase also includes dealing with your military generals, each of which bring their own personalities, problems and histories to the war room.  In addition, you will enjoy a diplomatic marriage that will bolster your approval rating, at least initially, with one of the races; but your wife adds an entirely new substory to navigate through, with multiple possible outcomes.
The diplomacy phase of this game is rich enough to not only play the game for, but to replay it until you have exhausted all the diplomatic possibilities.  And since maintaining high enough favor with a faction will open up surprising new avenues, there is a lot of possibilites to explore and enjoy.

As the only person in my friends list to have purchased this game, I feel its only fair to leave a review,
Miasmata is essentially a realistic survival horror (minus the need for food)
Your goal is to find various plants and combine them to make a medicine that will cure you of your disease, its sort of like a more complex form of slender
To my knowledge, there are no monsters, no people, no ghosts or anything supernatural, just wild animals and one in particular that wants to kill you.
Miasmata does not go out of its way to scare you, but I feel this works more in its favor then against it. The fear comes from concepts that are very real and very obvious, you can die in the wilderness, or get lost.
there are scraps of a map scattered throughout the game, but there is no pointer that shows where on the map you are, so i suggest relying on bodies of water and your compass to tell you where you are and which way you need to go.
TL;DR
more of an amnesia style of horror, except with no monsters and its in the wild, is it worth 15 dollars? Probably not, but they do seem like they put a lot of work and originality behind it, so i'd suggest either wait for a sale or pay them the full 15 to show your support.

As someone who cares deeply about science and discovery, this game was very refreshing and engaging for me, despite its nagging technical and design issues.
I highly recommend that anyone with a similar passion for science, discovery, and adventure give Miasmata a try. It is very rough around the edges, but its dedication to its novel niche concept makes it worthwhile. It's a game that is geared towards a specific audience, and that audience will likely love the game. For anyone else, it could be a passable diversion, but you might find it too dull and boring to play to completion.

Miasmata is an "exploration" game, you wake up on an island and have to find plants to create an cure for the disease you're suffering from. You have to wander through the forests, spot and collect plants, then carry them back to somewhere you can identify them and their effects.
You are also chased by "something" during all this, but I won't tell more about it here ;)
What makes the essence of that game is the Cartography Mechanic. Basically, you'll have to build your map on your own, not to get lost. To reveal the map, you have to stand at a particular spot and aim with your compass to 2 known objects (houses / statues / ruins) that you know, so you'll be able to triangulate your position and reveal the map.
Then, the "how to get in the forest without being lost" will make your brain cells works.
The graphics are beautiful, every tree has been "hand-placed" by the two developpers (they have made the entire game, including the physics engine, on their own... that's incredible).
[Pros] :
+ Awesome graphics, really (but don't hope playing with a low-end GC), better than some AAA Games
+ The feeling of being "lost" on that Island ; this is the sole game where I really had the feeling that I was lost xD
+ A real "exploration game", where you're thrown in and don't know what to do at first
+ The Cartography mechanics, quite unique if you like it. It serves the "I am lost" feeling
[Cons] :
- English only, do not buy if you only speak your native language (other than English)
- Your character has soap under its feet (not actually, it's realistic, but too realistic xD)
~ The whole game relies on exploration, there is (almost) no ennemy (except the controls)
~ If you don't like the cartogrpahy system, you won't like that game
[Conclusion] : If you're ok with English, like exploration, wouldn't be bothered by a lack of ennemies, have a good GC and want to really feel "lost" in a game, give it a try ;) 8.5/10

Wargame Airland Battle
Description:
This is great real-time strategy.Wargame is set in the year 1970-1990 on the Scandinavia.Wargame is not Company of Heroes or command and conquer. It just not building strategy with action elements. In this game you have to think.Wargame developers added aircrafts and other units, in wargame is 864 units and two free dlc are available.
Summary:
Wargame is a realistic strategy that requires patience. It's a little harder in the beginning to get oriented in the indication of units and on map find out where what you have.

The multiplayer is perfect.  The single player is a different story...
First off, the AI cheats.  I am talking about a "zero fog of war" senario for the AI.  It may not be able to blind fire on your units, but it will send a worthless one point truck out towards one of your hidden units.  This will occur seemingly without fail.  While I can accept this happening every once in a while due to blind luck, this happens EVERY TIME I try to send spec ops. behind enemy lines.  That thenpaves the way for every aircraft in the pact's arsenal to drop half the planet's stockpile of bombs on my units.
Next, the AI spams.  As in, it will spam T-55s and BTR by the hundreds, while I, if I were playing pact, would be unable to field 20.  My units only have so much ammo and can only fire so fast.  They will almost always get overrun just by sheer numbers.  When playing the AI, it becomes less of an RTS and more of a tower defense, "Spam everything you've got," game.
Then there is the lack of intelligent AI in your own units.  I want to be maing strategic plays, not frantically telling every radar guided AA gun to turn off its radar to avoid being destroyed by a SEED (suppression of enemy air defense) aircraft, or telling an unarmed recon hellicopter to get its a-- out of a Tungustka's (Russian made AA gun) range.  For the enemy AI though, its a different story.  After all, when you can make 3.7 billion computations a second, its pretty easy to micromanage every unit.
As said above, when you are playing multiplayer, its a differnt story.  Yes, unfortunatly you do still have to micromanage every unit you have.  But so does your opponent.  And they are not micromanageing unitsat a rate of 3.7 billion a second.
This game has an unparalleled level of depth for a "game" RTS (i.e. not Command.)  Armored Vehlicals (Steam really needs spell check :)) have varying armor thicknesses based on where a shot hits.  (Front, side rear, top.)  Infantry can hide in forests and towns, making ambushes a snap.  Fuel and ammo is limited with logistic vehlicals (once again, I need spell check) resupplying your units.  You have full control over your aircraft while they are over the battlefield, if you tell them otherwise, they will NOT fly a straight line to thier target (not recommended as AA will likely shoot them down.)  Your units are irreplacable.  Although you can reinforce, your reinforcements are not unlimited.  There are so many features in this game that I would likely need to type five pages to list all the features in this game.
Would I recommend this game?  That depends.
Single player: HELL NO.  This is an exercise in frustration with the amount of AI cheating present.
Multiplayer: Absoultly.  This is a well made RTS game that, IMO should be just as famous as Starcraft or C&C.
The AI is very hard to play against. Even on the "easy" setting.  Pretty useless game for those who likes to play with AI. :/

I will be the first to admit that I originally bought this 10 dollar game because I saw that you could defeat the final boss in the first 2 minutes of the game. Sadly, this glitch has been patched by this point. :( Major disappointment. Oh well. I bought it also because I like open world rpgs, so here are my first impressions in the 2.8 hours I have played of it.
Complaints:
1. The voice acting is UNBEARABLY bad. I mean, I guess if you don't care that much about voice acting then it won't be a huge deal, but for me voice acting is a huge part of my story immersion and when it is terribad, it is really difficult to keep going.
2. Good news! You can get a horse early on into the game! But you're probably better off without it. The horse on a keyboard is ridiculously difficult to control. So difficult that my boyfriend started sending me horse puns to ease the pain of it. I told him to get out. It may be better once my horseback riding skill is better, but I doubt it.
3. The tutorial sort of barely touches upon a lot of important things. They kind of leave it up to you to figure out a lot of mechanics.
4. There are .... some graphic glitches. Not too terrible though, and this may be a result of my graphics card.
5. Character customization isn't that great, plus you only have the option of playing as a male. Which sucks because I usually play females and enjoy having the option. There is probably a story reason for this, but so far I don't see why the option to have a female main character couldn't have been there? Especially if this game was supposed to compete with ES Oblivion at the time it was made.
Good Stuff:
1. THE ALCHEMY SYSTEM IS LEGITIMATELY THE BEST THING ABOUT THIS GAME. You can do alchemy from anywhere with ingredients in your inventory and even better, you can NAME your potions. This leads to me naming my potions and my inventions a whole bunch of ridiculous things.
2. Because this game is pretty old, it runs really nicely on my computer. Your mileage may vary on this one, but I assume most people on steam have at least a decent running computer so that may be a plus.
3. Combat mechanics aren't too bad. It's pretty easy.
4. Despite a few glitches, the graphics are pretty nice! Except the human models, a lot of them looks weird in the face.
5. The soundtrack is gorgeous and I would recommend getting it at some point.
So, there's a bit of the good and the not so good. Overall, it's not a terrible game, but it's definitely not the greatest thing I've seen. The story is something I can't really put under good or bad at this point, because I haven't seen too much of the main story just yet, and I haven't really had the time to get attached to any characters. I'd recommend the game for the current price, because it's not a lot of money (even less if you're buying it during a steam sale), but it is a pretty decent game for the money you do pay for it.

Terrible "Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure" game, worth $1 at most. The HO scenes are lazy cut-and-paste of stock photos, and objects aren't "hidden" at all, just lined up, large and obvious. Puzzles are not intuitive but once you look at the intructions, they're easy; you can solve some just by clicking around or dragging items randomly.
The game also crashed twice. I see Steam says I played 5.7 hours, but that means the game must have been open as a background process on my computer after it crashed, because this is 2-3 hours of gameplay at most. The English is very bad and confusing (example: it sends you looking for a watering can when you're supposed to find a funnel).
Story is awful. As usual in these games, you're in a car crash at the beginning. As usual, your companion goes missing and you have to look for them. Halfway through the game, your character suddenly reveals she and her boyfriend were driving to an old town because your character is an amnesiac searching for her past. The game might have been slightly more interesting if that had been mentioned at the beginning, rather than dropped in out of nowhere, halfway through. As it is, the amnesia thing was just pointless and silly.
Maybe it's better that the story is so boring, because the ending is unfinished. It seems to end on a sequel-bait cliffhanger, but no one could possibly care enough about this story to be left in any suspense by the lack of closure.
I've probably played over a hundred HO games, and this game is in the bottom 5. It's not even really worth your time, let alone your money.

Another amazing Game From Larian Studios. Although the graphics in the combat phase are a bit lacking, it is everything you should expect from the Divinity line of games. Easy learning curve, but hard play curve. Easy is Normal, Normal is Hard, and Hard is Hard.........er. Also, a beautiful mix of 4x, map control, and RTS elements. Even though the RTS elements are extremely basic, they should not be the make or break of this game. Every decision has positive and negative effects on the game. Want to specialize with a certain race, be prepared to have lower performance when battling on a corner of the map controlled by another. Want to generalize the races, that's fine too. Just don't expect too many advantages. All in all, it is a well rounded game that I feel is under appreciated because they did not focus on any one point to shine.

Here is my review of the game:
Pros:
-Politics:
This game has an extremely good politics system in place where you can make decisions that effect not only individuals but entire races as a whole. This phase is easily the best part of the game, it is well voice acted, well animated, and provides great enjoyment for most.
Cons:
-Map phase:
The map phase is shallow to say the least, here you can play cards that improve empire related things, or build buildings that will allow you to improve income and recruit units or mercenaries. But that is all, there is nothing more here, no diplomacy, no trading, nothing that would make you want to spend time strategizing here.
-Combat:
This should be the most interesting part of the game, since this is the part where you get to be the dragon...for about 2-5 mins. Here are the problems with this phase:
First the design choices, as in the way the units look, they are not only quite small(can't zoom in enough), but also look the same for all factions.
Second, the speed of the combat is waaaaay too fast, if you want to play defensively, you are screwed, you want to build up bases, you are screwed. The only way to win is if you blob all over the enemy at the start of the battle in which case the battle ends rather quickly because if your draw it out, the enemy becomes too strong and usually you can no longer overwhelm them before you run out of resources, enjoy your 5 mins long battle without strategies and being the dragon for about 5 mins. This problem however also relates to being the dragon.
Third, the dragon is strong at the beginning, but if you try and draw out the match to enjoy some base building, you will quickly find, that your dragon is becoming more and more useless as time passes on, since the enemy is improving their units all the time, they will take more hits and you will take less, in the end you will die extremely quickly, making becoming the dragon rather useless.
Fourth, the units have way too many skills you can't micromanage on the same level as the ai, which can make some fights rather one sided.
Fifth, and this is the largest problem with the combat by far. Mercenary cards. Why in the world would you even want to enter combat with such bad mechanics behind it when you can simply bypass it by spamming inns and mercenary cards and than using auto-combat?
-The length of the skirmish matches:
These only take anywhere from 25(min difficulty)-45(max difficulty) mins. I tested this by using only mercenary cards and lol i won all of my matches against highest difficulty ai in 45 mins max. This is a joke. Mercenary cards shouldn't be in the game or should be better balanced.
-Story:
What story? You mean the few cutscenes we get?
The campaign can be completed in about 2-3 hours, which is extremely short for a game like this. The enemies are quite generic, have no personality, don't taunt you and pretty much act the same on the battlefield, or at least i haven't noticed that they did anything differently from eachother.
To sum it up, the devs created a great politics mechanic in the game, unfortunately the game fails at the other parts, and for the title dragon commander, i was expecting to see more dragons or at least more often than about 2-5 mins in combat. I have the feeling that if they went with the original concept, instead of remaking the whole game halfway through in a single year, they could've achieved more, alas, it is not so.
Do i recommend this game for the current price(40eur)? NO
This game is not worth 40 eur.
But i do recommend you pick it up when it is on offer.
The game is worth about 15-20 eur, carried by the politics and the multiplayer may give you a few hours of amusement.

One of the best game I ever played, but probably not for everyone.
This game is terribly "hard", yet so immersive.
Because you will find youself lost as soon as you will wander without pinpointing your position, searching this one plant you hope will releave the pain.
Because you will fall, crippled by the plague you have to treat, that make you slide on every surface.
Because you will feel alone, surrounded only by the deep forest and the whisper of the wind.
Because you are not alone, and you will fear for your life, and your sanity.
You will experience a new kind of atmosphere, have adrenaline rushes, and feel the fear. Not because of some petty tricks to surprise you, but because you will find yourself hunted, while you are so terribly vulnerable and alone, as a sick man without a proper weapon, who can only run.
If you're into survival, this is your game.
Two advice: -Read the cartography manual you'll find ingame. If you don't grasp that mechanic, you won't manage to do it, nor apreciate the game.
-Think of it as a real adventure. I myself wrote some notes about how I felt during my "trip", because the atmosphere was so intense. I get lost once for a several hours, after I tried to run away from "it". It was one of the very few "total immersion" I ever had in a game.

After the Y2K, seven video interviews of a lady get fragmented into hundreds of clips. Your task is to uncover the truth by searching for keywords and getting results from the computer's automatic transcription. YouTube should really adopt that tech as the transcription is spot on.
The game doesn't explain much more than this. By watching the clips, you uncover pieces of the story and find more keywords to try, like names of people or words that you think she used elsewhere. Search results are limited by 5 at a time, so you're forced to narrow searches down in some cases. This limited and unstructured stream of information makes for an unconventional experience. Fitting the pieces together and discovering the truth on your own was very rewarding to me.
Some were turned off by the at times awkward acting and some of the story's twists. I can see where they're coming from, but overall I thought this was a very enjoyable experience. The range of emotion from the actress is pretty impressive, and the story has enough depth that I could spend four hours looking for every clip to make sure I didn't miss anything!

Miasmata is a minimalistic survival game where you play the researcher Robert Hughes. You're cast away on an island, suffering from some kind of plague, and your aim is to find a cure as soon as possible. Luckily, there has already been some kind of a research team on the island but something has happened to them...
I will start by saying that Miasmata is terribly beautiful. The graphics isn't always perfect but all in all the environments are amazing. I am incredibly impressed by the two brothers who made this game and the game engine on which it runs. Miasmata is immersive; My first night playing I couldn't stop until four in the morning, when I reluctantly realized it was getting light outside.
To find a cure for your plague you have to find and research the plants and fungi on the island. It sounds trivial, but in Miasmata there is noone to hold your hand. You have to make progress using the notebooks you find from the earlier research team and on your own findings. The game is completely open world and you have no checkpoints or route to follow.
There is also no automatic map. Instead, you draw your map using triangulation. Two known landmarks give you your position on the map and is what you use to update your map. Other than that you have to use your compass and your memory. (Orienteerers probably have an advantage!)
You have no classic menus or inventory, instead you check your log book where all your notes and research is saved. You can also check on how you are feeling and take drugs for fever or other conditions.
These three elements: Open world, the map system, and the log book creates a massively immersive feeling. Every menu, note or inventory has a "real" representation in the game.
Other than that Miasmata is a creepy game which gave me some big adrenaline rushes. Instead of jumpscares, Miasmata provides the unnerving feeling of always being followed (and the panic of being discovered). Nature is also an enemy: Climbing mountains isn't easy and if you run too fast down a slope you will fall. Hopefully you know where you are when you are back in control, but in worst case you are lost and have to start looking for known landmarks again.
On the negative side: I have to admit I was on several occations frustrated and annoyed when my assiduous exploration was interrupted. (By what, I will not mention...) I actually even rage quitted several times (but only to start it again after a minutes). At the same time, this is part of what is charming with the game and what creates intensity.
There are also some small bugs, but nothing that can't be easily solved.
A final warning to those who want to be able to close down a game quickly: You can save only at given save points. They are many and spread widely, but it can be good to know if you are the kind of gamer that have to be able to close down with just some seconds notice.
I guess I should have lower expectations from a team of two, but the game felt clunky and directionless.

Seriously one of the most profoundly underrated games I have ever played.
Things Miasmata did that were totally amazing and have not been properly replicated before or since:
*A completely original exploration based gameplay concept from the triangulation mapping
*A sense of maintained suspense and horror thanks to the complete unpredictability of the monster that can show up at any time or not show up for hours as you explore.
*A player character that feels legitimately weak and frail when injured. Your injuries and dehydration make the character more difficult to control and more prone to tripping and falling. Your characters momentum will frequently send you careening off cliffs in a panic unable to stop yourself in time, especially when running from the aforementioned monster.
It is a good game.

Miasmata is a fun and interesting game, but not without its flaws.
Pros:
-Disease survival aspect is done fairly well
-World is beautiful and huge
-Day/night cycles are realistic
-Variety of interesting plants to find
-Walking/gravity effect is also very realistic and makes the game more immersive (there's a real fear of momentum throwing you off a cliff instead of being able to magically stop at the last second.)
Cons:
-The "Creature" is a huge pain, and not in a good way. It feels broken most of the time and out of place.
-No food is necessary, which takes away from the survival aspect a bit
-A lot of the achievements are glitchy (search on the forums for the 3rd party fix before you start playing)
In summary:
If you're willing to put up with the annoyance of the Creature, it's worth picking up for people who like adventure/exploration and survival games.

I've enjoyed Miasmata. It took me a long time to play it, as I had the game for several years before I finished it. It was one of my "I have nothing to play... oh, wait, let's do something in this for a bit" games.
Miasmata utilizes a rather interesting mechanic: a triangulation process for mapping out the island and finding your location, which makes this game stand out a lot as I have not seen anything like it elsewhere. The AI for the monster is wonderful, as it seems to show up with enough frequency and has some great pathing and bahaviors, much like a real cat. The fact that it could show up at any time, especially when you are covering lots of ground quickly, adds to the tension and creates a great atmosphere. The snippets of story through notes create a chilling mystery set on a suprisingly beautiful island.
This game, if comparrisons are made, somewhat feels "slender-esque" as you are a plague victim scouring the island for plants to synthesize a cure, and medicines to keep you alive along the way. I feel like the monster shows up more as you get closer to completion of the cure and it seems to show up more in critical areas, such as places where X plant for the cure is guarenteed.
My only issue with the game revolved around the controls. The movement of the character can be wonky sometimes. I feel like it does a great job of simulating the rigors of climbing with sliding and exhaustion; however, there are many times I'd want to move a foot or so forward, maybe down a 2% grade, and the guy would either overstep or just take off running. Many a cliff have I fallen from due to this "over/undersensitivity." I've found that alternating between forward and backward as you walk down any slope can greatly reduce the threat of "tripping."
There are also times where you'd trip from one-foot drops, get stuck on stairs or small logs (which is terrible when you are being pursued), bump a tree the wrong way and bounce off sideways, be following a curved ledge and start sliding to the right. I just felt I, as a human being, would be able to have better control of my footing; the game makes me feel like a baby who has just learned how to walk, yet lacks basic control.
Other than movement mechanics, I have greatly enjoyed the game so far. I enjoy exploration games and find that the ability to triagulate on the map adds more to the exploration reward. Miasmata has just enough tension and "horror" to attract fans of those genres and manages to stay fresh, as the map is fairly well-sized, allowing for many hours of play.

Please do not let the technical flaws of this game (of which there are plenty) turn you away from it. If you're the kind of person who can allow yourself to get completely immersed into a virtual world, look past those flaws and give this world a try.
Yes, there are issues. The uphill/downhill momentum can at times feel a bit... overzealous. Graphical fidelity is all over the place - while the general environment and landscape looks beautiful from afar, certain ugly details are exposed given a close-up. Several Steam Achievements are broken. You should probably avoid Alt+Tabbing the game due to the dreaded "One Moment Please..." problem. Performance issues can bring the entire world to a complete standstill for several seconds at a time, and you'll eventually realize that the only thing that "no loading screens" really means is that loading can get you killed. As the game was made from scratch by a pair of brothers, this sort of stuff is to be expected. There is an unofficial community patch out there (along with other helpful game utilities), and I'd recommend that you check that out before taking things too far.
But to be perfectly honest, since I decided to give this game another try after a near-year-long hiatus taken shortly after the intro, I'm thankful that I didn't pass it up. As one of those aforementioned people who can immerse themselves in games quite easily, I found a tension in this game that few other games have ever made me feel. That moment when I'm standing on the porch of my safehouse, barren map in-hand, building up the courage to take my first step into the unknown. That moment when I've got my headphones cranked up, and I'm crouch-walking through the forest, eyes peeled, my heart stopping at the crunch of every twig. That moment when all hell has broken loose and I've gone into a full-on panic-sprint, knowing that my only chance at survival is to put myself at the complete mercy of the terrain and just
. Those moments are gaming gold.
Miasmata has a bit of a learning curve; anybody who has played it can attest to that. For all of the things that this game can give to you, there are just as many things that it will leave you to take for yourself. You'll struggle with movement. You'll struggle with cartography. You'll leave the house a
too late one night and find yourself completely lost, hopeless, and staring death in the face. But give this game your time and your effort, and it will give you a completely unreplicated experience in return.
Save early, save often. Stay alert, stay alive. You've been warned!

Are you a fan of Visual Novels? How about classic noir stories straight from the ’50s? Then “The Monster Inside” will be a small treat for you.
Read more at:

More like a proof of concept and based on a Ludum Dare entry, The Monster Inside provides a short and neat read that succeeds in quickly building an atmospheric setting. The graphics style, music and written story are all in itself solid with the music ranking foremost.
Presented in small tabletop dioramas, the black and white still scenes feature minimal movement within a minimalist setup. Since these scenes mostly accompany the writing, they are easy to take in and depict only the most essential set pieces to identify the locality. A smoking ashtray, crime scene tape and chalk outlines immediately invoke the clear theme of a detective mystery. The score intensifies this theme with a handful of fine orchestral jazz tunes.
As the sound and vision suggests, the story is a rather typical noir fiction with a little twist towards the ending. It doesn't matter if the story is predictable in any way, that's part of the noir theme, but the writing is good enough to plunge into darkness and wait and see what comes next.
There are only a few dialogue choices, which don't seem to make a difference within the story but let the player set a little bit of the personality of the protagonist. Every other chapter the player is prompted to investigate the scene via point and click and that is already how far the interaction goes. For such a short and linear audio-visual novella the interactive options are sufficient enough. The only thing that can be mildly intrusive is the popping of the “NEXT” button, which is delayed slightly. Since that is often the only thing that moves in a frame, it can be slightly distracting to wait for it.
All in all, The Monster Inside is an entertaining novella with a noir vibe and a great soundtrack.

Five bucks for a small game these days is pretty steep. Games like this are usually free on site like Itchio and Gamejolt, so is this worth your money?
I suppose that depends on how you approach the game. I certainly enjoyed my time with this.
The game is from a child's perspective, and takes place in the days following Christmas, which is a topic and style not usually tackled in horror games. The graphics are subpar at best, but the atmosphere created from the first moments of the game really set the tone for later.
*SPOILERS FOR THE STORY PAST THIS POINT ON*
Once Mama is introduced, everything is thrown on its head. The house becomes as wicked and scary as the buildup suggests, and more than likely you are going to die from sheer confusion and terror.
This leads me to one of my biggest problems with the game: Mama's kill method.
From the first time Mama is introduced, it seems as though her A.I. is programmed like the usual "She can't see you, but she can hear you" deal. Well, that seems the case, but I suffered from dying to what seemed like nothing. Apparently she can just warp all over the place, and if you're not prepared she can insta-kill you out of nowhere. Luckily the game supplements this with constantly saving checkpoints in the night.
The Tattletails alsohave a Hunger, Battery, and Brush meter that gradually decreases as they away from the things that regenerate those meters. I felt as though this was unneccessary, as I never encountered a time when the Tattletails yelling put me in peril.
The ending of the game is where I lost interest, however, as the last night was more tedious as it was scary. By this time I had already gotten the shock factor of dying out of the way (As my FNAF experience has conditioned me for) and dying was an annoyance rather than a terrifying plight,
Oh? But didn't I say that the game put up checkpoints every so often in case you died? I did. The last night puts checkpoints too, though only after surviving long, seemingly random Mama encounters, and fetch quests.
The story seemed unique, but several factors (Such as my parents not existing, though that could have been the horror trope) marred the experience I was ready to be over with.
The ending was lackluster, but I have et to get the "Secret Ending" I think you receive after obtaining all the easter eggs, so perhaps the True Ending isn't as bad.
Nevertheless, give this game a go if you're into Five Nights at Freddy's style games, or for a cool twist on the child's perspective/Christmas horror story genre.

Soul Gambler was a pretty cool VN. While the concept of selling your soul is already pretty norm, they play with the concept in a way that feels fresh, and enjoyable. Selling only bits and bits of your soul for what you want instead of going for broke with 1 wish that'll backfire. These actually work the way you want!
The game is creative, and enjoyable despite a few flaws. They have a Stat system of Strength, Manipulation, Intelligence, and Charisma. While these help make parts easier, it honestly seems pointless to invest in anything besides Intelligence, you can even raise your Charisma to 4, beyond the normal cap of 3 and it doesn't do ANYTHING if you get 4, literally no effect for going beyond human limit. I also wished the story was longer and we were able to explore the whole concept of how souls worked, increasing your soul currency, encounter more potential soulmates, and so on.
For a game of this length however, I was still happy, did my first playthrough in like 80 minutes, but with the replay value I'm going for longer, exlporing possibilities. The story is very promising, the characters are interesting, though a few really could have been expanded on to be better, and the choices you make are good. I bought it for like 30 cents, but I would have bought it full price, it's just that good.

Payday the Heist is one of the best FPS's I've played in a long time! It has everything to make you want to keep on playing, keep on grinding those achievements and unlockables... Nah, what am I kidding? It's the worlds best "Drill Fixing Simulator". Only buy this if you love fixing Drills for days!
Overall I recommened you buy this even if you don't like FPS's because you'll love this and I'll tell you why in the pros and cons:
Pros:
♦ AI that seem to just work (This makes for an epic single player experience)
♦ Huge amount of challenges, upgrades and unlockables (This is awesome for replay abilities)
♦ Amazing Achievements (These are the right balance of difficulty and help keep the game fresh)
♦ Graphics seem okay (Graphics could be slightly better, but for what they are, they are pretty good and suit the game)
♦ Voice Acting that's on point (Heaps of games lack voice acting but this one has everything voice acted to a T which enhances every heist that little bit more)
♦ Nice number of Masks and Playable Characters
♦ Only 2 paid DLC not 10 million like Payday 2 (Payday 2 has way too much pointless DLC)
♦ DLC that isn't just Skins (This is awesome as most paid DLC these days for games are just skins and not actual content, but this DLC expands the game and is well worth buying)
♦ Multiplayer server and hosting that just works (One of the best servers I've played on in terms of being able to host and have people play with little to no lag)
♦ Ingame Microphone (Every multiplayer game should have one of these, being able to rage at peole for dying is soo good)
♦ Awesome number of difficulties (Overkill is a bit exessive but it's worth the challenge for us pros)
♦ Good amount of Missions/Objectives per Heist (Isn't too many and isn't too few, just a great balanced amount)
Cons:
♦ Not many Heist Maps (This isn't really a problem due to the number of achievements, challenges and unlockables each map has... But after you do each heist map it can feel repetitive eventually due to the lack of Heist Maps to grind on)
♦ Eventually it turns into a grind (Once you've got the initial achievements and challenges it turns into a grind of doing the same heist over and over again just to unlock that next challenge, upgrade, unlockable or the next achievement)
♦ No tutorial to explain what is going on (It is pretty easy to pick up, but for a first timer it can be pretty daunting, I didn't know we could switch classes by tab until way into playing for example)
♦ Restoring Power within 5 seconds to get the achievement on No Mercy too hard (This seems almost impossible as you never know which power switch you have to press to turn back on and some are ages away...)
Overall, if you like Drill Fixing Simulators I suggest you buy this now, don't hesitate. But in all honesty there are way more Pros than Cons and the cons aren't even that bad. So, if you like FPS's that have a huge amount of challenges, upgrades, unlockables, achievements that you can play both online with friends and offline by yourself with epic AI this is for you,,, even if you don't, I'm sure this game will make you enjoy FPS's.
I give this a 9/10 (If you ignore the slight grinding once you get to a certain point, lack of tutorial and the fact there are not many Heist Maps... then it'd be a solid 10/10).

A little story for you all.
This game holds a special place in my heart. When I was younger I played this on my Xbox-360. I beat the whole game and got to the ending, after beating the boss, I did what most people would do, and saved. Not knowing that the game would end shortly after killing the boss, promptly booting me back to the title screen. I had planned on going back and doing more side quests and exploring more of the world, but since only one save was supported, I was buggered. I held a personal vendetta from then on, swearing to the heavens I would replay it one day, doing more side quests before seeing the end of the game.
And so here we are, years later. I did as many side quests as I could manage, and saw myself to the end, laughing at the terribly "amazing" voice acting all the way.. And now, seeing the credits scroll and knowing that I can pop back into the game at any time and explore (yes I learned my lesson, I saved just before the end boss this time) I felt a sense of peace.
So.. overall In summary, if you think you would appreciate satisfyingly cheesy voice acting in a cobbled together open-world RPG as much as I have, give this dirty gem a play, just make sure you save BEFORE the boss. 8/10

It's been a while since I've played this, so I'll just talk about all the things that still stand out in my mind whenever I think about this game. Just to start, I played this when I was about 13, so a lot of this was new to me and it shaped the way I saw a game. This was a good example to me of all the unique systems that could be in an RPG and what I would compare future games to.
1. Weapon and armor upgrade system - this is by far my favorite upgrade system ever in a game. When you own two of the same weapon or armor you can "stack" them to increase the stats, so you could wear the same gear for hours and just keep upgrading the stuff bandits drop frequently.
2. Magic - The magic system isn't really fleshed out, but out of magic, archery, and melee it's the most fun and visually pleasing. If I remember correctly there's a lot of variety, including summoning, and making your own spells, which again is so "out there" that no other game. compared to magicka 1 and 2, and two worlds 2, can make such a fun spell making system.
3. Leveling system - The way you level up feels so off in some way, but the sound the game makes when you level up is addicting, like the level up sound in call of duty multiplayer, it just fills you with happiness.
4. Potion making - THIS IS A BIG ONE. You can combine certain ingredients to make permanent stat boosting potions. This is pivitol to making your character a god. Also you can make a potion to make you walk on water, that way you can run to all the islands in the game without spending skill points on swimming or taking off your armor.
5. Teleport and personal teleport - Very early on in the game you get the ability to teleport to different locations using portals, but what makes this spectacular is that YOU can get your own and make your own teleport location. Kill some villagers and take over a house as storage; there is no stealing mechanism in this game as far as I remember.
6. The vast open world - This is one of the largest RPG games I've ever played, if not the largest. One of the main quests has you go to a swamp, desert, and a fog forest, and I didn't see any of these things for a long time, and even when I did I didn't want to explore because I saw so much of the game already I wanted to finish it.
7. The last time I played this I played it on a $200 non gaming laptop. This thing is so old and overall not visually stressing that you could play it on just about anything nowadays.
8. The fighting with staffs makes you look like a jedi.
9 Last thing - Don't hold this game to low standards because of visual quality, face graphics, conversational dialogue, etc. In this game you are having the most fun outside of the cities just doing what you want, exploring caves and killing cyclopses in tombs. Just pick a direction and see where the game takes you, after you get the teleportation skills of course.
Overall I'd give this game 10/10 when you review the game for its RPG elements and not the graphics.

If you've ever played PropHunt Garry's Mod, then this game will not be anything crazy new to you. It's basically that, but improved upon dramatically.
Every round you play as either a stereotypical looking witch that shapeshifts into pretty much whatever object they want to, and tries to blend in and not get caught for a set duration of time. Or you play as a fat hunter that hucks potatoes at things that seem suspicious and out of the ordinary. That's the game put simply.
While the game is still working out some kinks and adding things, I think at this stage it is well worth full price.
The only thing I would add to that is if you plan on playing, it is much better done with a couple of friends in some kind of voice chat. That makes it all the more fun.
You unlock customizations for your characters, which can be some hats or clothes, to things like changing your weapons to something outrageous like pizza.
There are a good chunks of maps currently in the game, and the objects on the map, from what I understand, are more or less randomized each time. So you can't just memorize where something is supposed to be and win consistently with knowledge like that.
Hunters and Witches in this game each have their own set of unique abilities, at the moment only three each. Some are far better than others. They do need some fine tweaking, but all in all they're pretty decent as they are.
My only real complaint is that the hunters can be punished very heavily if they are unfortunate enough to not have the hook ability(it lets you climb stuff essentially). As witches can fly, with the default ability. This means they can get up to some pretty high places that you might not be able to access just because you haven't unlocked/chosen the hook. Which I understand, because it's all about strategizing. But in most cases it's not viable if you are a lone hunter or something like that.
The best thing as of now, is that the devs for the game are constantly open to suggestions from the community and are more than ready to communicate with them if there are questions.
Also you can't buy four packs for the game because of steam, not the devs. It's annoying, but doesn't seem to be their fault.
So all in all, if you have some friends you can convince to get the game with you, you'll get your moneys worth in hours and hours of fun.

I'd like to begin by saying I really wanted to like this game, but in the end it just didn't deliver in my opinion.
This game is about 10 years too late on the scene. If it had come out in the early 2000's it would have been amazing (indeed this game weirdly reminded me of another slightly obtuse point n' click adventure called 'The Lighthouse'). As is, the story is very well crafted and I really wanted to forgive the game's other shortcomings for it, but in the end I couldn't wait to be done with it. I will say that the mix of sci-fi and mystery was unique and JULIA did some neat things with story telling (no spoilers) that I haven't seen in other games...but again, just not unique enough to warrant the time, cringiness of the voice acting, or - to be perfectly frank - patience to put up the the bugs to tease out of hiding.
As for gameplay, I feel like the developers took all of the tropes from point n click adventures from the last two decades and rolled them into one game and then spread them out unevenly. I didn't see a single puzzle in this game that DIDN'T remind me of another game and in some cases the puzzles were downright annoying (pixle hunting? REALLY?). Because of this, I found none of the puzzles were very difficult and this game could be a good gateway for more 'cognitively intense' puzzlers.
The thing that irritated me the most about this game though and was actually the reason I bothered to write this review at all were the technical bugs that plagued me in trying to struggle through this game (perhaps that was an inherrent puzzle build in by the devs?). First, for some reason the screen resolution chopped off about a third of the screen, an issue I didn't realize until after the first puzzle of the game. When I went into the video controls of the game (which - unless I missed a hotkey for it - can only be accessed by selecting the main menu option from the interface) I was shocked to see there was no way to change this. Also frustrating was the game erasing several of my save games for apparently no reason. This necessitated having to replay swaths of the game over and over again which was how I came to deeply dislike the lack lustre nature of the voice acting.
In summary, JULIA feels like a game company's first attempt at a game and does a decent-ish job but had I known the issues I'd experience and the frustration I'd have to sort through in order to simply play it before buying it I wouldn't have done it.
Pros

-'Classic' style point n' click puzzles
-Decent visuals
Cons
-Annoying bugs
-Annoying voice acting
-Forgettable gameplay
