The concept to me was awesome and from hearing about it for 5 minutes i realised it could be easil spoiled and i knew i wanted to experience this game for myself.
Her Storyis a really really great game. I've not seen anything like it before. If you have any interest in murder mysteries, shows based around detectives and their cases you'll love this game. You're not told anything about the case you're just thrown this database containing a bunch of clips of this woman and it's up to you to first of all piece together what the case is and then to solve it. What i found made it such a unique experience is that there is no way you can play it without a pen in hand and to be constantly taking notes on things you hear or things that dont sit right with you. I ended having a big board full of character details, timelines, keywords to search for and theories and ideas i had about the case. Never before has a game involved me so much outside of the computer screen.
Pros:
-Unique gameplay
-Involves you outside of the actual game itself
-Makes you come up with theories about the case without ever acknowleding what happens so its up to you when you think you've cracked it
-Complex story (at least what i think the story is) that is left to you to fabricate
-Makes you feel like a badass detective if you make some form of a breakthrough
-Very simple mechanics, you wont waste any time trying to get the hang of things
Cons:
-It was slightly annoying never being able to hear what the interviewer asked, only the womans responses
-Some clips seem to be broken down into very short pointless sentences
-Can't see any replayability value
To be perfectly honest it's tough to come up with many cons. Even with the ones i've chosen, i'm not completely happy with them it's really me nit picking with them. The reason i can't  come up with anymore cons is that i've nothing to compare it to, nothing that done it better or had one mechanic that really helped in playing the game.
Conclusion:
I love this game. Its unique and involves the player way more than any other game i've played. While other games are left to interpretation this whole game is open to interpretation. Whether you find that a bit annoying is completely up to you. Personally i love it. You go through the game coming up with whatever theories you can conjure up that you might think are solid but the next minute can seem ridiculous. Its a great game and definately worth the small price tag. It makes you feel like a proper detective, especially if you get a big notice board and write out everything your thinking.
Great game, really the biggest problem i have is that i cant see how you might replay it, but some games are just like that i guess

This a spectacular little piece of experimental gaming that's a total steal for five dollars.
First off: If you've ever - even once - argued against a video game for not being interactive enough, then you should avoid Her Story. It ain't for ya'.
The game is a little bit of a lot of things: L.A. Noire, Dear Esther, Gone Home and more -- all with the sensibilities of a 3DO game. You're a fly on the wall in this murder investigation, rummaging through a series of jumbled live-action confessionals from the murder suspect in an attempt to find cohesiveness in her story that sprawls over seven seperate interviews across several weeks.
If you're a fan of "true crime" or exposés the likes of the Serial podcast, The Stairs or The Jinx, you will absolutely love this game. It's a fantastic little murder mystery enhanced by the dated aesthetic and interactivity. It's wildly engaging.
Side note: This game would not have worked if the actress who plays the lone suspect was terrible. Thankfully, she's quite good and does a great job leading you through twists, turns and red herrings galore.

N++ is probably the best platformer ever created. You have the beautiful and complex platformers, and then you have N++. This game is so unique in its own way. Everything you do is your doing: no RNG, no unfair deaths, nothing but glorious platforming that will last you hours and hours and hours.
You are a ninja. Your goal is to exit the level by collecting gold and avoiding enemies, mines and other possible entities. The game's difficulty can range from really easy for causal players, to excruciatingly painfully difficult for those hardcore players. So no matter what your skill is, you can still enjoy this game. Just to warn you about beating everything: This game is HUGE! Over 4000 levels are currently in the game, pluss an infinite amount of user created levels, so there's pretty much no end to this game.
There's also a co-op mode and a race mode for up to 4 players. Unfortunately at this time, there is no online co-op which is my only disapointment.
Overall, I highly recommend this game.

If there is one thing I demand from HO's games, it's a good story. I'm far from disappointed, I'm in fact very happy with such amazing (
) game.
Vivian and her boyfriend search for clues about her past and the meanings of her recurring dreams. They end up in a mysterious town filled with dark secrets. Matt disappears and the player's journey to rescue him leads to an amazing adventure.
The story is simple but well articulated, most actions make sense when gathering objects, and sometimes the results will surprise you!
I really enjoyed the cutscenes, the graphics are OK, nothing extreme, but the developers put some effort into it, and for me is good enough! The locations are beautiful, I just wish they were native 1080p. The design is extremely well done, I felt emerged in each scene, and never in the same place twice.
The HO scenes are really good and interactive, which makes it even better. They are far from confusing, and avoid giving the player a dosage of frustration.
The puzzles are the ones I felt more difficult in. Some are extremely challenging, but all skippable if needed.
I wish there was a sequel somewhere because
really does need one. Maybe the end is exactly what the creators intended, but I cannot stop feeling there was so much more into this story.
Could this game have been longer? Maybe, HO's games usually don't take much longer than 5-10 hours (depending on your skills). The advanced mode always gives a reason to go back a second time, if not for the cool scenarios!
A fun game for HO's fans and everyone else who can't resist a good adventure.

The game is divided into three main sections: The RPG section - Aboard the ship, after every turn, you are going to have conversations with your generals and ministers to decide the fate of millions, having an impact over the strategy map and also make researchs to improve your units and your dragon form; The Strategy section - World map view of the regions, the races, population, gold and research points, your units and strategic buildings. Thats where you'll move your troops and play your cards to try to conquer a region; The RTS section - After you move your troops to attack or if you have to defend, you can choose to play cards and let the battle auto resolve with the help of one of your generals or you can choose to go into battle yourself and that is where you can turn into a dragon to help your units.
Unfortunately the RTS section is a bit messy and stiffy. This section is really fast paced, there is no fog of war, the camera controls are bad, the maps are small and you are quite limited to what you can do. You have to capture predetermined points on the map to start getting recruits and to build factories. There is a limited number of recruit that you can gather and wins the player who manages to maintain a greater number of units built. The dragon is cool, but it is too weak and dies very fast. The RTS section is the one I disliked the most. I found it quite boring and a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ so I turned the difficult to casual to focus on the section I really liked, the RPG one. Too bad you are still forced play the RTS sections as you can use auto resolve only once per turn. The turn based strategy map and the card sistems are not something out of the ordinary and the strenght is on the RPG sections, with great characters and choices that have real consequences on the theather of war.
I think that with this game the developers tried to fire at too many directions, with a weak third person shooter (as a dragon), a bad RTS, a ok turn based strategy and card systems and a good RPG wraped up with a great sound track and pretty graphics into a average game. So, if it is on sale why the ♥♥♥♥ not?

I'll cut straight to my main gripe which admittedly comes from my expectations compared to reality. Not only do blasters have nowhere near the impact they had in the movies (and they retain their clumsy and random nature) but also everyone has swords. When I first heard of this game, I said: "Oh. A Furby-themed horror? That sounds a little boring."
Boy, was I wrong.
Tattletail is a game that's based around a Furby-type virtual pet called a "Baby Talking Tattletail". You're tasked with grooming it, feeding it and charging it's battery, all whilst avoiding the grasp of it's bloodthirsty mama in a small, dark house. You are given only a flashlight to protect yourself, and while this might sound like the typical "Run away from the baddie in the dark" horror game, it's far from it.
Tattletail happens to be the one thing that will get you killed. When hiding from Mama, you'll have to be sure you've got plenty of light, Tattletail hates the dark, as well as having to keep him fed, clean and charged at the same time.
The story is pretty simple. YOu're a small, curious and naughty child that opened their Christmas present early, and inside was a Baby Talking Tattletail, the newest from the WayGetters electronics line of products. As you tend to the thing, you'll start being hunted by the previously discontinued "Mama Tattletail", who is no longer available to purchase for unknown reason.
Despite the story being so straightforward, the gameplay is something you'll NEVER forget.
tl;dr: Buy the game because spooky Furby hide and seek in the dark. It's fun.

This game has a decent enough premise, with the concept of giving away part of one's self to overcome the obstacles in his or her life. I REALLY like this concept, actually. But the game falls short in too many aspects for me to ever recommend it to anyone.
The first and most noticable error the game has is constant spelling and grammar errors. This isn't even a minor issue, as in some occasions it was actually rather difficult to decipher what my options actually were. This made sections that could've been simple much harder to interpret in the long run. This is made even more apparent by how short the game actually is. This game has a runtime of anywhere between 30 minutes to an hour.
The story of this game is also a dissapointment. The game builds up at the beginning at a decent pace. It was interesting and actually worth more than the asking price at first. The story just sort of stagnates at around 10-20 minutes in. The story tapers off into witchcraft for some reason, and never really explains the other world your find yourself in throughout. In a game that's entirely story driven, that is unacceptable.
For these reasons I really feel the game isn't worth it, even if it's less than a dollar. The game can be beaten in less than an hour, so if you rush you can beat the game and still have time to refund it like I did, OR, you can save yourself the trouble and buy something else.

Before we start, let's make one thing clear. This is not a game, and I don't mean that as an insult.
If you come into this expecting a traditional adventure game/detective game, you will be disappointed. If you use the right search words, you might figure out the story beats in under an hour. But, and this is key, you are not here to solve the mystery. "Her Story" is more than just a title, its the point of this whole thing. You're here to learn of this woman's story; to see the twists and turns her life went through after the mysterious disappearance of her husband. If you're the kind of person who wants a traditional game, have clear goals and progression, or isn't interested in character stories, this isn't going to be a good product for you.
So, if "Her Story" isn't a game, what is it? I argue this is a nonlinear, interactive movie. I know the term "interactive movie" has been thrown around a lot in the industry, especially back when FMV was more than just a punchline. Most of these things were poor games with cutscenes that just happened to have real people. The interactive portions and the movie portions were kept separate. "Her Story" breaks that convention, and is all the stronger for it. You start with a predetermined search word, and a few videos. From that point forward, you have control over how the story is shaped, though not its content.
Have you ever watched a mystery/detective film and thought something like, "These guys are totally missing something super obvious! If they just investigated *blank* everything would work out"? "Her Story" can be thought of as the response to that. You aren't stuck on a set path, forced to follow along a specific line of investigation. Instead, your intuition is what drives the story forward. You get exactly the story line you want. You get to check the leads you want and follow whatever theories you have. Personally, I found that to be really fun. It kept me more invested in the story, to the point that I was writing down notes for every video.
In a way, the interactivity also helps to mitigate the problem of stumbling onto the twists too soon. Sure, you might find a video that gives you key information, but you probably don't have any context for it. You still have to search for more videos to set up the twist you've found. In a way, every answer gives you another question to answer. This whole system works very well, and makes me wonder why I haven't seen anyone else do it.
"Her Story" isn't perfect. The biggest frustration is how they attempt to keep you from getting to later videos. See, the computer you're using is from the 90's, and the video watching software will only show you the first 5 results from any quere. In a way, it’s clever since this means that if you search generic terms you'll probably end up just getting video's from the first few interviews. Its trying to force you to actually make intelligent guesses if you want to get video's from later interviews. However, it gets real annoying to see the same few videos show up over and over. Video's differ wildly in length, which means longer video's are far more likely to show up than short ones since the longer the video, the more words spoken.
Not hearing the detectives who are interviewing her can also be problematic. Sure, this is her story and I understand that a part of the fun is working out what was asked. But, sometimes there's just not enough contextual clues to let you get a solid idea what she's responding to. It sucks a lot of the enjoyment out when you have no idea whats going on.
At the end of the day though, I had a lot of fun with "Her Story". I got a couple of hours of enjoyment, though I was pretty relaxed in my playthrough; I took notes, watched some video's over again, noodled around with the computer's desktop, and so on. I got all the achievements as well, though honestly for something like this the achievements don't really add much. If the idea of an interactive movie sounds good to you, and you're willing to work around some annoyances, it's a really solid product. However, if you're looking for something a little more structured or game like, this isn't going to be your thing. Plus, unless you're a weirdo like me who really likes watching movies multiple times, you'll probably not get any replay out of this. If you're the kind of person who counts every penny and expects so much game for so many dollars, "Her Story" isn't really the best 'value'.
I think, if you go into this with an open mind and an understanding of what this thing is trying to be, you can have a real engaging time. I don't know of anything else quite like it at the time of this review, and with the positive press/user reviews I'm interested to see if other people will be start pushing the boundaries between 'game' and 'movie'.

A detective noir with supernatural elements, The Monster Inside is an interesting and intriguing audio-visual novella.  The game is short and consists of seven chapters.  Even such, maybe especially so, I found it surprising how easily and effectively I was able to immerse myself into the story in such a short amount of time.  I imagine the ease was assisted greatly by the monochromatic visuals and the music, both of which added a level of ambiance that really helped set the scene.  Visually and audibly this is a quintessential example of detective noir done right.  The dialogue in the game was on point, and I especially enjoyed the internal monologues of the player character.  And as with every great detective noir game, you are able to investigate crime scenes.  I liked the ability to actually interact within the crime scenes during investigations, but I wish there was a little more interactivity while searching for clues and whatnot.  This section of the game I found a bit lacking; it was also too easy.  The final reveal, or the solving of the case, seemed a bit sudden, but I still loved it.
I really enjoyed this game and recommend it to any fans of detective noir style games.  The VN nature of the game may seem a bit off-putting to some, but I really urge those who are curious to try the game anyway.  If nothing else, it's free, short, and you can get some achievements out of playing it.  It's a win-win situation!

Overview: Worth getting when on sale - solid 7/10. Brave mix of genres and gameplay styles, has a certain charm to it.
If you can overlook the underdeveloped (but still serviceable and fun enough) RTS part of the game, then you'll find a refreshing mix of "RTS + Panzer Dragoon + Risk + Crusader Kings + Fox News + Tumblr + Japanese dating sim where you marry a skeleton or a lizard princess" to quote another reviewer. Campaign took me 20 hours on normal, and I'd happily play it through again on a harder difficulty if my steam library backlog wasn't so mighty. Replayability is good due to different choices you can make as emperor / different princesses to marry / different tactics to use. Has it's problems, but no more than a lot of other games I've sunk countless hours into. Haven't played multiplayer so can't comment on it.
Good:
- OK story, decent characters who have decent voice acting (rarer than you'd think)
- Good research/upgrade system for troops and dragon powers
- Fun dragon combat
- Game components work well together
- Nice colourful visual style (subjective to a degree I guess)
Bad:
- Weak RTS component
- Poor tutorial system (there's good guide on steam you may want to check out, among others)
- A few balance issues, but not game-breaking
- Campaign ending is underwhelming (though the fun is in the journey, no?)
In the end, the goods outweigh the bads, and the bads don't prevent you from having a fun experience with the game.
Personal tips:
- Change the game speed to 'slowest', this helps A LOT for RTS battles
- During RTS battles, rotate the camera so it's facing North and keep it that way, this makes the mini-map more usable and navigating the map a lot easier.
- Don't forget to use your dragon form, it's fun! Watch out though, you can get ripped apart fast by anti-air if you don't avoid them or dodge well.
- Read a guide or two, a lot of things aren't really explained well or at all.

Unusual mix of RPG (dialogues, decisions and personal stories of your crew aboard your ship, The Raven), TBS (Risk-like map, along with simplified building and research system, armies moving and such), RTS (real-time battles for provinces your invade in previous phase) and action game (when you turn into dragon during RTS battle).
Each part is rather simplified and unable to carry the game on its own - yet it is combination of all those modes makes the game unique and worth playing. How you carry dialogues with your crew - generals, ambassadors, your queen - and what political decisions you make (to set up public healthcare or even... ban violent books and games) changes your relations with 5 races of Rivellon and situation on Risk map. This, along with troops you bring, decide how the situation will handle in RTS battles you gonna take (if you have low popularity with race living in land you invade or defend, you might not get enough conscripts to defeat enemy - opposite situation is possible as well). This include one-use cards you might gather during gameplay and which alter battles in various ways - by giving you new skills, additional troops or buffing/debuffing various types of units.
Main campaign might be short, consider how good you are at such games - but there are always custom ones available.

I really wanted to like this game.  And for a while, for like 2 chapters or so of the game, I did!  Then, like so much other AAA bullcrap that comes out these days, the game ran out of steam and stopped being interesting.  Don't get me wrong, it looks amazing and all that, and the concept is a great one.  Even the first part of the execution is very well done.  It's just that it never really gets any meat on its bones.  It's all surface, all shell.  No center.
Examples:  You get the ability to turn into a dragon wearing a jetpack during the RTS battles and help out your troops.  Sounds great, but all your dragon abilities are weak and stupid, you die really quickly, and while you're in dragon form, controlling your troops is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
You get to choose which woman to marry (it'd be nice if I could've PLAYED as one, maybe they'd have some husband options or given me the choice to be gay one way or the other, or anything other than what's there), but then after she has like, one sidequest that takes place entirely in dialogue, that's it.  Your queen does exactly 1 thing.  Well, two things.  She's got a quest that does nothing, and she's got clothed boobs for you to look at as she says the same goddamn thing every time you visit her chamber.  That's it.
The RTS portions lack strategy.  Good board positioning between battles is about as tactical as it gets.  The story starts off sounding interesting but never really goes anywhere.  And then just when you think it's over, a stupid thing happens, not for any good reason mind you, and then you're still playing it, but nothing interesting is happening apart from just... more game.  Your generals all have maybe one interesting quest that they do, as well.  The political decisions were a nice concept, but then they have VERY minimal impact on gameplay.  It's all just shuffling around numbers.  Show me some CONSEQUENCES!  I consistently just did whatever I wanted, politically, and everyone loved me at the end of the game anyway.  I never had to change the way I played the game outside of the room where you Make The Pointless Decisions.  That shouldn't happen.  There's not enough tech or dragon abilities to research, either.  You'll have them all, easily, well before the end of the game.  It's like it was developed by lots of people, none of whom were talking to each other, and they all had like a page of notes at most to work from for content.
Very disappointing.  Lots of potential, utterly wasted.

The music is amazing. The storyline and political intrigue are fascinating. All of this will fade into a bitter, crusted memory, however, once you realize just how utterly ramshackle the balancing is, how precognizant you'll need to be to devise a workable strategy and how massively unfair the battles can get, even after you figure out how to slow the game down enough to actually strategize during the real-time sections. And you will need to go into those, or you'll literally have no chance of winning -which, incidentally, is the same chance you'll often have even if you do fight the battle in real-time, only with a heaping helping of frustration on top. Then if you survive long enough to summon yourself -that's odd, isn't it? Having to wait for yourself to arrive!- ...Then you'll realize that if you breathe too much fire, as in enough to actually dent half the units in the game, then you'll overheat and have to cool down. So in short, this game is a terrible, atrocious waste of a magnificent OST and a choice-studded storyline; more than anything, it makes one wish the devs had had at least some clue as to how one creates fun gameplay.

I was very aggravated while playing this game, because near the end of the game one of the puzzles is clearly broken.  It's a bit hard to describe, but it's a puzzle with two circles that spin around each other composed of an image of a beast and people in agony.  I messed around with this puzzle for longer than I should have, but the simple fix is that when you are able to solve it (all of the images you can rotate line up with the fixed background image) you hit the skip button (looks like a fast forward button) and the game counts it as a fully solved puzzle without the use of skips.  Thanks to those in the discussion area who worked this out and posted what needed to be done.   What's especially frustrating about this is that this issue has been raised to the developers for more than a year now, yet no fix was ever released.  Very poor developer support, considering this would theoretically be an easy enough matter to fix you'd think.  This is an otherwise harmless hidden object game, but I've played completely free versions of games just like this that didn't have broken puzzles.
Like always in these kind of games the storyline is absolutely cheesy and over the top.  What's worse is that several times you will come across puzzles that require a specific tool in order to advance, and there are many cases where if the woman didn't discard an object after using it once it could be utilized multiple times for a variety of purposes.  That or any handyman with a tool box could breeze through these issues.  I couldn't tell you how many times you needed something as simple as a knife or hammer, and kept having to refind the same basic kind of tool.  If there are going to be so many of these kinds of puzzles in the game they should know better than to recycle the same sort of necessary object when any reasonable person would hold onto that kind of item.  I'm fighting supernatural creatures all by myself - I don't really need to hold onto this axe now that I chopped this wood, do I?  Plus with how easy it was for her to waltz into town and clean up house, you'd think some townsfolk with access to weapons, let alone stakes and garlic, could have killed off 3 vampires.
I can't recommend this game at all, between its stupid storyline and a broken puzzle the developers won't even bother fixing.

It's a solid dungeons and dragons game masquerading as star wars. The base system for this game is quite obviously D20 from character creation to combat.
I'll cut straight to my main gripe which admittedly comes from my expectations compared to reality. Not only do blasters have nowhere near the impact they had in the movies (and they retain their clumsy and random nature) but also everyone has swords. At first this is confusing, but when you replace blaster with bow in your mind it starts to make sense. That's because weapon statlines are straight out of D20 analogues. Mechanically this is fine because it creates some balance between melee and ranged, but thematically it just ruins the experience when you just want to blast some thugs and move along.
That is not to say that the star wars paintjob is bad: the story and characters are great! I just was dissapointed with how the game played. I recommend it if you're desperate for a star wars RPG and can put up with the combat. I've enjoyed it, but only despite the gameplay rather than for it.

I'm not that far into the game, and my stupid controller keeps cutting out on me so I'm playing using a keyboard (which I"ve never been good at), but so far I'm interested to see how the plot works out. Anyway, I would definitely recommend the game just for the quirky but engaging story.

Very good game, but it's certainly not for everyone. Don't expect Michael Bay explosions and action.
The game itself is just walking around the island, making the map yourself with triangulation, picking various plants and turning them into potions/medicine and making sure you will not die from dehydration and going too fast (yes, that is a thing). All of this while you are chased by a wierd cat/lion/panther/demon/whatever hybrid.
It kind of feels like Robinson's Reqiem, but without everything trying to kill you.

A nice, beautiful game, different from any other out there. The beginning was a little weird and dull, but once you travel more into the island, you will begin to understand how you're supposed to play and think in this game. Such moment is when you realize this is a one-of-a-kind game.
The game tries to simulate realism, and although it may seem to go overboard on some parts, it does everything very well (except for nights, which are strangely pitch black even if moonlight should give a little help, so I reccommend you avoid being outside at night, but that's quite the only bad thing I see about this game).
The controls might as well be weird, but that's because it tries to simulate real life even more. You're not supposed to be able to turn around 180 degrees and run straight away just like that in real life, right? Well, you can't just do that in this game either. It's not something too bad though, and it's easy to get used to it.
I was surprised when I reached one of the primary objectives in a certain place of the island, where the scenery was just great, and the search for a specific rare plant, was an interesting experience like in no other game.
When I encountered the "Creature" (which I like to refer to as Miasmata, even if that's a bit cheesy and the creature has no official name), that's when the game turned much more into a survival game. I was always checking my surroundings carefully and hiding from a practically invincible beast, until the moment I'd notice the creature is nearby, and that always made my heart race, even if this game isn't a horror or anything scary based game. You have to manage to not only survive your sickness, but you also have to survive being hunted down by such predator.
Overral, this game is one of the greatest survival/adventure games out there in my opinion, as I really love this game and it got me addicted very soon after I began playing. Rating: 9.5/10, would have been a full 10 if it wasn't for the unfortunately frustrating pitch black nights.

What's amazing about Her Story is not so much WHAT you find out, but WHEN you find it out. Because the twists, as they come (and there are plenty), will vary from player to player. It is a fantastic excercise in nonlinear storytelling.
The gameplay is reminiscent of a long-forgotten experiment like Majestic. The better you are with Google, the more research-smarts you have, the more you can stick your nose in the business of this police investigation. You'll pore over clips, take notes, build upon your own theories and ultimately come to a conclusion.
Rest assured, there is a conclusion to this story, but when you come to it depends on when you believe you've all the facts in order. It's a good four hours to find most of the clips available.
My only complaint is that I spent in inordinate amount of time trying to rearrange clips in the order that they happened. The interface really makes this a struggle as your collection of clips grows large. I don't think this should be automated, but it should certainly be easier than it is.
A stellar game and an experience you won't find many other places. For five dollars, this is a steal.

If you're expecting much gameplay, Her Story might not be for you. If you wish to put your Google-fu skills to the test while uncovering an intriguing story, then grab a copy. Her Story is more an interactive film than a video game, but don't let that deter you; Her Story is an interesting experience that continues through discussions as players attempt to put together evidence supporting their different interpretations. For its price, the game is perfect for a single gaming session to spend a few hours.

Fantastic experience. Not for everyone, of course, it's mostly an exercise in Google-fu while you play detective and even though you are not really asking questions to the character, it totally feels like you are. Eventually you might get bored, especiallywhen it starts feeling like your pool of questions is drying up, and then is where the game asks you if you want to proceed to the ending, which I think it's a very clever mechanic for a game that is not supposed to be a challenge but instead a self-managed storytelling experiment. Picked this up for $5 on the Steam Holiday Sale. Was it worth it? For $5, I would say yes. Sniper: Ghost Warrior is an actioned filled sniper shooter that focuses on trying to provide realistic sniper combat as well as stealth. This game achieves at being fairly entertaining, enough so to keep me playing through the campaign. The storyline is decent, while predicatable at times. The level design was pretty good as a whole, and while the environments and scenery are quite beautiful, the game does feel very linear. That being said, most maps and missions do have some open areas and provide room to explore should you wish to do so. This game does have some major shortcomings nonetheless: it overall doesn't feel as polished as it could be, the voice acting is decent but the dialogue for enemies loops and isn't varied enough, the game has bugs and rendering issues, the AI is unbalanced, and I didn't find that the sniping realism was fully achieved. We'll see if the sequel improves upon this franchise.
